d: Be of the same sygnification, only A, goth before a worde, which begynneth with a cōsonāt: ab and abs goth before a word that doth begyn with a vowell.

Two wordes made of the preposition, a, & the ablatiue case plurell of Batus, whiche in englysshe is a measure, signifieth an officer, that hath the orderyng of measures,Esdra. as a clerke of the markette,
An officer, vnto whome it belōgeth to write such thingꝭ as do chance.
Officers deposed, or such as be constrayned to resygne their authoritie.
Of Plinie is taken for accompt.
He whom a mā putteth frō him
A ryuer in the coūtrey of Damaske vnder the hyll called Libanus.
A gyrdell that the priestes of Iewes dyd weare.
A cupboorde, or dresser, also an astronomers tables.
The tables inbowed, wheron pylars doo stande.
A countreye in Tartari, where men haue fete tourned backwarde, and be wonderfull swifte, and be wylde.
One of the horses of Pluto kyng of Helle.
A citie in the realme of Thracia.
To expell or put out of fauour, or resygne an offyce, or to refuse his sonne or kynsman.
He refused hym for his sonne. Abdicauit se magistratu, He hath resygned his offyce or dignitie.
The fatte aboute the kydneyes. It is also the vdder and teates of a sowe, full of mylke, whiche is in Italy hadde for a delycate meate.
To leade awaye, or leade out, or pull away, or take with.
Fylberdes of Abellino, a citie in Naples.
To take or putte of a garment. Abemito uestem, Put of thy cote.Plau, ce.
To forbid. Eam abercet domo, He forbyddeth hir his howse.
To erre or wāder very moche, to depart ferre of, or a sonder.
To wede out, or pluck out.
The name of a Iuge in Israel.
To seuer or take oute of the flocke, or to drawe sheepe.
To dryue away any thinge, that is euyll or noyous. also to driue awaye cattell by thefte or deceyte.
To cast away, to renoūce to despise.
To recouer or take away by iudgement.
To vnyoke, discharge, or putte asonder.
To denye by an othe, or to kepe a thinge wrongfully.
To rydde the erthe from trees or vynes, and cutte awaye the vpper rotes, that they may beare the more fruite.
To consume in banketting or farynge delycately.
To sette or let to an other.
A sonne in the fourthe degree in lyneall discent.
To deny or refuse with coū tenance or becke, to becke away.
Signifieth to do the same oftētimes
To put out, or rase out to anulle, or vndo for euer.
A Senatours habyte, or a sowldiours cloke.
To take for ylle lucke, or haue in detestation.
People, whyche fyrste helde the countrey aboute Rome, & lyued abrode hauynge no houses. They may also be taken for any other people, whose beginning is not knowen.
To be borne afore naturall tyme.
An vntymely byrthe, nygh to the conception: which may be called aborsion.
An vntymely byrthe, nyghe to the iuste tyme of delyueraunce, whereby the chylde dieth.
The byrthe dystroyed with some hurte, or other mysaduenture, or medycine.
To brynge forthe a chylde, 〈◊〉 be perfecte.
That thynge, whiche procureth the sayd vntymely byrthe.
Out of the matter, or out of the purpose▪ vnsemely, vnconuenient.
To take fro, or take by fors.
They whiche beinge at lybertie, 〈◊〉 them selūs to an other mans rule, by theyr consente.
To dissolue or repell a lawe.
To breke of, plucke 〈◊〉 cutte of.
A ryuer of Armeny, that incloseth the 〈◊〉 Armente.
Is of phisytions taken for an impos • ume or botche, or for a course of euyll humours to some parte of the body, wherby matter is ingendred.
That whiche in absence is doone.
The strake of a cart whele, wherin the spokes he sette
To departe from a place▪ sometyme it signifieth to absteine or leaue of.
To loose that whyche was bounden. also to performe or accomplyshe. Also to spare or forgyue, to pardon, to spede, to assoyle.
That whiche sowneth nat wel, or discordeth, or scantly may be herde.
To swalowe, or suppe of all, to deuoure or consume.
To prohybyte or lette, or putte fro.
Abstinence, a vertue in forbearynge to take an other mans goodes.
To absteyne or forbeare, or tempre.
To gette by force or tourmentes.
To take by force or by craft
He hath birefte, taken away, or borne away.
To be away, or ferre of, or to fayle, or to be distant or absent.
Inconuenient, foolysshe, discordinge, dishoneste, abhorringe, or odious.
Be ylandes in the Venitian see.
The brother of Medea, whome she dyd cutte into pieces, and threwe into the see, whan she fledde frome her father with Iason.
Habūdantly, plentuously, inough, and more than inough.
To habunde, to haue out of measure more than inough.
To abuse, to vse a thynge: dishonestely, vncomely, contrarye to that, that it serueth for, oute of order, or in vayne.
Trifles, thinges of smalle estimation, wanton toyes, thynges vnseemely for menne to vse.
A people in Asia, whyche hauynge their Cytie distressed with a longe Syege, felle into a furye, or madnesse, and slewe all their wiues, their chylderne, and afterwarde them selues.
The citie of the sayd people.
A hylle in the occean See agaynste Spayne, whiche is called oone of Hercules pylars.

Signifieth sometyme, and. as Doctus ac iustus es, Thou arte kunnyng and iuste. Sometyme it is taken for Than, as Haud secus ac iussi faciunt, They doo none otherwise than they be commanded. Sometyme it dothe signifie as, as Superbis perinde, ac si Rex esses, Thou arte as proude as if thou were a kynge.
Is the iuyce of a fruite called siliqua. It maye be called also in Englande veriuyse.
A vniuersitie, whiche toke that name of a place nighe to Athenes, where Plato the great phylosopher taught phylosophye.
Were a secte of phylosophers, whyche folowed and taughte the opynyons of Plato.

A byrde that feedeth on thystelles, and maketh her nest with claye, and is called in englysshe, a Tytmusse. It was also a boye, whiche the poetes doo fayne was transformed into a floure of his name. It is also a bushe, lyke a whyte thorne, with lasse leaues, mosy, and pryckynge. Dioscorides sayth, that it is an herbe, that groweth in stony and moyste grounde, and hath leaues broder and longer than letyse, in forme lyke to rockette, somwhat blacke, and in broysynge softe and fatty, hauynge a stalke of two cubytes high, of thyckenesse of a mans fynger, garnyshed vnder the top with lyttell longe leaues and pryckynge, wherevnto groweth a whyte floure.
A towne in the myddelle of Hungarye.
A parte of a royalme in Grece, named Epirus. It is also a lyttell countreye in Egypte: and it is a citie by Syracusis in the royalme of Sycile.
A verse, wherein one syllable lacketh.
The greattest sayll in the shyppe.
The name of her, that nourished Romulus and Remus, the fyrst builders of Rome.
To goo to, or approche. Sommetyme it sygnifyeth to gyue an eare or harken, to take hede, and to make moche of.
To kendle, inflame, prouoke, or gyue boldnes.

Were sowldiours appoynted to be aboute great offycers for defence of their persones. Festus saythe, that it were they, whiche after the dethe of souldiours were put in their places. Varro affirmeth, that they were ministers redy at the commaundementes of principall offycers.
An accēt or tune, wherby a sillable is pronounced.
In the stede of acceperim, I haue taken.
All vessayle or other thynge, that may receyue and kepe what soo euer shall be putte into it.

An acceptaunce, a word of the lawe, whyche hapneth in this wyse. One sayth to an other, Art thou contented with that that I haue promysed the? or that by my bargain I owe to the? The other saith, ye I am contented. This is Acceptilatio. Also wherin soo euer I haue bounden my selfe by receyuynge of any thynge, it maye be called Acceptilatio.
To knowledge my selfe to haue receyued, that is not yet payde, also to take thankfully.
To call forth, or sende for.
To goo to calle, or fetche.
Is an accident, whiche may be, or not be, without corruption of that, wherin it maye be.
To falle downe in doing reuerence.
To gyrde, to prepare, to make redye to do some thyng.
To take, to here, to suppose, to knowe, to vnderstande, to receiue, to intreate or entertayne.
Aui, are, to enclyne or bende to.
Rysynge vpwarde to a smalle toppe.
He that dwellethe nexte to the fielde. Also he that commeth oute of one countreye, and dwelleth in an other.
To dwell by or nyghe, specially hilles or waters.
To accommodate, appropre, to applye, make apte, set in order, gyue, or inclyne.
A bedde or couche to lye on by daye tyme, as it was the maner of the olde Romaynes, to eate lyenge on their beddis.
The lyenge in the said maner.
To lye by, or to sytte, or lye downe to cate.
To lye downe, to lye by, to lie or sytte downe at feastes and bankettes. Accūbere mensā, to syt at one table.
To accumulate or gather in heapes, to increase.
To rūne to, to spede thither
Siouthe, pen • ysenes, heuynesse of harte, werynesse.
To be wery, or to waxe slouthefull.
Thynges wherof the paynt in the myddes is not knowen.
A tree, the wodde wherof is moste gentyll to worke in, and is named in englyshe Dowgeon.
Sower as 〈◊〉 sommetyme it betokeneth stronge, sometyme sharpe. Acer inimi • us, a sharpe ennemye. Also sore, as Acres animaduersores, soore punysshers.
Bytternes of taste, sharpenes of tyme, crueltie in man.
To trouble, to make bytter, or abhomynable.
Vnrype, bytter, difficult, or peynefulle, as, Robustorum iuuenum acerba mors, The dethe of yonge menne is peynefulle, as who saythe, they dye with greatte difficultie.
He that neuer cuttethe his heare.
A heape or gatherynge togyther▪ specially of grayne.
To waxe sowre or tarte, specially in lykour.
A kynde of vessell, which may be called a charger, or a basyn, and was a vessell, wherin were thinges sacrified.
A salate of herbes. it is also a gardeyn, where salate herbes do growe.
People in Grecia. and somtyme they be taken for grekes generally.
Is of poetes taken for a ryuer of helle.
The mayne sayle of a shyppe.
Was the name of the companyon or mynton of Aeneas the Troiane. It is also the name of a precious stoone founde in Sicile, which is in colour browne, and hath cerkles blacke and whyte.
Gresshoppers, which chirpe loude and pleasantly.
A sponge, whiche is verye softe, and hath smalle holes.
A hatchet of brasse, which amonge the paynyms was vsed in sacrifice.
Betokeneth the edge of a knyfe, or other weapon or toole. Also the front of an hoste, at the ioynynge of battayle, more ouer that parte of the eie, whyche is called the syghte.
A crooked sworde that the Persyans vsed.
Be lyttell kernels, whiche be in grapis, raisons, pomegranates, & other beries.
A kynde of syshe whiche hathe the scales tourned towarde the hedde.
A weapon vsed in the olde tyme.
An herbe, wherin is mooste feruent poyson.
Certayne impressyons in the fyrmament lyke to fyrye dartes, whyche doo seeme to flie.
A precious stone lyke a glasse, with smalle golden dropes, wherwith yf oyle be heate, and the body therwith anoynted, it dissolueth all werynesse.
A tartenes lyke vnto vnripe wyne or pomegranates.
To leane, as to leane my heed or arme vppon any thynge. Also it signifieth to assent to other mens sayinges.
To attayne a thynge that is sought for.
Pure wyne, wtout a lay, or vnmixte.
The sharpnes that is in fruites, whiche be not rype.

Tartnes, which biteth the tūge, and perceth the heed, as in the taste of garlyke, oynions, and other lyke thynges. It signifieth sometyme sharpnes in speking or mynde: sometyme lyuelynes and quyckenesse of wytte.
A kind of wertes, as great as beanes, so small at the rootes, that they do seme to hange by a synewe.
A subtyll sentence or lesson, requiringe moche study and serche. it is also taken for all thynges to be recited or doone, to delyte the audience.

Water bākis, or which mē do cal strō des, wheron the see floweth. Also it is that which we cal actꝭ, cōcerning mens lyues or priuate busynes put in writing. also such dedes as haue hapned out of iugement. Acri • ata be those, whiche haue hapned in iugement, proprely they, which be in doyng.
The name of a mā, whom Diana, bicause he did se her nakid, turnid īto an hart, & so was he torne & slain of his own hoūdis.

Betokenith somtime pronunciation, sometime an oration writen, sometime an action in the lawe, sometyme an hystorie, sometyme a defence, otherwhyle a recompence in wordes for benefite receiued, as gratiarum actio, for thankes. generally it is taken for act or dede in euery thyng.
To practise, specially in ciuile causes.
Whiche bothe the dede. Also in the lawe the plaintife, complaynant, or demandaunt. Also a player of enterludes. Also a mannes factour or baylyffe, that hathe the charge of his busynesse.
Names, which do procede of acte, as Rex, a regendo, of gouernynge, Dux a ducendo, of leadynge.
A substantiue, signifieth a notary or scribe, or any other that writeth spedily. Also it betokenith a kynde of shippes, whiche be callid barkis.
Performed, also arryued, thrust in, brought to, or feared.
A dede, the partes of a comedie or play, a dayes warke in tyllage.
The sharpnes of euery thing. it signifieth also clerenes of witte.
To make sharpe, as a knyfe, or other thinge lyke. somtyme it betokenethe to teache, otherwhile to steere.
A fishe called a banstikle or bāning.
A nedell, also chaffe of corne, also an order in battayle.
Sharpe, but in voyce it betokeneth high and small, as a treble.

By hym selfe, or ioyned to an other word, signifieth to, or at, as Vado ad oppidum, I go to the towne. Erat ad ripam fluminis ingens arbor, There was at the ryuers iyde a great tree. Some tyme it signifieth agaynst, as, Ad illum mihi pugna est, Against him is my warre. Sometyme it betokeneth in comparyson, sometime cause, as, Ad quid hoc fecisti? For what cause, or wherto diddest thou this? Sometime about, as Ad duo millia hominū occisa sunt, There be slayne aboute two thousand men. Also after, as, Ad haec, After this.
It maketh for the matter, or is conuenient.
Semblably, so moche: as, Adaeque miser, so moche a wretche.
An olde wife, whiche late hadde a chylde.
A prouerbe, or as I mought say. an olde sayde sawe.
A precious stone, called a dyamant.
By rule, streight as a lyne.
A frothe or fome growyng on reedes in the fennes.
Signifieth Neuer. For the olde grekes had no calendes.
To saye, to iudge, to appoynte, or depute.
He that is iudged, appoynted, or deputed.
Openly solde. Also Addicere was whan the iuge in the old tyme delyuered the dettour to his credytours, to do with hym what they lysted.
To lerne wel, or adde to in lernynge.
To adde, ioyne, or put to.
To bryng to, or bring forth, sometyme to drawe or plucke togither.
A frownyng forcheed. somtyme •• ducere is to ertende or thrust out.
So moch, moreouer, surely, without doubte. Somtyme it signifieth euen, as Ture •• • o eras audies uerba, Thou thy self 〈…〉 shalte here his wordes.
To go to, to demaunde, to attempte, to make assaulte.
To cleane faste, to sette sure, to 〈◊〉 to.
To blowe or to breathe on a thyng.
To bynde to, or tye, or 〈◊〉 .
To put to, to haue by me.

Short battes of a cubyte longe and an halfe, hauynge pikes of yron in theym, and were tyed to a lyne, that whanne they were throwen, he that did cast thē, mought plucke them agayn vnto him, hurlebattes.
To procure or styre, to bynd by othe, or promyse, to bryng or dryue to, to fasten or ioyne to.
Feastes that pryestes made in the olde tyme.
To caste to, to adde or putte to, or increase.
Feastes that priestes were wonte to make.
To gette or optain: ioynid with a ꝑson it signifieth to ouertake.
To denye with an othe, to coniure.
A porter, whiche dothe kepe the vtter gate.
To sende to, to delyuer any thynge to one to bringe to an other.
The acte or tyme whan beastes doth their kinde in generation. Seasoning.
To admitte, to put to, to brynge in, to suffre, to susteyne, or take.
To moue to, or put to.
To begynne to grow, to do sacrifice with incense, or other fumes, to burne swete thynges.
Is the aege betwene chyldehode and mannes age, whiche is betwene xiiii. and .xxi.
To be wanton, or full of youthe.
Festiual dayes, which were kept in the honor of Adonis, the derling of Venꝰ.
The name of a chylde, whiche was sonne of Cynare, kyng of Cypres, whome Venus had for her derlynge, whiche was slayn with a bore, whom the poetes fained, that Venus turned into a purple floure.
Gardeyns for a lyttell tyme pleasant, whiche shortely decayen.
An election of an heyre out of the cours of inheritance, as by wyll or gyfte.
He that is adopted or taken in the stede of a sonne.
The son of him that is adopted.
To elect or apoint an heire.
Reuerence due to god, or saintes. also an inwarde deuotion and affection to hym that reuerence is doone vnto: and is an expresse mocyon or acte of reuerence done with the body.
A prayse that is giuen to them that haue victorie. Also a cake of fyne wheate, whiche they vsed in sacrifice.
To sette on sodaynly, to begynne. Adorior hunc, I sette on him.
To honour with inclination of the body, to bescche.
The dryfte of sheepe to the water.
To turne the erth in tyllage.
I am here, er presente, or at hande.
To bring to or cary to.
Goodes whiche doo come vnloked for.
Syckenes that cometh without our defaute, and of some menne is called an vncome.
He that commethe to a place by chaunce.
Commune resorters, or haunters to a place.
Seruantes, whiche do fetche home their maisters after dynar or supper.
To repugne or be contrarye, or to refuse.
To make or giue shadow, to represente or expresse, as peynters doo, that do shadowe ymages in playne tables, to make them shewe imboced or rounde.
To call to, or cal to help.
To flie to, or nygh a place.
After myn, or thin, or his appetite.
The chauncell or other secrete place of the temple, where none came but priestes, or persones sanctifyed.
To yelde vp the gost,Cicero ad Attic. to dye.
To make a slaughter of mē.Tit. Liuiꝰ.
To telle the names to be wrytten.
To sette forth such a boke.Cicero in V •• e.
An othe amonge gentyles, sygnyfyenge by Pollux house.
A hous. and if there be ioyned thervnto the name of god or of a saynt, it sygnifieth a churche, or temple. Aedes saluatoris, saynt Sauiours churche.
An oratorie, or place, where images were kepte.
Al the hole building of the hous.
Officers, whose charge was to see to the kepynge vp and maynteynyng of tē ples, and priuate houses, and to make prouision for solemne playes.
He that hadde ben ones in that authorytie.
A Iudge or arbitratour chosen of the one parte.
To rule ouer the tēple or hous
The prelate of the temple or churche, and may be nowe called the persone or paryshe prieste.
To set forthe or publyshe. Also it signyfyeth to brynge forthe by generacyon.
Beastes lyke to men, hauynge fete lyke to gotes.
To enuie without malyce, or to folowe, or studye to be lyke to an other.
He that foloweth or enuieth another, onely for desyre of glorie.
A derke question, harde to be vnderstanded.
Wherin is no varietie or ••• ble.
Equall, playne, lyke, of lyke age.
He that is neyther extolled with ꝓsperitie, nor discōforted in aduersite.
I take in good parte, I seeke not, or care not.
The tyme whan the dayes and the nightes be of one length.
He that vseth the one hand as well as the other.
The tyme of the yere, whan the day is as longe as the night, whyche is twise in the yere. In spryng time about the viii, Calendes of Aprile: And in Autumne aboute the .viii. calendes of October.
To haue lyke power, or be of lyke estimation.
To be equiualente, or of lyke valour.
The ayre sommetyme wynde, blaste, breathe, or sounde.
A tresory, where tresure is kept.
Sowdiours, whiche for some defaute were put out of wages.
Whiche is as swyfte as the wynd.
Of the ayre or lyke to the ayre.
Rust or canker in mettal, specially in copper or syluer.
Labour paynfull, care of minde, with heuynes, infelicitie.
Is proprely copper or brasse. It is oftentymes taken for money, sometyme for trumpettes.
Moneye that other menne do owe vnto vs.
Money that we doo owe to other men.
Money that other men doo owe vnto hym, whom we speake of.
Mettal that wol be sone moltē.
Places to be in for shadowe in the sommer tyme.
To dwelle or be in a sommer place.
Places whervnto the see floweth and ebbith, or meres, filled with salt water.
To waxe hotte, to bourne, to flowe lyke the see.
Heate of the wether, or burnynge of the sunne. Also the vyolence or troublous motion of the see.
A mā easy to be spokē vnto.
To seke affectualli, to trouble whan it is put with damno, or other lyke.
Affection or naturall motion, as gladnesse, desyre, and suche lyke.
To moue affection or disposition, either to good or to yll.
He gaue to hym his deathes wounde.
In fieldes betokeneth adioynyng: In men it betokeneth alyance by mariage.
Punyshement of the body with syckenesse.
The thyrde parte of the worlde, wherin is Carthage, Numidia, and all the countreys nowe called Barbarye.
A man of Affrike. Also the most noble capitayne Scipio, was called Affricanus, bycause he subdewed that countrey to the Romaynes.

o: A fronte at que à tergo,
n: a fronte at que a tergo
d: A prouerbe signifieng the conferrynge of thynges passed, with the state of thinges present.
Was the generall Capytayne of the grekes, atte the syege of Troye.
A fielde. Somtyme a territorie belongynge to a towne, wherin is includid fieldes, medowes, woddes, and waters. Sommetime a manour with the demeanes. sometyme the arable felde onely.
A heape of stones or turfe. also a bulworke, or a countremure to a fortresse or campe in battayle. sometyme it sygnyfieth a caulsey.
To make vppe on heape, by addynge to.
To goo to, or come to, to inuade, to begynne, to attempt.
Wherin the beame of a payre of balance is hanged.
He that is meuid with a litle gain.
To do often, to pryck, to cōpell, to trouble, to persecute, to vexe, to consyder, to reuolue, to solycite.
That whyche is in byrthe more than nede requireth.
The surname that I haue by my father.

To do, to leade, to dryue, to labour, to here, to speake, to pronounce, to fayne, to goo. Nudi agunt, They go naked. I extende or sprede. Radices agunt, Pom. Mel. They sprede their rootes. I treate of a thynge, I gyue. Ago gratias, I gyue thankes. I brynge forthe, also to expell. Venena membris agit, It expellethe poyson oute of the membres.
A staffe to dryue cattell with.
Fere & heuines, or vexatiō of mynd.
He that makethe a commune game, and payethe the rewarde to theym that do wynne it.
He that setteth the pryce of vyttayle, a talker.
A markette manne, a haunter of markettes.
A landed man. Also he that fauoreth the lawes, whiche be made for the orderynge of possessions.
A greste, wylde growen, withoute culture. Also he that is rude and beastlye, without gentyll maners.
They that do aske their portion in diuision of landes.
They whiche be borne with their feete forewarde.
A porte to heate in drynke.
A vesselle of whyte brasse or copper, whyche is bryghte bothe within and without.
I saye, thou sayest, he sayth.
A wynge of a byrde, and a wyng of a battayle, whyche is proprelye of horsemenne.

Quycke of spirite, 〈◊〉 wytte, lusty of courage, mery, and he that lyueth in hope: proprely he that is in a meane betwene glad and sorte. Somtime it betokeneth a man redy and willing, therof commeth Alacritas, redynes or promptnes of wyll. also feruentnes of mynde.
A whyte spotte in the eyen. also the whyte of an egge.
A table openly sette vp, wherin eyther the names of officers, or some publike decree is wrytten.
The fatte that is in some tree.

Are byrdes of the see, whiche do hatche their yong chykens on the lande, and do lay their egges on the sandes, in myddes of the wynter, and whā the see is mooste troublous, if they do lay, it becommeth sodaynly calme, and the stormes and wyndes do ceasse, vntyl these birdes haue all hatched, and brought vp theyr chykens, and made them redy to flee: whiche is in the space of .xiiii. days. This birde is lyttell more than a sparowe, his fethers be purple of colour, myxt with whyte, and hath a longe necke and a smal, his byl somwhat grene, longe, and sclender, and this byrde is sene very seldome.
A dye, playinge at dyes. somtyme it signifieth chance. Alea fortunae, The chance of fortune. somtyme peryll.
A byrde, sometyme it signifyeth swyfte in fleing, or runnyng: as Alite planta, swyfte of foote.
A remedy to putte away myschiefe, or any yll thyng.
The generall name of medicines, whiche do expell syckenes.
Reyte, or wedes of the see.
To be in peyne, proprely for colde, to chyll for colde.
An aduerbe, sygnifieth, or els, elles where, an other tyme, sometyme.
Thou takest no heede what is spoken.
A drynke made of wheate brayed in a stone morter, the huskes of the wheate beinge taken cleane away.
That whiche comethe out of an other countrey.
To alienate, to putte away, or putte of.
To separate, to put a sonder.
He that anoynteth a man, and a surgion that healeth woundes.
In some parte, by some reason.
Some man. Aliquis est, He is a man of no small estimation.
To flow by, sayl by, or rowe by
To allure or drawe to, by fayrenes, to allure.
To ascrybe, to cheese, to assygne.
To sende, to allege, or bring forthe, to depute, or gyue auctoritie.
A figure or inuersion of wordes, where it is in wordes one, and an other in sentence or meanynge.
The greatte toe, whanne he lyeth ouer the nexte toe.
To squatte or throw any thing agaynst the grounde or walles.
To doo it gladdely, to obeye, to fauour, to consente.
To be deceyued in opynyon, to fantasye.
To doo a thynge in iape, to speake merily, or consent. somtyme it sygnifieth to speake some thynge, which secretely hath some other vnderstandyng.
To speke or do some thynge agreable with somme hystorie before wrytten.
To flowe nigh to, to washe as the water dothe the grounde, whan it floweth ouer it.
A floode caused by rayne, or by ryuers whan they rise.
Is whan abundance of water mixt with claye, couereth the grounde.
Al thinge that norysheth vs, properly the erth is so called, Alma tellus, bycause we haue therof our sustinance. Sometyme it signifieth quiete, Almus dies, A quiete day. in Virgile.
An alder tree. Somtyme it signifyeth a shyppe or bote.
A syckenes of the heed, whereby the heares do falle of.
The mountaynes, whiche do depart nowe Italy and Fraunce.
An other, the other, one of the two.
An other, the other. Alter, the other, the seconde. Sometyme it sygnifieth both. Vnus aut alter, one or bothe. Vnus et alter, The one and the other.
Poyses of lead, made to lyfte vp with bothe handes, to exercyse men, whyche may not otherwyse labour: wherof there be now many in England, specially in the chambres of stud • tes.
To contende with wordes one with an other on sondry partes.
By tourne, one at one tyme, an other at an other tyme.
Sondrye dayes, where one day is betwene.
To do thynges by tourne, nowe one and than an other.
Bothe the one and the other. also or the tone or the tother.
All thynge that is franked to make fatte, be it beaste, fyshe, or foule. Altilis gallina, a henne franked or fed
He that maketh noyse frō aboue,
He that thoundereth, whiche name the paynyms gaue to their god Iupyter.
To the tone or the tother,Apuleius. to the tone parte, betwene the one and the other, in the higher parte.
High, depe, proprely in the see.Vergilius. it sygnifieth also excellent, glorious, anciēt.
A place where hiues be sette. also a stocke of hyues.
A basket or mawnde, also a culuerhole, a chessebourde, or tables to playe on.
A hyue for bees, a vessaile to washe in, the bealy of any thing that lacketh lyfe. sometyme it signifieth a shyppe.
They whiche be moche vexed with freattynges in the bealy.
A sonne or scolar that is brought vp of a man, as of his owne father, eyther with sustinance, maners, or lernynge.
Lether properly tawed. somtime it is put for a bagge or a pourse.
Of felowship, a good felowshyp, a familiar word vsed among frendes.
He that is a great louer, or amorous.
A louer be it man or womā.
A clerke or secretarye, alway attendynge.
To waxe bytter, or to be bytter.
He or she that louethe, 〈◊〉 loued.
A louer, or he that is amorous.
A drynke charmed, to make a 〈…〉 .
That whyche per • th to loue.
A cyrcuite of wordes, or a tale • wen in length.
That aboundeth in suche fourme of speakynge.
He that vseth bothe handes lyke welle.
To compasse, to seke for promotion, to desyre, to praye, or intreate.
Inordynate desyre of honour or auctoritie.
A cyrcute: also the offence of ambition, made by the lawes.
Was called of the Paynyms the meate of goddis. Some do saye, that it is an herbe of the kynde of Mugworte.
A priuate place to walke in, a walke or galerie.
A thonge, or that which is bounden to the myddes of a darte, or iauelyne, to caste it.
A canne or potte, wherout they powre wyne.
To clothe, to putte on a garmente.
Ioyned to a thyng, lacking lyfe, signifieth profitable, or holsome.
To suffre to depart, to lose to sende, to lette passe, to take fro.
Pleasaunt or dilectable. Locus amaenus, A delectable place.
I put to, or sette vpon a thinge.
To remoue, to put from a place or a thynge.
A measure, whiche euery waye contayneth a foote it may be vsed for euery potte that is caryed aboute.
He that beareth the potte, a tankarde bearer.
To make more, to draw to.
A manne repried, or delayed in iugement, vpon some difficultie or consyderation.
Greatnesse of power or maiestie, sometyme it sygnifyeth largenes, Terrae amplitudo, The largenes of the coūtrey
An oyle potte. Also a bottelle or flagon. sometyme it signifyeth a thyng that is blowen or puffed.Suetonius in Domitiano. Suetonius vseth that worde for a drynkyng glasse.
A water pot, and it may be vsed for holy water potte. See Calepine.
Any thinge that is ordeyned agaynst poysonynge.
The mother or some of all oyles.
In holy Scripture betokeneth separation, els where it signifyeth a thyng offered or sette vp in a temple or churche, as thynges offered and hanged vp.
To curse or gyue to the deuylle.
Anotomie or cuttyng of men by phisytions, to consyder the inwarde partes and membres.
A shielde without corners, such one in the tyme that Numa was king of Rome, was sene falle out of the skye.
A mayden seruant it was proprely taken for a bondewoman.
To drawe wyne or other lykoure.
Windinges and turnynges, specially in the grounde.
A disease in the throote, called the Quynse.

A great hole in the erthe with many tournynges, or that whyche hathe none issue out, or a lane in a towne, whyche leadeth the nexte waye to a strete, or that whiche lyeth on an hauen, whereby marchandyse is caried frome the water, or recaryed.
Brethe or wynde of a man.
To fetch wind, or draw breth.
He that drawethe his breathe peynefullye.
To consyder, to take heede, to sette my mynde, to beholde, and to thynke.
All thynge that hathe lyfe, and is sensyble, commonly it is taken for a beaste.
Sauynge that it is more larger. For it maye sygnyfye all thynge that hath spirite, as welle in heuen, as on erthe.
To gyue courage or boldenesse, to quycken:
The mynde, the wyl. somtime it is put for the soule: sometyme for affection or delectation, sometyme for wynde or blast, somtyme for wrathe, sometyme for a sowne.
To resyste, or to helpe, to sette to my mynde.
To grow or to be borne by a place or manne.
That whyche is of done yere olde.
An olde wyues tale, or a tale without fruite.
Vyttayles, sustynance, or lyuynge. Somtyme it betokeneth fyndyng in borde and apparayle.
The corde wherwith the sayle is bounde to the maste.
The eare or handel of a potte or cup. And sometyme it sygnifieth occasion. somtyme a bouckle.
The poostes on euerye syde of the doore.
Aboue other, before other, more than other, or besyde other.
A colation or drynkynge betwene dynar and supper.
To precede or excell, or goo before.
To putte before, or set more by.
Before this tyme, or before that tyme.
The crosse piece wherto the sayle 〈◊〉 .
Outwarde pyllars or postes, wherby 〈…〉 , or frame to susteyned.
They whiche be next the stan • appoynted for to defende it.
The beare of a woman, that is layde
Foreheed, nowe gentylwomen do 〈…〉 their rolles.
He that sercheth for antyquities, or redethe olde warkes, or vseth olde forme of speakynge or writinge.
To make voyde, to reduce to the fyrste state, to repelle. Antiquare legem, to repell a lawe.
Auncient or olde. sometime it signifieth noble or worshypfull.
He that hathe ouer other preemynence.
Remoue, putte away, or dryue away. Also it hath a signification of a more vehemency: as Apage hanccaniculā, Away with this bytche: or, hens away with this bytche.
Withoute a skynne. So be the Iewes called of Horacius, bycause they be cyrcuncyded.
To open, to disclose, to expownde.
The crowne of the heed, the toppe of euery thynge. it sometyme sygnifyeth a mytar.
The gutte whiche is ful of blode, mixte with grease.
One of the thre partis of the world wherof the inhabitantes be at this day called generallye Moores or Morynes, the countreyes be nowe called Tunyse, Fese, Marocke.
The place where as hyues be sette.
A byrde whiche doothe deuowre Bees.
Shepe, hauynge smalle bodies, and lyttell wolle.
Rounde appulles, whyche I take to be they, that are called pomeroyall.
An herbe called ache, somtyme it is taken for our commune persely.
A defence or aunswere to a rebuke.
A fable, wherin beastes or trees doo speake.
A Rebelle. It is nowe vsed for them, whiche do forsake the relygion, that they haue ones receyued.
An impostume, wherin corrupted humours haue recourse in any parte of the bodye.
An apostel. it proprely signifieth a messanger.
A wyne seller, or shoppe, wherin thinges be sette to sale.
Officers of iustice, attendyng on the great ministers, to somon or attache whom they wyll commaunde.
The offyce of a Sergeaunt or baylyffe.
A namynge, or appelynge to a hygher iuge.

To name or calle familiarly to me. Also Vlpian the great lawyer wyl haue it to sygnyfye, to wowe a mayden to haue her virginitie. sometyme it sygnifieth to arryue: Sommetyme to appeale to a higher iudge.
To aryue. sometyme to apply or sette my mynde, to direct.
That which hangeth at an other thynge.
To hange vp, to waye in a balance or beame.

To desyre moche, to go to. sometyme it signifieth to be at hande. Dies appatebat, The daye was come, or at hand. somtyme to wounde or stryke at, as, Leuās se alis, os oculos que hostis, rostro et unguibus appetit, Rysynge with his wynges, his talons and beke, he wounded the face & eies of him that faught on the other parte.
To moue handes or feete for ioye, or to beate any thyng to the ground.

o: Applico, applicaui, applicare, uel applicui applicere,
n: applico applicaui applicare uel applicui applicere
d: To ioyne to, to laye to, or sette to, or to applye.
Put to, or set to. somtime it signifieth conuenient, or to the purpose.
To sytre or go abrode in the ayre, or in the sonne.
A place sette agaynste the sonne.
To ioyne, to agree two thinges togither.
At, whan it is ioyned with a person, it signifieth with.
A basyne to wasshe in mennes handes.
A place, wherin water is caste.
That whyche haunteth the water, or lyueth therin.
That, wherinto water is putte. Vinum aquatum, Alayed wyne.
He that sercheth for water, or cō uayeth it.
The standarde bearer of the Romaynes.
A ploughmanne. and sommetyme a ploughe oxe.
To trowe, to iudge, or awarde.
A place where trees be sette, proprelye Elmes, wythye, or Salowe, it may be taken for an orchard, or a hoppeyarde, or a vyneyarde, where vynes doo growe vp by trees.
A vyne that rūneth vp in height by a tree or a pole.
A thynge secrete, or of fewe knowen.
To strayne, to putte of, to dryue away.
A diuiser of buil •••• , or a maister of the warkes.
The treasone of Minumentes 〈…〉 belongynge to a kynge or a 〈◊〉 .
A relle that womenne doo weare 〈…〉 beedes, to beare water or mylke 〈◊〉 .
A bowe, the rant of a roufe.
A by ••• e called an heron.
A b • sy manne medlynge with many thynges.
To burne, to loue ardently, or excedyngly▪ to make haste, to be cō sum • d, to desyre.
High and difficult, hard to com to.

A large place in a Cytie kepte euer cleane, where marchauntes do assemble: as I haue sene in dyuers cyties in Almayne. Also it is euerye place marked oute to buyld or to set an house in. Also a floore, where corne is thrashed.
To waxe drye, or to be made drye.
A bragger or a vaunter of his owne vertues, sometyme a forger of lyes, to make men merye.
He maketh or occupieth a banke for exchaunge.
A banker, with whom men doo make their exchaunge of money.
That whiche is done with great reason.

Is a raison, makyng a profe, wherby one thinge is gathered by an nother, and the whiche confirmeth that, whiche is doubtefulle, by that whiche is not doubtefull. somtyme it signifyeth a mattier, sommetyme coiecture, sometyme a shorte exposition of that whiche foloweth, other while sentence.
To reproue, to impute, to accuse, to shewe.
To speke sharply, shrewdly, or pertely.
Reproued. sometyme it sygnyfyeth shrewde, and he that can in speakynge sharpely inserche a mans mynd. Also shryll of voyce.
They that speake moche in fewe wordes.
A Ramme. Also a piece of ordynaunce or engyne, made lyke a rammes heed, to beate downe a walle. It is also oone of the .xii. sygnes that the Sunne passeth by.
The berde of corne, sometyme it is putte for wheate.
Harneyes and weapon. Also the instrumentes of all maner of craftes, Also standardes and baners, sommetyme battayles.
Tooles, instrumentes, all store for warres or shyppes.
An armorie or storehouse for shyppes or ordinance.
A study where bokes are laide, or a drye larder.
Store of horse or nete. somtyme it sygnifyeth cattell.
Proprely an esquyer for the body, as he, whiche alwaye attendynge about a knyght, beareth his hedpiece, his speare, and his shielde, a custrell.
Rynges that gentylmenne vsed to weare aboute their armes, as at this daye some men and women do vse, called bracelettes.
A vessel wherin they vsid in their sacrifice to put wyne.
The shoulder of a beaste, or the pynion of a fowle.
He that is obsessed with an ylle spyrite.
To gyue to moche, to presume, to make myne heyre.
A synewe lyke to a vayne, wherein the spirite of lyfe doth walke, as the blode dothe in vaynes.
To ioyne one ioynte to an nother.
A ioynt. also a moment or parcel of tyme. also a colour of Rhetorike.
To strayne, to thraste togyther, to wrynge.
Breadde made of wheat, whiche to harde and soore dryed, biskatte.
A place where reedes doo growe.
He that telleth of thinges to come by lokynge in beastes bowelles.
A fortresse or castelle, specyally standynge hyghe.
A pounde weyghte. In the olde tyme in the partition of lande, or other lyke thynge inherytable, they called the hole, As, and the partes diuided, ounces.
Peynted pament, whiche maye not be swepte.
To clymme, to ascende, to goo vp.
To chyppe or cutte with an axe.
To presume, to take vpon me a thinge.
To admytte, to take to me.
To adde to, to attribute, to impute.
He that is added to the nombre of other.
He that foloweth the example of an other, or he that writeth many copies of others exaumples.
One of the thre partes of the worlde.
Vnpleasant, as well in sight and herynge, as in taste, also harde or greuous.
He that is worthy to be dispysed, or refused.
To despyse, to refuse, to abhorre.
The deed see. Also a certayne claye there founden, whiche ones burning, wyll neuer be quenched.
To aspire, to loke to come to a thynge, to blowe, to fauoure, to gyue ayde, to gyue all my studye and wytte to optayne a thynge, to touche, to go to.
A page, and he that foloweth in all thynge the wylle of an other man.
To flatter in commendyng an other mans actes that be yll.
To folowe, to gette, to optayne.
To sowe, or plante by. Also to clayme, to affirme or approue, to manumise or make free.
Associate to a man in offyce or auctorytie.
To kepe diligentely, to take heede of one.
〈◊〉 lytte with or by an other, or I am assocyate.
To reste me, to sytte downe, t • sytte by.
To leape forth also Assilire, is to leape, as a horse leapeth a mare.
To be here, to defende a mannes cause.
To take proprely it sygnyfyeth to take to moche on me.
To ryse to an other better than my selfe, to gyue place, to growe vpwarde,
But. also therfore, as well, moreouer.
A lyttell marke in wrytynge like a Sterre,
He that drawethe his wynde shorte.
To stande by, to be present.
To playe at dyse or tables.
To ioyne, or bynde togyther, to bynde by couenant or promyse.
An Astrolabe or instrumente of astronomy.
The parte of astronomye that concerneth iudicials and practise.
The speculation and reasonyng cōcernyng the celestial or heuenly motiōs.
A celestial body compacte of many sterres, as a sygne.
To buylde, to ioyne oone house to an other, to fortifie, to affirme.
A voyce, whiche signifieth in the wordes that do folowe, wrath or indignation. Sommetyme it signifieth (but yet) whyche is a discrepaunce in the wordes that are spoken. Sommetyme it sygnifyeth Sed.
A greatte wrastler, or a great runner at commune games.
The craft of wrastlyng or rūnyng.
The iuge in games of wrastling or runnynge.
A thynge so small, that it may not be deuyded or made smaller. Also Atomi, be motes of the sonne.
Ynke, blache, that showmakers do occupie.
A mourner that gothe in blacke.
A porter that kepeth a gate.
Cruell, terrible, or sowre in countenaunce.
To take hede, to consyder, to intende.
A peculyare eloquence vsed in Athenes.
To speake like a man of Athenes,
To pertayne. Attiner, it besemeth, it is conuement.
To auaunce, to lyfte vp, to brynge to, to take away.
To attribute, to put vpon one by blamynge or accusynge, to assygne, to commytte.
An increase, or an open sale of priuate goodes.
Portesale of the goodes of men attaynted for treason or felonye.
He that begynneth any act, or is the fyrste causer or procurer of any thynge.
An indenture or obligation wherby a man is bounden to do seruice. Also ernest money.
To bynde by erneste or wrytynge to serue.
He that is bounde to serue, specyally in warres.
To go a byrdynge, or a foulyng, or hawkynge. Also it signifieth, to serche by craftye meanes.
Hardye, spoken in derisyon, or contempte.
Bolde or hardy, or trustyng well in hym selfe.
To bere, to consyder, to perceyne, to graunt that whiche is asked, to do the thynge that is cōmanded.
A place where menne do here lessons, or propositions.
Heryng, one of the flue wyttꝭ.
Somtime it is put for an ote strawe, or a wheate strawe, or reede.
Be thou gladde or ioyfull, as the vulgar people sayth, Reste you mery.
Backewarde, or on the backehalf. also angrye.
To disdayne. sommetyme it signifyeth to tourne away, to tourne fro.
To tourne away, or putte awaye.
To waxe greatte, or be great, to be growen.
He that tellethe by byrdes voyces, or by their flyeng or sytting, what shall happen.

o: Auguro, as et auguror, aris, rari,
n: auguro as et auguror aris rari
d: To telle by suche crafte, what shall happen.
Noble, or full of maiestie, wherfore the emperours of Rome were and yet be called Augusti. Augustus is also the moneth nexte after Iuly.
A thycke wodde without waye. Also a place where byrdes be kepte and nourysshed.
That whiche is lefte by auncetours. Auitus ager, Olde inheritance.
A haule. somtyme the palaice or court of a prince.
Tapesry, hangynges of noble mennes houses.
Sometyme betokeneth a softe wynd, somtyme brightnes, somtime fauour.
A piece of golde in money.
Be that hath heare as bryghte as golde.
A carter or driuer of a cart.
To driue a cart or some thing lyke. Also to gouerne.
To bere diligently, or giue good care.
Also it signifieth the persone that maketh the maryage on the mannes parte. Also the chiefe capytayne in warres.
The sygne or token shewed by • yrdes of thynges that shall folowe. Also if betokeneth fortune gouernance, or disposition of a capytayn. Also it is a token or signification of thynges to come.
To take lykelyhode. Also to begynne or entre into a busynesse.
Sowre or sharpe. Also soore or without pitie.
The vncle of the mothers side.
He that commethe in ayde of an nother.

Is a lyne imagined to go streight from the north to the south, dyuydynge the worlde as it were in two partes: at the endes are supposed to be two poyntes in heuen, whiche are called the northe pole and the southe pole.
A berye, as a baye bery, an hawe berye, an eglantine berie.
The place where the solemnitie of Bacchus was kepte.
Feastes of the paynyms, whiche they dydde celebrate with all abhominations of lechery.
A wyne porte. It maye be called a quaxinge potte.
To celebrate the feaste of Bacchus, to runne vppe and downe lyke a madde man.
Amonge the Paynims the god of wyne or drunkennes.
A place in the royalme of Naples, where be naturalle bathes of warme water bothe plesant and holsome: And by translation some poetes do so call all other naturall hote bathes.
A porter or cariar of bourdens.
A greatte fishe, whiche I suppose to be a thurlepoll.
A kynd of acornes. it is also a suppositorie to helpe them that be costife. Also a swete oyntmēt made of Mirabolanes.
He that can not pronounce well his wordes whan he speaketh.
A crossebowe, or a brake. It may be vsed for a gunne.
All thinges belongyng to a bain.
The keper of a bayne, or he that serueth in a bayne.
A bathe or vessell to wasshe in the body. A dienge vate, a fonte.
An vnthrift that in lechery & glottony deuoureth his substance.

In the olde tyme were all people, excepte grekes. proprely it be they, which do speake grossely, without obseruynge of congruite, or pronounce not perfectly, specially Greke or latyne. Also they that abhorre all elegancie. Moreouer it signifieth them, whyche be without letters, fiers or cruelle of maners or countenaunce, barbarouse.
The countreye where dwellythe people rude or beastly.
The corrupte fourme of speakynge or pronouncynge.
An instrument of musyke, whiche I suppose is that, that men call doulsimers.
A thrummed hatte, or a shepardes cloke.
A foole. Somtyme a mynstrel that syngeth iestes or fables.

A place where people do assemble for suites in the lawe, and ciuile iugementis be exercised, and counsayles holden. Also it maye be taken for a halle, or other large place, where suiters do attende, or men do wayte on rulers, or great feastes be kepte. It also sygnifyeth a cathedral churche.
He that kepeth the place called Basilica.

A Cocatrice, whiche is a serpent in the desertes of Aphrica, with a whyte cyrkle aboute his heed, hauynge a sharpe heed, redde eyen, and is somewhat blacke of colour, and is so venymous, that he sleeth men and beastes with his breth, & with the syght of his eyen.
The foote of a pylar, or that whiche susteyneth any lyke thynge. Also it signifieth the foundation or grounde of a matter.
A vessell with a longe handell.
A measure for wyne or oyle.
Slyppers, proprely of phylosophers, or suche other.
Is he, whiche hath abundaunce of all thynge that is good, and is perfecte in all thynges that be worthy prayse, or ought to be desyred of a good man. sometyme it is taken for noble or fortunate.
Is a heape of good thynges gathered togyther, of it selfe sufficient without lacke, and a very perfection accordyng to vertue.
Bankettynge dysshes, as tartes, marchepaynes, and other lyke.
A wanton worde, whyche is as moche to say, as lyttell fayre one, well fauoured chylde, praty mayden.
Signifieth al the tyme that the warres do contynue. also battayle or warre.
A great cruell beast or a monster.
Tapesry, wherin is wrought or painted the fygures of beastes.
Beastely. Beluina rabies, A beastly furye.
I intreate the wel, Thou arte beholden vnto me.
To prayse, to saye welle of a manne.
A man wel tunged, or faire spokē
He that receyueth a benefitte or good tourne of an other.
He that is beneficiall or lyberall.
To turne to good. Precor deū, ut haec res bene uertat tibi, I pray god this thynge may tourne the to good, or maye be for thy profite.
Fauour or good wylle, an intente to do well.
Is that whiche is commonly called Crystalle.
Men whiche in olde tyme faughte with beastes in the syghte of the people.
The wyfe of Duilius the Romayne, whiche was of so greate chastitie, that she was at that tyme an example, whan it was a thynge monstrous to here of vnchastitie.
A stacyoner, or a boke sellar.
A place where they vsed to sacryfyce shepe, whan any house was bourned with lyghtnynge.
Shepe with .ii. teth, called in some place hogrelles, or hogattes.
Any thing of two yeres old.
In two partes, or two maner of wayes.
That beareth twyse in a yere.
A double thefe, or he that hath stol ••• 〈◊〉 .
A carte drawen with two horses.
He that hath badde two wyues.
Beastes commen of two sondry kyndes.
Cattaylle or beastes yoked two togyther.
The humour of Melancoly, proprely that whiche bryngeth a man to fransy or madnesse.
He that hath abundaunce of that humour.
He that hath had two wiues.
Of two partes, hauynge two membres.
Two monthes olde, or two yere, accompted of the moone.

o: Binus, na, num, two, idem quod duo. Binae litterae, two letters. Bini tabellarii,
n: binus na num two idem quod duo binae litterae two letters bini tabellarii
d: Two messangers, bina iuga boum, two yoke of oxen Binarius numerus, the numbre of two.
She that hath had two byrthes.
Hauynge twoo wynges. Also a twyebyll, wherwith carpenters doo make theyr mortaises.
A seate or fourme, wheron two men onely may sytte.
One day added to, in foure yeres.
A beeste hauyng oone horne, and a very longe mane.
A citie, and also a greate meare or poole in the countrey of Thrace.
A royalme in Asia, whiche nowe the turke hath.
A kynde of naturall lyme, wherof the olde walles of the Cytie of Babylon were made.
A cytie of Thracia,Plin, li. 4, of Plynie called Bizian.
He that stamereth, omittynge some letters in speakynge.
To flatter, to speake fayre for aduauntage.
Cursynge, reprochynge, commonly blasphemy, whiche is nowe onely referred to the despite of god.
To curse, to reproche, to speake in the derogation or despyte of an nother.
To bable in vayne, and from the pourpose.

Is proprely the longe flye that flyeth in the leame of a candell, and is of the kynde of mothes. It is also a silke worme: and blatteus, beinge an adiectiue, is purple colour. Vestis blattea, a purple garment.
Softe, delicate, wanton, that can not decerne thinges, and whiche vaynely bosteth hym selfe.
A people in Aphrike, whiche haue their visages in their breastes.
An herbe being of the kynde of betes, hauynge no sente, Blittea meretrix, an vnsauorie queane.
A serpent in Italy, so greatte and large, that on a tyme whan one was kylde, there was a chylde all hoole founde in his bealy,Plin. lib. 8. capi. 14. as Plinie writeth.
The markette place, where oxen be solde.
A kynde of sweete smellynge gumme.
A countrey in Grece, wherin was the cytie of Thebes.
A ryuer in Spayne by the countrey of Granado.
A masse or lumpe of mettall, or other lyke thynge.
A great sowne or noyse, as it were of a trumpe, or gunne, a bownce.
Of sylke, Bombycina uestis, A garment of sylke.
By your lycence, No displeasure to you.
Good, whiche is contrary to yll.
A good man: Also beneuolent, peasyble, lyberall, playne, easye to speake to, worshypfull, treatable, mercyfull.
A sterre whiche foloweth Charles wayne.
The northe sterre, callyd the lode sterre.
A great ryuer in the countreye of Scythia.
A rother beaste, be it bulle, oxe, or Cowe.
The name of a parte of the see, whiche lyeth in two sondry costes: one by Constantinople, the other more northe.
A precious stone lyke to womennes heare.
A precious stone lyke to a blacke graape.
A puddinge made of the inwarde of a rother beaste.
A town not far from Rome.
He that with great noyse crieth out on a nother man.
To belowe out lyke a cowe.
He that is ordeyned a iuge in any game of wrastlynge, runnynge, or leapynge.
That kynde of mantell, which nowe commeth out of Irelande, or a longe garment made of rough frise.
Bracelettes, whiche some gentylmen and gentyll women doo vse aboute theyr armes.
That whyche lyke an arme holdeth any thinge vp, a proppe, or shore.
Thynne plates of mettalle, horne, or wodde.
The rewme or cattarre, whiche falleth downe by the chekes.
The rewarde for wrastlynge, runnynge, or leapynge, commonly called the chiefe game.
A capitayne or leader of the frenchemen called Galli, whiche, buylded Verona a citie of Venece.
An hospitalle, where chyldren be kepte and nouryshed.
He that speaketh his mynd a fewe wordes.
A gyant, whiche was of an excedynge greatnesse.
Brytayne, whiche doth contein Englande, Scotlande, and wales.
The inner parte of the throte,
They whyche haue their mouthe and tethe standyng farre out, tut mouthed.
A flye, whyche eateth corne, as it groweth.
A citie in the royalme of Naples.
An herbour or hedge made with thornes and briers wounde togither.
People in the royalme of Naples, ioynynge to Sycile.
Dul and grosse witted like to a beest.
A shriche oule. also a botche.
That whiche longeth to an oxe or cowe, as Lac bubalum, cowe mylke.
A stone lyke to a bugles harte.
A lytell cheke. Also that parte of a helmet, wherby wynde is taken.
An oxe heed. and the horse of Alexander the great was so called.
Herdes of nete, Bucolica, the same.
An herbe called langedebefe. Also a fyshe called a sole.
To caste durte on one: proprely it is of chyldren, whiche nourysses do name cackynge.
Wyld garlyke hauynge a leafe lyke to a lylly. it is taken generally for all rotes that be rounde.
A male of lether, wherin clothes be caried.
A tablette or other thynge hanged aboute ones necke, proprely whan it is holowe. A bobell of water, somtyme the heed of a nayle, otherwhyles studdes in girdels or other thinges.
He that is garnyshed with tablettes or studdes.
To bubble, as water whan it boyleth.
The hynder part of a plough whiche is croked.
An ile in the occean of Germany.
A tyraunt, whyche was kynge of Aegypte.
A place where deade bodyes haue ben brente.
A kynde of hawkes, whyche hathe thre stoones.
Was called a great sacrifice, suche as Hecatombe is.
A towne that the grekes calle Pyxunta.
A place where boxe trees growe.

A citie of Thrace now called Constantinople, whiche was somtyme buylded by a kynge of Spartane, called Pausania, wherof the people and inhabitantes were called Byzanta • . Afterward it was augmented by Constantine the emperour. and was the chiefe and heed of all the empire orientall.
Fantasticall men, and of straunge inuentions.
A maner of fyne flaxe or lynnen. I suppose it to be cotten.
An horse, yet in some partes of Englande, they doo calle an horse a cable.
A cytie of the lower Asia, all thoughe Cabytli, be people in India.
A pot or cauldron, wherin meate is sodden.
A gyant, whome Hercules dyd slee.
A scorne, or a lowde lawghter in derysyon.
To laugh immoderately and with a loude voyce.
To be nonsuite in an action.
Fallynge, decayinge. Caducus morbus, the fallynge euyll.
That whiche falleth by it selfe, as Cadiua folla, leaues fallyn downe by them selfe. Cadiua poma, appulles fallen from the tree.
A wine vessel, it may be takē for a pipe.
A rodde, whiche poetes supposid that Mercury bare in his hande, as messanger of Iupiter.
An ambassatour or Herault sent for peace, or to take a truse.
A keuerlede of lynnen, mooste proprely a quilte.
A vessell wherin lottes for election or consent of a multitude be put.
The name of a Prynce, whyche browghte oute of Phaenicia into Greece syxetene letters, and was the fyrste that wrate in profe, and founde out the fusynge and castynge of mettalles.
Syckenesses which be not apparant▪ the causes wherof, be hydde from phisitions.
To se but lyttell, to be half blynde.
To beate, or whyp▪ to cutte, to stryke, to kylle, to me • ke. Caedere ianuam saxis, to breake the doore with stoones.
To departe, to gyue place, to obeye.
To gyue ouer a ryght or tytle.
Say, Cedo cuium puerum, Tel or say, whose chylde or seruant.
Gyue, Quin tu mihi argentum cedo, But yet gyue thou me thy money.
Woddes vsed to be cutte, Copeyses.
Edgelinge. Also at one cutte or choppe.
Heuen or the firmament. also a granynge yron.
A syngle man or woman. Also euery chaste persone.
Morter, or any other grosse matter, wherwith walles be made.
Daubers, pargetters, rowghe masons, whiche do make onely walles.
The preter perfect tense of Capio, I haue taken.
Waxe. Also Caere were writynge tables couered with waxe.
To laye waxe on any thinge.
Of waxe. Also fatte or tydye.

o: Caerulus, la, lum, et Caeruleus, lea, leu,
n: caerulus la lum et caeruleus lea leu

d: That whiche is myxte with waxe.
A soore, whiche is lyke to a honye combe.
An oyntment made with oyle and netes dunge, wherwith men that wrastlyd vsed to anoynte their bodies. Also it sygnifyeth the place where wrastlers were annoynted.
Thre leaued grasse, whiche bringeth furth whyte hony suckles, called clyuer grasse.
A citie in the coūtrey of Palestina.
A citie in the realme of Arragon.
Heare, or a bushe of heare.
A waipon, somtyme vsed in Fraunce. it is also a parte of an oration, not concludynge a sentence: as it were a pyece of a sentence.
A piece as it were cut of from the remenaunt, proprely of a verse.
An instrumente, wherwith iuorye •• e bored. Also a weapon lyke a dagger.
Gray of colour or blunket. Also he whiche hath grey eyen.
They whiche be cutte oute of the mothers or dames belyes.
A weapon hauyng great plummates hangyng at the ende of a clubbe.
A gyrdell or corse, whiche the husbande dydde putte aboute his wyfe, whan he was maried, and at nyght dydde plucke it of.
Be aduerbes sygnyfyenge, sometyme moreouer, somtyme from hensforthe, sometyme Caeterum, is a coniunction, and signifieth sed, but.
The name of a ryuer in Phrigia.
A propre name of a man.
A conuocation place, where matters concernynge deuotion were treated.
An herb called calamēt or nep.

A philosopher of Inde, whiche in the presence of the greate Alexander, beinge of the age of .lxxiii. yeres, felynge hym selfe sycke, made a bonefyre, and wente into the toppe therof, and bourned hym selfe.

A rede, or wheate strawe, Also a penne. It is also taken for a pype, or whystell. Also a fyshynge rodde, and a twigge, wheron birde lyme is put. Also small branches of trees, also it is a pole to mete with, conteynynge syxe cubytes and a spanne, a mette polle.
A pynne of wodde or iuorye, wherwith men and womē do set or trimme vppe their heare.
A tyre or burlette for a woman.
Boyes and knaues, which do folowe hostes, and do either carye the weapons of souldiours, or serue them of wode or water.
The heele. it sometyme signifieth the ende of a matter. sommetyme a stroke with the heele.
A horse that dothe flynge or kycke.
A peble stone. Also the stoone in the body. Also a chesse man. also accompt. also the leste weight or poyse that may be. Moreouer a knyfe made of a stone.
He that is moche diseased with the stone. Calculosus locus, a stonye place.
To make darke, or be darke.
That whiche makethe hotte or warme.
Brawn, or hardnes of the fete made with goinge.
To be harde as drawne. Also to knowe perfectly.
The firste day of euery monthe.
The mother of Archias, whiche gaue the name to the countreye of Archadia, whom poetes fained to be transformed into a beare.
The name of an yle, also of a woman, whiche receyued Vlysses whanne he escapyd drownynge.
Oone of the vyrgines, whiche be named Musae.
A cuppe to drynke wyne in. Also a potte, wherin potage is sodden.
The parynge or skynne of an apple, or other lyke fruite. Also a keueryng made of clay. Also that parte, wherout springeth a floure, whiche is grene.
A medycyne to make the eyen fayre.
A citie in Grece, also it was a great forest and wodde in Brytain, nowe called Englande.
The doughter of Athlas, a Nimph or woman of the see.
A beaste in Syria, which with his hornes throweth downe great trees.
A citie in the countrey of Naples.
A mountayne in the southwest part of Spayne.
All the heed, whanne the flesshe is awaye.
He that accusethe or seweth a many vniustly.
To accuse or sue a man vniustely.
A swyne fed with graines, and suche other vyle thynges.
An herbe growynge amonge corne, hauynge a yelowe flowre.
To chaunge. In the olde tyme it signified to fyght, to begyn a iournay, or to tourne in a iourney.
A kynge of Persia, grandfather of Cyrus. It is also the name of a ryuer in the countrey of Hyrcania.
The false roufe of a house, sollar, or chamber.
To make a fauce roufe of a hous, or to make a solar, or to sylde.
A towne of Italy in the countrey of Picenum.
The inhabitauntes of Camerine, a towne in Sycile.
An herbe, whiche beinge brused, prouoketh a man to vomite: wherof camme this prouerbe, Ne moueas camerinam, for, procure not harme to thy selfe.
Was in old tyme a boy, or a wenche that seruyd the byshop, whan he dydde sacrifyce. Also the name of a man or womanne.
Made lyke a fournayse or chymney.
A worme which eateth herbes, & is rough with many fete, & is callyd a palmer.
A bytte or snaffyll. also a rayne or corde, wherwith men beinge condempned were bounde.
A cane, also an oyle pot or canne.
Pipes, wherby water doth runne into a cundyte.
Latteses, or any thynge made lattese wyse. Also secrete places to looke oute. Also windowes made with barres of wodde or yron with dyuers holes.
To rase or put out, to cut or teare any thyng that is written.
A kynd of fyshe called a crabbe, also a signe in heuen.
Is the same that Cancelli be.
To make whyte, to bleache, to make to glowe lyke a burnyng cole.
To glowe lyke a burnynge cole. Also to be white.
To be whyte, or to make whyte.

Was be amonge the Romains whiche laboured for some of the great offyces in the publyke weale: and they were so named by cause they dydde weare in the tyme of their election white apparayle. It maye be taken by translation at this tyme, for them that in vniuersities be called incep • oars, or regent maisters. Also for theym that be lately christened, or newely entred into some honorable or worshypfull state.
Whyte. It is somtymes taken for gentyll or easye: as Candidus lector, a gentyll reder, whiche dothe not openly reproue that which he redeth. Candidus index, A gentyll or easy iuge.
Sometyme sygnifyeth fortunate, and it sygnifyeth more than Albus, as oryente whyte.
Were of the olde Romaynes named the apparayle pertainyng to the heed.
To be hore, or gray heared.
A mayden, whiche bare on her heed a basket or cofer, wherin were iewels or images of the goddes.
Be taken for white heares for age.
A beaste, whiche hathe onely the face of a dogge.
A lyttell dogge or bytche. Also a sterre, wherof canicular or dogge days be named Dies caniculares.
A dogge, a kynd of fyshe called dogfishe, a play at tables, a signe in heuē, wherof there be two sterres, oone called Canis maior, the other canis minor.
A poete whiche was in the tyme of Martialis.
A cane or rede. also a canne or pot. also a village in the countrey of Galilee.
A towne in the countrey of Apulia, where a greatte hooste of Romayns was slayne by Hanniball.
A place where kanes or reedes do growe.
To synge, to playe on the shalme or other instrument. Also to praise, to prophecye.
To blowe the retraicte in battayle.
A rule, also the inner parte of a targate, whiche keuereth the hande.
A stone whiche hath the prynte of a blacke flye called a byttell.
A greene worme shynynge with a glosse of golde, whiche is bredde in the toppe of asshes, and laide to a mannes body, maketh it to blyster.
A pot or a iugge. Also a beaste, whereof there is founde noo female. Also a kynde of fysshe. also the blacke flye called the bytill.
A maner of a charyot or wagen. also a perche or a rayle.
A geldynge. Also a traunsome of timber.
The yron wherwith the extremytie of wheeles be bounden, the straake of a carte.
A towne in the countreye of Apulia.
That taketh or conteyneth any thynge, able to receiue.
The greatnesse of a vessell, or lyke thynge that contayneth.
A gelded gote. sometyme it is taken for the bucke gote. it also was the name of an olde grammarion.
To take, or to goo aboute to take, to receyue. sommetyme it sygnifyeth to brynge in.Plautus.
The heare of a mans heed. somtyme the toppes of herbes, where the seedes do growe.

To take wyllyngely, or vnwyllyngly. Sommetyme it sygnifieth to delyte, to mitigate, to deceyue, Capti dolis, deceyued with cautels. somtyme to cō teyne. Du boni, quid turbae? aedes nostrae uix capiunt, Good lorde, what a company? vsieth our house woll conteyne theym. Also to make.
Blynde, also great louers be named capti.
To halter, or putte on a rope, or corde.
A man that deserueth deth. Also that is prone and redy to murder.
That growethe greatte in the heade.
Were amonge the Romaynes the poore▪ sorte of the people, whiche were discharged of all exactions, and remayned in the citie onely for generation.
A lytell heed or top of a thing. Also the hyghest parte of a pyllar.
Any thing that couereth the heed, commonly they do call it a hoode.

A condemnation, wherby a man loseth either libertie of his person, • is made bond: or is banished his countrey, or put out of the kynges protection, or renouncynge his owne familie, is adopted or take into an other, whiche is not now vsed.
Was the surname of hym, that found the heed, whan the Capitole shulde be buylded.
The palaice of the citie of Rome.
He that hath a great heed, also heddy or obstinate in opinion.
He that hath a great heed, or a dull heed.
Any thynge that is growen to a heed.
A lytle heed, also a chapiter.
The name of a greke letter, for whiche the latins vse C.
A countrey in the lesse Asia.
A frute called Capers, wherwith we do make salates & sauce for mutton, whiche eatē before meles, be very good for the stomake, & ageinst diseases of the splene.
An yle in the see called Ligusticū.
A beaste whiche doth see wonderfull quickly. It is also a kynde of vynes soo named. Moreouer an yle by Naples.
A beaste called a roo. It is also the tendrell of a vyne, whiche wyndeth diuers ways, called also Pampinus.
That whiche is of a gote. Caprillus, a, um, idem.
A sygne in heuen, conteininge xx. sterres.
The paryng away of the barke of a tree.
A wylde fygge tree, which runneth vp by walles.
That whiche is of the kynde of a goote.
A stable or pen, where got▪ be kept.
Birdes like to gulles, which appere not by day, but in the night they come into gote pennes, and do souke the gotes, wherby the vdders of them be mortified.
The coppe of lyttel mane, that is in the forheed of a horse, or other beast.
A vessell wherin oyle is kept.
He that kepith chestis, or apparel.
The acte of takynge or deceyuynge, or that wherby any thynge is taken.
A prysoner taken in warres, or a sclaue.
To gette the fauour of oone with tayre wordes, pleasant dedes, or rewardes. Also to deceyue or take quyckely.
The acte or crafte to gette fauor. also deceyte or subtyltie.

Chaunce. also deceyte, perceyuynge of a thinge, or capacitie. Captus hominum, Mens capacitie. sometyme dilectation, Non possum adduci et suscipere è pecunia captum, I may not be brought therto, and take dilectation of the money.
A citie in the royalme of Naples.
An olde manne redye to be layde in his beere.
What so euer may receyue any thynge into it: proprelye it is a beere, wherin deed corpsis are borne: also the hyltes or handell of a sworde.
A heed. Also the begynnynge of euery thynge. Also a chapiter of a boke.
To gather a soore to a heed.
A mans name that buylded Capua.
A kynd of lynnen cypres: also the saylle clothe of a shyppe. Moreouer it is a syne garment of women of sylke or lynnen.
A cole. It was also the name of a Romayne.
To haue a Carbouncle or botche.

A botche, whiche commeth of inflamation. it is also a kynde of precyouse stones, whiche do shyne lyke a bournynge cole. Moreouer a defaulte in a vyne, and other trees, wherby they ar burned, whiche happeneth about the canicular dayes. Also it signifyeth erthe, wherin is founde blacke slatte stones.
A pryson. Also Carceres were stables, wherin horses were sette, whanne they shulde runne.
A kynde of frogges, hauyng on their bealyes yelowe spottes.
A syckenes which hapneth by weakenes of the body, with moch sweatte and feblenesse of the stomake.
An herbe, whiche some do suppose is Cressis.
The poste, whereon the doore hangeth, and is moued. Also a mere or boū des, whiche passith through the felde from the southe to the northe.
The effect of the matter or thing: the chiefe poynte of the matter.
To lack proprely those good thynges, which ones were had. Somtyme it sygnifieth to be without a thyng: as Careo culpa, I am without faute. Careo febre, I am without feuer.
The name of a caruer, the scholar of Lysyppus.
A region in Asia the lasse.
A lyttel worme that eateth wodde: It is also putrifaction or fylthe growen by age or contynuance.
The keele or bottom of the shyppe.
A strete in Rome, wherein Pompey dwelled.
To make a thyng of the facion of a shyppes bottome. Also to speake to a mannes reproche.
Scarcitie, proprely of that whiche serueth for the sustinance of man.
A countrey of the lasse Asia.
The name of two sondry hylles in Iudea.
A verse or metre. Also the hole warke whiche is made in versis. Somtyme it signifieth a charme.
The name of a lady, whiche had the spirite of prophecy, and gaue aunswere in verses.
To carde wulle, or other lyke thynge.
They that do pike or make clene wulle, or carde.
A place in Messenia, and the temple of Appollo in Laconia.
A larder, wherin hangeth salte fleshe, sometyme it sygnifyeth a bowchers shambles.
The name of certain people in Italy.
A boucher of men, or hangman, that cutteth theym in pieces.
The place where suche execution is doone. Also the offyce or acte of a hangemanne.
The mydle region of al France.
A towne in the border of Germanye.
Fleshe, proprely of that whiche is deade.
Plowghemens bootes, made of vntāned lether, they may be called cokers.
An Ile agaynste Aegypte, the myddes betwene Rhodes and Candy.
A carte horse, or charyotte horse.
To gather or plucke. Also to chese, to reproue, or taunt, to vse .i. fruor. Also carpere uires, is to make feble.
The cytie of Cartage in Affryke.
The name of a citie in Grece.
The images of women holding garlandes, or other lyke thynge sette vp to garnyshe howses.
The woman that kepeth the cotage
A hyll, in the borders of Aegypte.
A spice, whiche hathe the vertue of Cynamome, and is wonderfull soote in sauoure.
The see whiche ioyneth to the sayde hylles.
Nettꝭ which may be called hays. Also an helmette, but than it hath Cassidis in the genitife case.
A signe in heuen, that hathe .xiii. sterres, and is figured lyke to a woman, sittynge in a chayre.
The gumme that droppeth out of afirre tree.
To put oute, or make of none effecte.
A propre name of a man.
A fountayn in the fote of the hill of Pernassus, whiche was dedicate to the Musis.
Was a kynde of sacrifice, that the vyrgins Vestales made.
The inhabitauntes of a lyttelle walled towne.
One lyttelle walled towne after an other.
A lyttell walled towne. It is also a cundyte, oute of the whyche water rounnethe.
A docke where shippꝭ be laid vp.
To chastise with wordis. also to correcte or amende▪
A Beuer, whiche hath the taile of a fyshe, in the residue is like to an ottar.
Were bretherne both atte one byrth, which were honored for goddi.
An armie of men of warre, whan they lye or abyde in any place. Also the place where the hoste lodgethe. Also the Pauilions beinge pyched.
To lay or lodge an army.
To gelde. Sometyme to cut of generally.
Castrense, that which pertaineth to an hooste or armye.
Lynnen clothe, wherwith maidens dyd gyrde them selfe vnder their pappes.
Chaste, honeste, and contynent, or vncorrupted.
Happe, ruyne, mysfortune, or myserie. also a case.
Instruction or informacyon to hym that begynneth any thynge.
To instructe, to infourme or teache.
The place where horses be coursed.
A verse wherein one onely syllable lacketh.
Speche or writyng where thinges be recyted in order and numbre, a rehersalle.
Certayne heretikes, whiche sayde that the holy goste was not in the apostels, but onely in them selfes.
A playster made with herbes and sewet.
A portculious, Also cloudes. somtyme caues in the erthe.
Gret courses of water, falling downe from highe places. Also the places from whens they do falle.
A rewme or styllynge downe of water or fleme from the heed.
A shyppe that watcheth or espieth for other.
A cage, wherin men be sette, whiche are to be solde. also wherin they were punysshed.
Parte of a shyppe or pauemēt.
A company of men of warre. some tyme a multitude of people.
They that doo assemble in companyes.
A kynde of erthe, wherof latyne mettall is made.
Vniuersalle. nowe it is vsed for hym that kepeth the faithe, as the vniuersall churche hath obseruyd it.
A great reproche layde to gentylmen, whiche had robbed the countreis, that were alied to the Romaynes, and had riottously consumed the goodes.
The ouer stone of a mylle, callyd the runner.
The righte worke of vertue, a ryght dede.
Wyse, or wytty. Also the name of a noble and wyse familye in Rome.
One of the gates of Rome.
The desyre of female kynd, to cō pany with the male kynde, proprely to goo assaute, to rudder, to horsynge, or to blyssonynge.
A kytten or yonge catte. Also it is putte generally for the yonge kynde of all beastis. also for a dogge.
A hole, wherin byrdes do brede.
Is a place at large, hauyng many porches, whiche serueth to a commune, lyke a market place.
A very hygh mountayne in Inde.
A tayle of a beaste. somtyme a mans priuye membre.
The lower part of a tree next the roote. Also a table, hauynge many leaues or tables.
A caue or darke place in the groūd. Also a cage or cowpe, wherein byrdes be kept. Moreouer a place where a comedy or enterlude is playde.
To beware, to eschue: also to prouyde diligently, to take hede. Caue tibi, Take hede of thy selfe.
A caue or holowe place in the grounde.

o: Cauillo, aui, are, uel cauillor, ari,
n: cauillo aui are uel cauillor ari
d: To ieste to mocke, to bourde.
A shepe house, but proprely a folde.
A stalke or stem of an herbe or tree. Also it is an herbe called colewortes. It is somtyme taken for all pot herbes, the rūpe of a beaste, and for a shafte or iauelyn.
A towne, whiche of Plinie is situate in the fyrste region of Italy.
An yle in the occean see.
A howkster that selleth meare and drynke.
A woman that selleth wyne. Also the tauerner.
Was an yle, whiche afterward was called Andros, and after that Antandros.
A hatte or cappe after the facion of Macedonye.
A cause or matter in suite.
Souldiours, which for causes reasonable, were discharged oute of the armye.
A discharge of a souldiour for a reasonable cause.
That is cause that a thynge is done.
To complayn me of a thing that dothe greue me.
To fynd the matter, or to bring for excuse.
Medicines, whiche do burne the skynne or the fleshe.
Is a markynge yron, or an instrument, wherwith soores ar burned.
Marked or burned with that instrument, or marked with an yron.
A ragged rocke, or hylle fulle of greatte stoones.
It is ordeyned or prouided by an acte of parlyament or counsayle.
It is nede to prouide or beware.
A man or womanne, commynge of hym.
A rocke in the see, or an yle.
To gyue place, to goo away, to voyde, to withdrawe, to graunte, to gyue.
I leue my goodes to an other.
To procede no further, to admytte the contrary.
Those goodes ar com or happened vnto me.
In the imperatiue mode, Tell thou.
Amonge lawyers is, The tyme is come, that the dette is due to be payde.
The first swearyng of the pitche tre.
The fruite of the cedre tree.
An yland in the costis of Germany.

A kynde of trees, whiche is excellent for buyldinge, forasmoche as the tymbre therof is great, & very lyght: also it dureth longe, and is neuer eaten with wormes, and is soote in sauour, hauyng leaues lyke to a cypresse tree.
I am in greate fame, or am renoumed.
To celebrate or brynge in renoume, to make good reporte. Also to haunte, to honour, or worship.
To doo a thynge quyckely, to make haste.
He that calleth on the mariners, to rowe or labour.
The shoute or crye that shypmen or botemen do make, whan the master doth whystell or calle.
A cellar, wherin any thyng is kepte. Also where we be pryuily wasshed. Also a secrete place in the temple.
He that hathe the charge of a cellar or storehouse.
To hyde, or wyll not knowe.
A people in Spayne, of Celtis, Frenche men, and Iberis Spayniardes assocyate togyther.
A kynde of sweete trees growynge in Affryke.
A byrd lyke an hauke, which maketh a great sowne whan he crieth. Also it is the name of a town or coūtrey in Grece.
A tombe, where no manne is buryedde.
To suppose, to shewe myne opinion or sentence, to determyne, to be discontent, to numbre people, to the intent to take them, whiche be apte for the warres, or to leuye or taxe a subsidie.
A iudge of mens maners. Also suche as was appoynted to valewe mennes goodes.
He that hath bene a Censour, or is worthy for his grauitie to iuge and correcte other mens maners.
He that dothe assiste or accompany the iuges of maners called censors.
Were those fieldes, whiche by the lawe ciuile mought be boughte & solde.
The authoritie or iudgement of a censour. Also correction of maners, lawe, or decree, concernynge maners.
Yerely reuenues. Also valuation of goodes. Also a subsidie, the numbring of the people.
He that is assessed or taxed, capite censi, taxed by the polle, or he that payeth heed syluer.
A kynde of herbe called Cētory
A people in the coūtrey of Thessaly, whom the poetes dyd fayne to be the one half lyke a man, the other halfe lyke a hors. Also they be certayne great shyppes.
A ryuer, whiche was fyrste called Euenus.
A worme called a Palmer, whiche is heary, and hath many feete.
A quylte, or a iakke, or other lyke thynge stuffed with linnen, floxe, or cotten, or a cushyn made of pieces of cloth of dyuers colours.
The poynt, whiche is in the very myddes of a thynge.
Certayne iudges in Rome, beinge of the numbre of a hundred and fiue. And their iugementes were called Centum uiralia iudicia.
A parte of an hoste, conteynynge an hundred men. Also a porcion of ground in the felde, contayning an hundred acres.
By a hundred togyther. Also plentuousely, or in a great numbre.
A capitayn ouer one hundred of foote men.
To diuide men into a company, contaynyng an hundred persons: or feldes into a hundred acres of lande.
A hundred pounde weyghte, or a hundred pieces of that money that were called Asses.
The heed ache, whan al the heed dothe ake.
The name of a man, and of a fishe.
The name of a kynge of Ethiope.
A laake nere to the see Athlanticū
A precious stoone, hauynge manye whyte strikes.
A place in Athenes, where men beinge slayne in battayle, were buryed. Also an nother place, where commune women dwellyd.
A serpente, whiche hathe hornes lyke a ramme.
A smalle weight or poyse, whyche is the fourth part of a scrippule, the .xlviii. parte of an vnce.
Is of Quint. called a spece of reasonynge inexplycable.
The porter of hell. Also a dogge with thre heedes, which Hercules drewe out of Helle.
A mā being braynsycke, or wild brayned, trustynge onely to his owne wyl.
The goddesse of corne. sometyme it is vsed of Poetes for the selfe corne, or breadde.
A thynge which is founde in hony combes, wheron bees do feede.
To see or perceyue also to consyder: sometyme to iuge, or determine. somtyme to trie out. Also to syght in battayle, to entre into lande, which is happened vnto me by inheritance or gifte.
Oone contendynge or stryuynge with an other.
Certayn, sure without dout. sometyme it sygnifyeth euen as we wolde haue it.
A harte, or a forke, wherwith cotages be propped vp.
The hynder part of the necke.
Ceruse, or whyte leade, wherwith some women be paynted, and colde playsters be made of it.
A tirfe. some do call theym sottes, grasse and erthe togither.
To ceasse, to leaue warke, to abyde.
He that is slowe in dooinge his dewtie.
An instrument, wherwith iuorie is made holow. also a dagger, or a wunbyl. also an herbe, whiche is called Berayne.
Places nyghe the see syde, where Tunye and other greatte fysshes be taken and saltyd.
A fyshemonger, or taker of great fysshes.
A great fyshe called a whale.

The name of a noble philopher & capitayne of Athenes, which vsed to say, that more terrible was an hoste of hartes, hauynge to their capitayn a lyon, than an hoste of lyons, hauyng an harte their capitayne.
A citie of Perse, whiche nowe is called Aetisiphon.
A gatherynge vnder the skynne lyke the disease called Bubo.
A citie in Asie agaynste Constantynople.
The name of a citie in Grece. also of an yle, and of a byrde.
A stone of the colour of brasse, but more blacke.
A region in Asia, ioyning to Arabie, wherin was the great cite of Babylon.
Be taken for greate astronomers of the contrey of Assiria.
A citie of Thessaly on the se cost.
