He that hath had two wiues, cō monly called Bigamus.
A womanne that hathe hadde two husbandes.
To dispose, to order, to interprete or make playne, to deuyde, to dygeste.
Sygnifyeth in a sentence, a lyttell or smalle distaunce. Digitum transuersum ab eo non discedebat, He went not from hym a fynger bredde.
To fight togither with swordes. by translation to contende or stryue.
Honour gyuen or dewe to a man for his merites. sommetyme astate of nobilitie, or great authorytie. sommetyme beautie, proprely of a man, specially in gesture and communication.

n: digno aui are amp dignor ari
d: To iuge one to be worthy, or to be estemed worthy.
To discerne or knowe by dyuers meanes.
To marke, as men marke beastes to knowe them.
To slyppe or go awaye, to falle downe, as • howse doeth. sometyme it signyfieth to fayle.
To teare or rent in pieces.
To consume goodes, or spende ryotrously or wastefully.
An argument, whiche on euery parte taunteth him, to whom it is spoken.
To fauour or loue meanly somtyme to diuyde.
To vndo, or cutte a cote, or other thynge beinge sowed.
An aduerbe, whiche signifieth betyme in the mornynge.
To waxe daye, to appere to be daye.
That porcion of daye, whiche is before that the sonne ryseth.
The leauyng of play, or the space betwene recreations or playes.
To wasshe, to make cleane, to putte away, to release, to alaye, as wyne is alayde with water: or to tempre, to purge, or discharge a crime.
A faynt colour, or vnperfect coloure.
Is wyne or other lycour, wherein any herbe or other thing is depid by a certayne space, whiche some phisytions calle infused.
Is whan the erth is surrounded or drowned with moche rayne.
To flowe abrode, as diuers streames out of one springe.
To syght or contende with some thynge.
The halfe deale of that whiche is diuided.
Is spoken where a mā intendeth to shewe that that the meane is beste.
The halfe deale of that whiche is not seuered or diuided.
Letters sent from oone to an nother.
To sende dyuers persones into dyuers places. Somtyme it sygnifieth to let to departe, to gyue leaue, to ceasse, to leaue, to lette passe, to suffre, to humble.

o: Deiecit uultu & dimissa uoce locuta est,
n: deiecit uultu amp dimissa uoce locuta est
d: She dyd cast downe hir loke, and with an humble voyce sayde. Also to gyue, to let down.
One of the names of Cybele, called the mother of the goddꝭ
The rydge of the hylle of Ida in Phrigia.
Harlottes, whyche be hyred for lyttell moneye.
Harlottes, whiche kepe abrode in the feldes and woddes.
A iurisdiction, a gouernance. Also the diocese of a byshop.
A philosopher of Socrates sect, and Diodorus Siculus, a story writer. and an other Diodorus, Ci. in Br • to. & Tus. lib. 5. a stoike phylosopher, of whom Cicero writeth.
A goddesse of the see, mother of Venus.
A geometricall instrument, to discerne altitudes and distaunce. Victrunius vseth it for wayinge or pluckynge vppe of water.
An yle in the borders of Italy.
A cytie of Aegypte. There be foure other of the same name in Aegypte, but very small cities in comparyson of this.
Vessels of erth with handels, wherin wyne was kepte.
A shepeherdes cote made with shepe skynnes.
Two vowels ioyned togither called a dipthonge, as ae, oe, au, ei.
A Charter of a prince or cytie, or a wrytte.
Any garmente lyned, but it is taken for a doublette.
A serpent, of whom if a man be bitten, he dyeth for thyrste.
A citie in the realme of Naples.
A womans name, the wyfe of Lycus kynge of Thebans.
Distrybuters of money, or paye maysters.
To shrynke for colde, or for feare.
Streight, or in a right fourme.
To breke or leaue of. Eares consilium diremit, That thynge brake or dissolued the counsayle. also to put of, or deferre.
An hygh hylle of Maurytayne nowe callyd Atlas.
To braste or breake a sonder.
To wede out, or purge that whiche is nought.
Callyd the god of rychesse, sometyme it signifieth ryche.

To departe. sometyme it signifieth an exception as, Quum discesserim a fratre, nemo est mihi te charior, Excepte my brother, no manne is to me more dere than thou arte. Also it sygnifieth dyuysion or openynge. as,Ci. 1. 〈◊〉 Quum terra discessisset, magnis quibusdam imbribus, discendit in illum ••• atum, whan the erthe by thoccasyon of moche rayne opened, he wente downe into the cleft or swalowe.
To depart or sundre one thyng from an other. Also to striue or varie, to knowe distinctly.
To pluck or teare in piecis.
Dissolute, or neglygent, or vnable for the warres, cowarde.
Lerning as it is ꝑceyued of the scholer. It is also a good forme of lyuing.
To forgette that whiche was ones lerned.
He that agreeth not with an nother.
A separation. somtyme election of good from yll, discretion.
Seuered or parted. Valla saythe, that it is he that discerneth the qualyties of men, and value of thinges.
Diuersite or difference. also the shedynge or partynge of the heare. Also it sygnifieth peryll.
An instrument, wherwith the heare is parted or shadde.
To be moche vexed or troubled in mynde.
Opened wih a wedge or other lyke thynge.
To runne hither and thither, or wander.
A dyshe. Also a rounde thynge of wodde or mettalle, whiche in playinge is throwen from one man to an nother. It is sometyme taken for the hole fygure of the sonne or the moone.
To caste or shake downe, to remoue, to examyne, or discusse.
To expelle or put from many places or many wayes.
Losse by neclygence, or superfluous expenses. Also it signifieth harme.
To spēde, also to stretch out.
A stewarde, or other offycer, layinge out money for howseholde: a disposer of thinges.
To sowe abrode, or to scatter.
To gyue parte to one, part to an nother.
To dryue beastes frome their pasture.
To discerne, to espye, to consyder.
A fote in meter, that hath four syllables longe, as Oratores.
To take accompt, or examyne any maner of thinge writen.
To dispute, to make plain to be vnderstande.
Where euery mans opinyon is asked in a matter, whiche requyreth iugemente.
To make thynne that whiche is thycke.
To kysse swetely, and with moche delectation.
Cutte as a bodye is in an anotomye.
To think contrary, or to disagree.
To sowe sedes, sometyme to dispute or declare.
To be at variance or discorde.
To lepe down from a place, somtyme to braste.
To dissemble or fayne a thynge, whiche is not as it semeth to be.
To scatter or sprede abrode or dispatche, also to bringe vnto noughte.
To lose or vnbynd, to spede to paye seuerall dettes.
To do agaynst the relygion, to breake the relygion.
To stratche out, or retche, to fyll, as a bottell is fylled.
To breake smalle, to pounde or to braye syne.
A distyllyng, specyally from the heed, callid a reume or catarf, the pose.
To lette or withholde with busynesse, or vrgente causes, to holde or putte backe.
To dyuide. Also to make dystinction.
To stande aparte, or be dystant one from an other.

To plucke away, or to dyuide, or to withdrawe a thynge. sometyme by translation it is taken for to sell. Also to fynisshe or conclude matters in variaunce. Controuersias distrahere, to ende controuersies or suites.
To dystrybute, or gyue in sondry partes to dyuers persones.

To bynd fast, or to strain harde, to rubbe of or clense the fylthe or soyle of the body, to thretten to stryke, or to drawe out a swerde. Gladium distrinxit, He drewe out his sworde. Sommetyme to gather,Columel. as, Sereno caelo manibus distringi oliuam opertet, In a fayre cleere daye the olyues must be gathered by hande. Districtus negotiis, lette with busynesse.
An hogge, which hath the bristils of his necke deuided.
To make ryche, or be ryche.
A verse made in the honoure of Bacchus.
A fote of four sillables in verse, hauynge one longe, an other shorte, an nother longe, the fourthe shorte.
Longe tyme. also the day tyme. wherof commeth Interdiu, in the day tyme.
To wāder from place to place.
To stryde, or to spred wide one from an other, as bowghes of a tree.
To selle to dyuers persones, or in dyuers parcelles.
The partes of a comedy or interlude, where many persons speke togither.
To turne often to a thing, or to resorte.
To resort, or repaire to a place.
Wherto men in iourney doo resorte to bayte or be lodged: a lodgynge.
Pertaynynge to an inne, or lodgynge.
A by waye, or syde way, oute of the high way.
To tourne from one thinge to an other, to take lodgynge, or to bayte.

n: diuerto ad te amp apud te
d: I come to lodge with the, or to tary for a tyme with the.
To diuide or parte in sonder.
That whiche may be seuered or diuyded.
He that hath power in diuine thynges.
To telle truthe, as well of thynges present, as of thinges passed. for the more parte it signifyeth to coniecte of thinges present, what shall happen.
A foreiugement or coniecture. Also where a matter cometh in iugement, without writinge or wytnesse on any of the partes, that iudgement may be called Diuinatio, a diuination.
That whiche pertayneth to god, diuine.
Wherby we declare what is in variance, or whereby we doo expresse of what thinges we wyll treate. Also a diuysyon into sondry partes.
Amonge the olde Romaynes was he, whiche at the election of greatte officers, diuidid or gaue money to the people, in the names of them whiche sued for the office, to thintent for to attayne it.
The day light vnder the fyrmament. whan we say, Sub dio aliquid fieri, it sygnifieth some thynge to be doone abroode, or out of the house.
Old writers vsed for dant, they giue.
A dyuorse, or separation of a mā and his wyfe. sometyme a departyng from any other thynge.
Pertayninge to daye, as Diurni libri, bokes conteynynge the actis done euery day. sometime a dayes hyre.
Worthy a diuine remēbrāce, Nowe they take Diuum, & diuam, for a man or woman saynct.

To gyue. Also to offre, or proffre. Vt tes dant sese, As thynges offre them selfes.Vergilius. Also to bryng. Magnam dabit ille ruinā arboribus, He shall brynge a great fall vnto trees. Also to say, Quamobrem has partes didicerim paucis da bo, For what cause I lerned that parte, I wyll telle the in fewe wordes. Also to obeye,Terentius to conforme. Da te mihi, Conforme the to my wylle. Also to committe or doo. O Aeschine, pol haud paternum istue dedisti, O Eschines, in good faith in this thou hast not done lyke a father.
To applye, to gyue or take hede, or to helpe.
I rēder me, or I am vāquished.
To commytte authoritie or power, or remyt a thinge to an other mans pleasure or lybertie. Suarum ominum rerū illi potestarē dederat, He gaue hym the rule of all that he had.
To gyue lybertie or power to do a thynge.
To putte into his hande pryuily, as they do to men of lawe, or priuy solyciters, or corrupt offycers.
To pay damages, or to make satisfaction.
To flatter, or speake to please.
To assigne or appoynte busynesse, or a thynge to be done.
To deceyue by fayre promyses, or pleasant demonstration.
To teache or gyue knowelege, or to informe, to aduyse.
Doctrine, whiche procedeth of the teacher. Disciplina, lernynge taken of the scholer.
Lerned, that is to say, knowynge a thynge without experience. Vide peritus.
A citie in Greece, whereby was a woode, in the whiche men thoughte that trees spake.
The daughter of Iupiter and Europa.
Was a drinke made of nine thinges, herbes, iuyse, water, wyne, salt, oyle, bread, hony, and pepper.
A certayn determination, whiche in sectes of philosophers euery oone had, without the whiche the secte fayled. sometyme they be called placita.
The heed, fete, or eyen to ake.
I am sory for thy mysfortune or trouble.
I am sorye on thy behalfe.
Any great vessel of wine, as a tūne, pipe, butre, or hoggisheed.
Great as a tunne. Doliaris heluo, a gorbelyed glutton.
A space of grounde contaynyng xii. furlonges.
To cutte or hewe with an axe or sythe.
The propre name of a man of Troy,Varro. that was very swifte of fote.
A scourge, hauynge a dagger, or other lyke thyng closed within it.Seruius. Liuius. It is also a certayne taklynge of shyppes. Also a lyttell sayle called a trynkette.
Griefe or paine of body or mynd, also sorowe.
That whiche makethe griefe or sorowe.
Euery crafty deceite to compasse a man, wherby he receiueth damage.
A solar or flatte keuerynge of a howse. it is somtyme taken for the house.
Pertainynge to housholde. sometyme it sygnifieth tame.
A pylar or other lyke thynge, that beareth vp an house.
A lord or maister, to whom other doo seruyce.
A lordeshyp or rule ouer other.
Was taken of olde wryters for dominus.
Apte to be tamed or broken.
The acte of tamynge or brekyng of any wylde beaste.
To make tame, sommetyme to vaynquyshe, as Domare hostes, to vaynquyshe ennemyes.
A tamer or breaker of that, whyche is wylde.
A howse, where suche thynges were kepte, that were gyuen to the goddes. It is sometyme taken for a gyft or rewarde.
A gyfte in money or grayn, giuen by emperours vnto the people. also to sowldiours aboue their wages.
He that is able to gyue.
He to whom any thynge is giuen. rewarded.
A reede or cane, whereof they made arowes.
Vatyll. sometyme as longe. Donec uiuo, as longe as I lyue.
An yle in the see Aegeum.
Names of countreys ioynynge to Athenes.
People in Grece nygh to Aetolia.
A Nimph of the see, and is interpretate bytternesse.
Panels, which horses do weare on their backes, whan they carie or drawe.
That whiche beareth or carieth any thinge on the backe.
A backe of man or beaste.
The name of a riuer in Phrigia.
A yoman of the gard, or other lyke, whiche for gardyng of his maysters person, beareth alway a iauelyn or byll.
Dowery, lande gyuen in maryage, to the husbande or wyfe, for cause of the mariage onely.
Indowmentes of the sowle, that is to say, vertues and good maners.
Indowmentes of the body, that is to say, beautie, strength, helth. &c.
That pertayneth to dowerie, as bona dotalia.
A poise or weyght, ponderynge .lx. where cornes, taken out of the myddes of the eare. Also a coyne of Athenes, signed with a bullocke.
Of Plinie be taken for old branches of vynes. also it is an herbe, which is otherwise called Pyretum, it bourneth and byteth the tongue, as welle the lease as the roote.
A precious stone, taken out of the heed of a dragon, whyle he lyueth.
Where in a comedy or interlude, dyuers personages be broughte in, some abydyng, some departynge.
A prouince in Asia the more.
A beaste lyke to a camell, but of a wonderfull swiftenes.
The place where men do rounne horses.
The name of a Romayne, of ryght noble lynage, and eloquence: but he was proude and ambicious.
The propre name of a man of Thessaly, frende of Nestor.
Siue Druidae, were in the olde tyme religious, or rather superstitious persones in Fraunce, whiche vsed arte magike.
Afterwarde Pelasgus, is nowe called Archadie.
He is in doubte, what he shulde do.
To be in doubte, or to tracte tyme.
Doubtfull, Dubius is he that hath two wayes, and woteth not whiche to take.
The act of a capteyn, or guyde. Also a duchy. also Ducatus, ti, a coyne callid a ducat.

To leade them that be wyllynge, to haue respecte to a thynge. some tyme it signifieth to allecte or styrre with some pleasaunt meane. also to reuolue: also to drawe, as a man draweth a sworde, also to gette. sometyme it signifieth doinge, as Ducere somnos, to slepe. Also to buylde or make vp. somtyme to tourne away. as Ducere uultus, to tourne awaye the visage. to delaye or prolonge. to go downe. Ego me duco ab arbore, I wente downe of the tree. Also to wedde, or do the act of mariage.
A poyse, contaynynge .ii. drammes and .ii scruples.
To fyghte within lystes, or in battayle.
Men in olde tyme called Bellona.
A citesens name of Rome, whiche Duelium, battayle. fyrst tryumphed for victorie on the see.
Of the auncient writers was vsed for dederis.
A marchepayn made with almondes and sugar.
The seruyce of a bondeman or slaue.
An ile in the see Maliake, or as some saye, Ionio.

Sometyme signifieth whan, or whiles, as, Dum dormis, fures domū intram, whyles thou slepest, theues entre in to the house. somtyme vntyll, somtyme as longe. Also it signifieth wherfore: also, so that. somtyme it doth but make vp a worde: as, Adesdū, paucis te uolo, Come hyther, I wolde a fewe thynges with the.
All kyndes of thornes or breres.
Knyghtes, or suche souldiours as had double alowaunce.
Double, or two.Cato de re rustie.
Some thinke to be the name of a ryuer, nere to whiche the gyantes made the towre Babel: Some woll it to be a fielde,Daniel. 3. as in Daniel.
The Spayniardes call a vessell, that they vse to wasshe and bayne them in.
The name of a ryuer nere to Valentia.
To indure, to sustaine or suffre.
A lorde, a prince, a ruler.
A citie in Cicile, whiche fyrst was called Epidānus.
In composition, signifieth yuell, difficile, or impossible.
A syckenes, whiche letteth a man that he can not pysse, called the strangurie.
The name of a story wryter, whiche was in that age, that Pygmalion reigned in the east parte.
Vnto that, in that maner of wyse.

A tree, which is blacke in colour, and is odoriferous, whanne it is bourned, it hath vertue to clense the eyen. This tree groweth in India, which beinge cutte, wareth as harde as stone. Sola India nigrum fert ebenum, India alone bryngeth forth blacke Ebenus. Virg. 2. Geor.
An yle, betwene the Iles Ophiusa and Pythiusa, the erthe of whyche yle serpentes can not abyde.
Yles in the see aboute Englande, where the people do lyue by whyte meate and fysshe.
The sonne of Iupyter and Pros •• pine.
To braste out, or bubble vp, as water dothe whan it rayneth.
An herbe, of some called walwort.
People of the countreye called Liege, or Luke, beyonde Brabant.
A fygure in speakynge, callyd digression, where a manne leaueth for the tyme the principall matter.
The chiefe citie of the royalme of Mede. There is a citie in Syria of the same name, sommetyme called Ephiphania, and maye be writen Egbatana.
An aduerbe demonstratiue, whiche sygnyfyeth, Lo, see, proprely where a thyng sodaynly happeneth. Ecce tibi, wylt thou see, take hede.
An assembly, a counsayle. Amonge christen authours, it signifieth the congregation of people in the faythe of Christe.
Lo he is here: lo she is here, lo these men be here, loo these women be here.
A lyttell fysshe, whyche retayneth a shyppe vnder saylle, that he canne not moue.
Bene Ilandes in the see Malyake.
The vttermooste shaale of a cheston nutte. It is also an Hedgehogge. Also a fyshe lyke to the same beast, also a vessell of tynne, wherein cuppes be wasshed. Also the name of a citie.
Thebans, soo callyd of Echyon, oone of the fyue, that holpe Cadruus to buylde Thebes.
A stone specked lyke a Serpent.
A sounde, whyche reboundeth to the noyse or voyce, that is made in a valay, or in great woddes.
A medycyne, whyche muste not be eaten or chewed: but beinge in the mouthe, suffred to styll downe into the stomacke by lyttell and lyttell.
A playne interpretation of the letter.
At what tyme, or lo whan.
A stonye, a dampe, a traunse, whan a man forgetteth hym selfe.
A fygure, whereby a syllable naturally shorte, is produced.
Where, in, ioyned with a vowell, is not sowned.
Whanne the nether lydde of the eye falleth, and canne not ioyne with the ouer lydde.
A Cytie beyonde the ryuer of Euphrates.
To commaunde, to ordeyne, to declare.
Ordinaunces or commaundementes of them, whiche be in great authoritie.

n: edo es edi esum uel tum

d: Is applied to a cull & grosse persone: and for as moche as Nasturtium, called Cressis, being eaten, dothe make the nose tynkell, and therby causeth the dulle spirites to wake, therfore by this proueth is ment, Plucke vp thy spirites: or, awake dullarde or luske.
All thynges that appertayne to be eaten.
To explane, to declare. Edissere fabulam hanc, Declare this fable.
To hewe or cutte cleane and smothe.
Esau was soo called, and the countrey where he reigned.
A hylle nere to Pangcum in the borders of Thessalye.
People of Thrace, nere to the see cooste.
Were women which slutred with a diuyne furoure, dydde celebrate the mysteryes of Bacchus.
A hyll, where the same people inhabyteth.
To bryng forth, also to drawe out,Virgilius. as, Hoc dicens, eduxit corpore telum, That sayenge, he drewe the weapon oute of his bodye. Sometyme to reyse vp.
To nouryshe or brynge vppe from chyldehoode.
Nourishyng or bryngyng vppe of chyldren.
Is what so euer is set on the table at diner & supper to be eatē, saue the breed.
Andromaches father, that reygned at Thebes in Cilicie.
To stuffe or fil a thīg.
To cut of by the arme pit.
To cary out or put out. sometyme to ouercome or subdue. also to cōmende: somtyme to holde vp, to set forth: somtyme to mynisshe or appayre.
To make ymages of wylde beastes.
A signe made to the l •• ely similitude of man or beast.Plaut.
To desyre or aske a thynge impo ••• nately.
To blowe away, or blow forth.
To blo, as a flour doth at the first commynge out.
To flowe or rounne out, as water dothe out of a fountayne.
M • nne wanton and delicate, or tender, enduryng no hardnesse.
She that hath lately brought forthe a chylde. Also a womanne paste teemynge. Terra effoeta, land: spent or worne with bearynge of moche grayne.
To powre out. somtyme it signifyeth to consume, to put out.
Discomfited, scattered, putte oute, or powred out.
To speake vnaduisedly, or folyshely, or hastily.
A towne in the hyther Spayn.
To relent or dissolue, as yse that thawith.
A citie in Sicile, whiche Aeneas buylded.
Necessitie or lacke of thynges necessary, pouertie.
To go forth, or go out.
To drawe out, as lycoure out of a place.
An Interiection of callynge. it signifieth howe. Eho dum ad me, Howe come hyther to me.
h: E ante H, & E ante I.

d: Sommetyme it exhorteth, sommetyme it blameth.
h: E ante H, & E ante I.

d: To cast out, or put out.
h: E ante H, & E ante I.
E ante H, & E ante I.
E ante H, & E ante I.
E ante H, & E ante I.
E ante H, & E ante I.

d: Of the same sort or cōdiciō.
h: E ante H, & E ante I.

d: Of the same estimatiō or state.
h: E ante H, & E ante I.

d: To slyppe or slyde. sometyme to escape.
A sawce vsed in the olde tyme.
Be called the prynces of Porsyanes, of Elam the sonne of Sem, as Iosephus sayth.
A citie in the countrey of Lucania.
That whiche is in englishe called ambre, wherof beades be made, It is also taken for a mettalle, parte golde, parte syluer. Plin.
Tis, elegaunte, fresshe, gorgyous, cleane, polyte.
Elegancy, gorgiousnes, clennes, beautie in wordes.
A writer of lamentable versis, or balades.
People in Grece in the countrey some tyme called Peloponessus, nowe Morea.
The fyrste or pryncipall mattier, wherof al thinges do take their beginning: whiche be foure in numbre, fyre, ayre, water, and erthe. Also the letters, wherof sillables be made, are called elementa.

An argument, reprouynge subtilly an other argument. It is also a table in a boke, to shew the places by letter or other wise. It is moreouer a great perle, or other precious stone, whiche women were wont to hange at their cares.
A beast, callyd an olyphaunt. It is sometyme taken for yuory. sometyme a syckenes callyd lepry.
Be called these peynters, whiche peynt with yuorie.
A kynde of leprie, wherin the flesshe dothe swelle, and is full of spottes.
Amonge the olde Romaynes were bokes, wherin their lawes were written, whiche concerned the nobilitie.
A ryuer, whiche watereth a greatte parte of Media.
To lyfte vp. somtyme to take away, to mynyshe, to extenuate.
A Cytie in the prouynce of Africa, not farre from Athenes.
The name of a man, and is interpretate, free, gentyll.
Sorowes in the fieldes, to conueye water.
To brynge out, to drawe out, to prouoke.
He that tourneth thynges oute of order.
To hytte agaynste a thynge, to breake, to presse out, to exclude, to strangle, to kylle.
To putte or cast forth from a place ferre of.
One of the names of Dido.
The matche, whiche is in a lāpe, and standeth in oyle.
A testification or witnesse in wordes, of praise or dispraise, of honoure or reproche.
A propre fourme of wordes and sentences.
To remoue fer of, to make longe, to deferre.
To speke, ꝓprely it is, whā I set a thynge forth in speking, that the herers may vnderstād it, as I conceyue it.
Among the Lacedemonians was as moche to saye, as commune mynysters or seruauntes, as sergeauntes, or suche as in London they do call yomen.
A companion of Vlysses, whiche with other, Circe tourned into an bogge.
He that is sycke of the drynke of yesterday. Also a louer of trifles.
To shyne or make bryghte outewarde.
To mocke or deceyue, Also to leaue playenge.
He that hath feble loines, and can not stande vpright.
To lyue in glotony, or to spend superfluousely.
To powre out of one vessell into an other.
Ordure or fyithe caused of aboundance of water, or other lycour.
A place where poetes dyd suppose the sowles of good men to dwell.

To infraunchyse or make free, or sette at lybertie. somme time it is vsed in the cōtrary sence, to bynd or make bonde. It is most cōmonly where a man dispossesseth him selfe, and doth alienate his lande to an other.
To dwelle out of a place.
He that wandreth longe, and at the laste retourneth home: a lurker.
To take awaye scurfe aboute the brymmes of woundes or soores.
To gelde, or to take away the courage of a man, or to abuse a manne chylde in lechery.
A citie that is nowe called Antioch.
A parte of the realme of Macedonia.
A notable citie of Palestine, which nowe is called Nicopolis.
He or she that is redye to bye any thynge.
Pictures made of wod, stone, or mettal, of one colour, set in wodde stone or mettall of an other coloure: as we see in chesse bourdes or tables, callid coū ters: it is moche vsed in Italy.
Signifieth the childe conceyued before it receiueth perfecte shappe of a man or woman.
To aske in fourme of beggynge.
To issue or come oute of the place where a thinge is drowned.
Old worne souldiours, whiche were pardoned of warres, & not withstandynge had pencyons, which were called Emerita stipendia.
To shewe or excel aboue all other, to be higher than other.
A sluse, or place to lette water out of a ponde or ryuer.

Sommetyme it signyfieth hym, whiche is sent before in battayle to espie, or to skyrmyshe. sometyme a seruant, whiche is alway at, hand, redy to be sent forth. Also it signifieth suche a persone, whyche is ordeyned of him that is in any great office or authoritie, to aduaunce his bribery. Also it sygnifyeth a horse stalyon, whiche serueth to gette coltes.
To sende forth, to publyshe, to manumise.
A hyll, whiche aboute the border of Indie, is diuided into two bowghtes.
The name of a Phylosopher, which supposed all thynges to haue theyr beinge of amitie, and variance.
An expresse signification of that, whiche is intended.
The making of a thynge better than it was, whan it was receyued or letten, as lande.
He that taketh a thynge, and promyseth or couenaunteth to make it better than he receyued it.
Is graffyng betwene the bark and the wodde.
Paper, wherin marchantes or grossers do putte their wares.
A place wherin is kept a marte or fayre.
That whiche is or maye be boughte.
An instrument, wherwith the shuffe of a candell is taken away, a shuffer.
To snuffe a candelle. Also to make cleane a mans nose. somtyme it signifyeth to dispoyle a man of money, proprely by crafte.
Of a cleane and sure iudgemente.
A demōstration, whan a thing is so discryued, that it seemeth to the reder or herer, that he beholdeth it, as it were in doinge.
An innouation or renewynge. It was amonge Iewes the feaste of dedication of their temple.
Vernyshe, enamyll, or other pycture, wrought with fyre.
A handell of a thyng. somtime a dagger, somtyme that part of an ore, that the water man holdeth. It is vsurped for a boke in so lyttell a volume, that a man maye alway carye it with hym.
A beaste bredde in the oriente, as great as a bull.
The cyrkle or course of all doctrines.
That lernynge whiche comprehendeth all lyberall sciences & studies.
A consuminate perfection, whiche Aristotle dyd put besides the foure elementes.
Whan men wente oute of the campe vnto battayle.
A mantell suche as Irishe men and women do nowe weare.
The name of a manne, whiche founde the course of the mone. wherfore the poetes fayned, that the moone loued hym, and descended downe to kysse hym, whyles he slepte.
A citie in Iudea, from whens the precious balme cometh.
Forsothe. sometyme it is expletine, and dothe but fylle vp a sentence, to make it sounde well. sometyme it is a copulatiue: Sed enim, but forasmoche.
A ryuer of Thessaly, nere to whiche the battayle was fought betwene Cesar and Pompey.
To indeuour, to inforce to do a thynge.

o: Enitor, teris, enixus sum, eniti, idem quod eniteo.
n: enitor teris enixus sum eniti idem quod eniteo

d: A cytie of Sycile, sytuate in a hyghe place.
The name of an auncient poete.
A mans name in holy scripture.
To cutte away the knottes, or to vnknytte.
To take out the kernell of a nutte. It is also to declare or make playne a sentence.
To growe or sprynge of a thynge.
The name of a valiant capitayne of the Thebans.
The sonne of Iupiter that builded Memphis in Aegipte.
The age wherin oone entreth into the state of a man .xv. or .xvi. yeres.
He that is of that age.
A boke, wherin is written that, which is done daily, or a boke of reckning.
The harneis of a horse or mule.
Greate officers amonge the Lacedemonians, by whome the kynges power was restrayned.
A towne of Achaie, whiche nowe is called Corinthus.
The ladder that gothe vp to the toppe castell.
The name of an excellent phylosopher of Syracuse.
Versis in cōmēdacion of a deed man, a gay laude.
The name of a stoik philosopher.
The name of hym, which dyd put the principal goodnes in voluptuositie.
A cytie in Sycile, but the Romaynes after they had subdued it, wolde haue it called Dyrrachium.
A small thynge in the innermost parte of the tunge, lyke a littell tunge.
He that wryteth verses, called Epigrammata.
He that hath a croked nose.
A cōclusion in writing or speking.
A wheale or pushe, whiche ryseth on the skynne by nyght.
A manyfestation. It is also a solemne feaste in the churche.
A byshoppes palays or house, or a place to espie out of.
A byshoppe, sometyme an espie. sometyme a clerke of the markette.
A letter sent from one to an other.
A spowte sendynge forth water from a cundite.
A scripture written on a graue or sepulchre.
A songe beinge songe atte a weddynge, or verses made in the praise of them that are maried.
A medicine layde to the regyon of the harte or lyuer, to coole it.

An addition, proprelye applyed to a thyng for some notable qualitie, which it sygnifieth, as Seuū mare, The rough see. Garrula pica, The chatterynge pie. Crudelis Nero, The cruel Nero. Campi florigeri, The flouryshynge fieldes.
A garment worne vpon a gowne.
A foote of foure sillables, of whiche one differeth euer from the other thre.

A kynde of verse, or songe, which contayneth thynges concernyng as well god as manne. Also whiche hath the fyrst verse lengar than the seconde, as, Beatus ille, qui procul negoriis Vt prisca gens mortalium.

A greate feaste, whervnto all the people assembled, whiche amonge the olde Romayns was made either to the honour of some of their goddes, or at the burieng of some notable personage. It may be now taken for a churche feest, or feest of a brotherheed,Cicero & L. Planco • or dyner made at a buriall or interment. It hath bene sometyme vsed for a uate bankette.
Bilongynge to a feaste or banket, as Epularis sermo, cōmunication mete for a feaste or bankette.
To eate at feastes or bankettes.
Apt to be eaten at a feest or bankette.
Fleshe that groweth on the gūmes about a mans tethe.
Men boden to a great feaste, or they which come vnboden, to eate the reuercion. Amonge the gentils they were called by the pristes, to eate that whiche was lefte of the sacrifice.
A horseman, contrary to a fote man. sometime it is taken for a knight. But I suppose, that amonge the Romaynes, Equites, were taken for theym, whome we calle gentylmen.
Pertaynynge to eques, as, Equestris ordo, the state or degree of gentylmen. Equestres copiae, the numbre or company of horsemen.
The places assigned to gentilmen, where they satte to beholde any solempne syghtes or playes.
The hyre of a stallyon to season a mare.
Whan a mare desyreth to be seasoned.
Runnynge with horses: a playe dedicate to Mars.
Able to be ridē, also a place in whiche horses might easily walke.
An hoste of horsemen. also the acte of ridynge. sometyme the state or order of gentylmen.
The esquirie or companye of the stable.
The propre name of a manne, and surname of a familye in Rome.
A horsecolt. Also a maner of turment made of bournynge plates, lyke to a horse, wherin men were tourmented.
Asi, ere, to scrape of, or out of a thynge.
The name of a famous physytion.
The name of one of the Musts.
Of householde to be deuided or parted amonge dyuers heires.
A wonderfull greatte wodde in Germany.
One of the names of Iupiter.
One of the ryuers of Hell.
People in Arabia, which go naked.
A discontynuance of action, doone throughe absence or neglygence of the parties.
For the profyte of the publyke weale.
Towarde. Erga festum natalis Christi, Agayne Christmasse.
A house, where men were compelled to worke on stone or mettall. Nowe is it taken for a prysone, and sometyme for the prisoners.
The gayler or keper of the prysone.
A gayler. sometyme it signifieth a labourer.
The propre name of a man.
Was a tyranne, whiche Hercules subdued and slewe.

Therfore. somtyme it is spoken dysdaynously. Fac ergo quod libet, Than doo as the lyste. sometyme exhortynge. Ergo age, go to. sometyme it signifyeth bycause, Illius ergo, for his sake. Virtutis ergo, bycause of vertue.
An engyne to drawe vp thynges of great poise or weight, callid a crane.
A mā possessed with an yl spirite
An herbe growynge in woddes, and is lyke to maioram.
The fyrste kynge of Athenes, whiche inuented a chariotte.
A ryuer in Italy, now called Po.
The name of oone of the furyes of helle.
The wyfe of Amphiaraus, & systar of Adrastus, whiche betrayed hir husbande for a bracelette at the siege of Thebes.
Thou haste taken my money from me. Eripuisti me a periculo, Thou haste delyuered me frome perylle.
Thou haste taken my boke from me. sommetyme to make haste.
An herbe growynge in Aegypte, and may be interpretate contention.
A fowle, the greattest that fleeth̄, and ouercometh and eateth the Egle.
That crepeth here & there, as, Vitis erratica, a crepyng vine, that shoteth out in dyuers places.
Errour, properly where falsehode 〈◊〉 affirmed or taken for trouth▪ or trouth for falsehode.
But, bescere, to be ashamed, or to blusshe.
An herbe called Rokat. also a worme called the canker worme, whiche cōmonly is vpon • olewortes.
To belke or broake wynde out of the stomacke.
To throwe out, or cary awaye rubbell, as morter, stones, and other lyke thynges of olde buyldynge decayed, or pulled downe.
To teache any arte or science.
An vnkindly moisture, wherby corne growynge is putrified.
A mountayn in Archady, where Hercules ouercame a bore, that destroyed the fieldes. There are also a wodde and a ryuer of the same name.
An Ile, the countraye of Gerion, where the ayre is so benigne, that men well nere are there immortall.
An herbe called redde betes, as I do suppose.
Is called the redde see, this see is betwene the Indie & Aethiope occean.
The name of a mountayn in Cicile, and of a citie theron buylded, wherin was edified a temple to Venus, wherof of Venus is called Erycina.

o: Quid geminas Erycina meos sine sine dolores?
n: quid geminas erycina meos sine sine dolores
d: O Venus, why doest thou continually double my sorowes?
All maner of meate, as welle for men, as beastes.
A table, wherat men do eate meate.
Certayn religious men of the Iewes.
A people, whiche • oo eate theyr frende • ; whan they be deed, and drynke in the sculles of their heedes.

And, as well, Te admirantur & ciues & hospites, As well thy countrey men as straungers do wonder at the. sometyme it signifieth but, by an interrogation, sometyme, That is to saye, Annos natus 〈◊〉 sexaginta, & senex, Nowe thre score yeres olde, that is to say an olde man.
Wyndes which do cōmonly blowe in sommer, about the canicular dayes.
The name of an yle in the see called mare ligusticum, whiche is by Ieane.
The name of a certayne vessell.
The sunne of Oedipus and Iocasia his mother.
The myddell brydge of the nose.
He which with voyce, gesture, and countenance expresseth the maners of menne.
True sayenge, or true exposytion, or reason.
An imytation of other mennes maners.
Paynters, whiche in pyctures doo lyuely sette out the maners and affections of men.
To escape, to passe with daunger, to appere, to clymme, to delyuer, to be, to come to.

Mars daughter, of Thebes, the wyfe of Aesopu • : and the wyfe of Capanei was soo called, whyche louyd her husbande so feruētly, that whan she harde he was take at Thebes, she fell nere deed in a swowne, and after whan his funerall was celebrate, she l • pte into the fyre.
To putte or sette out of the doores.
An exclamation to the praise of Bacchus, and is as moche to saye, as Bone puer, O good chylde.

The propre name of Carmentis sonne, and is interpretate a good man: he lefte his countrey Archadia, and came into Italy, and entryng into the mouth of Cyber, and expulsyng the inhabitantes, rested in the hylle Palatine, where he beganne to buylde the towne Palanteum.
An interiection of reioycynge. Euax iurgio uxorem tandem abegi, Heida, I haue yet at the laste dryuen my wyfe away with chydynge.
An yle in the greke see, & the name of a citie situate in the same.
The name of a storie writer, and is interpretate prudente.
A citie of Phrigia, where growe great plentie of very fayre grapes.
Good grace, a renderynge of thanke. It is nowe taken for the sacramēt of the aultar.
The name of a famous Geometrycian.
Euexi, euehere, to cary out. somtyme it sygnifyeth to extoll or lyfte vp.
The name of an old story writer
A ryuer descendyng from Thrace, and deuydynge Calydonie.
Happe. somtyme it is taken for the ende▪ or conclusion of a thynge.
To waraunt al that, whiche shall happen.
He that hath goodes of the testatour with condicion, that if he performe not his laste wyll, or do distourbe it, he shal lese all that he hath.
By and by, at an instant.
A countrey in the orient, aboute the whiche the ryuer Phison, whiche we calle Ganges, that commeth out of Paradyse, dothe rounne.
Of womanly or chyldyshe condicions. also he that lacketh his genitours.
To take away a mannes membres of generation.
To bowel or drawe out the guttes of any thinge.
To flee, to eschew, or beware.
A worde well spoken, a praise, a benediction.
The sonne of Admetus, kynge of Thessaly, gotten on Alcesta his wyfe.
A mās name of Athenes, whom Suidas writeth to be the sonne of Museus the poete.
A iuste constitution or ordynance of lawes.
To call out, to call forthe, or calle away. Euocare testes, to brynge forth wytnesse.
Souldyours, whiche for some necessitie be sodaynely called out of the fieldes vnto battayle.
A towne in Locris, whiche somme call Eupalion, and some Eupolyon.
A poetis name of Calcidonye, whom Gallus did translate.
One of the ryuers, that comme out of Paradyse, whiche passeth through the citie of Babylon.
The propre name of a woman.
The daughter of kynge Minois, whiche brought forth to Neptune, Orion. ther was an other of that name, the daughter of Proetus, kyng of Argiue.
The name of one of the princis of Peloponnese. Virgil feineth a Troyane to be so callyd.
The name of an excellente poete amonge the Grekes.
A small cundyte rysynge of a great height. Also a diche made to inclose places to play in, in the stede of hedges. some do take it for a small ponde or stewe.
An arme of the see, or a narrowe passage betwene two places.
That parte of the worlde, whyche we do inhabyte, so named and called of Europa, the daughter of Agenor, kynge of Phenice.
A ryuer that rounneth before the towne of Lacedemona.
Was the wyfe of Leutichis, kynge of Spartans.
The kyng of Phlegia, whiche distroyd Thebes, before Cadmꝰ buildid it.
One of the sonnes of Hercules that reigned in the yle Cous.
Quietenesse, suertie of mynde, or hartis ease.

o: Ex fide, fama. Cic. ad Atticum, Summa erit haec, statues, ut ex fide fama, re que mea uidebitur,
n: ex fide fama cic ad atticum summa erit haec statues ut ex fide fama re que mea uidebitur
d: This shall be the hoole effecte, that thou doo, as it shall seeme to be for myne honestie, accordynge to the trust that I putte in the, and for my profyte.

o: Ex dignitate tua, et ex repub. facis,
n: ex dignitate tua et ex repub facis
d: Thou doest accordynge to thyne auctoritie, and for the weale of thy countrey.
A demaunder of money. some englyshe it a Comtroller.
To buylde perfectely. also to dryue out of the house.
To mounte or lyfte vp, some tyme to prayse very moche.
A swarme of bees, Also the nedyll or tounge in balaunces and beames. Sommetyme it sygnyfyeth a iuste examynacyon.
To drawe oyle cleane from the mother.
To drawe oute cleane, to emptye, sommetyme to suffre, to make. Non potest hic sine tu • opera exāclari clauꝰ, Pac. This nayle can not be made without thy helpe.
I do it with my good wyll, or as my mynde gyueth me.
Accordynge to myn appetyte, or as I wolde desyre it.
I fauour hym with all my harte.

To kyll,Plaut. somtyme to make aferde. Prius quam intus redii exauimatus fui, Or euer I came in agayn, I was made aferde.Q. Cut • iꝰ. Multos exanimauii rigor insolitus niuis, The vnaccustomed chyllyng of the snowe depriued many of their lyues.

n: exanimus ma mum amp exanimis exanime

d: Made aferde, or troubled in mynde: somtime it signifyeth deed.
A wheale or a pusshe in a mannes skynne.
To make tame, proprelye to breake the tethe of wylde beastes.
To vnarme, or to take harneysse from a man.
To take away the taklyng from a shyppe.
To make the accyon faynte or feble.
To eare well, also to write.
To polyshe, or make playn, as carpentars doo after that they haue hewed.
To make sharpe, Also to make very angrye.
Of the hole. Haeredem fecit ex asse, He made him heire of all the hole.
To putte out of wages, somtime to disgrade a knight, or other like.
Souldiours or seruantes putte out of wages, or dismissed of their seruice.
Deposed, or put out of office.

o: Ego hunc communem meum, at que nostrum omnium hostem exbalistabo lepidè,
n: ego hunc communem meum at que nostrum omnium hostem exbalistabo lepide
d: I wolie feately deceyue this min enmy, and al ours in commune.
To charme. sommetyme to shutte out.
To chaufe, or make angry, or to make very hote.
To rente or cutte in pieces.
To departe or go forthe, to passe or excede.
He that wryteth faste that whiche other men do speake.
To beate out the braynes of any thynge.
A serpent, of whom the heed being cutte of, thre came vp for it. It was also called Hydra.
To shite. proprely it is to trye out the yll from the good.
To gather here and there the chiefe of any thynge.
The sackynge of a towne or citie, or the vtter destruction therof.
To fall out of a thynge.
To cutte out of a thynge.
To moue vehemently, or to call out, to waken.
To excepte, to take or receyue, to trye or inserche, to separate, to take by crafte, to gather, to hyde, to succede, to resyst without any busynesse.
To wryte in cyfer, or other compendiouse fourme.
To crop, to teare, or to beate.
To crye oute, to calle for al • wde.
To shytte out, to deliuer, to hatche egges, to make to appiere.
To plucke of the skynne or hyde of a beaste.
A foole, or a man hartles.
Thinges of dygestion expulsed moyste or drie, vrine, or siege.
To grow oute, or to growe moche.
The refuse or of fall of any thing.
Watche, as well by daye as by nyghte.
So contrarye the one to the other, that they may neuer agree.
To watche, as they whiche in battaylle, or in the garde of a pryncis personne doo.
To beate or stryke out, sometyme to fynde out with study. V • primum silicis, scintillam excudit Achates, Verg • As soone as Achales had stryken fyre of the flynte. Also to hatche.
To put out of court▪ Apollonium ideo excuriauit, quia nihil habebat, Ve ••• ▪ Therfore dyd he put Apolonius out of the courte, bycause he had nothyng.
To be pacified,C • s •• ▪ to be assuagid of ire
A digression in speakynge, a skyrmyshe in warres.
A rengyng syue. also a bulter.
By an order, of a purpose.
To eate, as a worme or soore dothe, to eate vp.
A parlour, or other lyke place.
A forme of spekyng, where the poete onely speaketh.
An example to folowe, eschewe, or beware.
A sample, wherby we attempt to make a thynge lyke to it. somtyme the one is vsed for the other. oftentymes they both do signifye an example, where one thynge is compared with an other.
That whiche may be taken away, or taken out.

To go out, to exchewe, to braste oute. In memoriam exire, to be in remembraunce. Exit in fabellam, It is made a fable. Exit de potestate, He is not able to gouerne hym selfe: he is in warde, or vnder a gardayne.
To make a hole in a thing.
Funeralles, the whiche are doone in the buriall of any person.
To do or execute. somtime to declare or expresse.

To exercyse. sometyme to driue out of the house, to sette on warke, to vse. Exercere discordias, et simultates, To haue variance or contencion. also to get or wynne. Exercere sumptus, To gette theyr expenses. Exercere tellurem, to tylle welle the grounde.
An hoost of 〈◊〉 of wa • te.
To go forth, to drawe out, as a man wyll drawe out a sworde. Fulgentē que exerit ensem, And he drewe oute his bryght sworde. Also to lyfte vp.
To drawe oute cleane, to make empty.
To plucke vp herbes or wedes.
To pros • re, to set abrode, for all men to beholde.
To putte to busynesse, or trouble.
To feare horryblye, or with tremblynge.
To whistyll or hisse a manne out of the place. Exifilare, idem.
To expell or shutt out. also to require, to inquyre, to do.
Expelled, demanded, perfectly done, or perfourmed.
To goo out hastilye, or to leape out.
I am acquite or discharged of the offence or trespas.
I am clerely discharged of all paymentes.
To emptye, to brynge to nowghte.
Vnloked for, whiche no manne hooped.
To trowe or suppose, to decerne or iudge.
To be, to appere, to be sette vp, or aduanced.
Deadely, or that causeth dethe, or myschiefe.
To detayne battayle in the triall of ryght.
He that lyueth without loue, or oute of loue.
A songe at the ende of a comedy or interlude. also the ende of a matter.
To leaue growynge. sometyme to growe mightily.
He that is passed growynge. also olde, or out of vse, it signifieth also a manne childe abused agaynst nature.
To vnbynd, to pay al clerely, to recompence or gyue in rewarde, to delyuer. Suspitione exoluere, to deliuer frō suspicion. Exoluere religione, to discharge from vowe or conscience.
He that hath his eien put out.
A garmente without sleues, a taberde or chymere, or suche as hermytes do weare, or mūkes whan they do ride.
He that dwelleth in the subbarbes of a towne or citie.
A crafty forme of desyryng or askynge a thynge.
To go out of the track or carte lose, or to go out of the right way.
To be borne, to appere out, to ryse, as the sunne dothe, to inuade.
To garnyshe or make faire, to apparayle rychely, to ordeyne. Somme tyme to make foule, or out of apparayle.
To induce or optayne by desyre, to desyre hartily.
To bone, or plucke out boones. Also to pulle oute the strynge of a lamprey.
A stranger, that is come out of another countrey, and dwelleth here.
To make nakyd to the pappes.
To come abrode, or into an open place.

To tarye or abyde, to obserue or take hede. Expecto quid uelis, I marke what thou wylt saye: or elles I desyre to knowe what thou woldest. Also to hope. Expectate uenis, Thou comest euen as I wolde haue the.
To put out of the breste or stomacke.
He that hathe nothynge of his owne.
To delyuer, to spede, to carye out. Expedire manus, to holde vp the handes. Expedit, signifyeth also, It is expedient or necessary. it is come to passe.
To ponder or weye, to examyne straytely, to paye truely, to spende moneye.
To spend or lay out money.
To wake a man out of his slepe.
To attempte, or assaye, or proue.
Without any parte, lackyng experience. Expers doloris, withoute peyne.
Neuer dyenge. Expers lucis, without lyght.
To desyre moche, or coueyte, to happen, to wylle. sommetyme to take, to passe ouer.
To robbe, polle, or take by extorcion, or deceyte, to spoyle.
To pacyfie god with satisfaction or prayer, whan we thynke that he is displeasyd.
To seke for fysshe, to fishe out, or serche priuilye, to gette or wynne. Tandem nescio quid ab eo expiscatur, Fynally I can not telle what he wynneth or getteth by hym.
To fylle, fulfylle. also to sacyate, to comforte.
To extende. Also so to vnfolde,Ouidius, to declare. Explicat ensem, He draweth out his sword. Explicat & caenas unica mensa duas, Martialis. He maketh two suppers at one table.
To dryue oute with noise or rebukes, or clappynge of handes.
To bewayle with exclamation, to serch out diligently, to proue with serchynge, to be aduysed, to drye or exhauste.
To expowne or declare, to set or brynge a thyng out of that, wherin it is. sometyme to caste out a thynge, to thintent that it may perishe. Also to spend, to sette forthe.
An exposytion or declaration, of anye thynge diffyculte or harde to be vnderstande.
Chyldern cast out, to be perished.
To complayne, to make a quarell. also to wyl. Expostulare iniuriam, To complayne of wronge or displeasure, to hym that dothe wronge.
He that cōplayneth of wrong done by his frende.
To presse or wring out, to expresse or declare playnely.
To imbraide or twyte. also to lay in reproche.
To promyse or vndertake for an other.
He that promiseth, or is suretie for an other.
To wynne by assault or force.
To meue a thyng with moche thrustynge, or to put awaye.
A putter awaye, man or womanne.
To be cancelled or put out, or rased. it is also spoken of iuges, whan they be put out of cōmission. It is also to quyte, as, Munus munere expungitur, One good tourne is quyte with an other.
Were souldiours discharged, or put out of wages.
To shrede or loppe a tree, to vnderstande perfytely.
A mountayne in Rome, where watche was kepte.
To do thinges extremly or rigorously: as it were that one sued another vpon an oblygation sealyd.
The inwarde: as the harte, the lyuer, the lunges or lightes, and the splene.
Sodaynly, without study, or for the tyme.
An oration or matter spoken or wrytten without studye.
To perce through. Also to enserche curiously.
To dryue out, or pulle downe.
Whyche is not of that countrey, a straunger.
To beate out. also to whette or grynde.
To put out, proprely as fyre, whiche may be efteloones kendlyd: sometyme it signifieth to flee, or destroye: sometyme to make a distynction or dyuersitie betwene thynges.
Sothesayers by lookynge in the inwardes of beastes.
To be, to remayne, to be apparant.
To fynde oute the trouthe by tourmentes, to take awaye by force, or plucke away.
Is he that is made to voyde, or is dryuen out of his countrey: also a vagabūd.
Whan we speake of thynges, whiche are very true, and nat to be douted, as it were spoken of goddis own mouthe.
He that is not of the same house or kynredde.
Is spoken, where a man wold signifie a thing to be laste, & after all other.
To towche with the fynger toppes, is spoken, where is sygnified, that a manne hath vnneth touched or felte a thynge.
Out of arowe shotte, out of gunne shotte, signifieth out of daunger, or in safegarde.
Sometyme it signifyeth the begynnynge, sommetyme the ende, somme tyme the warste.
To delyuer, to shake of any thynge that letteth.
To ordeyne, to buylde or sette vppe.
To fynde oute with moche labour.
To put away, or to put oute or from a thynge by vyolence.
To be banysshed, to lyue in exyle.
To reioyce excedyngely, to bragge, to leape oute.
To putte of, to dispoyle, or vnclothe.
Clothynge. Also hydes or skynnes of beastes. Exuuiae serpentis, an Adders skynne.
The beane shall be knockyd on me, sygnyfyeth the peine or blame shal light on me.
The refuse or offall of beanes.
Almoost euerye craftes manne that warkethe with the hande. Faber lignarius, a carpenter: Faber ferrarius, a smith. Auri faber, a goldesmythe.
The propre name of a man.
In the ancient tyme was taken for a maynteyner.
The name of a noble Romayne.
A warkehouse, or forge, sometyme the frame or warke.

A noble Romayne, who beinge wonderful pore, not withstandyng refused a great some of money, sent to him by king Pirrhus, towchynge with his handes all his membres, and saying vnto the kynges messangers: As longe as he mought rule all that, whiche he touched, he coulde lacke nothynge.

n: fabrico caui are amp fabricor cari

d: To go aboute to doo a thynge▪ somme tyme to go awaye. Facesse hinc, Get the hens. Facessit ubi negotium, he putteth the to busynesse.
Mery wordes or deedes withoute dishonestie.
A face, sometyme the proporcion of all the body.
Lyghtly, or easily, withoute lette or doubte.
Lighte, easye, good to be entreated.
An acte or dede. sommetyme an ylle dede.

To doo, to be occupied, to make. Facio plurimi, I make moch of. Floccifacio, I sette not a strawe by it. Facere uerba, to speake. Facere lucrum, to wynne. Facere sumptum, to bestowe coste. Facere iter, to go or ryde. Facere terrorem, to put in feare. Facere copiam, to gyue leaue. Facere iacturam, damnum, naufragium, to lose, to take harme, to go to wrecke. Facere, is also to sacrifyce, to profyte. Faciam ut te plarimum amem, I woll loue the moche. Fac te esse qui sum, ymagin that thou were as I am. Facere conuicium, to rebuke, or putte to rebuke. Facere nomina, to gette dettours, as by lendyng: as they do nowe by exchaunge, and in shyftes, proprely called vsury: and in bargaynes of corne, cattell, and other lyke, or in letting of landes.
A diuisyon of people in sondry opynions. also an acte.
Done and brought to good passe.
Power to do or speake. some tyme rychesse. also facultie.
Eloquence, or sweete and pleasant speche.
Wyne that drynketh of the lyes.
Grapes, whereof commethe wyne, hauynge moche lyes.
Lyes, dregges, or groundes of any kynde of lycour.
He that fyghteth with a byll.
Hooked, also any thynge, wheron be hookes or other lyke thynge.
Wherby legacies were defalcate or cutte of, where the fourthe part of the goodis were not assignid to the heires.
He that beareth a byll or booke.
To cut with a byll or hooke.
A countrey in Campania, now in the royalme of Naples, wherin grewe the beste wynes of Italy, callyd falernum.
People in Italye. Also a kynde of puddynges.
To deceyue, also to be hydde.
To forge dedes, writinges, or seales.
A tellar of newes or tydynges, or a spreder of fame.
A householde, a family, or kynred.
Were places of buryall for men and their seruantes.
Famous, as well in good, as in ylle.

Madde. In the olde tyme before that Christe expelled the dyuel, whan that dyuelles were honoured in ydols, certaine persones, aswell men as women, were possessed with dyuels, which lad them, where they lysted, agaynste their propre wylles, and caused them to speke wonderful thinges, some also sodaynely, and often tymes telle what shoulde happen: wherfore they were thought to be inspired with goddis: those persons were called Fanatici. Some tyme Fanaticus, is taken for the keper of the Temple or chappell, where the deuyll gaue answeres.
People in the northe partes of the worlde, whose eares be so great, that with them they keuer all their bodies.
A Temple, where the dyuell gaue answeres out of an ydoll.
Sometyme sygnyfyeth all maner of corne. All be it among auncient phisytions it is taken for wheat meale.
Amonge the olde Romaines were the ceremonies of matrimonie.
To stuffe. Also to franke or fede, to be farre, to cramme.
A myxture of sondrye kyndes of grayne and corne. Sometyme it is taken for a myxture of thynges good and badde.

o: Farrinus, na, num, & farrinaceus, a, um,
n: farrinus na num amp farrinaceus a um

d: A place where wheate or meale is kepte.
Stuffynge, or that wherewith any foule is crammed or franked.
The crafte or maner of stuffynge or crammynge.
A swathell or swathynge bande, or other lyke thynge. sometyme any gyrdell.
A grype, or thyng bounden togither. It is also a nosegay, or any thynge knytte togyther, whiche maye be borne in a mannes hande.
To transforme by inchauntment, or to bewytche.
An inchauntmente to transfourme or disfygure any thynge. whiche so inchanted, is of the cōmune people called, taken, or forspoken, or forlooked.
Is a burdeyn or knytche of wodde, or any other thyng. Also Fascis sagittarum is taken for a sheffe of arrowes.
Roddes bounden togyther, and an axe in the myddell, whiche were borne before the chiefe offycers of Rome, in declarynge their authoritie, whereof some had syxe, and some mo.
Were certayne days, wherin the offycer of Rome, called Praetor, mowghte speake onely these three wordes, Do, dico, addico. It maye be nowe vsed for holy dayes.

Were certayne bokes, wherin were conteyned certayne ceremonies and causes of sondrye thynges amonge the Romaynes, concerninge their feastes and solemnities, whyche were longe kepte from the knowlege of the common people, vntyll they at the laste were deuulgate by one Caius Flauius.
To contemne with disdayne, to abhorre or haue in abomination.
Hated, proprely where one abhorreth the sight or presence of any thing.
To make or rayse vp in heyght.
An altitude, or the top or height of any thynge. Sometyme it signifieth the state of a persone in any dignitie, somtyme the ende of a thynge.
Is spoken whan a man wyll signifye a matter or thynge to be fynysshed and brought to a poynt.
Pertaynynge to destenye, fatall. somtyme mortall.
To gape wyde, as the erthe dothe in a great drythe.
A reder or teller of destenyes, or a southsayer.
A brynger of deth or pestylence.
To make wery, to trouble moche, to stryke, to stere or prouoke, to restrayne or lette.
The ordinance and disposition of almyghty god. Desteny, goddis prouidence. somtyme deth.
An ydiote, that lacketh naturall knowlege.
One of the wyndes, called the southwest wynde.
A shepeherde, whiche was the nourisher of Romulus and Remus.
A torche, a candell, or other lyke thynge, whiche brennynge gyueth lyght.
To be sycke in a feuer.
He that hath often the Feuer.
To pourge sowles by sacrifyce or prayer.
Sacrifices and ceremonies for purgynge of sowles.
In the Sabines tounge is callyd purgynge or clensynge.

Was a certayne offycer of armes, whiche denounced warre or peace, where as was hostilitie or cause of battayle: whiche may nowe be taken for an ambassadour, sent for suche a purpose, or for an Heralde.
The gaulle. sometyme it is taken for griefe of the mynde.
A Catte: sommetyme it sygnifyeth a weasyll.
The inner and backe parte of the thygh.
The thygh. some englysshe it the hamme.
The propre name of a story wryter, whiche flourished in the later dayes of Tyberius Cesar.
A wyndowe, sometyme an entrie into a thynge.

o: Fenestratus, ta, tum, open. Plaut. Nulla est fenestratior domus,
n: fenestratus ta tum open plaut nulla est fenestratior domus

d: A day dedicate to the infernall goddis, to pacifie them towarde the soules departed.
Were also the sacryfyces doone for sowles.
Wyndynge shetes, and suche lyke thynges, wherin deade bodyes were lappyd.
Fruiteful, or that bryngeth forth moche fruite.
A dysshe with meate. Also a pagent, caryed or borne to be loked on. sometyme it signifieth the stage or place, wherin the pagent is.
Men armed in lygyt harnes, redy to come quickly to socours: whiche sought with dartes, swordes, or slynges.
A citie, whiche after Plini. standeth in the fyrst region of Italye.
A towne of the Sabius, or Samnites.
A name of Iupiter, gyuen by Romulus, the first kynge of Romanes.
A beere, wheron deed bodies are borne. somtyme a thinge, wheron ymages, relikes, or iewelles are borne.
A mountayne, of whiche the house of Pheretre was named, of which the duke of Vrbyne is descended.
To stryke, to stablyshe, to knocke.
To make a league or truse.
To slee, to hit the marke.
To meddel or myxt well togyther, as leuen with dow. also to leuen.

To beare, to suffre, to leade or brynge, to saye, to name, to desyre, to brynge forth, to haue, to boste. Ferre ad populū, to aske the people aduyse. To take away, to receyue, to optayne, to accustome.
To vse fortune: Ferre in oculis, to fauour moche.
To receyue, to wryte that whiche is receyued, to knowlege to haue receyued a benefyte or profyte.
To spende or laye out, to wryte expenses, to bestowe.
The goddesse of woodes. also a citie vnder the hyll Soractes.
An instrumēt or tole of yron.
Ꝑtaynyng to yron, or of yron.
To agree to the sentence or iudgement.
Hauyng yron on it, or closyd in yron.
Ruite of yron, a murray colour, some calleth it a sadde blewe.
Glewe, syse, sowder, or suche other byndynge or cleauynge matter.
To ioyne or myxe togyther, proprely mettalles, to sowlder.
A Cake made of sondry graynes and spyces.
A rodde or stycke, wherwith chyldrens handes be striken in schooles. also a cane or rede. also a potte stycke.
To make hast, to be troublid.

Spede the slowely, is spoken, where a man wyll sygnifye a thynge to be done, neither to hastyly nor to slowely, but in a conuenient temperance. See my booke of the Gouernour, in the chapiter of Maturytie.
Mery, prouokynge myrthe, ioyous. also pertaynyng to holy dayes.
The yonge tender spring of a tree, or herbe. Also a moote.
A beaste called a beuer, whiche is also called Castor, whose stoones are vsed in medicine, and are called Castoreum. It is also a kynde of waspes.
Are the extreme partes of the liuer, the hart, or the lunges, or of other thinges wherin is any diuysyon, they maye be called lappes, brymmes. Also the spires of herbes or trees newe sprongen.
A buckle of a girdell, or other thing lyke therto.
To buckle, to ioyne togither tymber, or bordes, or other lyke thinges.
A place where figge trees do grow.
He that loueth or gadereth fygges.
A staffe or stake of a fygge tree.
Full of sores in the heed or berde.

o: Ficulneus, a, um, & ficulnus, a, um,
n: ficulneus a um amp ficulnus a um

d: In the masculyne gender is a fygge: in the feminine gender, is a figge tree. it is also a soore or scabbe, growyng in the places of a mans body, where that heare is.
A vesselle seruynge to dyuers pourposes.
Belefe, truste, promyse. It is a stablenes and truthe in promyses and couenauntes. It is also a faythfull execution of thinges commytted or promysed.
The strynge of any instrument. sometyme a harpe or lute.
The credence or promyse of all the people and rulers.
A harpe: it maye be called a fyddell. it is also he that playeth on the instrument.
A tourment made with cordes or strynges, wherwith menne be tourmented, to make them to confesse treason or felonye.
Trust, confidence: somtyme hope: it is proprely that truste, wherin any thyng is deliueryd by one man to an other, to the intent that he shall redelyuer it, whan he is required.
A possession to an other mans vse, or vpon condicion.
A state in landes made vpon confidence of truste, or a morgage.
The warke or warkemanshyp: sometyme a lye, or a thing fayned.

To thruste in.Columel. Virg. Ge. lib. 4. sommetyme it sygnifyeth to driue or fasten in the erthe. Palum humi fixit, He droue the stake into the grounde. also to plant or sette. Ipse feraces Figat humo plantas, He wolle sette in the grounde the fruitefull plantes.Iunenal. Sometyme to stryke.
A potters warkehowse, or potters crafte.
A sonne in lawe by an other wyfe, or an other husbande.
A newe begunne gentylman, or a gentylman of the fyrste heed.
Ferne growynge on trees, callid in a greke name polypodion.
Somtime dothe conteyne both sonnes and doughters.
A countreye, that is nowe callyd Ascalon.
A threde. sometyme the proporcion of a thynge.
To spynne or make a threde.
The skyrtes or hemme of a garmente.
A boxe, out of the whiche men doo caste dyse.
To make, to forme, to fayn.
The ende, the conclusyon. also intente or purpose, whervnto any other thing hath relation, or is made or done for.
The borders or marches of a countrey, boundes.
A suertie or stabylitie. also that, whyche is called the grounde of a cause or matter. Also the firmament or heuen vysyble.
A chiefe fate. Also it is a thynge made with withes and halters, wherewith cattell were so moselled, that they mought not byte anye yonge sprynges or buddes of trees.
A lyttell hyll in Italye, not farre from Tyber.
Greate sachels, wherin were put great sommes of money.
That maye be cutte or slytte. fiscilis, the same.

A pype, as well to conuey water, as an instrument of musyke. Also the we sell or throte bolle. also a tappe or faucette. also a disease or soore, whiche commeth of a putrified humour, and contynually rūneth.
Full of holes lyke a spunge▪
An instrumente, wherwith pi •• s of wodde be dryuen into the ground. and stones in pauynge, called a rammer.
Be beastis of Aethiope, of a browne colour, hauynge two pappes in the breste, as man hath: nor they be not so wylde, but they may be tamed, nor so tame, but they woll hurte those, that greue them.
An instrument, wherwith in the heate of sommer wynde is fanned blowen into mēs visages, to koole thē.
A blowynge or puffe of wynde.
Wythered, feeble, weake, hangynge downewarde, lollynge, or flaggynge.
The smalle braunches or twigges of trees or vynes. sometyme scourges or flayles, wherwith corne is threshed.
To scourge, to the thresshe, to blame or rebuke.
An vngracious persone, full of myschiefe.
An yll or myscheuous dede, worthy rebuke and punyshement.
To aske importunately and with clamoure.
They whiche for moneye doo suffre them selfes to be beaten.
To bourne with a flame of fyre. Sommetyme to loue or desyre inordynately.
Clothe or sylke of vyolette colour.
The priestes wyfe, or a wedding gowne of vyolet colour.
A typpet of vyolet sylke, whiche the newe wedded wyfe dyd weare.
The great prieste amonge the gentyles.
To be lyke golde, or of yelowe colour.
Yelowe, or of the coloure of golde.
To bowe, to bende, to leade.
An oration or spech, wherby a mans mynde is stirred to pitie, reioysynge, or other lyke affection.
Any thynge that may be easylye bowed or bente.
To blowe. also to make coyne of mettall.
Flockes of the shearynge of wollen clothes.
Plays made in the honour of Flora, an harlotte, whiche gaue a great treasure vnto the people of Rome.

o: Floreo, rui, ere, & florido, aui, are,
n: floreo rui ere amp florido aui are
d: To flourish or to haue floures. Also to excell. somtime to prosper.
To bourgen or to brynge forth floures.
Garnyshed with floures. sometyme freshe or lusty.
To be tossed as a shyppe is in the see. also to doubte.
A floudde, a waue of water styred by tempeste.
To flowe contynually, sometyme to flytte or swymme.
A great ryuer. sometyme the course of the water.
To rounne, as water dothe, to procede or come of a thynge, or to growe.
A fyshe, lyke to an eele, callyd a Lampreye.
That whiche is in the ryuer.
Vnstable, or that whyche dureth but a whyle, large, or wyde, relented, lecherous, and wanton.
A kerchiefe, whiche menne and womenne dydde weare aboute theyr cheekes.
A braunche of a vyne, whyche groweth out of a twyste or forked bough.
Bread baken on the hote coles.
A little panne, wherin fyre is borne.
A panne or herthe, wherein fyre is. sometyme it sygnifieth fyre. somtyme priuate houses or tenementes.
A place where a thyng is dygged.
To polute or defyle, to destroye, to rent or teare, to consume.
A breaker of leage or truse, or entercourse.
A leage betwene princis, an entercourse, a truse after battayle: sometyme it signifyeth a lawe made in the tyme of warres.
Felycitie, prosperitie, abundaunce of all thynges.
Hauing abūdance of al thinges, prosperous, commodious, or profytable.
A womanne. Also in beastes the female.
Pertaynynge to haye, as Falces foenariae, hookes or sythes for to cutte haye.
Pertaynyng to vsurye, or vnreasonable gayne.
An vsurer or lender for vnreasonable gayne.

o: Foenero, aui, are, & foeneror, rari, cum datino,
n: foenero aui are amp foeneror rari cum datino
d: To lende for vsurie. Foeneror cum ablatiuo, To borowe, or make a shyfte, or to laye to morgage.
Vsurye, vnreasonable, or vnlefull gayne, commyng of that thyng, whiche is lente.
To brynge forth, most cō monly as a beast or a byrde dothe.
The tyme from the conception vnto the byrthe. Also the increase of cattell. sometyme it signifieth the increase or commynge forth of other thinges.
All thynge that is brought forth by generation, somtyme the fruite of trees.
Full, or great with yonge, as a woman with chylde or a beaste.
To snuffe or fetche backe wynde with the nosethrylles.
The huske, wherein the eare of wheate or other corne is inclosed, whan it is grene, called the hose. Also for a sacke, wherin corne is putte.
A belowe, wherwith fyre is blowen. also a ball blowen full of wynde: semblably a bedde stuffed onely with wynde. it is also a bagge, wherin money is.
A nourishment of natural heate. It is also any thynge layde to the bodye in the fourme of a playster, to mytygate the peyne or griefe of any disease, callyd fomentation.
Any matter, wherwith fire is kendlyd and kepte burnynge. sometyme it sygnifieth that, whych feruently styreth vs to do any thynge.
Of a fountayne: as Aqua fontana, well water.
A market woman, whyche selleth egges, chykens, and other lyke thynges at the markette.
A payre of tonges or other lyke instrument.
A propre name of a man.
A mylche cowe that bryngeth forth caulfes.
I shuld or had be, thou shuldest or had be, he shulde or had ben.
Habytes or robes, worne onely in places of iugement.
Pertaynyng to places of iugemente or courtes, where lawes be exercysed: also a iurrour.
The hatches of a shyp, or place where men beinge in the shyppe, do walke vp and down. Also stages or galeries, from whēs the noble men of Rome beheld the playes callyd Circenses.
Huches, wherin bokes were kepte: nowe be they taken for keuerynges of bookes.
Dunge that is lyquide or thynne.
To discharge the bealy of ordure.
Lose bealy, or he that hath a laske.
An Emote, or Ant, or Pismere.
That whiche is commonly callyd a rynge worme.
That whiche is to be drad.
He that feareth other: also he that is feared of other.
To forme, to make in facion.
An instrument or dede in writing. a style in wrytynge, and a fourme in pleadynge.
Dayes whan the women dydde nought els but bake breadde.
They which haue stalles or bouthes vnder the vaultes or arches of churches or palayces, where they sel theyr wares to them that passe by, as they do in west mynster halle.
To make an arch or a vault.
To perce or boore a hole.
Stronge, puissant, valyant of corage. also fayre, sometyme ryche.
The fortunate ilandes, be so callyd of the abundaunce of fruites, of whiche Strabo writeth .li.i.
To make prosperous, to augment with good fortune.

A market, where thynges be solde. Also a place where iudgementes are practised, and matters in lawe pleaded. Forum whan it is taken for a market, hath cōmonly an other worde ioyned therwith, as Forum boatium, the markette where cattell to solde. Forum holitorium, the markette where herbes be solde. Forum piscarium, the fyshe markette.
A region or coūtrey of Italy whiche somtyme was called Iapidia.
A cytie of Italye, whyche nowe is callyd Imola.
A dyche, or dyke, or a mote.
That whiche is dygged, or maye be dygged.
To nouryshe, to sustayne, to maynteyne, to weate or washe a thynge, to ordeyne or sette, to defende.
More than rype, rotten as fruite is.
To take the bytte in the teethe, sygnifieth to set naught by.
The two great veynes, whyche do appere on eyther syde of the necke.
A pece or gobette of a thynge broken.
The noyse, whyche is made at the fallynge of any great thynge, rushyng.
The fringe of tapesry, that hangeth next the grounde.
Proprely is sayde of chyldernes brestes, whan they do growe, to waxe imbocyd.
Not to satisfie the necessitie of nature, or carnall appetite.
A rorynge, proprelye of waters. sometyme a murmuryng, rumble, or noyse of people assemblyd togyther.
To rore or make a noyse lyke great waters.
To grynde the tethe togyther for angre or payne. Also to grunte or grone for peyne.
Acustomed, moche hanted, also assembled togither, abundant.
Greatte haunte, and companye of folke.
A narowe parte of the see, where it is mouynge and troublous. Sometyme it is taken generally for the see.
A byrde, which syngeth in the cold wether, a ruddocke.
To breake smalle, specially betwyxte the fyngers.
The grayne in the toppe of the eare, whiche is lasse than a corne.
A boxe, out of the which dise were caste on the tables.
He that selleth stuffe of lyttell valewe.
Vayne, lyght, of none estymation or value.
A slyppynge of of leaues. Also brousynge.
The foreheed, the frunt. Also it signifieth shamefastnes. also countenance.
Is spoken where a man sygnyfyeth, that one disdayneth extremely an nother.
The leafe of a tree, with the braunches.
He that hath a brode forhed.
Hauynge a greatte forehed, or not abashed.
He that taketh the frute or profite of a thynge. Pernour of profytes.
That whiche beareth fruite, or doth pertayne to fruite.
Fruite. also al profite or reuenues that cometh of the grounde.
Increase of all those thynges, whiche the erth bryngeth forth, moste proprely of grayne or corne. sometyme it signifieth rent or reuenues.
A good man, a thryfty man, an honest man, temperate in expenses.
Moderation in liuing, speciallye in apparaylle and dyete, sobre rule, also suffyciencye.
The vppermost part of the throte, the gargyll.
A taker or pourueyour of corne.
All corne, that hath berdes or eyles. it is moste vsed for wheate or rye.
Wyse in vsynge of a thynge.
To vse with dilectation and profyte.

o: Frustro, aui, are, & frustror, aris, ari,
n: frustro aui are amp frustror aris ari
d: To deceyue. also to do a thyng in vayne, or vainly to employe.
A kynde of brembyls, whose pryckes be not hooked.
That which hath a great stalke, and yet it is no tree, as fenelle, caules, certayne malowes, and other lyke herbes. somtyme it is taken for the stemme or stalke.
Hauynge abundaunce of suche great herbes.
A place where groweth herbes with great stēmes or stalkes.

o: Frutico, aui, are, & fruticor, fruticaris, ari,
n: frutico aui are amp fruticor fruticaris ari

d: Coloured or paynted, as some women be.
A dorre or bee without stynge, whyche entreth into hyues, and eateth vp hony. Also payntynge, where oone colour is layde on an nother. It is also vsed for desceyte or falsehode.
He that flyeth lyghtly. Also it signifieth swyfte.
To flye, to runne awaye, to escape, to forgette.
Waters, which be taken out of a commune ryuer by stelthe.
He that runneth frome his maister, wyllyng neuer to returne, or goth to a place, from whens he supposeth that his mayster can neuer recouer hym.

o: Fulgeo, si, gere, & fulgo, gi, ere,
n: fulgeo si gere amp fulgo gi ere

d: The lyghtnynge whenne it is in the clowdes.
A se byrd, more thā a culuer, & black.
A colour mixte of grene and redde, a darke yelowe.
A smoky place, where wine was layde, to the intent that it moughte the soner ware olde. also the shanke or tonell of a chymneye.
Horses, whiche coupled with an halter, dyd go before the charyot.
He that walketh on a rope.
A slynge. Also a castinge nette, a sach • ll or purse lyke a nette. Also a cerkle of golde, or other mettalle, wherein stones he sette.
To yette or cast mettall, to powre out, to sheede, to throwe downe, to scatter, to gyue aboundantlye, to speake moche, to lay downe.
That whyche is vsed to be callyd lande or soyle.
To vyolate a place with a deed bodye.
Vyolated with deade bodies. Also mortalle, blouddy. also pertaynynge to deed bodies or dethe.
Bowed or howped, as somme vynes be.
To exercyse an office. Fungi uita, to lyue. Functus uita, He that hath fynished his lyfe.
Funerall exequies, or solemnitie of burienge. Sometyme it sygnyfieth the deed corps.

A seruant, whiche for some lyghte offence, was compelled to beare a forke on his necke, hauynge both his handes bounden faste thereto, and so to goo through the towne, confessynge his defaut, and exhortynge other, that they shulde not in lyke case offende, whyche was a greate reproche.
The furyes of Helle, whyche were thre, Alecto, Tisiphone, Megêra.
Bakers crafte. Also a womanne baker.
Madnesse: Also furye, whyche is a vehement concytation or styrrynge of the mynde.
That which is done by stelth, or very pryuyly.

Thefte. it is defyned to be a deceitfull handlynge or vsynge of any thynge, or the possession therof, to haue therby gayne or auauntage, whiche is by the lawe of nature prohibited to be suffred. It is somtime any act that is done priuily, or to the intent it shuld be secrete.
Sacrifice doone to Pluto and Proserpine.
A litle thefe, also a beest called a Stote, that killeth rabettis. It is also a sore callid a felon. also a sore callid a cattisheer.
A speare with many teethe, wherwith fyshers do take troutes, or yeles, by throwynge of it, a troute speare, an yele speare.
Browne of colour, not fully blacke.
Pertaynynge to meltynge, As Ars fusoria, the crafte of meltyng. Vas fusorium, a meltynge potte.
That whiche wyll be soone powred out.
He that speketh all that he knoweth shortely or vnaduisedly.
A galowe tree or gybet, whereon men be hanged.
A garment with two lappes, wherof the one caste backward, dyd gyrde him that did were it. whych garment the consule ware, whan he denounced warres.
Two yles by the further partes of Spayne, beyonde Granade.
A gumme of a certayn tree, whiche is moche vsed in playsters.
Thynges whiche do hange on cypresse trees, lyke small heares.
The name of a noble phisition.
A royalme in Spayne, callydde Galyce.
The tyme whanne the Cocke croweth.
A place where pultry is kept.
He or she that kepeth pultrye.
A countreye in Asia, callyd also Galatia.
A cocke, a Frencheman, a prieste of Cybeles, callyd the mother of the goddes,
A brothell house, a hous of baudry and ryotte. Also Ganea, is taken for gluttonye.
A Ruffyan, a haunter of bandy houses, a ryotter. Also a rauyner of delycates, a frauncher.
A greatte ryuer, whiche enuyronneth India, wherin is founde bothe golde and precyous stones.
A Troyane chylde, whyche was fayned to be rauyshed of Iupyter, and made his butlar.
To bark or houle lyke a dogge.
A mountayn, & also a citie in Asia.
To gargaryshe or washe the mouthe and throte of a man.
Ioye, myrthe, an affection of the mynde, conceiued of an opinion of a thing good or pleasaunt.
A mantell to caste on a bedde: also a carpette to lay on a table, some calle it a daggeswayne.
A place where tresure is kept
A hyll and towne in Sauoy, nowe called Geneura.
The name of a iuge in Israel.
Is taken in holy scripture for hell.
The Fooreteethe, whiche be shewed in laughynge.
He that laugheth to make other men laughe.
The noumbre of two. Also geminus, is a twynne, where many chyldren are borne at one burdeyne, althoughe they be thre or mo. Also it is the name of a man, whiche in hebrewe is Thomas.
The yonge budde of a vyne. Also a precious stone.
To budde or sprynge, as a yonge graffe or vyne dothe.
To grone, or to wayle, or to make a lamentable noyse.
A place frome whense the bodyes of personnes condempned were throwen downe.
A corne, or lyke griefe vnder the • yttell too.
The eye lydde. It is sommetyme taken for the chekes.
Of a gentyl or noble kind.
An astronomer, or other lyke, whiche by the sterres set at a mannes natiuitie, telleth his fortune.
A manne in his house verye lyberall and freshe.
Ioynted, as a wheate straw is.
The ioynt of a strawe, or stalke of an herbe.

Pertayning to the byrthe of a man. genitale solum, the naturall countrey or place, where a manne is borne. genitalis dies, the daye of natiuitie. genitale semen, the sede of generation, genitalia, the membres of generation.
Sometyme generation, sometyme the sede of generation.
That hath power to ingender, or that whiche procedeth with generation. genitiuae notae, markes, wherewith a man is borne.

An aungell. Amonge the Paynims some supposed it to be the spirite of a man. Some dydde put two gouernours of the sowle, a good and an euyll, Bonus genius, & malus genius, whyche neuer departed from vs. sometyme it is taken for nature it selfe, or dilectation meued by nature.
Men, whiche do gyue all their studye to eatynge and drynkynge.
To absteyne from all thynges pleasaunt.
A beast lasse than a fox, of colour betwene blacke & yelow, medlid with black spottes, whiche wyll soone be made tame.
A kynseman of the same name and stocke. sometyme it signyfyeth a gentyle or paynyme. somtyme a countrey man.
Propre, or familyar to that people, or kynrede.
