Gentilitie, the multitude of the people or famyly.
The surname or ancyent name of a mans auncetours.
Of the people or nation, gentilitia sacra, ceremonyes of that countrey or people.
The natural speche or mother tunge.

Is the begynnynge of euerye thynge, eyther of the persone that ingendred it, or of the place, where it was ingendred. Orestes a Tantalo ducit genus, Orestes hathe his begynnynge of Tantalus, or is of the bloudde of Tantalus. Plato genere Atheniensis est, Plato is of his bloudde or auncetrye an Athenyens. Also it sygnifieth kynde. genus uitae, a kynd of lyfe. genus mortis, a kynd of deth. genus animalium, a kynde of beastes. Also it signifieth that, whiche conteineth many sondry kyndes, as Animal comprehendeth a man, a byrde, a fyshe, and euery of them is genus to that, whiche in theym is comprehended. As a brute beast is genus to a horse, a lyon, a bulle, a dogge, &c. A byrde is genus to an egle, a crowe, a larke, a sparowe. &c. A fishe is genus to a whale, a porpese, a haddocke, a playce. &c.
Superstitious warkinge in sorcerye, by cerkles and prickes in the erthe.
Geometry, measuring and proporcionyng of fygures in the erthe.
Germaynes, or Almayns, They be also bretherne of one father and oone mother.
The countrey named Germany, or Almayne.
A branche of a tree or herbe.
To beare. sometyme it signifieth to haue.
Fyshe of the kynde of herrynges, it may be called pylchardes.
Talkers of tryfelyng thinges, or lyght matters.
A porter, or a man hyred to carye bourdeynes.
A mayde that kepeth a chylde.
A place where the Senate dyd assemble, a parlyament house.
The name of a king of Spain, whiche was slayne by Hercules.
As some men do suppose, was the towne, whiche is now named Caleys.
What soo euer is borne, a burdeyn or caryage.
That wherin any thyng is caried or borne, a flagon, a horse lytter.
The exercise, where a man is borne or caried on any thinge.
Pertaynyng to sygnes or tokens of myrthe, with meuyng the body or handes.
To make suche sygnes or tokens of myrthe, as in daunsynge.
To shewe the affections of the mynde by meuyng of the body, or any part therof▪ somtyme it signifieth to delite.
To beare longe. Gestat ventrē, she to with chylde.
Gesture, or coūtenance with menynge of the body.
A littell ile in the see called Ionium, wher vnto menne condempned were exyled.
He which hath a croked backe, or a great bunche on any parte of the body.
A mete made of sondry kindes of fleshe, or of garbage of foule.
The iawes, wherin the teth be set.
A greate ryuer in Egypte, otherwise callyd Nylus.
A rele, wheron threde is woūden Gith, a sede, whiche is nowe callyd Nigella Romana: it is blacke lyke to oynyon sede, and is very soote, and the sauoure thereof exhausteth reumes of the heed.
To be without heer, or smothe.
A place, hauynge nothynge growynge in it.
To make a noise like a gander.
Were men, whiche faught vnarmed with swordes.
Pertainynge to that maner of fyghtynge.
The arte or feate to fyghte with a sworde.
A lytel sworde or wodknyfe. also the name of an herbe lyke to sedge.
A sword, also a kind of fishe, which hath a bone in his forheed like to a sworde.
Fedynge of swyne with maste, callyd paunage.
The parte of a bore next the necke, the shelde or gammonde.

Mast growing on okes, bech, chestons, and other lyke, it is also a pellette of leade. Also a kernell growyng betwene the skynne and the flesshe, it is more ouer the foreparte or nutte of a mans yerde.
Iocunde, plesant, ingraued, polyte, holow, famous, subtyll.
An herbe lyke to plantayne, whiche maketh a blewe colour,Caesar. wherwith the auncient Butons dyed their vysages. some men englyshe it woadde.
Oyle, whiche dothe come from the olyues before they be pressed.
A horse with a wall eye.
An herbe, which crepeth on the erthe nygh to salt waters.

o: Glaucoma, matis, & glaucomatum, ti, & glaucoma, mae,
n: glaucoma matis amp glaucomatum ti amp glaucoma mae
d: An humour in the eien, lyke crystall, whiche letteth the syght.
A man or womanne with graye eyes.
A god of the see. also many men were called by that name. also the name of a fysshe.
A turfe or piece of erthe.
A fielde mous, whiche slepeth all the wynter.
To growe, to waxe fatte, to couerte or desyre feruently.
A boule, or other thing very rounde. Also a multitude of menne or beastes gathered rounde togither.
To cackle as a henne doth.
To wynde in rounde. also to gather togither in an heape.
The consent of good mē in the praise of a man or woman, callid renome, glory.
To auaunt, to thintent to haue praises, to extolle with bostynge.
Renomed, somtyme in the yll part, vaynglorious, or bosting him selfe.
The systers husbande, or brothers wyfe.
A glose, or exposition of dark spech.
He that maketh a commente on a boke.
To pulle of the barke or rynde of a tree.
The teethe, wherby the age of an horse is knowen. They be sommetyme taken for that, whiche sheweth the houres in a clocke or diall.
A citie in Iudea whyche was consumed for horryble synne agaynst nature.
A disease, wherby a mans seede gothe from hym vnwyttyngly.
The name of a great rhetorician.
Monstruous womenne, whyche were vanquyshed by Perseus.
The Iaye hath nought to do with the harpe. whyche is spoken of theym, whyche lackynge eloquence or good letters, doo scorne theym that haue it.
The name of a noble famylye or house in Rome.
A greese or steppe, a degree in consanguinitie.
To be caste downe from his place: wherby is sygnifyed to be abasshed or moued from constancy of mynde.
To go by steppes, or steppe.
A fourme of speakynge, when of the fyrst sentence springeth the seconde, of the seconde the thyrde, and so forthe.
One of the names of Mars.
A man borne in Grece, a Greeke.
A place where Ambassadours adode, vntylle they were sente for into the Senate.
To ryotte in bankettynge and rybaudrye.
They whiche do go on styltes.
He that teacheth grammer, or expoundethe authours, a profounde grammaryan.
A smatterer in grammer, a meane grammarian.
He that wrytethe on his knee.
The place where the recordes, or commune writinges be kepte.
Grasse: sometyme all herbes togyther, the swarthe.
Hayle. Also a pushe lyke to a boyle in the flesshe, whiche greueth a man whan it is touched.
Somwhat great, or of good age, well stryken in yeres.
Eloquente, he that speaketh as it were with a greatte magnyfycence in wordes.
A gray • arde, wherein corne is kepte.
A pensyll, wherwith menne doo write in tables.
A case, wherin pensiles were kepte, it may be called a pennar.
He that by highe wayes, lyeth in awayt to robbe or slee men, an extorcioner.

To robbe or slee men passynge by the hyghe wayes. Also to goo or come on one with a violent rage. Therfore in a sodayn and violent pestilence, it is said, morbus grassatur, The sycknes kylleth mē sodaynely.
Grace, somtyme it signifieth thanke, sometyme a benefyte, sometyme rewarde▪ also peace or loue, sometyme cause or respect, also prayse.
Very thankfull. Also in fauour, with the people, or well estemed.
An aduerbe, betokenynge withoute rewarde: sometyme without deserte.
An aduerbe sygnifienge, of good wyll, without benefite.
To gratifie, or doo a thynge thankfull, or to conferre a benefite, or doo a good tourne.
To giue thankes to god with offrynges, also to reioyce of good fortune.

With a datiue case, to be ioyous for hym selfe or an other for any good thynge that hath hapned.Liuius. Tibi de hac tua fcelicitate gratulor, I am ioyous with the, or as gladde as thou arte, of this prosperitie that thou arte in. Sometyme it sygnifyeth to gyue thankes vnto god: but with an accusatiue case it signifieth to take thankfully any acte.

Heuy, greuouse, sommetyme substancial, graue, or hauyng grauitie, contrary to lyghtnes or wantonnes, also great or puissant, sometime olde or aged, somtime sure or constent, sommetyme plentuous or full. Terra grauts, lande laded with corne.
Greuousely, heuily, substancially, moche, wisely, sadly.
Heuynesse, griefe, disease. Somtyme the mutre or reume of the heed.
He that hath a heuye heed.
That whiche maketh a heuy heed.
To greue, to burden, or lade.
To be grieued, or to take grieuouselye.
To gette a woman with chyld.
A flocke, as well of menne, as of cattelle.
A souldiour taken at aduenture, not chosen.
The chiefe shepard, whiche hath the charge of the hole flocke.
Cattell, whiche is in the flocke.
A thynge, wherwith grounde is measured.
A mydde place, from whense goth foure wayes.
A beaste, more than a grassehoppe, whiche destroyeth corne.
A grype or gryffon. also a captious, an insoluble, or diffuse argumente, a ryddyll.
A nose rysynge in the myddell.
The grene shale of the walle nutte.
A swallowe or depe pyll in a water, or a goulfe.
The gully or gargylle of the throote, or throote bolle. It is also a worme that bredeth in barnes, and eateth vppe corne.
A darke and vyle habitation, a cabban or cotage.
A cruet, or other lyke thynge, oute of the whiche lycour is poured dropping.
He that hath a swollen throte.
A lyttell hylle, not farre from Thessalye.
The name of a kynge of Lydia, also a ryuer of Lydia was callydde by the same name.
He that teacheth chylderne to exercyse them in wrastlynge, or other like.
A place, where is commune exercyse of the bodye. Sommetyme a schoolehouse.
The chiefe mayster of the schole or place of exercyse.
Phylosophers of Inde, whiche went alway naked.
A beaste, whyche commethe of a horse and an asse mare.
That parte of the house, whyche serueth onely for women.
To compasse or goo in cyrcuite.
A towne, whiche Hercules and Apollo, layenge there asyde theyr stryfe and debate, buylded togyther, and the inhabytauntes of the same towne are called Gyttlietes.

To haue, to hold, to possede or occupie, to esteme or suppose, to call, to dwelle, Pensi habere, to take hede. Frustra habere, to deceyue. Habere bene seu male, to doo or prosper well or yll. Bene haber, it is wel. Res ita se habet, the thinge is at this point. In custodiis haberi, to be kepte in prysone. Fortunas suas uenales habuit, he hath solde all his goodes. Habeo tibi fidem, I put my truste in the. Habeo rationem, I haue busynes, or I haue to do. Habere rem, to medle with a woman. Habere rem cum aduersario, to contend. Habere gratiam, to thanke. Habeo audire, I can here. Habeo polliceri, I canne promyse. Habet frustra, He is dysappoynted.

The fourme or state of the body, sometyme of other thynges, Also apparayle. Also it sygnyfyethe a qualytie or propretie, whiche a manne hath conceiued by education, longe exercyse, or custome, habyte.
A kynde of swete smellynge gumme, that groweth in Media.
People in Fraunce, whiche be nowe callid Burgonyons, and Burbonoyses.
A stable, wherin kyddes be kepte.
A disease in the fundemēt lyke teates or wartes, out of the whiche issueth bloudde, callyd emorrodes or pyles. Also a serpent, of whom if a man be stryken, he bledeth to dethe.
To cleaue or stycke to a thynge. sometyme to doubte.
In the is putte all the blame.
To sticke fast, or be thruste in.

o: Haesito, aui, are, idem quod haereo.
n: haesito aui are idem quod haereo

d: An heyre, or he, which succedeth an other in his landes or goodes.
Pertaynynge to inheritance. Bona haereditaria, goodes whiche do come by inheritaunce.
Crauers of goodes, flatteryng men to be their heires.
Lande, wherin a man hath a state of inheritaunce.
A secte, an heresy, an obstynate opynion.
A fysshe callyd herryng. Also a sawce made of fyshe.
A ryuer nat farre from Aetna.
An Egle, that haunteth aboute the see.
Bokes contayninge the properties of fyshes.
A thorne lyke to a whyte thorne, growynge by the see syde, and hath leaues lyke to an olyue tree, but they be broder.
The cirkle or garlande aboute the Moone.
A citie in the lasse Asia.
People of Paphlagonie, so called bycause they ar inuironned about with the See.
To be in a dreame, to be deceyued, to erre, or to take a matter wrong.
Nymphes or fayries of the woddes.
An angler or fyssher with an angle or hoke.
Pertaynynge to a hoke. piscatus hamatilis, fysshynge with a hooke, or anglynge.
A colour on the body, lyke to them that be leperous.
A sworde lyke to a sythe.
A grapull of a shyppe. also a coupers instrument, wherwith he dryueth on howpes, an addysse.
A grapelyng yron, for to close shyppes togyther: also a poll with a hoke on the ende, that shypmen vse.
A womans name, the doughter of Harpalus kynge of Thrace.
Monstruous byrdes, hauyng maydens vysages, and talons of a meruaylous rapacitie. wherfore men that be rauenous, and great gatherers of goodes, be named sometyme Harpy • ae.
A dyuynatour, or tellar of thynges to come by the lokynge in the bowelles of beastes. Also he, whiche obserueth tymes in doinge of thynges.
The arte of hym, whyche is a dyuinatour.
The diuynation or tellynge of thynges to comme, by the lokynge in beasts bowelles.
The bowyng made lyke a cer •••• • n roufes of houses, or of a whele.
Were without yron: and in the olde tyme were gyuen for a price to theym that vanquished firste in battayle.
Sygnifieth to leaue sute, to dispayre of the matter in variance.
Reunnynge at the tylte with speares.
To drawe or take out, to here, to see, to take a thyng gredylye, to wounde, to fatigate or make wery, to make empty, to consume. Haurire supplicia, to suffre punyshement or peynes.
The name of one of the comedyes of Terentius, whiche is as moche to saye, as tourmentynge hym selfe.
A wike. Also the numbre of seuen in dayes, yeres, or other tyme.
A tree, wherof the wod is blacke lyke geate, and it beareth neyther leaues, nor fruite.
To be dustre or made darke.
Of men in olde tyme were callid poore folkes.
The daughter of Arsinoi, whiche was gyuen to Nestor for a gyfte.
A sacrifice, wherein were kylled a hundred beastes.
A countrey hauyng an hundred cities therin.
He that hath an hundred fete.
The yexinge of a man. also a lyttelle puffe, whiche riseth in breadde whanne it is baken.
A place whiche is hette with the sonne.
The harneys of carthorses, wherby they drawe.
An herbe commonly called Enula campana, in englyshe Helycampane.
A cytie in Grecia called also Corinthus.
An herbe hauynge a yelowe floure. A marygolde.
A lyttell tree lyke to a fygge tree, and hath leaues lyke a plane, but greatter and blacker.
An herbe lyke to Smallage, whyche groweth in watery groundes, and hath but one lease.
A flowre whiche in the sonne rysynge dothe open, and at the sonne sette closeth. Some supposeth it to be Marygoldes or ruddes.
Of some men is taken for a kynde of wyllowe tree, of some men for yuie.
An herbe, the rote wherof purgeth melancoly.
The sonne of Deucalion, of whom the Grekes were named Hellenes.
An arme of the see. whyche deuideth Grece and As • e.
A garment which was vsed in Lidia, and was of the color of a cowes hyde.
People called Suycers, or Suyches, by desyre of warres, ennemyes to all mankynd: subiectes neither to god not to Prynce.
He whiche in eatyng and drinkyng spendeth al his substance, a reueller. somtyme a glutton onely.
A colour betwene redde & white lyke the coloure of clothe, called frenche tawnye.
An herbe, which hath stalkes somwhat redde, and smal burres on the toppe, whiche do cleaue faste vnto clothes.
An interiection of blamynge, disdaynynge, meruaylynge, or shewynge.
A currour, which runneth many myles in one day.
A peyne in halfe the heed, callyd the mygrim.
A measure of licour or corne, whiche may nowe be taken for a pottell.
Gayne of all, and halfe as moche, as of .iiii. s. be gotten .vi. s.
A proportion in Arithmetike, cō taynynge the hole noumbre, and halfe that nombre: as one to thre .xv to ten.
An herbe good agaynst all yexis.
Half the compasse of the visyble heuen or firmament.
An halfe tercian feuer, whose course is in euery .xxxvi. houres, or whych hath the course of a tercyan.
Certayne iles in the douche see.
One dayes sustynaunce. also a worme, whiche lyueth but one day.
A mountayne in Grece in the realm of Thrace, which is syxe myles in height.
A flye lyke a butterflye, whyche flyeth at nyght into the leame of a candell.
Muste boiled to the thyrd part.
Was sommetyme the name of Egypte, by reason of seuen cities, whyche fyrste were in it.
Where a syllable naturally short, is made longe in a verse, which doth happe in the begynnynge of the fyrst fote.
A town in the cōfines of Europa.
A towne very nere to Naples.

An herbe lyke to Organum, it groweth in watry places, and hath a floure lyke a lylle: and whan the floure is fallen, it hath a heed lyke popie. It is also an nother herbe growynge in plashes, hauynge a lyttell stalke, whiche excedeth not foure fyngers hygh, hauynge a redde floure, and leaues lyke Coriander: this herbe healeth all woundes, if it be layde vnto them. It is called Heraclion syderion.
A philosopher, whiche alwayes wepte, whan he behelde the people: his warkes of a purpose were obscure • harde to be vnderstande.
The name of an Emperour, it is also a touche stone.
An herbe. Also generally all thynge that groweth on the erthe, not being wod. somtyme a wede.
Where a manne yeldeth hym, or confesseth hym selfe to be vanquyshed.
He whiche knoweth the propreties of herbes, and maketh medycynes of theym.
One of the surnames of Iupiter.
A great wodde in Get many, whiche is in breadth .ix. dayes iourney.
A Romayne, whiche fauoured the parte of Marius.
An ymage of Mercurius. It is also an image, the heed wherof may be chāgid.
Be also Images ferte or layde on Sepulchres.
An ymage contaynyng the figures of Mercury and Pallas.
The sonne of Mercurye & Venus. Also he that is both man & woman.
Small images, proprely of lytell chyldren with whynges.
A lyttelle hylle that standethe on Iordane.
The name of a citie that Hermes buylded.
A ryuer, which in the middes, parteth the fyldes of Smyrnee: and fallynge from the hylle Dorylao, dyuideth Phrigia from Car • a.
The disease, wherof men be called brosten: for that their bowels, or other matter, is fallen into their coddes.
The sonne of Antipater, whyche in the .x. yere of Augustus, was of the Romaynes declared kynge of Iewes, and he reigned .xxxvii. yeres.
The thre daughters of Atlas, whiche kepte the gardens, wherin grewe the golden appuls, that were taken awaye by Hercules.
The gardeynes, wherein were the golden appulies, nowe callyd Orenges.
Is a parte of Thessaly sayth Strabo, and Ptol. and in Homerus, it is a town in Euboea. Stephanus sayth, it is a Cytie in Acarnania.
The countrey of Thuscan wherin the citie of Florence is.
A parlour, wherein syxe persones may soupe.
The sonne of Iupiter, whiche was kynge of the Getulians.
An herbe with a pourple floure, and hath a rounde roote.
An herbe lyke to malowes, hauing a gretter lefe, and a heary stalke, holyhok.
This man. also here or in this place.
An yle betwene Sicile and Liparis. Also the name of a way, of a womanne, the wyfe of Thelaphus kynge of Misie.
The floure of the herbe Camamele.
A medycyne to pourge flewme and cholere.
An yle in Cyprus, nere to Paphꝰ.
The declarer of mysteries or holy scripture.
The propre name of a man.
A small gutte or ars gutte.
The .viii. calendes of Aprile, whan the day & nyght haue equall houres.
The propre name of a man.
To make one mery or ioyous.
A synger of a wanton and delycate songe.
The lyttell blacke, whyche is in the ende of a beane. It is sometyme taken for nothynge or nought.
A ryuer in Sycile, deuided into two partes, the oone fresshe water, the other salte.
A measure of the Iewes, whiche contayned of wyne or water, the weyghte of xviii. pounde.
A philosopher, whiche was expert in all sciences and craftes.
A beaste beynge halfe a man, halfe an horse.
The name of a phisytion moste excellente.
A brode way, wherin many horses may runne togither.

The sonne of Theseus, who at the complaynte of Phedra his stepmother, was pursewed by his father, and he in a charyot fleynge, was ouerthrowen amonge the sharpe stones, and rente all to pieces. Afterwarde Aesculapius reuyued hym, and restored hym to helthe. wherefore he wolde be called Vi • bius, that is to saye, twyse a manne, forasmoche as he had twise lyued.

An herbe, wherof yf horses bone eate, they forthewith rounne madde. It is also a venomous humour, rounnynge out of the shappe of a mare, whiche yf a man happe to receyue inwarde, he shall be madde. Plinius saythe, that it is a lyttelle fleshe in the forheed of a colte, whan he is newe foled, blacke, and as moche as a date, whiche the mare plucketh awaye with hyrrethe, as soone as she hath foled: and if any man do take it away before her, she neuer after wyll loue hir fole.
An herbe lyke fenell, but hauynge greatter leaues.
A herde or keper of horses.
People in the Scythik occean whiche haue fete lyke horses.
A beast lyuyng in the ryuer of Nyle, hauyng fere lyke an oxe, his back and mane lyke a hors, & neyeth like a hors, a wynding tayle, and tusked lyke a boore.
An herbe lyke parcely, and groweth in drye groundes, whereof horses do gladly eate.
An herbe called in latine Equisetū, or cauda equina, in englyshe, horsetayle.
The gutte, whiche is called Ieiunum.
A man that is hear • e.
A chylde, whiche passethe the age of .xiiii. yeres, and begynneth to be styrred with lecherye.
To enter into that age, or aptnes to lecherye.
The corner of the eie, also he that is gog • e eyed.
A gote bucke. it is also the ranke sauour, which issueth out of the arme holes.
To narre lyke a madde dogge.
To gape as one doth for sluggishenes, after slepe, or for lacke of slepe. Also it is to proffre to speake, or open the mouthe to speake.
A citie in Spayne, nowe callydde Sibyle.

A countreye in the weste parte of Europa callyd Spayne, and was sometyme callid Iberia, and Hesperia, & is inuyronned on the southe part with the see, callid Mare mediterraneum, whiche dyuydeth Europa from Affrica: on the northe parte with the see called Mare Cantabricum, on the weste with the great occian see with the mountaynes called Pyrenei, and the royalme of Fraunce. And this countrey is diuided by Pthelome into thre regiōs, Bethicā, wherin is Granado, Siuyle, Corduba. &c. Lusytaniā, wherin is Portugal, Galicia. &c. Tarraconenicin, wherin is Castyl, Lyons, and Arragon. At this tyme it conteyneth fyue relmes, Granado on the south part toward Affrike, Portugall on the west, Galicia and Biscay on the north, Arragon on the caste part, Castyl and Lions in the myddell.
A player in enterludes and stage players.
• beaste hauyng sharpe prickes on his backe, called a porkpine.
To make to gape or chinke.
Gapynge, or chynked, as the grounde to in a great drythe.
A robber by the hyghe waye.
A boke to carie in iourney, whiche may be called a iournall.
Proprely the beaste, whiche hauynge his bowelles taken out, is layde hole on the aulter and bourned.
A testament all writen with the hande of the testatour.
The reprocher of Homere, generally Homeromastices, be taken for all reprochers, and false correctours of lerned menne.

The poete of all other moste famous and excellent, who wrate the battaile betwene the Grekes and Troyanes wonderfull eloquently: but howe truely, wyse me may coniect. Also he wrote the trauayle of the prudent Vlysses. Finally both wor ••• are worthy to be radde, for the meruailous inuention, and profytable sentences in them contayned.
A lyuynge creature, hauynge capacitie of reason, subiecte to death, a manne, woman, or chylde.
A man, whiche sitteth alway in the smoke, or by the fyre.
Of the same tonge or lāgage.
A cappe of the olde facion.
The propre name of a woman, wherby is signified concorde.

Signified somtime in mokage a man of a noble linage, bicause noble men wrate their forenames,Erasmꝰ in Chiliad. their names & surnames with thre letters, as. P. Cor. Scipio, C.I. Caes. It is sommetyme taken for a thefe, bycause in Fur are but thre letters.
They whyche sleepe together vnder one ruffe.
Honour, dignitie, sometyme beautie, also reuerence, honesty.
A present giuē to ambassadors, great officers, and iustices at their first cō myng, or executing of their autorities.
To speake with reuerēce, as whan a thinge shall be spoken, which is vyle or dishoneste.
Playes made at Rome, to the honour of Bacchus.
To do honor, or to honor
Sommer honye. It is also a sauce made of fyshe.
The sonne of kyng Agamemnon, whiche slewe his mother, bycause she conspired with Aegisthus her aduouterer, to slee his father.
A cerkle dyuidynge the halfe sphere, or ouer part of the firmament, from the other halfe, where, to our syght, it seemeth that the heuen toucheth the erthe.
A precious stone of the colour of fyre.
A grene stone, compassed with a cerkle of the colour of golde.
Of this yeres, Hagnus hornus, this yeres lambe. Homae fruges, This yeres grayne.
Among the Caldees was named the good god.
The diligent markynge of the tyme of the byrthe of a chylde.
That part of the firmamēt, whiche euery houre riseth from the cast, astronomers do call it the ascendent.
Euery, thynge, wherein howres be marked.
Whan a man thynketh that his heare doth ryse, also to quake for cold or feare. somtime to feare moche.
Whan a man feleth within hym great colde or tremblynge to begyn, as in a feuer, or in a greatte feare: Somme tyme to quake.
A barne, wherin corne is layde. Sometyme a store house, wherin any other thynge is kepte.
Hauynge a terryble sowne or voyce.
Tremblyng for colde or feare, also horryblenes.
The daughter of Hortensius, a woman moste eloquent.
An excellent oratour of Rome, of a wonderfull memorie.
A knotte gardeyne, or a gardeyne for pleasure, or an orcharde.
A geste, or mutual frendes dwellyng in sondry countrays. also a stranger or a mā, inhabiting out of the coūtrey.
A countrey, wherby a manne maye peasibly passe.
Vsynge a gentyll entertaynement, or gladly receyuynge a straunger.
To receyue frendely into his howse.
They that be borne without nosethrylles.
An hooste or sacrifice offered to attayne vyctorie of ennemies.
To recompence, to asswage, or abate, to offende.
A measure of a hundred and forty bushels. Also a doore.
The staffe, wherwith all measures be made euen, a stryke.
To that place. Also to him or her.
Humanitie or nature of man. also doctrine, pertainynge to man.
Gentyll, tractable, courteyse, mercyfull and frendely.
Base, lowe. also simple or pore, abiecte, vyle.
To make lowe, poore, or abiecte.
Basenes, or lowenesse, humilitie, whiche as Speusippus defyneth, is a gentylnesse of the mynde, lackyng wrath or angre.
People which came out of Scithia, and inhabyted Hungarye.

Is a precious stone, of the colour of fyne golde, whiche beinge worne in suche wise, that it toucheth the fleshe agaynst the hart, or the vain, whiche comith from the hart into the left hād, preserueth one frome the pestilence. It is also a purple floure, whiche hath a rounde roote, some do suppose it to be callyd in englyshe, flowre gentyll.
Were solempne ceremonyes done in the nyght.Hieronimus cōtra Iouinianū
Seuen sterres, in whose rysynge & goinge downe it alway rayneth.
A region in Asia, ioyning to Armenie, enuyronned with the mountayns, callid Cauca •• . It is also the olde name of Spayn.
Places where men of warre doo reste them in wynter.
A greatte ryuer in Spayne, nigh to Tarrhacon.
A cytie in Sycile, and a mountayne nygh to it, whiche doth growe full of tyme: And therfore the hony, whiche is there, is of all other moste pleasant.
Is a dogge, ingendred betwyxte a hounde and a mastyue, called a lymmar, or mongrell.
A kynde of hawkes, whyche seldome is sene in the daye, but seeketh his pray in the night.
A disease, whan the skynne is fylled with water.
A water serpent. It was also a monster, with whom Hercules faught: and as soone as he had stryken of one heed of the monster, immediately sprange vp an other.
To medle with an endelesse matter, or where after one myschiefe hapneth an nother.
Diuination in callyng of spirit 〈◊〉 to appere in water.
To rest in the wynter time.
A beaste lyke a wolfe, whiche hath a mane ouer all his backe and neck, but the heares be longer and harder.
A showre of rayne or hayle.
A skynne in the secrete place of a mayden, whiche whanne she is defloured, is broken.
Was called the God of maryage.
A hyll by Athenes, where was hony of all other moste precyous.
A citie, where were meruayllous fayre women.
An aley in a gardayne, or galerye without any couerynge.
An Instrumente, wherewith stones are polyshed.
A longe dependynge, or superfluous sentence.
Excesse in aduauncynge, or depressynge: As higher than heuen, whyter than snowe, swyfter than lyghtnynge, slower than a snayle, warse than the dyuell.
People in the northeaste parte of the worlde.
That whyche is nexte ouer the browe of a manne. Also somme saye
Where aboundeth one syllable or two.
Where diuers wordes be pronoū ced vnder one accent, as quādoquidem, utcun que ▪ &c.
Adders, which styngyng a man, he dyeth slepynge.
The inwarde parte of the body aboue the nauil, & vnder the stomake.
An vssher or substytute in teachynge.
Substaunce. it is also that, whiche dothe ryse in vryne, where there is good digestion, if the resydence be white, lyght, and rysynge in facion lyke a peare, the smalle ende vpwarde.
The doore, or rather the place open, where the doore is.
The wyfe of kynge Mythridates, whiche folowed hym in al his warres, beinge armed lyke a knyght.
A ladye, whyche loued Iason, and whanne he retourned not at the tyme, whiche he promysed, she threwe her selfe into the see.
A maner of speakynge, where the laste is sette before the fyrste, and as it is sayd, the cart before the horses.
One of the names of Bacchus, called god of wynes.

To ly. somtyme to be. In medio cā pus iacet, Salustius. In the middel is a feld. also to be deed. Ille iacet, Lucanus. Cic. de sinibus. he is deed. somtyme to be contēned or nought set by, Maximas uero uirtutes iacere necesse est, uoluptate domināte, Carnal dilectation ruling, nedes must excellent vertues be nothyng set by.
To throwe, caste, or shoote, sometyme to sette or lay. Iacere fundamenta, to laye the foundation.
To throwe, to reuolue, or tosse in the mynde, to vexe, to throwe downe & beate, to auaunt or glorie, to speake vaynly, to sette forth, to tosse, to caste out.
Damage or losse, proprely as whan a man hath moche goodes in a shyppe, and by force of tēpest, is constrayned to throw it into the see, leste the shyp shuld perishe.
A shot, or cast with a darte, or iauelyn.
Any thynge that maye be shotte or caste farre, moste commonly a dart or light iauelyn.
A serpent, that lyeth vnder trees, and sodaynly with a meruaylous vyolence perceth any beaste, whiche happeneth to passe by hym.
A fote in meter, whiche hathe the fyrst syllable short, the other longe.
Now late, but a whyle sens.
A lyttell whyle paste, but late. sometyme forthewith.
A towne not farre from Rome.

Some suppose to be Saturne, some to be Iaphet, one of the sonnes of Noe. Cicero calleth hym the superiour worlde, or heuen, he was made hauynge two visages, either bycause the heuen tournynge, the yere retourneth, where it beganne: orels bycause it knoweth what is passed, and aforeseeth what shall happen. This god, or rather ydoll, had a temple in Rome, which in the time of warres was alway open, and in the tyme of peace was shutte. And therfore whan in stories mencion is made, that the temple of Ianus was shutte, than is it to be vnderstande, that the Romaynes had peace vniuersally.
A coūtrey in the realme of Naples.
A wynde, which commeth out of the partes of Apulia, & is a western winde.
He whiche firste conquered the Fleece of golde.
A phisition or surgion, whiche cureth with oyntmentes.
The auncient name of Spayn, also an other countrey nye to Armeny.

A foule or byrde of Egypte, whych is high, and hath stiffe legges, and a long byl. They profytte moche to the countreye in kyllyng and eating serpentes, whiche oute of Libia be caried into Egypt, with a sowtherne wynde. Also it is taken for an enuyous person.
An yle in the see Icario, whiche is also called Icaros.

The father of the chast Penelope. There was also an other Icarus, whiche was the sonne of Dedalus, who hauinge winges, with his father flewe out of the yle of Crete: but whan he flewe higher than his father commanded him, the waxe, wherwith the fethers of his winges were glued, being molten with the heate of the sunne, and the fethers fallynge of, Icarus was constrayned to fall into the see, which was afterward callid Mare Icariū. Also Icarus is a mountain in the regiō of Athenes.
A beast in Egipte, of the greatnes of a catte, and is facioned like a mous, who crepeth into the body of a Cocodryl, whan he gapeth, & eatinge his bowels, sleeth hym. It is also a kynde of waspes.
An instrumente lyke a compasse, wherewith are made the descripcyons of the sonne.
People whiche doo lyue by eatynge of fyshe.
A fishmonger, or seller of fishe.
A ponde or stewe, wherein fyshes be fedde.
So paynted or fourmed, that in euery membre the very similitude is expressed.
A towne in the countreye of Capadocia, an other in Asie the lasse. it is also a mans owne image like him selfe.
A byrde called a yelowe hamer.
He that is disesed with the Iādis.
A white wesyll, whiche destroyeth bee stalles, and eateth the hony.
That, Id quod res est, which is trouth.
A mountayn, which lieth nigh Troy.
A cytie in the yle of Cypres.
A mountayne & a wodde in Cypres.
A famous ryuer, whiche passeth by Parthia and Inde, wherin is golden grauell, and precious stones.

A fygure conceyued in ymagynation, as it were a substance perpetuall: and lyke as of one seale procedeth manye pryntes, so of one Idea of a manne procedeth many thousandes of men, and semblably of other Ideas procedeth thynges innumerable. So that Ideae, be as it were eternal examples, wherby all other thynges be created: and this is Idea, wherof Plato speaketh.
The propre passion of a disease.
The same thynge, or the same man.
That which is offred to idols.
A shepe that was offred euery Idus to Iupyter.
A regyon in Syria, ioynynge to Egypte, and bordereth vpon Palestina.
Ides of monethes, whiche do diuide Honas from Calendes.
The lyuer of a mā, or other thynge lyuynge.
The gutte, whiche goth downe to the fundement.
To be sette on fyre, or to be made fyre.
Any thynge, oute of the whyche fyre may be beaten.
Certayne fautes, whiche erthen pottes haue in the inealynge.
Are certayne prouocations, naturally gyuen to imbrace vertue.
One of the surnames of Vulcanus.
The fyre. Sometyme it is taken for an harlotte.
A sore, wherin is an excedynge inflamation and burninge.
He that spytteth fyre: the sonne is sometyme so called.
Vnnoble, vnknowen, foolyshe, of none estimation.
Ignorance, lacke of knowlege, and is referred to the wyt of the persōne.
Lacke to be knowen, and pertaineth to the thynge or acte.
To lerne and knowe perfectly. Also to forgiue, to haue excused to knowe not, or be ignoraunt.
The leeste porcyon of a thynge, that may be imagined. Also the stuffynge of a puddynge, or other lyke thynge.
An ylande in the Tuscayne see.
Is that whiche is set in the highest part of a man.
The colycke, and he that hathe the colycke.
A tree callyd holy, or holme.
The warke of Homerus, of the syege of Troye.
A citie in the prouince of Narbone.
The propre name of a daughter of Priamus.
The propre name of a Troyane.
The name of a ryuer in the prouynce of Athenes.
Without myrthe, or lackynge myrthe or pleasure.
Thynges dilectable, whiche draweth and allurethe the mynde to imbrace them, flyckerynge intycementes.
Lawlesse, also wanton. Illex oculus, a wanton eie.
To driue or beate to a thyng.
To annoynte harde, to spotte or soyle.

Dark, whan the mone doth not shine

A countrey nowe called Slauonye, whiche hath on one parte Italy, on an nother part Germany, on the east side Grece, on the weste the Venyce see.
The kynge of Troyanes sonne, that buylded Ilium.
Baner bearers, wherin be ymages paynted.
Fygured or fourmed into an ymage.
To make ymages, or to counterfayte.
An ymage, a symylitude,Vergilsus. a shethe, or case.

The couerynge or eueisynge of the howse.

An Ilande of Thrace, and a towne in the same is so called.

To defalcate or mynyshe the auctoritie or state of a person.

Respicimus dita illuuies, immissa que barba, we behelde, O what an horryble fylthynesse and a bearde growen in lengthe. Also to bryng or sende on the contrary parte.Lact. li. 4. Hoc futurum esse dixerunt, ut post breue tempus immitteret deus regem, qui expugnater Iudaeos, It shoulde come to passe sayde they, that god shulde sende to the contrary parte a kynge, whiche shulde vanquyshe the Iewes. 〈1 paragraph〉 Alij Tarquinium a Cicerone immissum aiebant, ne C • a • ius, suscepto malorum patrocynio rempub. turbater, Some sayde, that Tarquine was brought in craftily by Cicero, lest that Crasius, in takynge on hym the defence of mysdoers, shulde therby brynge sedicyon into the weale publyke.
A tenon, whiche is put into the mortals, also a pynne, whiche is driuen into tymber, to make it ioyne and abyde.
Lette, impediment in warres. Impedimenta, is the caryage and trasyke, that goth with the hooste.
To lette, to staye, or supporte, to defyle.
Is proprelye he, that hathe his fere so bounde, that he can not goo.
To perswade instantly, to inforce, to plucke downe, or infeble.
To spende or lay out money, to bestowe, to lay out.

The chiefe capitayne in warres, nowe, the emperour.

Ful of rule, or ruling moch.
Not expert, easy to be deceiued.
A solemne commaundemente, a preeminence in gouernāce, autoritie royal.
That may be gotē by desire.
To gette by desyre or instaunce.
Infyxed, mortaysed, as it were in a stone.
To obtayne by desyre, or requeste.
Diligent, not slowe, valyant.Plautus 〈◊〉 capt. Terent. i • Phor.
To hytte oone in throwynge some thynge at hym. Impingere compedes, to putte on gyues. Dicam tibi, impingam grandem, I wyll laye a waighty matter vnto the.
To wrappe in, to tye faste,Plautus. to detayne. Implicat ad speculum caput, she bounde vp her heed at a glasse.
Wrapped or tied fast togyther. Implicitus morbo, attached or detained with syckenes.
A cloke to weare in the rayne.
A place in the house, where they vsed to receyue rayne water. It maye be englyshed a lowuer.
To put one thyng on an other. also to gyue, to inioyne, to laye to ones charge.
To make a balke in earing of lande.
Which hath no commoditie of tyme nor of place.
He that deceyueth with promises, or selleth false ware for good.
He that can not resyste his appetite or affections. sometyme it is vsurped for puissaunt.
Sometyme immoderate power▪ also vnabilitie to resyste.
At this time, or for this present tyme.
An yll man, dishonest, obstinate, wanton, malaperte, wyly, vnsacyable.
Dishonesty, vnthriftines, wantonnesse, obstynacy, malapertenes, raueny, wylynesse.
To imbrayde a manne with some defaute.
Vnware. Also not circumspecte.Vergilius. sometyme very circumspect.
A man chylde before the age of .xiiii. yeres, a mayden before .xii.
Without damage, without punyshment or griefe, in vayne.
Lacke of punyshement, libertie withoute punysshemente, pardon of punyshement.
To repute or ascribe, to lay the blame or defaute.
Sygnifieth in. Also In rempub. toward the publyke weale. In meam partem, on or for my part.
He went into the shyp. also it sygnifieth space of tyme. In noctem, vnto nyght. In lucem, vntyll day▪ also for.
To fel vpon condicon, that a thynge be done by a day.
For oone houre. In horas, frome houre to houre.
It is in his power, at hande, or easy, or in hande.
To be gyuen a parte or seuerally.
To bryng forthe to a cō mon vse or commoditie.
To come to mynde, or remembraunce, to be consydered.
To brynge downe from authoritie, to mynysshe estymation or power.
Budeus. where the landes in debate cometh in viewe, by the assignement of Iuges, vnto them whiche be called viewers, whiche shall see the boundes and quantitie of the lande in variance.
Plinius in epist. to brynge the matter to lyght, to expresse the thing perfectelye.
In a playn and euident matter.Quintii.
An ylande of Egypte, to the whiche is no commynge.
To be vayne, and of none estymation.
Empty, vacaunt, ydell, lyght in estimation.
An yle in the Tuscayne see. Also a mountayne.
Neuer harde of, straunge to here.
A rynge, or other lyke thynge, hangynge at the eare.
To be or waxe very hot.
To halter, or to bynde with a halter.
To go or walke, to goo stately, to enter.
To inflame, to sette fyre on a thynge.
A rayinge syue, wherin corne to clensed, or it be ground. also a sarcer.
To make angry, to do displesure to one, to accuse.
Is lechery cōmitted with one, whiche is nygh of kynne or aliance to him that commytteth it.Seruius. Also it sygnifyeth all maner of pollucion.
Loste. Spe incisa prius quam praedicta dies adesset, Hope beinge lost, er euer the sayd day was commen.
To happen, to fall sodaynely, to come by chaunce.
Trenches, to conuay water from a ryuer, into a medow, or other low ground.
To synge, proprely to fayne a small breste.
A cutte or garse. Also Incisurae, be the lynes in the palme of the hande.
A thynge wheron great vesselles of wyne are couched.
To call for one, to cry oute on one, rebukefully to call in.
A potte, wherin meate is sodden.
Not hauyng souped. It incoenatus cubitum, He goth to bed supperlesse.
Forgetfull, not consyderynge what he dothe.
He that dwelleth in an other countrey, than where he was borne.
To be callyd before the coūsell.
Stable, that can not be shaken.
Out of order or facyonrude. Also weryshe.
Lackynge aduyse, or consyderation, he that wyll not aske counsayle. Inconsultu meo, without my counsayle.
To sytte as women or taylours done without a stoole.
Incredible, not to be beleued, meruaylous.
To sounde or make noyse. also to rebuke, to prouoke.
A spyrite, whiche assumynge the fourme of a man, medleth with womenne. Also that whiche is called the mare, wherwith men be oppressed in their slepe.
To lye in or vpon, to cleaue to, to sytte ouer a thynge, to syt on egges, as a henne dothe, to occupie, to possede, to imbrace, to nouryshe, to dwell in, to care.
Lyenge in, syttynge to hatche egges.
He that warketh on an anuil.
To indeuour, to take in hād, to happe, to leane vppon, or fall on a thing.

He that is condempned withoute makynge aunswere.

He that accuseth or appeacheth an other man. Also he that for to escape punyshement, or for some rewarde, disclosith the conspiracie, wherevnto he was made priuie. It is also the forefinger, and a touch stone to trie golde, also the table of a boke, whereby certayne chapyters or notes be founden.
To disclose, to manyfeste, & make openly knowen, to demonstrate, to accuse, to sette or tell the price, to delyuer in possession that whiche is bought.
To denounce or declare solemnely, and for a greate cause. As battayle, fastynges, funeralles, counsayls, triumphes, and other great thinges. Also to sette a tribute or taxe, and to appoynte.
That whiche is declared or appoynted.
The cause or matter not knowen, declared or defended.
Dayly, from daye to daye. Crescente indies multitudine, The multitude or noumbre dayly increasynge.
Of the same countreye or towne borne and bredde.
Goddis made of mortall menne, some take them for priuate goddis, pertainyng to particular places.
Bokes contaynyng the names of goddis, and the mistycal sygnification of them.
To name, or cal by name.

A dullarde, that can not be taught.
Towardenes, & disposition to vertue, in chylderne, In men, token of vertue. Also very nobilitie, or honour, aptenesse to good or euyll.
That may not be made tame.
Truce, or peace for a certayn tyme.

To induce, to bryng in, to ꝑsuade, to illure, to incline, to deceiue, to cancelle, to defete, to put on, proprely hosen or shoen, to infix or stablish. Ita induxi in animū, I haue infyxed or stablyshed in my mynde.
A fourme of argument, proceding from the particulars vnto the vniuersalles. Also an argument, whyche by gettyng the assent in thinges not doubtfull, proueth the thynge, whiche is intended.

d: To graunte lyghtly, to consent to a request, to pardon.Ci. Tyr. Ter. Heau. Indulge ualetudini tuae, Take hede to thy helth. Nimiū illi indulges, Thou carist to moche for him. Also it is to gyue respite, to be gentyll and mercyfull.
To put on a garment, or other lyke thynge, to transfourme, or translate, to caste in, to annoynte.
A vertue comprehendynge bothe study and diligence, industrie.
He that is wytty and actyue.
To make dronke, or be dronk • n.
To begyn, to go in, to deserue, to gette, to wynne, to optayne, to treate.
To make a leage or treatie of peace.
To make peace. Inire bellum, to make warre. Inire uiam, to fynde the way. Also Inire, is to leape, as a horse doth on a mare. Inire fugam, to flee, as men do in batayle, to consyder, to vnderstande.
A tryflar, vsyng nothyng in order, 〈◊〉 to the purpose.
Without any science or craft, an 〈◊〉 persone, also vnprofitable.
A vyne, wherof the wyne is soo good, that none euyll procedeth therof.
That can not be shaken of, or dissolued.
Infamed. Infamis digitus, the myddel fynger.
A chylde that can not yet speake. it is also euery thyng that is very yong. Also it signifieth not eloquent, somtime an ideot that can not speake.
To infarce or stuffe, or • ylle.
A dyar, that dyeth clothe, wolle, or sylke.
Infected, dyed, stayned, poysoned. Also vndoone, or not doone, not made.
Displeased, moued with angre or hate towarde an other. Also he that beareth malyce.
To brynge in, to throw in, to adde to, to cast in, to conclude. Inferre arma, to make warre. Stuprū inferre, to cō mytte aduoutry or fornication with a kynswomanne.
Standerdes or baners displayd in battayle on bothe partes.
To do displeasure with sondry incursions or rodes.
The see occupied with pyrates and robbers.
That standethe agaynste a man, to the intent to indamage hym.
To dye clothe, to stayne o • infecte.
To inflame or set on fire.

To declare at the barre in a place of iugement, to pleade, also to perforate or make a hole.
Within, bynethe: In numbre it signifieth lasse or fewer.
Vnbroken, sure, Infractus animi, styffe of courage. sometyme it signifieth discouraged.
To crasshe the teethe for angre.
A foole, that knoweth not howe to vse a thynge.
Be the labelles, whiche do hang on euery syde of a mytar. It was in the olde tyme the attyre that priestes dyd weare on their heedes. They were also tapettes of linen, wherwith temples were hanged.
The shank or tonel of a chimney.
A tounnell, whereinto licour is poured, whan vessels are fylled.
A piele, wherwith breadde is put into the ouen.
To bowe the knee, or make courtesye.
The propre nature of a thynge. Also wytte.
Comme of an honeste stocke or kynrede.
A free man borne, or a gentylmā.
Gluttonie. Also the cray or gorge in byrdes.
Agaynst my wyll, or our wylle.
To inuade, to be imminēt, proprely spoken of battayle or tempest.
The pryuie membres of menne and womenne.
An herbe which cureth the diseases in pryuie membres.
To gape. also to couere moch.
To abhorre, to quake for feare.
To caste or throwe in, to cast at some thynge, to throwe with violence, to putte on.
To sease or take possessyon of a thynge. Manus iniectio, a sease • of lande.
Not euen or playne. Also not indifferent or iuste, sometyme great, strait, or narrowe.
To instructe in thynges concernynge relygion. Initiatus, instructed or entred in rules concerning religion. also to begyn to do a thynge.
To begynne: also to be weaned, as chylderne be.
A beginnyng, a sacrifice to Ceres.
Catell neuer yoked or broken, whiche were sometyme sacrificed.
To inioyne, to appoynt, to lay on, as a mā wil adde to a great burdein.
Wronge, iniurie, reproche, damage. Taken like an aduerbe, it signifyeth, without cause, without deserte.
Wrongfull, he that doth any thynge agaynst the lawe.
Vnharmefull, he that doth none harme.
Wherin is no damage, that whiche can do none harme.
To graunt or assent with noddynge of the heed.
The name of Cadmus daughter, the wyfe of Athamas kynge of Thebans.

He that dwelleth in a place, where neither he, nor his auncetoures were borne.
To be madde or peuysshe, to dote, to do vnaduisedly.
Madde, peuyshe, doting, regarding no counsell, frowarde, vntractable.
To write in or vpon, to name or intitle.
Vnwritten, written vpon, named, or intitled.
Be all flyes and wormes, that be diuided in their bodies, the heed and breaste from the bealy and tayle, as bees, waspes, emotes, or pismeres, and suche lyke.
To set in, to ioyn. whan it hath inseui, insitū, it sygnyfyeth to greffe.
The bond or thonge, wherwith a tergat or buckeler is hanged on a mans arme.
To sytte on, to sytte in, or be in, to besiege, to abyde in a place.
Wiles to intrap a mā, er he be ware.
To practyse wyles, to intrappe or betray a man.
To entre to thintēt to abide.

Signes or tokens of honour, wherby euery astate or great auctoritie is knowen, as robes, maces, swordes borne vpright, cappes of mayntenaunce, and other lyke thynges. Also somtyme tokens of doctrine and vertue: as staues typped with syluer, which bedels bere before doctors, hodes furred, crownes of laurell. &c.
To note with somme sygne. Also to doubbe knyghtes.
Notable, excellent, marked with some speciall token to be knowen.
To accuse or appeale, also to fayne or dissemble.
To bringe into, to conioyne, to put in a mans mynd couertly & craftily.
A colourable & crafty beginning of an oration, dissembling som thing. where the matter may not be fauorably herde.
To set fast and fyrmely, to indeuour, to prouoke or solicite. somtime to assyst.
The greffe. Also a iegot or other lyke meate stuffed with flesshe and egges chopped or mynced.
Not wont or accustomed, haut, arrogant, presumptuous.
Seldomnes of vse in any thynge. vnhauntynge of a place. Also presumption wanton pride.
To drie in the sonne, to blech.
Slepy, or he that slepith moch.
To beholde attentiuely▪ to wayte on.
To beholde, to ouersee, to controll, to consyder a thing throughly.
A beholdynge, an ouersyghte,Cicero. Ti. Liuiꝰ a controllemente.
To make a thyng smalle, like to a wheate reede.
An instant, the least part of time.
To new make, or begin any thīg. somtime to renue or reform, to reedify

It is nigh, it is com, it is at hand. Caesar ubi se diutius duci intellexit, et diē instare, qua die frumentum militibus metiri oportebat, whā Cesar ꝑceiued that he was delayed, & the day. was nigh come, whan he muste nedes delyuer corne to his men of warre.
A coūterpoynt. also it signifieth all tapisry, which serueth to couer any thing.
A chapman, a mercer, also he that selleth apparayle and fyne stuffe, goinge about therwith.
To institute, to begynne, to instructe or teache, to ordayne.
Ancient maners & customs, also ordināces. Pro meo instituto, for my purpose.
To require instantely, to solicite, to stycke to, to resiste, to persist, to prease on, to come on, or immediatly folowe. Instat, it is nowe.
The trappier or apparayle of an horse, a horseclothe.
An instrument or toole. Also ordinance of warre, vessell and all necessaries of household and husbandry. sometyme it signifieth a dede or charter, cōcernyng lande dettes or couenantes.
To sette in order or aray, to instructe, to fournyshe, to prepare.
Lumbardes, proprely menne of the duchy of Melayne.
An ile inuirōned with water. It is also a hous in a town, hauīg none other hous ioyned to it, but stretes on euery syde of it.
Mooste vyle, proprely men banyshed into Iles to dygge mettall.
To leape vppe, to scorne or speake in the reproche of a man.
A leapynge vp or into a thyng.
To spende or lay out money.
Yf it be spoken of age, it signifieth yong & lusty: if it be spokē of a mā it signifieth honest in al poyntes & qualites, in a thynge it sygnyfyeth entier or hoole.
It is in my power, or at my pleasure, at myne arbiterment.
Goddesses, hauynge power to doo harme.
Mydnyght, whan all thing is in sylence.
The caulme of the water,Salustiꝰ in Iugurth. whan there is no tempeste.
Thinge out of tyme or season. Intempestiue, vntymely.
To bende or stretche. Also to loke diligently on a thynge, to knytte or tie, to inforce with myght.
To set or fixe the mynde.
Signifieth to do a thynge vnaduisedly, and without any iugement.
Signifyeth not intente or purpose, but for the act that is apointed or executid.
In the poynte to peryshe and be vtterly loste.
The inwardes of man or beast.

o: Intercalaris, re, & inter calarius, a, um,
n: intercalaris re amp inter calarius a um
d: Put or set betwene. Intercalaris dies, the daye of the leape yere.
The moneth, in the whiche certayne dayes were sette, that lacked to make the yere complete, whych moneth is Februarye.
A syngular verse, often repeted amonge other verses. Some doo call it, in englyshe balades and songes, the foote or refrette of a ditie.
To make intercessiō. also to go betwene, or be betwene.
There is amite betwene the and me. Tribuni intercesserunt, The tribunes dyd let or prohibite.
A let or prohibition of the Tribunes agaynst the auctoritie of other offycers.
To cut asōder in ye middis.Vide Cale pinum.
To decaye or perisshe betwene this and that.
To synge betwene or in the myddell of a thynge.
To preuent or apprehēd one vnware, to take in the middes, or in the meane while, sometyme to take all.
Were dayes diuided, part holy day, parte warkedaye.
To shut in, to stoppe, to let.
A disease betwene the skinne and the fleshe: whan it is an adiectiue it signifieth inwarde. Intercutibus uitiis madentes, ouerwette with inwarde vices.
To prohibite greuousely: also to resyste or lette.
In the meane while, also neuer the lesse. Interea loci, in the meane space.

o: Interest mea, tua, sua, nostra, uestra,
n: interest mea tua sua nostra uestra
d: It behoueth me, the, him, vs, you, or it ꝑtaineth to me, the, hym, &c. also it maketh matter, or is a diuersitie. Nihil interest tui, It is no matter to the. Si nihil interest regis, peto ut dum dico, uinculis liberer, If it be noo matter to the kyng. I pray you, whiles I do speake, lette me be without gyues. Sometime it signifieth to be in the myddes.
A womans priuy tokē, wherby she is knowen from a man.
A wall added to an olde foundation or walle, to sustayne it.
To put betwene, to cast betwene.
In the myddell of that place.
In the mean space or time, in the mean reason also sometime, sodainly, otherwhile.
To speke in a mās tale.
To shyne betwene, or in the myddes.
To make a glade in the myddell of a wodde.
The space of tyme, in the whiche neither the old mone doth appere, nor the newe moone is seene.
To flowe betwene, to wasshe betwene meales, or other actes.
The newe mone at the very chaunge.
The tyme whan the moone is at the poynt to chaunge.
To leaue or put of for a time.
Warre to vtter distruction or dethe.
A ioynt in a mans fynger. also a ioynt in a strawe or rede.
To knowe a thynge amonge other thynges.
A messager, or meane betwene two persons being at variance.
That whiche is within, or inward.
A space betwene that which is in order. Interordo, dinis, idem.
To interrupt or lette one that speaketh or dothe any thynge, also to require, to aske or demaunde.
Certayne pieces of tymber, whiche are sette frome the corners of the walle, to the endes of the rafters, to conuaye rayne water into the spoutes.
Walles, which rise vppon an other walle, and haue no fundacion in the grounde.
To putte or sette betwene, to renewe or refreshe any thynge.
He or she that refresheth olde thynges, and do make them seme newe.
Salust • ▪ in Iugurth. to promise vpon the credence & consent of all the people.
An interpretour or translatour. Also a styckler betwene two, whiche are at varyaunce.
That whiche is playne betwyxte two partes grauen or imbosed.
He that ruleth in the meane tyme, betwene the cessynge of the auctoritie of one principall gouernour, by deth or otherwise, vntylle an other be elected into the same offyce.
The saide meane tyme of gouernaunce or rule.
To be tried by examinatiō, that they had offēded against the lawis.
The spaces betwene the oores in a bore or galey.
The space betwene the shulders vnder the necke.
To diuide in the middel with some inclosure.
The gristell, which maketh particion betwene the nosethrilles.
To sowe or set betwene or in the myddes.
To make noyse in the middes or betwene.
To spring vp in the middes.
To strawe betwene, or throwe thynges betwene.
To be present. also to differ, to be diuers. Stulto intelligēs quid interest? What diuersitie is there betwene a fole and a wise man?
Wouē or wrought betwene. or • inselde, as cloth of tinsyl, or bawdekyn.
Gallynge, whiche hapneth by the occasion of sweate betwene the legges, the toes, or fyngers.
The losse of bothe partes, or on bothe sydes.
To be vacant or void betwene
To come in the meane while, to be present amonge other.
To take away craftily or falsly.
To visite among, or now & thā.
He whiche by the law can make no testamēt. somtime it signifieth detestable.
He that dyeth without makynge any testament, intestate. Also he that dieth makyng none heyre by testament. also a mā out of credence, whome no manne wylle take for a wytnesse.
The bowelles, or inwarde parte of man, or other thynge lyuynge.
Where people do warre within their owne realme.
Hate with hart & mynde, mortall hatrede.
The inwarde buyldynge of tymber and pargette.
To depe, as one dothe his fynger into lycour.
To thrust in by throwing of a darte, or other lyke thynge. Also to tourne or wynde in.
Within. Intra modum, lesse thanne a meane, shorte of a meane.
Les thā the opiniō that mē haue.
Damage eyther to the gyuer, or to the receyuour.
Cicorie or white endiue.Galenus. Plinius. Columel.
To inuade, to entre, to app̄hēd.
To waxe stronge, to be confyrmed or stablyshed.
Orations made ageynst one in reprouyng his maners and lyuynge.
To carye in a thinge, to carye a thynge into a place.
To rebuke one vehemently, and with violent and soore wordes.
To fynde a thing, whiche a man seeketh for.
To be sworne as princis coū saylours and seruantes be sworne vnto thē. Also to do feaultie.
To tourne in, to tourne vppe so downe, to turne in and out after the vulgar speche, proprely to turne euery thyng contrary to the ryght fourme or facion.
Yonge children without heare on their bodies.
To seke out, to finde in seking.
That maye not be founde with sekynge.
To adorn or garnishe a thing.
Olde shrewes or vnthriftes, me • in lyuynge vnthriftily waxed olde.
To were out for age, to be oute of vse, to be aged or olde. Also worne out, almoste consumed.

Togither, one the other. Inuicem d •• gunt, they do loue one an other. also it signifieth for thy parte. Habes res urbanas, inuicem rusticas scribe, Nowe thou knowest the affaires of the citie, for thy parte write what is done in the countrey.
Enuy, griefe to beholde or here that an other man prospereth.
To haue enuy at an others prosperitie. Inuideo tibi doctrinam, I haue enuy at thy lernynge. Also to see inwardly or through a thynge.
The displeasure of his acte, or attemptate, or the dede wherfore he was enuied and hated.
A thynge, whiche bredeth enuye or hatred.
An enuyous persone. sometyme he, whiche is enuied.
To haue watche of a thynge, or to lay watche, to care.
Neuer sene. also hatid or odious.
Boden, as to a feaste or bankette.
To bydde. also to delyte, to fylle the bealy.
Vnwyllynge, or agaynste a mannes wylle.
Lackynge a way, or where nothynge can passe.
To make shadowe: somtyme it signifieth to defende.
To catche, as it were with an hooke.
To calle in, to call for helpe, also not to calle.
To steale, to lay violent handes on one, to flee out.
A byrde not redy to flee.
As a thinge whiche is wrappped togither.
A worme lyke a canker. whyche is on vynes, and whan he is taken of, he wrappeth hym selfe rounde togither.
An interiection, signifieng sometyme grefe, as in Tibullo. Vrorio, O I burne. Sometyme excessiue gladnesse. as in Ouidio. Dicite io paean.
To speke merily, or in disport.

n: iocosus a um amp iocularis lare

d: The sonne of Iphiclus, of whom the people of Sardinia, were named Iolenses.
The daughter of Euritus, kynge of Aetolia, whom Herculus loued.
A region of the lasse Asia, wherein were the citie of Ephesus, Milerum, & Clazomenae.
A stone of a vyolet colour.

o: Ionicus, ca, cum, & Ionius, a, um,
n: ionicus ca cum amp ionius a um

d: A citie of the countrey of Palestina, not farre from Ierusalem, standyng by the see, whiche some men do suppose to be the hauyn, callyd Port Iaffe.
A ryuer of Iudea, commonly callyd flume Iordane.
An yle where Homerus was buried.
Were men of armes, so called of Maximian the emperoure, whiche dydde valyantly in the countrey of Illiria.
The wyfe of Melāpos, whom for her beautie Iuno tourned into furye or madnesse.
The daughter of kyng Agamemnon, with whom he dydde sacrifice going to Troye.
A lyttell worme, bredynge in hornes and vynes.
He, she, that same, by demonstratynge or shewynge the persone or thynge spoken of.
Plates embosed like to fygures or images of men or women.
The sonne of Praxonidis, whiche fyrste ordayned the solempne playes callyd Olympiada.
The holownesse of the hande. sommetyme it sygnifieth the hole hande.
Wrathe, an appetite to punyshe him, of whom we be offended.
Angre, displeasure agaynst one, a desyre to be reuenged.
To consente to the sentence or raison of an other, which hath spoken, or to be of the same opinyon.
He whiche is in auctoritie to see peace kepte in a countreye or citie, which amonge vs may be callyd a Iustice of the peace.
The rayne bowe. it is also a floure deluce, the roote wherof is verye soote, and is commonly called Yreos.

Is a fygure in speakynge, whanne a man dissemblyth in speche that whyche he thynketh not: as in scoffyng or bourdyng, callynge that fayre, whyche is fowle in dede, that good, whiche is yl, that eloquēt, which is barbarous. Semblably reasoning contrary to that I thinke, to the intente to mocke hym, with whome I doo dyspute or reason.
He that vsethe that fasshyon in speakynge.
That may not be rewarded or recompensed.
That maye not be repaired or restored to the fyrste astate.
To be taken or holden in, as it were in a nette.
Taken, lapt in with crafte, or faire promyses.
To water grounde, to brynge water into the fieldes out of a ryuer.
The grounde or fielde that may be easyly watered. sometyme the water, whyche may be easyly diryuied into the fieldes.
To make voyde & of none effecte.
Voide, of none effect or force.
Hauynge the laste syllable sauynge one, longe, to prouoke, to kendyl wrathe, to styrre vppe.
To breake in, or enter with force. somtyme to breake asonder.
To rounne hastilye or furiousely into battayle, or vppon any thynge. sometyme to falle in, or cast in.
A famouse rhetorician, whiche inuētid to make euery matter cōpendious.
A waye to introduce, or begyn to teache.
A ryuer commynge oute of the Rone, where the hylle callyd Cemenus is ioyned to the Rone: and so runneth by Druentia into the goulfe of Venyse.
An yle ageynste Velia, callydde also Oenotris.
A region of the lasse Asia.
A cite in the countrey of Pāphilia.
The houckle bone. it is somtyme taken for the ache in the sayde bone, whiche vulgare phisicions do call Sciatica.
He that hathe the ache in the hyppe, cōmonly callid Sciatica.
The priestes of the goddesse Isis.
Called also Io, one of the harlottes of Iupiter, whom he tourned into a cowe for feare of Iuno his wyfe.
A certeyne puddynge. some calle it an Isynge.
The name of an excellent minstrel, whiche played on the shalmes.
A ryuer in the cuntrey of Boeotia.
Where two sentences are in lyke lengthe.
The name of a famous oratoure, of wonderfulle eloquence, oute of whose schole proceded the moste excellente oratours of Grece.
A fourme of buyldynge, where euery thynge is equally strayght.
Equalite of lawes, as where they be indifferent & like to al maner of persons.
An yle in the Venician see ioynynge to Slauonie.
A citie in Sicile, and a ryuer of Siria.
The great ryuer callyd Danubius, in • uche Danowe.
The greattest ryuer of Europa, called also Danubius, Danowe.
A narowe parte of the countreye, where two sees are but a small distaunce asonder. There be dyuers suche places in Grecia, and of them were certayn playes called Isthmia.
A parte of Italye, marchynge on Illiria, callyd nowe Slauonye.
A citie in Italia, whiche by an nother name is called Confiniū, There is an other in Spayn, where Silius Italicus was borne.
A iourneye. also a way. Iter habeo ad Caesarem, I take my iorney to the emperour.
To do a thynge eftesoones, to goo backe agayne.
A towne in Peloponeso, an nother in Thessaly.
A towne on the mountain of Taurꝰ.
The name of Priapus the most dishonest and abhominable ydoll. Also the secrete membre being in prosperite.

A commentarye or boke of remembraunce, contaynynge thynges commytted in iourneyes. Also it is a kalender of myles in the distance of places, with the tyme of abode in euerye place, lyke to iestes of princis.
A region in Arabia, or Siria, of whiche the people are callyd Ituraei.
A goinge. Quid noster itus & reditus, what our goinge and commyng.
The sonne of Tereus and Prognes, who, as poetes doo fayne, was tourned into a fesaunt.
The mane of a beaste. Also the name of a kynge of Barbarye.
A sterre, whiche is also callid Lucyfer and Hesperus. it is sometyme taken for bryghtenesse.
To commande, to desire, to wyshe, to exhorte, to decree.
To declare in the voyce, the ioye and gladnesse of the harte, whiche maye not be expressed with wordes.
Ioye and gladnes in voyce, not expressed in wordes.
He or that, whiche is the cause that an nother reioyseth, dylectable, pleasaunt to see or here.
Iewry, or the countrey of Iewes.
He that hath auctoritie of his propre iurysdiction, to sytte in iugemēt without commission. As the chiefe Iustice of Englande, the Mayre of a cytie incorporate, and a Coroner.
He that sytteth by cōmission, as all other iudges and iustices.
Pertaynynge to a iuge, or that whiche is to be iuged.
To iudge or deeme, to suppose,Lau. Vall • in Barpt, i • ciū. lib. • . to gyue sentence, to condemne.
Was amonge paynyms the god, whom they supposed to haue auctoritie ouer the rydges of hylles.
A streete in Rome, where was an aultar of Iuno, whyche men supposed dyd ioyne matrimonie surely.

As moche grounde as one yoke of oxen wyll eare in a day. som suppose it to contayne in length 240. feete, in bredth halfe so moche. some saye, that it is more. Leonardus Portius saythe, by the auctoritie of Columella, that Iugerum containeth .xxviii. thousand & .viii. hūdred fete.
Oxen lyke in greatnes, callid yokes, or payres.
A celestyalle Sygne, contaynynge thre sterres.
To slee, not onely with weapon, but also with syckenes. Quartana neminem ingulat, The feuer quartayn sleeth no mā.
The foreparte of the necke, whyche is dyuided in two great synewes.Cels. Is. 4. Dexter, & sinister.
To slee proprely in the neck.

Whan an oratour or man of lawe, toucheth vehemently the poynte of the matter, and with manyfest and sore argumentes and reasons, seemeth to assaulte and oppresse the contrarie parte, as it were with sharpe weapons.

A yoke. also the rydge of an hyll or banke, also the beame, wheron weauers do tourne their webbe. Also a thynge lyke to a galowes, vnder the whiche in sygne of reproche, they whiche were vanquisshed, were constrayned to creepe, whiche was made with two speares standynge, and one speare ouerthwarte. Also a frame, wheron vynes are ioyned. Also a beame, whereon balāces do hange. Also the syde beames in a shyppe, in the whyche the traunsomes are fastened.
A citie in the yle of Caea, the countrey of Simonides the poete.
A kynred, whiche proceded from Ascanius, sonne of Aeneas, callyd Iulus. also a towne in Cales, in the coūtrey of Spain.
The moneth of Iuly, which toke his name of Iulius Cesar.

Otherwise namid Ascanius, the sonne of Aeneas. Iulus, is also a litle worme with many fete, bredynge in vynes & okes, whiche is also callyd Conuoluolus, Inuoluolus, & Voluola. It is also the mosynesse of the outwarde parte of fruites. Also the yonge fruite immediately after that the flowres be fallen.
Be also the mosynesse or softe heares, whiche do growe on the beardes & visages of yong men, before that they be shauē: and somtyme it signifieth the same yonge men.
Is also a fyshe, whiche is guyde vnto whales: whiche also is called Hegeter. it is moreouer a songe dedicate to Diana.
Euerye beaste that drawethe or beareth burdeyns. also a lyttel carre.
Meate callid iunkettes: also a freshe chese made on rushes, callid a iackeman.
A spyce that is medicinable, specially to make the brethe swete.
People in the coūtrey of Liguria.
The monethe callyd Iune. also a mannes name.
The wyfe of Iupyter, it is sometyme taken for the ayre.
Be two of the fortunate Iles.

The name of a greate prynce, whiche for his wysedom and prowes was honoured of the gentyles for chiefe of all goddes, It is also the name of a planette, whiche is alwaye beneuolent in his influence and course.
A braulynge, or a small contention.
Accordynge to the lawe, or belongynge to the lawe.
Power, or auctoritie to ministre and execute lawes.

Lawe, auctoritie, lybertie, power, ryght. somtyme the place, where the lawe is ministred. Also lycour or iuyce. De iure meo, tuo, suo decedere, to omytte some part of the rygour or extremitie of the lawe. Pro suo iure agere, & summo: iure agere, to take the extremite of the lawe. Summū ius, the rygour of the lawe.
Brothe, wherein meate hath den sodden.
A solempne othe or promyse made to GOD.
Sacrifices done for deed men: now it may be vsed for funerall exequies.
Cicer pro Roscio. is proprely in funeralle obsequies, to do and performe al thinges thervnto necessarie.
A cessynge for a tyme from minystration of lawes in places iudiciall.
A iuste or rightuous man, an vpright and true meanynge manne. It is taken ofte tymes in holy scripture for a vertuouse mā or good man.

Equall. meane betwene twoo extremities. Iusta magnitudo, neither more nor lesse, the iuste quantitie. somtyme it sygnifyeth greatnesse. Iusta pars, the greatte parte. Iusto labore, with great labour. Iustas inimicitias, great hostilitie. sometyme it signifieth amonge lawyers, true or very. Iustus filius, his very sonne.
Playes vowed for the helthe of yonge menne.
Is also the name of a poete, whiche wrate Satyres.
Yonge, not onely men but also beastes. Iuuenculus, idem.
Youthe. sometyme a multitude of yonge men.

Nighe, ioyntly or togither, euen like, accordynge.Salustiꝰ in Catalinar. Nunc uero quo in loco res nostrae sint, iuxta mecum oēs intelligitis, Nowe howe the matter standeth, ye all knowe as well as I: or els, in what case our busynes is, ye vnderstande all as moche as I do.
A greate whyte byrde, of the kynde of Rauens.
A manne or womanne hauynge greatte lyppes.
A spotte, whiche sodeynely hapneth to thynges that are smothe, a blemyshe.

Lyppes. Also Labrum is the brymme or brynke of a ryuer or fountayne. Also a fatte or lyke vessell necessarie to be bayned in. somtyme a fatte for wyne after that it is pressed. It may be vsed for a keele vate, wherinto ale or beere is putte.
Was the name of the sonne of Minos, who was named also Glaucus.
Vnstable, whyche wylle soone falle, slypper.
To slyde, to dye, to fayle, to fall downe by lyttell and lyttell.
The name of a countrey in Italye, vulgarly called Terra laboris, the lande of laboure.
A felde in Campania, where the stubbyll of corne is so great, that the people do burne it in stede of wodde.
To laboure, to be in heuynesse or griefe.
A maase, or any buildyng made like a maase, out of the which it were hard to gette forthe.
A kynde of apparayle. also a woman of Lacedemonia.
A citie in the parte of Grece, which is nowe called Moraea, wherof Menelaus was kynge.
A shorte cloke, whiche menne of warre be wont to weare.
Cloked, or cladde in a cloke.
To teare in pieces, or to gyue many woundes.
A Lyzerde, an Euet: also the parte of a mannes arme, from the elbowe to the wreste of the hande, proprely the brawne and synewes of the arme.

To rent, or goo aboute to rent the good renoume of a man. Also to prouoke a man to wrathe or displesure, with wordes, writynge, or acte: to rayle on a man, to prycke a man with some yll language or acte.
One of the thre ladies called Parcae, whiche poetes dyd fayne, to haue the rule and contynuance of mans lyfe.
Gardinges of a garment, proprely where the skirtes be cutte in sondry facion. In lacinias, in peces. Lacinia, is also a redde musheron, whiche springeth at the rote of a chesten tree.
Cutte in sondrye facions, wyndyng and tournynge dyuers wayes.
An elbowe of lande, lyenge betwene the see, called Hadriaticum, and the see callyd Ionium.
Meate made of mylke, all herbes, whiche haue iuyce lyke mylke.
He that maketh sondry meates of mylke.
Places within the rybbes of a man, benethe the nauyll, soo tender, that it maye not suffre any wounde or stroke, as Probus sayth. Some say that they be caules, wherin the small bowelles do lye.
To be tourned into mylke, or to be fylled with mylke.
Of mylke or lyke milke, also that whiche is nourished with mylke.
To fede with milk, also to deceiue with faire wordes.
A dyche, wherin water standeth. also a trenche, wherby fieldes are drayned, Some englyshe it, a synke.
A beame of tymber. Also suche a thynge as doth yet hange in marchauntes houses, ouerthwart their halles, whereon be set a great numbre of candelles.

A depe place alway full of water whiche is deriuied into brokes and riuers, also the vesselle, whyche receyueth wyne, whanne the grapes are pressed. Also the pryncipalle beame that gothe ouerthwarte the howse.
A swete gumme, whiche goth into the makynge of pommanders.
To derogate anye thynge of the kynges auctorytie or prerogatiue.
Heresye, or lollardy, contempt of religion or ceremonies.
The rewarde gyuen to hym that vanquyshed at playenge or fyghtynge with weapons.
A garment lyned, whiche the dyuynours callyd augures, dyd weare.
The name of one, which wrate the lyues of Phylosophers.
Compasse or mucke layde in the fieldes, to make corne and grasse to growe plentuousely.
Gladnesse, reioycynge of the mind, whiche doth also appere outwardly.
To be gladde, or to reioyce with outwarde sygnes.

A good shepe. Laeta seges, & letū legumen, plentyfull corne and grayne. All other thynges, not hauynge lyfe, beinge called Laeta, do sygnifye dilectable to beholde, or that do please the eye of the beholder.
To plane, or make playne, or to polyshe.
Verses, whiche do halt in the myddes of the foote.
Be thynne cakes made with floure and water, wherto was putte fatte brothe, pepper, saffron, and cynnamom.
One of the names of the ile of Delos.
A kynde of fyshe, whiche maye be called the hare fyshe.
He that hathe eien lyke a hare, or in whom the ouerlyds of the eien do not meue downewarde.
A warren or parke of hares.
The name of a famouse harlotte, vnto whom for her beautie repaired the richest men of Grece.

To speake lyke a baby: in the whiche worde the greke doth approche nerer to the englishe than to the latine, as babazin, whiche made a latine worde, 〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉 is babare, it maye be transferred to the mother or norice, that babeleth with hir childe whan she giueth to it the dugge.
To lycke with the tounge. also to touche, to flowe, or runne softly.
A ryuer in Italy, whiche meteth with the ryuer of Po, called Padus.
People dwellyng about the sayd ryuer of Lambrus.

Be women, whyche beholdynge, chyldren, or gyuyng to theym gyftes, doo alter the fourme of them, whiche children be afterwarde called elfes, or taken with the fayrye. And some suche women wylle sucke the bloudde from chyldern. They be also those, whyche be called ladyes of the fayry, whiche do allure yong men to company carnally with them, & after that they be consumed in the acte of lecherye, they coueyte to deuoure them.
Is also a beaste, whiche hath a womans face, and the fete of a horse. It was also the surname of a noble Romayne, and also of a famous harlot.
One of the sonnes of Hercules.
A leame of fyre, or brightenes of the sonne, moste vsed for a lampe.
A citie on the border of Asia, vpon the ryuer called Hellespontus.
A gloo worme, or a worme callid a globerde.
A wulle man, or he that occupieth or selleth wolle.
A fishe so called for his whitenes and softenes.
A spanish iauelin with a brode heed.
Armed with a iauelyn. also woū ded with a iauelyn.
A dyshe, whiche of some is callid a potenger. also a balance.
To strike, to rent with the teth.
A garment made of vndied woll.
A beast, whiche is found aboute the ryuer of Po.
To languyshe, to be sycke, to be faynt, to be aferd, to be idell.
Langettes of aumbre, lyke to longe beadestones.
Languour, faylyng of strēgth and naturall all moysture.
The flesh shambles, or shop where fleshe is solde. Sommetyme it sygnyfyethe dismembrynge.
He that dothe worke woulle, to make it mete for the clothyar. It maye be called also a woll wynder.
He that had the reule ouer sworde players, and caused them to be taught, and after solde them. Also that ordayned byrdes to fyghte.
To put in woll, or to dresse wt woll.
The soft heares or mosynes in the vysages of chylderne and women. Also on fruites called peaches, and some herbes as longe wort, clary, and suche other.
An herbe called Clote ▪ whiche beareth bourres, that cleauen to clothes and cattell.
To be made or tourned into a stoone.
To strike with stoones. also to strike somtyme without stones.
A lytle stone, also a precious stone.
To make harde as a stone.
A stone but lasse than that, whiche is called Saxum.
Is sommetyme taken for a myle. Ad tertium aut quartum lapidem, at the thirde or the fourthe myle. De lapide empti, were slaues or bondmen solde.
People of Thessalie, of whom Perithous was kynge.
A falle. Also a small offence done by neglygence, an ouersight.
A citie in the yle of Cypres.
The roufe of a chaumber, which is imbowed or fretted. also a playne beame in a rouffe.
Haltered, snarled, tyed or bounde faste. sommetyme it sygnyfieth holowe or bowynge.

Goddes, whiche the paynyms didde suppose euery person had belongyng vnto hym▪ which were also called Penates, both the whiche wordes be also taken for pryuate dwellynges or houses. Mei lares, mei penares, my house or dwellynge place.
A priuate chappell or closette in a mannes house.
Larde, or the fat of an hogge. sometyme swynes flesshe salted.
A famous harlotte, which bycause she made the people of Rome her heyre, they named her a goddesse, and callydde hyr Flora.
Lyberalle expenses, to wynne a mannes pourpose.
The name of one citie in Thessalia, an other in Asia, the thyrde in Italy.
A brooke by the citie of Comum.
A tree of the kynde of firre, out of the whiche issueth a soote gumme.
A spyrite, whiche apperethe in the nyght time. Some do call it a hegge, some a goblyn. Also a masker, or he that weareth a visour. it is sometyme taken for the same visour.
He that is feared with a spirite, & is becomme madde. It sommetime signyfieth a masker.
An ymage defourmed, pale, leane, and horrible to beholde.
The iuyce of an herbe called Laserpitium, commendable in sondry medicines.

n: lasseo amp lassesco lassus sum sere

d: An yle in the see called Egeū. It was also called Andros.
A priuye place, where men do hyde them. Sommetyme it sygnifieth an excuse.
Where as be many priuye places.
The name of a cōsul of Rome, of whose hous was made a church of sainte Iohn̄, whiche is nowe callid Lateranensis.
All maner of lycour: but it is moste commonly taken for water.
A dungeon in the prison at Rome.
Of latin, of that part of Italy, whiche was called Latium.
A denne or bury, where beastis do hyde them. somtime it is vsed for a secrete place or caue, wherin men be hidde.
A greatte or large felde, great and large possessions.
Sacrifyces to Iupiter named of the latins, who fyrst dyd ordayne them.
Latin, or of the people callyd latines.
The propre name of Aeneas father in lawe.
A mountayne in Ionia, where poetes say the mone kyssed Endymion.
Was a strayte prison in the citie of Syracusis in Sicilia, an other in Spartha. It is also a quarry, out of the whiche stones are dygged.
Was mother of Apollo and Diana.
Called also Diana, and is also taken for the moone.
The honour and seruyce, wherewith god onely is worshypped.
To barke as a dogge dothe.
To robe, also to serue in warres.

Robbers by the high waye. Also souldyours retayned. Amonge the Romaynes it were those, whyche were alwaye aboute the kynges or Emperoures persone, as the garde is aboute the king. Also Latrones, seu Latrunculi, be chessemenne, with whiche menne doo playe at the chesse.
