A citie in Italy, now callid Narnia.
In the olde tyme they vsed for nequeunt, they may not.
Nymphes or maidens of the see.
Was called oone of the goddis of the see, and somtime it is put for the see.
The wife of Mars, called god of battayle.
A certayne kynde of shelle fysshe. see Plinie.
An yle or citie nyghe to Epirus, a countrey of Grece.
Where saint Iames the apostelle lyeth. It is also a lyttell tree, hauyng leaues lyke to an almonde tree, but greatter and fatter.
The name of an emperour, of a monstruous and cruell nature.
He that hath pein in his sinewes.
A towne in the countreye callyd Lucania.
That whiche hath many sinewes. It is somtyme taken for stronge.
A synewe, it signifieth sommetyme strength. Also stockes, wherin offenders be put. Nerui be also stringes of an instrument. Sometyme it sygnifieth the priuye membre of a manne.
A countrey in Sicile, ioynynge to the hyll of Ethna, which alway sendeth forth flames of fyre or smoke.
To not know, to be ignorant of a thynge.
He that dothe not knowe, or is not knowen.
A nymphe or mayden of the see.
A place, where duckes are kepte to be made fatte.
A Capytayne of the Grekes, which were at Troy, who lyued the ages of thre olde men, and in gyuynge counsell was excellent.
A citie of Vmbria, whyche is a parte of Italy.
In no maner of wyse, in no condicion.
Neyther on the one parte, nor the other.
A marke in the vysage or body of a manne or womanne, as a mole, a redde or blacke warte.
Any thynge that may be knit.

n: nexo as amp is nexui nexere

d: Free men, that do bynde theym selues to labour or seruyce,Var •• . to be acquited of the dettes, whiche they owe.
To be bounde by oblygation or couenaunt. also to be wrapped in bondes, as is the commune sayenge.
The propre name of a man.
Thynges gyuen for vyctorie, as rynges, colers of golde, and crownes or garlandes.
A citie in Egipte, where the emperour Octauian vanquysshed Antonie & Cleopatra.
A citie in the countrey of Bithinia, in the lasse Asia.
The mother of Euander the old kynge of latynes.
To vent as the hound doth, whiche foloweth the dere or hare, or other game.
A wynkynge, as whan one doth sygnifie his mynde to an other by loking.
Somtime to sauor, somtime to shine.
A sauour or smell of some thing burned or rosted: sometyme it signifyeth grennynge. also brightnes.
To brede as a byrde dothe, to make a neste, or eyre.
A neste, sommetyme it signifieth the byrde that bredeth. Also a vesselle lyke to a neste. Also Nidi be coffyns, wherin marchantes do lay their sondry wares.
A wiede growinge in corne, callyd also Lolium, cockle. Also a blacke seede, good to smelle vnto agaynste rewmes or distillations.
Blacke, fowle. Also it is sometyme vsed for deed.
A fountayne in Ethiopia, whiche is of somme men supposed to be the heed of the greatte ryuer Nilus.
To make blacke, also to be black.

o: Nihil cum fidibus graculo, Nihil cum amacino sui,
n: nihil cum fidibus graculo nihil cum amacino sui
d: The dawe hathe nothynge to doo with the lute: nor the sowe with maiorā: A prouerbe applyed to them, whiche presumynge to moche of their owne wyttes, do meddel malapertly with thinges, wherof they can no skylle.
A stone lyke a Topace, but that it is more duskyshe.
A great ryuer in Egipte, callyd also Geon, and is one of the greattest ryuers of the worlde.
The bringer of storms or shoures.
An yle in the see called Ionium.
A sodayne great showre or storme of rayne or hayle. Also a cloude or a great wynde, also a vessell, oute of the whyche wyne is drawen or powred.
Vndoubtedly, surely. somtyme it signifieth but yet, no meruayle.
To good. Nimis malus, to ylle.
Wherof is to moch, or excesse.
A great cite in Assyria, also an other greatte citie in the corner of Iudea, towarde Arabia.
A great kynge of Assiria, & Babilon.

A woman, who hauynge a greatte numbre of chyldren, and they beyng deed all at ones, so moche lamented and sorowed, that she loste hir speche: wherfore the paynyms fayned, that she was turned to a stone.
A ryuer in the coūtrey of Scithia
Was of olde tyme vsed for nobis.
A place in Media, where fayre horses were bredde.
A kynges name, of whome it is fayned, that he had one golden heare. It is also a kynde of haukes.
A seld mouse. Also a glow worme that shineth by nighte.
A toothe pike. sometyme it signifyeth elegancy in speche.
To be styffe, or to resyste agaynste a burdeyn, to indeuour, to leane on a thynge, to flee, to be sustayned, to inforce hym selfe, or take pein, to trauayle.
A region or Contray in Egypte, also the name of two cities in Egypte, aboue the citie of Memphis.
Full of snowe, or where it snoweth often.
I will endeuour me, I will assay to do a thinge.
To make noble, or to adde to dignitie, or estimation, to cause to be knowen.
A booke that Aulus Gellius made, which was so called, bycause it was writen in the wynter nyghtes at Athenes.
He that fleeth or exchuith the night.
Is a name, whereby the Moone is called bycause that she doeth shyne by night, also a lytle beest, which shyneth by nyght.
A wanderar or goar by nyghte.
At night, or in the nyght, by nyght.
Oules to Athenes, a prouerbe, whereby is signified any thinge to be abundant, and more than ynoughe.
Where there can be founde nor begynnynge nor endinge, that whiche may neuer be losed.
Is also in an host in batayle, a throng of men, so thicke, that it can not be perced.
Thou sekest for a knot in a rushe, it is applyed to him, which is scrupulouse in a thing that is not doubtfull, but playne.
The wertes, which be in the chekis of a gote or swyne.
A ryuer in Thracia, whiche runneth into the ryuer of Ister, or Danow.
People in Scithia, called nowe Tartary.
A name, or nowne, sometyme it signifieth worshyp, auctoritie, noblenesse of bloode, kynred. Also cause. Eo nomine, for that cause. Meo nomine, for my sake.
An officer, which called euery man by his name.
A towne in Italy by Rome.
Besyde the commune signification, doeth also signifie dettours or dettes, also articles writen.
To demaunde or calle for dettes.
For an honest pretence or consyderation.
A iurisdiction, as a mayraltie, a baylywyke, or prouostshyp of a towne.
A place in the countray of Arcadia.
Nyne dayes in euery moneth before the Idus.
A contray in Germany, wherein is the duchy of Bauaria, or Beuar, also the towne of Nurenbergh.
A contraye in Fraunce called Normandy.
An hospytalle or place, where sycke folke are kepte.
Notes, cyfers, markes, made for remembraunce of some thynge.
A clerke, whiche wryteth instrumentes or plees.
To be knowen or made knowen.
That whiche by some lawes is appoynted to a mans bastarde.
To note or marke, to make a mark or token, to write after an example.
Knowen: also a frende, or of acqueyntaunce.
To tylle newe grounde, or set newe vynes.
Ceremonies the nynth day after the burienge.
Newe, fresshe, late commen vp or begonne.
Men of late commen vppe, whiche are not gentylmenne of an auncyent stocke.
Peyne, offence, or trespace. somtyme it signifieth hurte or harme.
A howse, wherinto corne is caryed for feare of rayne.
Maryable, of ful age to be wedded.
To be wedded, or to wedde, proprely of the womans part.
Thynges hangynge downe from the boughes of trees or pitchtrees, and are no leaues.
The day before yesterdaye: Nudius quartus, Nudius quintus, Fowre dayes passed, fyue dayes sens.
To make naked, to discouer, or opē.
To tryfle, or go about vayne thynges.
Withoute peyne or laboure, without any difficultie.
No man yet, none to this day.
For an, or vtrum, whiche hapneth in a demaunde or question. Num ego te spoliaui? Dyd I robbe the?
Was the seconde kynge of Romaynes.
A tumbrelle, wherein menne be punysshed, hauyng their heedes and fete put into it.
Proprelye is the wylle of God. Sommetyme the power of god, somme tyme it sygnyfyeth god, sommetyme apparayle.
He that casteth accompt, or reckneth a thyng in numbres.Augustinꝰ

Promptely, redily, sometyme in accompt or reckenynge.Fab. Quin. v • . De Actore facile dicente ex tempore dictum est ingenium eū in numerato habere, of the plaintyfe, whā he speaketh quyckely and without study, it is sayde, that he hath a quycke wytte and a redy. Claudius Isidorus testamento suo dixit, Plin. li. 31. quamuis multa Ciuili bello perdidisset, tamen relinquere seruorum quatuor millia, iuga boum tria millia sexcenta, reliqui poecoris ducenta quinquaginta millia, In numerato pōdo sexcenta millia, Claude Isidore sayde, that not withstandynge that he hadde loste moche in the Ciuyle warres: yet hadde he lefte in his testament foure thousande slaues, three thousande and syxe hundred yoke of oxen, of other cattel two hundred and fyfty thousande, In money redy tolde syx hundred thousande pounde.
To numbre or counte, to telle money, to reken catell.

Sometyme quantitie, as of grayne, it is also a precise order in harmony, in lengthe and shortenesse of syllables. And therfore sommetyme verses be called Numeri. 〈◊〉 , in 〈◊〉 Also it signifyeth company or feloweshyp. It is also taken for the warste sorte of the people.
A ryuer in Italy by Lauinium.
A keper and louer of money.
The grandfather of Romulus and Remus on the mothers syde.
He with whome exchaunge of money is made.
A lytle coine or piece of money
Moneye. It was a coyne, whiche was the tenthe parte of a golden peny.
A payre of shakelles, or fetters for a horse.
To declare a wylle or testament by mouthe.
A namynge, a declaration of a wylle.
The market days, whiche in olde time was the nynthe daye: and than dyd the husbande men come to the citie to bie and selle, and also to here their lawes declared, whiche were newe made.

n: nudinalis le amp nudinarius a um
d: Pertaining to a market or fayre.
To selle openly: sometyme to bye often.
A demaunde. Nunquid ego sum? Is it not I?
Wylle ye anye thynge with me? or, Is there any thynge that I maye do for you?
Late, awhyle agoone. Sommetyme longe ago.
Signifieth late done, or hapned, or newe begonne.Plautus in • apt.
A daughter in law, the sonnes wyfe.
A becke, or countenaunce with mouynge the eye or hande.
With a becke and rebecke, with a calle and a becke.
A reremous or backe, with litel fete, that they seme to haue none.
A nyghte crowe, or shryche crowe.
He that dothe see nothynge by nyght, and lyttell in the euenynge.
The daughter of Nictes, which lay with her father, and afterwarde was tourned into an owle, who wolde not be seene but at nyght.
Goddesses of the waters, or spirited, beinge conuersaunt aboute waters, elfes, women of the fayrie. sometyme the Muses be so called. also yonge bees, as sone as they haue receyued their fourme.
He that is wedded, the brydegroome.
A mans name. also a citie in Arabia.
A kynd of Iuie, hauyng black beries.
A ryuer in the yle of Crete or Candy.
A cytie in Crete or Candye.
For at, ob rem, for my profyte, ob oculos, Plaut. before myn eyes.
To lette a man that he can not telle out his tale.
To walke a gaynst an other. also to walke togither, or with an other.
To here hardly, or vnwillingly. sometyme to obey.
To thruste agayne, or put to.
To lay ouer, or couer a thing somtyme to vncouer or open. also to bring agaynst or ouerthwart a place.

n: obdureo rui ere amp obduresco scere
d: To be harde. Obduro, are, to make harde.
To consume or eate al aboute.
A great stone, square like a butte, waxing smaller & smaller, vntyl the toppe, of a great height, made plaine by a warkman: there were of them diuers in Rome.
A spyt or broche, also a longe strike in writing like a spit, for a note or diuersite.
To go to, to go aboute, to be at hande, to mete with one.
To take possession of landes, wherein a manne hath a state of inherytaunce.
Was in the old time vsed for obediam, I shall obey.
A man that is very fatte.
In Virgil is fatte,Vergilius. Suetonius in Neuio it sygnifieth leane or lyttell. it is most commonly taken for fatte in the bodye.
To whister in ons eare. Also to tell a thynge often.
To growe vppe as herbes doone.
To obiect, or often impute, or lay to ones charge, also to caste out.
Any thinge that is before a mannes eyen, and may be sene.
The layenge or settynge of a thynge before ones eyes.
To lay or throwe against, or to lay before one.
To stere or moue before.Sex. Pom.
By the waye, incidently, besyde the purpose, in the meane tyme, precisely.
The dieng or decesse of a mā. somtime the cōming of one. The ancient writers toke obitum for the accesse of one.
He or she that chydeth or rebuketh.
To delite. Oblectatio oblectamē & oblectamentū, recreatiō
To eate delicate meates gredily or rauenousely, and to consume goodes in feastynge and bankettynge.
To couer with mudde or softe claye. sometyme to stoppe or daube.
To scrape out, or putte out of remembraunce.
A scrapynge or blottynge oute of a worde.
To speake agaynste or contrarie, to reporte ylle, to curse.
As we communely say, I holde my peace, I speake not, I hold my tonge.

Bounden, subiecte, apt, in daunger. sometyme it sygnifyeth gyltie or fautie. Sum tibi obnoxius, I am bounden vnto the, obnoxius morbis, subiect to sicknesse. Periculis obnoxius, subiecte to perylles. &c. Minari interdū ferro, nisi sibi obnoxia foret, And thretned hir sommetyme with his weapon, yf she wold not be obediente to his requestes.Salustius. Colum. 5. Ci. ad At. Obnoxium feris, Caste out to wylde beastes.
To couer the heed or body.
To denie, to resyste agaynste a thynge purposed.
A poyse wayinge halfe a scruple. it was also a coyne of syluer, whiche varied in poyse after the countrey, as obolus Atticus, Salu. in orati. Memmii. obolus Romanus, obolus Hebraicus.
To begin to spring or come forth
Begonne or spronge, as rumor obortus, tydynges spronge.
To come priuily or steale in, to come vnwares or vnloked for.
Ci. in 〈◊〉 to come or attayne to honour by crafty dissimulation.
The gettynge or obteynynge of a thynge in fourme aforesayde.
Letters opteyned by the sayde meanes.
To laugh at one, or to mock one. Obsio, a mocke.

n: obrigeo gui gere amp obrigesco scere
d: To be or waxe styffe for colde.
One of the yles called fortunate.
Is in hydynge somme thyng, whiche shuld be spoken, to atteyne the thynge that we desyre.
To checke or interrupte a man in his speeche. Obrogare legem, to derogate one lawe by an other.
To ouerthrow, to couer a thing in castynge an other thynge ouer it.
Lyghtnynges, which sodaynely happen, throwynge downe and burnynge thynges, before they be procured or loked for.
To be fylled to moche with a thynge.
To offre my selfe to salute one.
To be wode angry against one.Plaut •• in Epid.
To brynge or cause yll lucke.
Abhomynable, all thyng whiche is to be eschewed, dysshonest, vncleane, pernicious, Also brynging yl lucke.
Darke, hydde, dysfuse, vnknowen, of no gentyll bloode.
To make darke, to shadow, to hide, to kepe in silence or from the knowlege of other, to make of no reputation.
To besech or hartily pray, Obsecrare ab aliquo, to desyre of one.
Is somtyme an aduerbe. Hem, obsecro anis est? Howe, I pray the is that he?Terent in Eunuc • o.
To make prosperouse, also to obey or do all thing at an other mās wil, to make a thing better than it semeth to be.
To inclose about wt an hedge
Thynges done to the pleasure or appetite of hym, that they be done for.
Take thy plesure, make good chere.
Diligent, redy to do that, whiche is commaunded.
Redynes to do all that is commaunded. sometyme it sygnifieth flattery.
To folow an other mannes pleasure.
To sowe or sette aboute, to plante.
To locke or shutte a doore.
Mete to be obserued, worthy to be had in reuerence.
To awayte diligently with the eyes, and also the mynde, to honoure, to take good hede, to haue in reuerence.
An hostage, or pledge in warres
They whiche ar besieged, that they may not issu out of the place where they ar.
Lyenge in awayte, to take away any thynge craftily.
A glasse whiche is pure blacke.
A garlande gyuen to them, whyche delyuered a towne or fortresse besyeged with ennemyes, whyche was of grasse.
To ly in await to take one.
A syege about a towne or fortresse.
To close letters & seale them. Also to sygne them.
He that putteth to his sele or sygne to a dede or instrument.
To throwe or caste, as whanne men of the countrey do say.
Wrapped, sette about with herbes or trees.
To decaye, to waxe olde, to be out of vse.
Decayed, olde, oute of vse, worne, as a garment, whan it is bare.
All meates, excepte breade and potage.
That whiche hathe an yll sowne.
He or she that maketh feastes or bankettes.

o: Obsorbeo, bui, bere, & obsorbo, psi, bere,
n: obsorbeo bui bere amp obsorbo psi bere

d: To be fylthye or vncleane, or sluttyshe. Nonius declaryth it to waxe olde.
To do the offyce of a mydwyfe.
To be obstinate, or persist firme in one sentence or purpose.
To crye out on one, or make a noyse.
To resist or repugne against, to speake in detraction of one.
To hyde, to stoppe a mans throte, that he can not eate meate.Plautus in Stich. Pom. Fest.
To sette that a manne canne not loke out of his wyndowes,Cice. pro domo sua. or to stoppe his lyghtes.
To abasshe,Plautus in Milite. or make abashed.
To hurte or hynder, or indamage.
To obey, or be at commaundement.
To treade or thruste downe, to suffocate, to bruyse.
An humble desyre, proprely not to do a thyng. Also to take god or some other thynge to wytnesse.
Humbly to beseche, to desyre for goddes sake, or for the remembraunce of some thinge, whyche to hym that is desyred, is thankfully herde.
To keepe sylence, not to speake.
To opteyne, to holde, to retayne styll, to gete, sometyme to haue. Si istam animi firmitudinē obtines, salui sumꝰ, If thou haste that firmenesse of courage, we be saulfe.
To be verye slow or dull.
To ylle reporte, to depraue, to haue in de • pyte.
To thruste downe, to putte to with force. Obtrudit fores, He pullid to the doore. 〈◊〉 in 〈◊〉 . Also to set forth. Aliquid prius obtrudamus, Lette vs fyrste sette forthe sommewhat.
To gyue to a man a wyfe against his will or appetite.
To slee, also to stryke of a mans heed.
To stryke, to breake, to make dull, to hurte a man with speking, to make werye.
To crye oute, as a childe.
To enuyronne or compasse aboute with a dyche or walle.
He that tourneth one out of the ryght waye, or letteth hym that he maye not passe.
To stoppe or lette oone of his passage.
To comme agaynste, to mete with. also to happen.
To be presente, to come in remembraunce.
To tourne agayne, or backe. Sed mihi ante oculos obuersabatur reipub. dignitas, quae me ad se rapit. But before myne eyes camme the estate of the publyque weale, whiche plucketh me vnto hyr.
An aduerbe, which signifieth before in the waye, against one. Obuiam ire, to go against one, to preuent.
To make darke with a shadowe: sometyme to defende.
The auncient Romayns vsed for obsecro, I beseche you.
An harowe or dragge, whyche hath yron teeth, wherwith cloddes are broken.
A breakynge of cloddes, or harrowynge.
To waxe or be harde flesshed, or brauned, lyke as a bore is.

o: Occano, & occino, occanui, & occini, occanere, & occinere,
n: occano amp occino occanui amp occini occanere amp occinere
d: To synge agaynst one, to laye in rebuke.
To be loste, or vndone.Plautus in Casi.
Dethe of manne or beaste. Also the goynge downe of the sonne, or sonneglade.
They shal gyue rebukes or wordes of reproche.
To crye oute against one with rebukefull wordes.
Where one syngeth against another. It maye be also taken for a countretenor.
To slee or wounde to deth, to fall greuously.
For frequenter occiduntur, they be slayne here and there, or in dyuers places.
To fall downe, to perysshe vtterly, to dye, to goo downe, as the sunne doeth, and other sterres.
Oure hope is lost.Plautus in Pseudo •• ▪
This thinge is lost or in despayre.
The place where the sunne goeth downe.
Of all other mooste lost or desperate.
A slaughter or deth of men or catell.
I am deed, I am lost.
The hynder parte of the heed.
To stoppe a man frome speakynge.
To harrowe and breake cloddes and balkes in the corne fieldes, Also to couer with erthe.
To be slayne, to be deedly wounded.
The fielde, whiche is neglected of the owner, & labored by other.
To occupie, to get or take before an other man, to vse in commune, to take or holde a thynge with force, to lette or empeche, to possede, somtyme to lende for auauntage.
He that dothe occupie or vse a thynge, the occupier.
A colour in rhetorike, where the playntyfe in preuentynge the wordes of the defendaunt, reherceth that whiche he will laye for excuse, and disproueth it.
To fynde aduyse or coū sayle.
To take or kepe a place with force.Liui, li. 33.
To meete with, to come to remembraunce, to offre hym selfe. Also to resiste, to runne, to come to mynde, or remembrance, also to be proffred.
The frequentatiue of occurro, to come often to remembraunce, to mete ofte, or runne agaynste one.
The see, whiche gothe aboute all the worlde. Alsoo a great poole made in Rome, for many persones to swymme in.
That whiche hath eyen, or holes lyke to eyen.
A ryuer which passeth throughe Acarnania, a countray in grece.
To be vnoccupyed, or withoute busynesse.
Vacation from labour, leyser, quietnes, ydelnes, lacke of busynes.
Boted or harneised on the leggis.
The numbre of eight, in sondry partis.
Hauynge eight feete.Sueton. in Cali. Quint.
Full of eyen, also quick sigted, circumspect, espyenge a thinge shortly.
A witnesse whiche sawe the thinge.
He loueth her as well as his owne eyen.
An eye, alsoo a yonge budde of a tree.
To be in loue with the thing, which is sene.
I hate, or haue hated: Odisse, to hate, or haue hated.
He that is hated, displesant, troublous, tediouse.

n: odit eum cane peius amp angue
d: He hatethe him wars than a dogge or a serpente: as who sayth, mortally without hope of reconcylynge.
Oone of the sonnes of Ixion the Centaure.
An Itenerary, wherin is writen the distance of one place from an nother, or a lyke thyng, as the iestes of princis are, assignynge their iourneys.
Euery thynge that sauoureth well. also sauour.
A maker or seller of thinges that smelle swete.
That which is perfumed. sometyme that whiche doth sauour, odoriferous, or smellynge swete.
A hounde made to the sute.
A hounde or spanell, which hunteth by sent.
That whiche sendeth furthe sauour, or hath a good sauour.
A ryuer in the countraye of Thracia.
A citie, alsoo the floure of a vyne.
Kynge Darius horsekepar, by whose polycye he atteyned to the kyngedome of Persia.
The countraye in Grece, called also Laconia.
The orderinge and prouydinge of thinges concernyng housholde, alsoo an order in writinge, whereby euery thinge is set in his propre place.
Where women do sitte & worke with woull or sylke.
Vniuersall, pertayninge to all the worlde.
A general counsail, wherein thinges are vniuersally treated concerninge all countreys.
A man, which dissolued subtyll and darke questions.
The bery of a wylde vyne.
An oynemente made of the sayde bery.
The father of Deianira, the last wife of Hercules.
A seruaunte, whyche bringeth wyne to the table.
A potte wherein wyne is caryed.
The fylthy oyle, which is in wull, that is in the flankes of a shepe, or aboute his necke, which oyle is soden oute, & vsed for medicyne.
Woodnesse, or madde fury: alsoo a fly, which maketh a great noyse, whan he flyeth, some do suppose it to be, a dor, lyke to a bee, but that he is blacke & grettar.
The father of Medea, wyfe of Iason.
A poodinge, also a dish made with fatt broth, harde chese, peper, and cynamom, or other lyke iunkat. somtyme it is taken for a morsell.
A lytell morsell, as of fleshe mynced, also a potage made with pieces of flesshe, as stuyd brothe or forced gruell.
To meete with, to fall into, to fynde by chaunce, to stryke or hytte any thinge vnware, to offende. Offendere apud aliquem, to do a thinge, whyche lyketh not theym that do see it done.
An impediment or let, an obstacle.
The knotte of a ribon or lase, wherewith a bonet or hatte is knytte fast to the heed.
That which is layd in a mans waye, whereat he stumbleth.
He that stackereth in redinge, as yf he were not perfyte in reding,Quint. or redeth otherwyse than it is wryten.
To hytte ofte, or to lette.
To offre, or present, to gyue willyngly, to promyse.

Strypes.Plau i • Rudes. Ne offerumentas habebis plureis in tergo tuo, quam vlla nauis lōga clauos, tum ego ero mendacissimus, and yf thou haue not moo strypes on the skyn of thy backe, than a galy hath nayles, I shall be the falsyst lyar that euer was.
Iustin. to put a complaynte against one.

o: Offerre incendium, Cice. ad Pont, Cicero in •ael•• Domus ardebat in Palatio non fortuiro, sed oblato incedio,
n: offerre incendium cice ad pont cicero in ael domus ardebat in palatio non fortuiro sed oblato incedio
d: My house in the Palaice dyd burne not by any chaunce, but by fyre thrast in by some man.
To hurte, sometyme to do, also to dy cloth.
A seruysable man, or he that is glad to please, or doeth well his duetye.
A grief which procedeth of a good cause or raison.

Office, duetye, or a thinge, whiche ought to be done. It is sometyme taken for honour done to one, and it may be vsed for that, whyche we do calle homage, done in suche fourme as our lawe doeth appoynt it, it is also taken for benefyte.
To abyde in one purpose or opinion, to be obstinate.
To tourne a thinge contrary or aboute.
To powre water into the mouth of a man or beast.
To breake with a plough, lande cared before.
To powre aboute, to make darke or blynde, to stayne, to cast in, or bringe in.
To put water or other lycour into a mannes mouthe, to sowke downe, as they vse to do to lyke men, which for feoblenesse canne not by them selfes take any sustenaunce.
A kynge of Egypte, whyche first buylded the citie of Memphis.
A ryuer which commeth oute of the hilles called Alpes, and runneth to Rome.
To prate, to braule, to speake with chydinge.
To caste or set the eyes on one.
He which first buylded the citie of Thebes.
An Ile betwene Phenicea and Syria.
An exclamation, signifienge that he, which speketh that worde • s saciate or wery of that, which he seeth or heereth.
Is moost proprely the frute of an olyue: yet sometyme it is vsed for an olyue tree.
A colour, which is mixt with grene, blacke, yelowe, and whyte.

n: olearis re amp olearius a um

d: One of the Iles called Ciclades.
The tyme of gatheringe of olyues.
Thinges which haue an yll sauour.
A place where olyues do growe, also the dung or ordure of a man, proprely it is a draught or iakes.
That which hath a great sauour, eyther good or badde, mooste communely stinkinge.
They whiche doo aduaunce the state of noble men and ryche men, aboue the popular astate.
Sometyme, as well in the tyme passed as in the tyme to come, nowe late, longe tyme passed.
A gardynar, or sellar of herbes and rootes.
The tyme of gatherynge of olyue beryes.
A place where doo growe olyue trees.
Plenty of olyues, alsoo reuenues, which do come of olyues.
The qualytie of olyues, the gatheringe tyme of olyues.
Herbes which serue for potage, pot herbes.
A citie betwene the hilles of Ossa and Olympus.
Playes and greate games, on the hyll of Olympus, made to the honour of Iupiter.
Pertaynynge to that playes or hyll.
The space of fyue yeres, whereby the olde grekes dyd account, as we do now by the yeres of oure lorde: as • he first Olympias, the seconde, the third. and so forth.
He that hath had victory in the games at Olympus.
A mountayne or hyll in Grece, aboue the which appereth no clowde: and therfore amonge the Poetes it is vsurped for heuen.
A ryuer in Grece by the place called Thermopylas.
A citie in portugall, nowe called Vlysbona, in englysh Lusseborn.
Lucke, also a worde or sentence sodaynly spoken, after the which some thing hapneth to folowe according thervnto, aboue the expectation of them which herde it.
The call or sewet, wherein all the bowelles are lapped, also the thynne skyn in the heed, wherein the brayne is contayned: of some called the ryme of the brayne, and of surgeons Pia mater.

o: Ominor, aris, ari, & omino, aui, are,
n: ominor aris ari amp omino aui are
d: To gesse what shall happen or folowe.
He that telleth a mans lucke or fortune.
Left, not medled with. Omisso animo, Vbi te vidi animo esse omisso, whā I sawe that thou caryddest for nothinge.
To forbeare, to leue, to neglect.
Let hym alone, pardon hym.Terea. Phor •• .
He touched euery point, A prouerb. applyed to hym, whiche omitteth nothinge expedient or necessary, and is therfore of all men commendyd.
In all poyntes. Res est omnibus numeris absoluta, it is a thing perfyte in all poyntes.
All maner of wayes, of euery kynde.
They which do eate raw fleshe.
Licour made of frute that is not ripe, as of grapes, and than is it called veriuyse.
A grene wyne not pleasaunt or swete.
Oyle made of olyues, not beinge rype.
To be dombe, and can not speke.
To put impositions or taxes on the people.
A worme, which bendeth him selfe lyke a bow whan he goeth, which is reed, and founde vnder trees, which haue lyen longe on the grounde.
A beast halfe a man, halfe an asse.
A byrde lyke to a swanne, whiche putting his heed into the water, brayeth lyke an asse.
A worde made of sowne or pronouncinge, as bletinge of a shepe, lowinge of a cow, hissinge of an adder.
A whyte stone, lyke to a mannes nayle, also some be founde in Inde, which are of dyuerse colours, hauynge whyte spottes lyke vnto eyen.
Made of the stone called Onyx.

o: Operam do, operam impendo, operam nauo,
n: operam do operam impendo operam nauo
d: I do myne yndeuour, I put to my diligēce I spend my labour.
That whiche is done with labour.
Profytable, necessary, a ioyfull thinge, moche to be estemed.
The wark, or that wheraboute a man laboureth.
Busy, diligent in labouringe laboriouse, paynefull.
Pertaynynge to serpentes, they were bookes, which Nicander, and Petridius wrate, of the nature of serpentes.
People in Ethiope, whiche do eate serpentes.
The name of Esculapius, bycause that he is ymagyned to holde a serpent in his hande.
A stone hauynge spottes lyke a serpente.
Iuno, Iuno was so called of women, bycause they supposed, that she holpe them when they trauayled.
The spoyle, which by one chief Capytayne is taken frome another in batayle, as his cote armure or harneys.
Wyne whiche moughe endure good, two hundred yeres.
That maye be conceyned in opinion.
To suppose,Plautus in Bacch. to haue opinion.
Aboundaunt, fresh, or gaye. Coena opipara, a delicate souper.
A lady, companyon to Diana, she was also wyfe to Saturnus, and by her is signified the erth amonge the Poetes.
A booke wryten on the back syde.
He that can not tourne his necke.
The cricke, or disease, whiche letteth a man to tourne his necke.
He whose father deyed before his grandfather.
Iupiter, Iupiter the helpar at neede.
The iuyce of an herbe called blacke Popye, alsoo Opius, is he that fighteth in armure.
Balme naturall, whyche in a part of Iudea, called Ierocinthe, stilleth oute of a lytle thorne.
The iuyce of an herbe, called Panax.
All fruites whiche do growe in the last ende of somer.
A place, wherein frute is kept.
It behoueth, it is expedient or necessary.
To dye: also to be slayne.
An aduerbe, signifienge very moch, sometyme it signifieth furthwith, veryly.
That whiche is in due tyme, and as it ought to be.
Fete or apte to take wronge.
Opportunatly conuenientely, as it ought to be.
To oppresse, to kepe or shit in, to take sodaynely, to rauyshe a woman, to grieue, to thrust harde.
To obiect against one, to reproche.
The suster and wyfe of Saturne: also it signifieth ayde or helpe.
A puruayour of vytayles, or Catar.
To prepare often for dyner or souper.
Al thinge belonginge to a meale, except bred and drynke.
To prepare thynges necessarye for dyner, souper, or bankat.
The science whereby the raison of sight is knowen.
The heed men of a citie, also they whiche defende the parte of nobilitie and riche men.
The state or condiciō of heed men of a towne or contraye.
The choyse, the request or desyre. It was also to a captayne in warres, a ministre to do his commaundement, and be assistent vnto hym.
To desyre, to chouse, to require. Adopto, coopto, exopto, vide suis locis.
He that syngethe lyke to a sheparde.
A warke, a laboure. Eius opere by his meane or diligence.
It is necessary, or nede. Si opus sit, yf nede be.
That which most communly is called implemētes of houshoulde, proprely of tymber, as fourmes, stooles, cupboordes and other lyke thinges.

o: Opus est conuento. Ita res subita est, celeriter mihi hoc homine opus est,
n: opus est conuento ita res subita est celeriter mihi hoc homine opus est
d: The chaunce is so sodayne, or the mater requireth suche hast, that I must nedes speke with the man shortly or quickely.
It must nedes be done, or executed.

o: Opus est remissam. Terent. i• Hecyra. Vosmet videte ia Laches & tu Pamphile, remissam opus sit nobis an reductam domum,
n: opus est remissam terent i hecyra vosmet videte ia laches amp tu pamphile remissam opus sit nobis an reductam domum
d: Now Laches and Pā phile aduyse your selfes wel, whither it be necessary, that she be sent home, or fetched home.

Thou hast nede of them.Plautus in Capt. Terent. in Heau. Vt cū desponderim, des qui aurum ac vestem, at que alia quae opus sunt, That whan I haue affiauncyd her, thou delyuer money and apparayle, and all other thinges nedefull.Plautus 〈◊〉 Music.

With all meanes possible, in most harty wyse. Rex Seleucus me opere orauit maxumo, vt sibi lationes cogerem, Kynge Seleucus desyred me, as moche as he possibly mought, that I wolde geate him souldiours to be aboute his persone.Terent. in Eunuc •• Thais maximo te orabat, opere vt cras redires, Thais desyred the as hartyly as she can, that thou woldeste come agayne to morowe.

Where aunsweres were gyuen by ydolles: sometyme the aunswere, somtyme the sayinge of some wise man.

Lyke an oratour, or in fourme of Rhetorike.

Thyrty Iles in the see by Scotlande.

Wherin order is obserued ordinarye. sometyme a scoffer or gester.
Order, the dewe place, the astate of menne.
To keepe oone within his boundes, that he doo not excede his degree.
Is in battayle that, whyche is callyd the raye.
To breake or scatter the raye.
Is moste taken for vomyte, all be it sygnifieth appetite.
An instrumente pertaynynge to buyldynge, also an ordinance of warres.

A measure contaynynge .vi. foote. Suidas dothe write, that it is the space, whiche is conteyned betweene the handes stretched abrode, whyche I suppose is a spanne.

To be borne, to ryse, to appiere.
Commen by auncetours oute of some countrey or citie. sommetyme borne, Nati Carthagine, sed orundi a Syracusis, Borne at Carthage, but by auncetoures descended frome Syracuse in Sicile.

To gape, as menne do for lacke of sleepe.
Battaylle, wherein they, whyche were before vaynquysshed, haue the vyctorie.
A lyttell mouthe, also a kysse.
The sonne of Iupiter begot on Neobe, the daughter of Phoroneus, which succeded Phoroneus in the kingdome of the Argiues, and afterward was kyng of Egypt, who after his death was honoured for a god.
One boone from an nother in pieces.
A shryne or lyke thyng, where the bones of deed men are put.
To shewe often. Alsoo to booste.
A thynge, whiche happeneth seldome, and betokeneth, that some strange thynge shall happen. As a blasyng sterre, thunder on a fayre daye. Sometyme it signifieth a thynge monstruous.
The entrees of greatte ryuers, sometyme hauens.

A maner of exylynge of men atte Athenes, whyche excellyd other in power or authorytie: whyche exyle was doone by delyuerynge of oyster shelles, wherin the name of hym, whiche should be exyled, was wryten.
Browne breadde, the whyche menne are wonte to eate with oysters.

A garlande of myrtels, gyuen to hym, whiche had vyctory without effusion of bloudde.

A small triumph of a prince or captayne, whiche had victorie of his enmies without slaughter of men, or where battayle was not denounced: in the whyche tryumph the capitayne went on foote, or onely dyd ryde on a horse, with a garland of myrtelles on his heed, and his souldyours syngynge aboute hym.
Whiche is in symylitude of an egge.

Of oone father and mother, or brought vp vnder one maister, or in one schoole.

Suger and vynegre sodden togither, of somme menne called Syrupus acerosus symplex.
Medicines to make a womanne to brynge forth hyr byrthe quyckely.
Soores aboute the nose, which haue an yll sauour.
Pertaynynge to fourrage or meate for beastis.

By thy lycence, by your leaue, or lycence.

To mitigate, to apease, to accorde.
Platted, Pactilis corona, a platted garlande.
A ryuer in Lydia, hauynge golden grauelle.
Sometyme a participle sygnifienge couenanted, promysed, somtime a nowne, signifienge a couenant.
A safe conduite,Ti. L • uius. to passe from one countrey to an other, a pasport.
The name of a noble poete.
A Cytie in Italye, by Venyce.
A ryuer in Italye callyd the Po.
A ryuer, whyche somme saye is an arme of the Po.
An hymne in the prayse of Apollo. sommetyme the same Apollo. It is nowe taken for any hymne, made to the lande of God, or our Ladye.
He that is appoynted to await on chyldern to see them well ordred.
A louer of chylderne in vnhoneste wyse.
Erudition and institution in good artes, as Gellius teacheth.
A foote in metre, whiche is of oone longe syllable and thre shorte.
An herbe callydde Pyonye. Also a countreye in Europa, and is a parte of Macedonye.
A citie in Lucania, where there is abundance of Roses.
He that loketh a squynte vpward.
Ploughmens holyday, as wakes be nowe adayes.
A man of the countreye, or of the vyllage: sommetyme it is taken for hym that goth not to battayle.
A towne of Thessaly, whiche after was called Demetrias.
The syde of a leafe in a boke.
A lyttell syde of a leafe in a boke.
The name of a ryuer and of a citie, of whiche the people are called Pagyritae.
A spade, also a p • ele to put in breadde into the ouen. Also a fanne to make wind. Also the brodest parte of a rynge.
Wedges or pieces, or gaddes of mettall whan it is fyned.
Was callid a god of the see.
A countrey in Syrie, ioynynge to Arabie, called in holy scripture Philist • im.
A wras • lyng place: also the exercyse of wrastlynge.Ci. de ora tare primo It is also the comelynesse of mouynge and gesture, according to the state or degree of the person, which sheweth it.
Openly, before men, that all menne may see it.
A noble greke, whyche sounde certayne letters of greeke, Also to sette an arraye in an hooste, and the fourme of watches, with the watche worde.
Leauers or porters, wherewith they left and beare tymbre, and suche like thynges of greatte weight.
To beare on leyuars or porters.
Men, whyche do beare on leyuers or porters, thynges of great poyse or weyghte.
A Sacrifyce doone at Rome on the hylle callyd Palatinum.
Vitrunius▪ li. 2. a foundacyon made in a maryse grounde with pyles of tymber.
They that wander about, and wote not whither to go.

A palaise of an emperour or great kynge.
Chaffe of corne, also a gristell, whyche fallethe downe frome the necke of a cocke or capon.
The Dewelappe of a Rudder beaste. Also a place, wherein chaffe is kepte.
Called goddesse of shepeherdes and of pasture.
A cytie, soo called of Pallena, the daughter of Sython, and wife of Cletus.
Shepeherdes holydayes kept in the honour of Pales.
A contrarye songe, or retractynge of that, whiche oone hathe spoken or wryten: Nowe of somme menne called a recantynge.
To retracte that, whyche one hath spoken or writen.
Was the Mayster of the shyppe, wherin Aeneas camme into Italye. Alsoo an Elbowe of the lande of Sycile into the See.
A bryer, whiche beareth a codde, wherin are thre or foure blacke sedes.

A mantelle, suche as knyghtes of the garter do weare.

To take the praise or honour from an other.
An acte worthy the palme or sygne of vyctorie.
Worthye the sygne or token of vyctorie.
A garmente of bawdekyn, whiche the consule dyd weare in tyme of peace, and the vyctour in tyme of warre.
The small and tender branches, moste proprely of a vyne.

That beareth palme, or date trees.
A measure of a foote and a handebrede.
All byrdes, whyche hau • hole fete, as cōmonly al water foules haue.

Pappe made with mylke and floure.

Of paper, or of the sayd rushe.

Two lyke one to the other in fourme or degree.
To be sufficient, to do or sustayne a thinge.
Payres, two togither of any thinge.
To requyte, to do one thinge for another, lyke for lyke.

That which may be sone goten, or will be sone redy.

A man infamed, yll reported of.

Left oute, vnspoken, or vnwriten, which ought to haue bene spoken or wryten.

Was double wages, gyuen to horsmen for hauinge two horsis.
A myle in Persya, contaynynge fifty furlonges.

He that countresayteth him that is called Parasitus.
Certayne stones in pyiars. Parastata also one of the bones in the shanke of the legge.
Stones, which do sustayne bothe sydes of a doore, called Iambes.
To bragge or crake, to speke grete or hyghe wordes.
Ladyes of desteny, also it signifieth the selfe destyny, or disposicion in prolonging or shortnynge lyfe.
To spare, to forgyue, or pardone, to let or prohibite, to leue, to forbeare or absteyne.

Father, mother, or any other auncetour.

To celebrate the funeralles of auncetours or frendes.
The floures of thistels, whiche be lyke fethers.
A figure in spekinge, where one worde is lyke to another, but of dyuers sygnifications. Nam inceptio est amē tium, non amantium, this begynnynge is of madde men, not of louers.
To appiere, to be seene, to obeye.
Some thinge added to, beinge no part of the matter, as whan a payntour doeth make an ymage, he doeth adde to trees, or townes.
A whyte colour that peynters do laye, whiche is fonde in Egypte.
For pariet, she shall bringe forth a childe.
Iuges assigned for capitall causes, as murdre or felony that requireth deth.

Of the yle called Parus, frome whens is brought marbelle stone, called Parium marmor.

To prepare, to geate, to apparell.

Parysshonars, or they, whiche do dwell within one parishe.
A countrey in Grecia, called also Archadia.
Murderars of their parentes, betrayours of their countray, somtyme murdre generally.
Murdre of kynsfolke, or traison to the propre countraye.
The pretertence of parco, I haue spared.

Is an herbe whiche hath small leues lyke to Coriander, & a floure whyte somewhat yelowe within, and hath a greuouse sauour. Some poticaryes do take it for the lasse mugwort, but I fynde not, that it is taken for feuerfue. Celsus wryteth, that it groweth on walles.
The olde name of the citye of Naples.
To gyue part, or take part, to make another man partner, or of counsayl.
Coheyres, or comperceners, which haue inheritaunce togither.
Partly, in part, some tyme part. Partim hominum venerunt, part of the men dyd come.

The chamber of the Sexten, or him which kepeth the Temple.
Pertayninge to the shepharde or herdman.
Of fedynge or grasinge of catell.

The craftysmen that maketh such clokes.

A citie in Italy called Padua, nigh vnto Venice.
To make open, to declare, to disclose.

To whome it pertaynyd, whā trues shulde be takē, to receyue the othes and appoyntement of bothe partes, and was there in, chief and principall ambassadour.

That which happeneth to one by his father.
To defende them, which be poure, or be falsely accused.

Defence of men beinge in trouble or suyte.

A poore man, or poore woman.
A herdeman, also he that doeth hyar catell.

A wayuers lowme, also a combe. it is also the place aboute the pryuy membres, where heare doeth growe, it is also the stickes, wherwith a mā stryketh doulcemers whan he doeth playe on them, also a fishe, sometyme a harowe.
In the facion of a combe.
To kembe, or trymme heare, to carde woulle, to sette a harpe or other lyke instrument.
Pertayninge to the brest. Fascia pectoralis, a brest kerchef.
A certayne carte sometyme vsed in Fraunce.
Store of catell: alsoo places where they be kept, also multitude of catell, alsoo reuenues that commeth of catell.
In the plurell numbre, catell, beastes.
He and she that stealeth a commune treasor.
Robbery of the cōmune treasour, or of a prince.
Substaunce, that rychesse, which is onely in money and catell.
To steale a commune treasour, or any thinge frome a prince.
Money, it is taken of the olde Ciuilions, for all thynges, whyche we calle catell.
All maner of catell: sometyme the multitude or flocke of catell, sometyme it is taken onely for shepe or gotes.
The steppe or token of a mannes foote.
A stake or forke, whereby a vyne, hoppes, or other lyke thinge is sustayned, or borne vppe.
Of the quantitie of a foote, in length, or distaunce.
Inferior iuges, which went on foote.

Were Senatours, whiche dyd not shewe their opynions in wordes, but onely meuynge them selfes towardes those personnes, whiche had raysonned, whose sentences they dyd approue, lyke as they do in the parliament house.
Where one fote goeth with the other, foote by foote.
To take him to his feete, to runne awaye.
To retreate or go backe.Caesar. Cicer. pro Plan.
To come to a point of a mater in controuersy.
A foote, somtyme it is taken for al the legge, frome the thyghe to the sole of the foote.
He that goeth on foote, or is on foote.
Softely and fayre, by lytle and lytle.
To set proppes, or to prop vp a vyne or tree, that it shal not fall or bowe downe.
A numerouse speakynge or wrytinge in the fourme of a verse, or metre allthoughe it be not a verse.
A lytle worme, whyche breedeth betwene the skynne and the flesshe.
Any thinge whiche hath a stalke, as the moost part of frute.
Any thinge, wherewith the foote is tyed, as a fettar, a payre of gyues, or stockes.
A fisshe, the stalke of an apple or peare, or other frute: also a louse.
A seruaunte, who foloweth allwaye the master, or mastres.
The herbe called Rue, or herbe grace.
A horse, which was fayned to haue wynges: it is also a signe or numbre of sterres in heuen.
A stage, whereon pageantes be set: or whereon plate & iewels do stand to be loked on.
A countraye in Grece called Arachadia.
People whiche came out of Grece, & inhabited Italy: they be also Arcadiens.
A kynge of Thessalia, vncle to Iason.
A prince, of whom the people called Peligni toke their name.
People in Italy, which came out of Illiria.
A citie in Macedonia. alsoo a payle, whereinto kyne are mylked.
He that deceyueth with fayre wordes.
She that is a wedded mannes harlot.
The acte or lyfe of her, which companieth with a weddyd man, aduoutry on her part.
To deceyue with fayre wordes, to moue a man pleasauntly to do a thynge.
To shyne bryght, to shyne through.
A bason, wherein mens fete are wasshed.
A countraye in Grece, called nowe Morea: and lyeth betwene the see called Ionium, and the see called Aegeum.
Whiche vaynquysshed on horsbacke in runnynge Oenomaus, father of Hippodamia, and wedded her.
A hill in Sicile on the see syde.
A Targat or buckler, lyke an halfe moone.
They whyche do weare suche bucklars.
The gentyles called goddis of mās lyfe: they be somtyme taken for the mooste secrete partes of the house.
To hange, or be hanged, to depende, somtyme to be in payne.
To be troubled in mynde, to doubte what to do, to cesse frome all other thinges, and to attende to one thynge, to be in suspence.
To ponder or waye, to consyder, to esteme or value, to paye, to sustayne or suffre, looke for dependo, suspē do, expendo, in their first lettres.
Signifieth to do & vndo, to take moche labour in vayne.
That maye perce, or be perced.
The inner part of the house.
A ryuer in Grecia, which dyuydeth the countrayes of Elis and Achaia.
A paynters pencell, wherewith he paynteth.
The hemme of a garment, the skirtes.
Any thinge whyche serueth to brusshe or wype cleane any thynge.
A tayle: also the secrete membre of a man.
Tayled, hauynge a tayle, also pénitus inwarde.
An aduerbe, vtterly, to the vttermoost, farre of.
That whyche is payed for a thynge bought, the payement. Pensa, in the plurell numbre, thredes of flax or woull, whan it is spunne, whyche maye be called yarne.
That whych hangeth, or stondeth on hyghe.
A garnard, where corn is kept
To ponder or consyder no thynge,Val. in po. not to ponder or consyder any thynge.
To ponder welle a mattier, to pay money, to make recompence.
A ponderer or wayer. Verborum pensitatores subtilissimi, Gellius. The mooste subtyll ponderers of wordes.
To ponder or way a thynge.
Wayed, examyned, somtyme it sygnifieth good and wyse.

The flaxe, whyche is bounden on the distaffe,Ci. de ora. out of the whiche the threde is drawen. sommetyme it sygnifieth the threde that is spunne. It is also the execution or mynystration of an offyce. Also regarde that one hath to a thynge.
A gardeyne made vpon the roufe of a house, or vpon pyllars.
An herbe called cinkefoyle, whiche hath fyue leaues,
A countray betwene Palestina and Arabia, wherin were the cities of Sodom and Gomor, bourned by the vengeance of god for synne agaynst nature.
He that is captayn of fyue men.
The volume of the fyue bookes of Moyses, that is to saye, Genesis, Exodi, Numeri, Leuiticum, Deuteronomium.
He that exercyseth any of these fyue games, castynge of the ball, or tryndell, runnynge, leapynge, wrastlyng, and throwynge the darte.
A queene of Amazon, whyche was slayne at the syege of Troye.
Is a parte of a verse, where a sentence is fynysshed in the fyrste syllable of the thyrde foote.
A Cloke, worne whanne hit raynethe.

n: penus penoris amp penum amp penu amp penuarium
d: A storehouse. Sometyme stoore or prouysion of vytayles.
An herbe callyd Pyonie, whyche beareth a redde floure, and great rounde sede, wherin is meruailous vertue against the fallyng euylle.
A kerchiefe or other lyke couerynge of the heed.
I haue spared, or forborne, or pardoned.
The preter tence of pungo. Also pepigi is the preter tence of pango. Pepigit foedus, He made a league or alyaunce.
Sygnifyeth by, ioyned with an nother worde it sygnyfyeth perfection. Perpulchrum, Verye fayre. Pergraue, Veraye greuouse. Peraetatem, for or by reasone of his age.
Medycines, whiche do make good concoction in a man, that the meate caten, maye digeste welle. Also salues and oyntementes, whyche doo make impostumes rype.
To perfourme, to make perfyte, to consyder, to drawe or cause to be drawen with force.
To accuse one, and to sewe hym to a condemnation.
To walke or go about a place.
To contynewe or lyue ouer yere.
To drie vp, to be very drye.
To quafte or drynke all out.Plautus in Pom. Fest. Cicer. ibi.
To synge stylle, to contynewe syngynge.
A meale, where men eate hūgrely.
To perceyue, to take, or receyue.
To bryng into a lytel roume.
To runne apace, to runne by.
Loste, perysshed, withoute recouerie, out of hope.
Abydynge all the day, or watching all the day, or he whiche doth any thynge in the daye tyme.
To bryng to an ende, to brynge or leade by force.
Treason agaynst the king, or the countrey. Also a traytour.
Out of a mannes propre countrey. Peregre uado, I go out of the countreye, or on pylgremage. Peregre uenio, I come out of straunge countrayes, or from pylgremage.
To go into strange countreys, or on pylgremage.
The daye nexte after to morowe.
A course of water that cometh with rayne, or a brooke that is only made with rayne.
To be loste or consumed, also to dye.
To go or ryde al aboute.
The auncient wryters vsed for facile, lyghtly.
By ryght or wronge, by one waye and other.
He that bryngeth a thynge to passe, or to a poynte.
To brynge in conclusion. Also to brynge or telle tidinges. somtime to suffre or endure.
To accomplyshe, to brynge to a poynte, to optayne.
False of promyse, he that dothe any thynge against the trust that is put in him, disloyall.
Falsehode against promyse or trust, disloyaltie.
To rūne out as water both out of a broken vessell.
To dore or perce through, •• stryke through, to dygge through, or to the dottome or depest of any thynge.
To perce, or to make an hoole throughe.
Perced through, stryken or dygged through.
Aut or, Is in a prouerbe as mohe to saye, as he hath layde aparte shame, or he is shameles, or without abashement.
He hathe taken the fruite or pleasure of a thynge, he hath vsed or exercysed a thynge, or hathe lefte the vse or exercise therof.

o: Perfruor, perfructus, perfretus, aut perfruitus, perfrui,
n: perfruor perfructus perfretus aut perfruitus perfrui
d: To take all the profyte or cō moditie, to take pleasure or recreation in any thynge.
He that fleeth to the contrary part in battayle, or forsaketh his capitayne.
To rounne vnto oone for succour.
A place, wherevnto a manne runneth to haue succoure, or to be kept frome daunger: It is also taken for anye thynge, whereby a manne maye be succoured.
That whyche passethe lyghtly away, or tarieth not longe.
He that hath doone diligently his offyce or duetie.
To poure out, or droppe out, or stylle oute. Perfundit que genas lachrimis, • uidi •• . The teares dropped downe on his chekes.
A towne in Pamphilia, wherof Diana was called Pergaea.
A Cytie in Asya, the countrey of Galene, the famous Phisycion.
Playe the man, goo to lyke a man, go to hardily.
Wylte thou not leaue? wylte thou not be gone.

To go, to procede▪ to endeuour to do a thyng, to continue, to make haaste, to assaye▪ 〈…〉 deuoured to go.Terent. in Phor •• . Suspen • o g • adu 〈…〉 perrexi, I assayed with a • yght pass to go softely.
To •• ryottous, in eatynge, drynkynge, and hauntynge harlottes.

A galerye, proprely. where it is open on bothe sydes, It is also the place in a shyppe, wherein menne doo, walke. Also a vyne raysed in the fourme of an herber▪ Sommetyme the companye of warkemenne, obeyenge to the chyefe warkeman.
To say, to gyue, to set a price. Praetium perhibere.
Oone of the seuen wyse menne of Grecia.
A noble man of Athenes, in whom was a naturall eloquence incomparable.
To be in peryl, also to experyence or proue a thynge.
Peryll or daunger. somtyme experience or profe.
A clause, a circute in wordes, or contynuance in speakynge.
Feuers, whyche come by courses or fyttes.

Was an artifycer, which made a bul of br • sse wherinto (being glowing hotte) men shuld be put, that in tourmentynge of them, by they • crienge, a noyse shulde issue out lyke the mowynge or belowynge of a bulle, the whiche engine whanne Perillus hadde gyuen to Phalaris, the cruell tyraunt, he caused the craftes manne to be fyrste putte into it, to proue his owne experience.
A compasse or • y • cuy • e.
My harte or courage is gone.
Soo, in lyke wise, euen ly • e, verye moche, euen as, in this facion.
A cytie of Thra ••• , which • nowe is called Heracl • a.
Th • • ethe and commeth by courses.
A 〈…〉 commeth by courses, 〈◊〉 tercians and 〈◊〉 .
Companions or dwellers togyther in one house.
The hangyng of a house, with tapisrye or other lyke thynge.
A philosopher of Aristotels secte▪ or opinion.
Circumlocution, one word expressed by many.
A fygure, whanne a part of a sentence nothynge necessary, is added vnto a verse.
Syckenesse of the lounges with the coughe.
The powder or dust that commeth of fylynge or shauynge of mettalle or wodde.
Sloppes, whyche womenne were wont to weare.
Tapesry, or couerlyds of Aras or Verdure.
A place set about with pyllers.
To sweare vntrewely,Plautus in Bacch. Plautus in truculen. to be periured.
A manne whiche is often forsworne.
A corse or brode gyrth, wherwith maydens were wont to be gyrte vnder their pappes.
A thynge whiche pleasauntlye draweth a man to fauoure it.
To speake out all to an ende, to speake perf • tely.
Cleere, that • manne may see through, as water, glasse, horne.
To be moche wette, or to be made very moyste.
To make verye moyste, or to wette moche.

n: permano amp permanesco are amp nescere
d: To be disclosed, knowen, or diuulgate.
To runne all ouer, or to fall into, to be declared openly.
That whyche is lefte from one to an other, or is taught by one to an other: As the father telleth or leaueth to his sonne, and he to his sonne, and so contynually by lyne.

o: Perme, aut te, aut illum, aut aliquid aliud stare,
n: perme aut te aut illum aut aliquid aliud stare
d: Whanne we, or anye other thynge is the cause,Plinius. that a thynge is not doone. Omnia iam parata erant, nisi per eum stetisset, Nowe al thynges were redy, if by his occasyon it had not be lette▪
A Ryuer in Grece, dedicate to the Muses.
To suffre, to yelde, or delyuer, to thraste in, to throwe downe, to cōmytte, to sende forthe, to let downe, us to lette downe one by a rope, or other lyke thynge.
To appease, addoulce, or mytigate a mans displeasure.
To chaunge oone thynge for an nother.
The pestyll and also the gammonde of bakon.
Wars, more dangerous, more full of myschiefe.
Swyfte, flyghty, sometyme stubborne, also deedly.
To tarye all the nyghte, to watche, to praye, to reste, to walke, to stande, to dwelle, to slepe, to lye oute of his owne house.
A showe of rawe lether, Also a sacke.
He that puttethe a stalyon to the mare, to season her.
He that weareth rawe lether shoen, boteux or cokers lyke a plough mā.
To begyn, spryng, or growe by the occasion of some thynge.
To speake or raison to an ende,Qui •• . to reason perfectly, somtyme to moue the herers to indignation.
The last part of an oration, wherin the affectes of the herers are chiefelye styrred.
To sette all thynge in peace.
Very scarsely, verye nyghely, or nygardely.
To constrayne, to moue or induce one to do a thynge.
A plumlyne, such as masons and carpenters haue, with leadde at the ende, whereby they doo proue the euennesse of their squares.
He that suffreth with moch peyn.
Proprely to doo or to committe an acte good or vlle.
Perpetuall euerlastynge, contynualle, holl, not in porcyens or dyuyded.
To aske importunately without cessynge, to perfourme.
Aduerbes, sygnifienge continually, alway, for euer.
To bynde or twyste harde or faste, to meddle so togyther, that a manne can not know what the thynge meaneth.
To speake nowe one thyng, nowe an other, that a manne wotteth not what he meaneth.

To speake doubtefullye, as wordes, wherin are two intendementes.Plautus in Aulularia. At scio, quo vos pacto soleatis, perplexarier, pactum, non pactum est, Non pactum, pactum, est, quod vobis lubet, well, I knowe wel ynough, in what facion you are wonte to speake, that a manne canne not telle howe to take you: It was promysed, It was not promysed, It was not promysed, It was promysed, euen as hit lysteth you.
A worde spoken, whych hath twoo dyuers vnderstandynges, or that whyche is one thynge in herynge, an nother in vnderstandynge.
Perplexed, twysted togyther, or harde to be lowsed, intrycate, doubtefull.
To rayne in the myddell of a howse.

An othe, sygnyfyenge by Pollux. Sommetyme the worde Per, dothe pertayne to the wordes folowynge. Perpol quam paucos reperias meretricibus fideles euenire amatores, Terent. in Hecyra. By God thou fyndeste verye fewe trewe louers happen to commune womenne. Where per belongethe to quam paucos, and not to Pol.
To drynke all day, or to drynke stylle, or contynually, or vntyl one be drunke.
To haue a greate ytche, or desyre to clawe or scratche.
To make all thynge cleane, or nette.
To declare al.Plautus in Cistel. Nunc operam date, ut ego argumentum hoc uobis plane perputem, Nowe take ye hede, that I maye playnly declare al this matter vnto you.
Added to any nowne adiectiue, augmentethe his power. Perquàm doctus, Verye well lerned. Perquàm stolidus, very foolyshe.
To make dilygente serche, to examyne.
To goo softely, or with moche peyne.
To scorne, to laugh at one,Perottus. or to make an nother to laugh.
To breake on sender, or in the myddes.
A manne or woman of the countrey of Persia.
To wryte a thynge throughe, or to an ende, to regyster or inrolle a thynge.
A deede of a mans owne wrytynge.
The olde and auncyente writers vsyd for perfacile, verye lyghtely,Pom. Fes • . or verye easyly.
The Surname of Proserpina, and sygnyfyeth the vertue of seedes in spryngynge.
A Cytie in the countreye of Persya.
To pursewe, to contynue in that, whiche is begonne, to persecute, to be auenged.
A stable abyding in any thing reasonable.
To contynewe with a stedfaste mynde.
A noble knyghte, whyche delyuered a fayre lady callyd Andromeds frō a whale, and also slewe Medusa, whyche tourned men into stones. Also it is a signe amonge the sterres.
A countreye in the easte parte of the worlde, where nowe Sophy reigneth.
To pay truely, to paye all, to accomplyshe.
A vysour lyke to a mans face. also person or personage, amonge dyuynes and late philosophers: somtyme the qualitie of a man.
A masker, or he that weareth a visour.
An herbe, whyche groweth by the water syde, hauynge great brode leaues lyke gourdes, but that they be greatter & harder: I suppose it to be the herbe, which in some countrey is called Donye.
To sowne oute, or sowne perfectely.
He that seeth quyckely, and doth all thynges with consyderation.
Clerenesse, proprelye in wordes or sentences, easynesse.
To sette a pryce on a thynge.

To wrynge harde, to towche a thynge shortely in speakynge or wrytynge, to dull or darke with to moche lyght. Perstringere aures, to fylle the eares with noyse. Perstringere nomen aut famam, to gyue a man an ylle name.
To induce one to beleue or truste, to aduyse, to styre vehementely.
In suche wyse as it may perswade.
A perswader or inducer to do a thynge.
A woman,Plautus in Bacch. whiche inducethe or moueth one to do an acte.
To tempte, to assay or proue moche.
To rubbe or frotte a thynge.
Displeased, annoyed. Sermonis pertesus, werye of the communication.Plaut. in Mostell. Suetonius in Caesar.
To make an ende, to cō clude, proprely to wayue out, or to weaue perfectely.
A staffe, a cogell, a perche or polle, wherwith grounde is mette.
To touche moche, to ioyn harde vnto a thynge.
To indure to the ende, to sustayne valyantely.
To loke on a thing ferre of, or on parte, and not all.
To stryke harde, or breake a thynge in strykynge.
To pertayne or belonge, to be ioyned to.
Vesselles cracked or broken in somme parte.
To come to a place or to an ende.
To make yll, to peruerte, or depraue.
He that seketh or loketh for a thinge.
Harde ouerthwart, yll to intreate, stubbourne, obstinate, sometyme constaunt.
Obstinacy: but sometyme it is vsed in a good part, and taken for a perseueraunce and constancy in a good act. Pertinacia allwaye in an yll part.
More obstynate, more stubbourne: sometyme more constaunt.
He that watcheth. alsoo diligent and industriouse.
Moche watche: alsoo watchinges▪ or vigiles before solemne dayes.
The olde wrytars vsed, for perire, to be lost, to peryshe.

To lyue longe, or vntyll the vttermoste.Plautus in Cap. Et si peruiuo vs que ad summā aetatem, tamen breue spacium est perferundi, quae minitas mihi: Althoughe I lyue yet to the vttermooste age, yet is the tyme lytle to suffre all: wherewith thou thretteste me.
That maye be gone in, penetrable.
To flee oute, or to the ende.
To burne all, or euery where.
A foote, whiche now contayneth xii. ynches, the olde foote contayned .xvi. fyngres bredeth.

Put for an aduerbe, signifieth on foote. Pedes agmen circuibat, the hoste went about on foote. In agmine non nunquam equo, Suetonius in Caes. saepius pedibus ante • bar, In the hooste, he wente allwaye afore, sometyme on horsebacke, but moore often on foote.
To be a foote man in warres.
A louse: allsoo a corde, wherewith the sayle in a shyp is bent.
Olde wrytars vsed for pennas.Pom. Fest.
In olde tyme vsyd for Pestis, Pom. Fest. Pestilence.
To go backewarde, to be lost or destroyed, to be nowght set by.
A barre or bolt, wherewith doores or gates be made fast.
An aduerbe, which signifieth backewarde, downewarde, vnder foote.
To cast vnder foote, to put to the warie.
A pestilence, a mortalitie of men.
A hatte, a rounde kouerynge of a house.
A corde, or a staffe, or a bourde,Iu • . pol▪ or other lyke thinge, whereon lyghte personages do daunce and proue maistryes. it is also a rouste, where pultry doeth syt in the nyght.
A tettar that runneth ouer all a mannes face.
The howfe of a whyte horse.Pom. Fest.

A floure whyche groweth amonge brembilles, in the later ende of somer,Plinius. and is lyke a wylde rose in coloure, and hath fyue small leues, the budde of dyuerse colours, hauynge within it yelowe sedes.
A sore in the shoulders of beastes,Pom. Fest. which I suppose is a fassion.
Olde wrytars vsed for Peto, Pe • ot. to aske or demaunde.
He that asketh or demaundeth: amonge lawyers he is called the demaundaunt: also it is a beggar, which asketh allmes from doore to doore.
A lytle foote: also a perche whereon frutes or onyons be hanged.

To aske, to gette or attayn, to desyre, to laye awayt, to abide, to strike, to go to a place, to seke. Petere gladio, to stryke with a sworde. Petere veneno, to poyson. Petere blandicijs, to • later. Petere tactu, to feele. Petere mutuum, to borowe: also to remembre. Petere iugulum, to kill, to folowe. Petere auribus, to heere. Petere naribus, to smelle. Petere oculis, to behold. Petere osculis, to kisse. Petere vi, to inforce. Petere, is also to assayle or make assault on one.
Carles of the countraye: also a wether shepe.
Want on dishonest, reprocheful, prowde, viciouse, redy to do wronge.
An oyle, which naturally runneth out of a stone.
He that hath one eye lasse than the other.
Some men in expoundynge Pliny, do suppose Pexas vestes, to be of suche thynge, as is shorne, as syne woullen clothe, or veluet.
They which do weare suche maner of cloth, or sylke.
Moussherons, growynge at the rootes of trees.
People of the Ile of Corcira.
The wyfe of Theseus, & stepmother to Hypolytus.
Runnyng cancre or pock, whiche shortly eateth the flesh vnto the bones.
A water crowe, it maye signifie a coote.
To moue or dryue a thynge vppon rollers.
A cruell tyraunt, which raigned in the citie of Agrigentum.
Staues, whereon men doo carye packes, playne staues, also leauars, to lifte thinges that be heuy.
An hooste of footemen, sette in suche order, that they maye incountre with their ennemyes, foote to foote, man to man, shylde to shylde. It is also the beame of a balaunce.
Are the ioyntes or spaces in the fyngars: they be also rollers, whereon shippes or greate pieces of tymber be remoued.
An instrument of warre, wherein wylde fyre is inclosed, that whan it is by shot fastened to tymber, it burneth all shortly.
A traper or bardes for a horse.
Trapyd, or bardyd.Do •• . in Teren. Phor ••
Frenetyke, he that hath vayne vysions.
One of the names of Bacchus.Orpheus.
Fantasyes, which happen to men in dremes.
A Pharyze, whych was of a secte of Iewes, which lyued in a more strayghter fourme than the commun people dyd.
A serpent, whiche maketh a furrowe in the grounde with his tayle, as he creapeth, and so lyfteth hym self vppe.
That part of physike, which healeth with medicynes.
A medycyne: sometyme it signifieth poyson.
A countraye in Thessalya, where the batayle was betwene Iulius Caesar and Pompey.
A worde of Hebrue, which signifieth a departynge.
A kynde of poulse corne. I suppose it be that, which is called Tares.
A greate ryuer in the countraye of Colchos.
A famouse Phylosopher and wrytar of Tragoedies, which dyed of the lousy sickenesse.
Thinges borne at great feastis or triumphes, as pageantes or iewels of gold or siluer, images, and suche lyke thinges.
A thinge, wheron pageantes are borne: also deed corpsis.
The generall name to all plate, whiche serueth for wyne.
A potte or cuppe of golde or siluer, which serueth for wyne.
An excellent w • rkman, in makinge great images of golde or yuory.
The soupers, whiche the Lacedemonians vsed, whyche were openly kepte with a meruaylouse temperaunce, euery man bringynge his measurable porcion of meate and wyne.
A louer of mankynde: also gē tyll and kynde.
A good man, a clenly man, or elegaunt.
A nightingale: also a fayre mayden, whyche was defloured by Thereus, husbonde to her sister, whome poetes do fayne was transfourmed to a nightingale.
A brawler: sometyme a louer of victory.
Philosophy, the loue or fauorynge of wysedome.
He that wolde be lyke a philosopher.
A solemne feaste amonge the Grekes.
A drinke charmed, whiche causeth a man to be madde for loue.
Smalle thynges hangynge downe of trees or herbes, like vnto heares.
A sore on the fynger, whyche maye be called a whytblowe.
The instrument, wherewith bloode is leten, a fleme.
A ryuer of hell, which allwaye burneth.
The son of Mars, a kynge in Thessaly, and father of Ixion.
A yelowe floure lyke a violet.
An inflammacion of bloode, which groweth into an impostume.
A se calf, it maye be supposed to be a Seale, whych is fisshe, and breedith on the lande.
A noble counsaylour of Athenes, whose lyfe is a myrroure to all counsayllours, which let theym rede in the warke of Plutarchus, intytled the lyues of noble men.
A great byrde, hauing redde fethers.

A byrde, whiche lyueth aboue syx hundred yeres, and finally caryenge swete spices vppe to a hyghe mountayne, by the heate of the sunne, and labour of hir wyngis, kyndleth fyre, whereby she being all burned, of her axen ryseth another like byrde: it is also a date tree, or palme, also a lytell ryuer in Grecia: it was also the brother of Cadmus, which raygned in Phoenicia.
A mountayne in Archadia, full of woode.
He that techeth one to pronoūce and moderate his voyce.
A shepeharde that founde Oedippum, after that he was hanged vpp by the feete.
One of the sonnes of Neptunus, whyche was taken for a god of the see.
The mooste auncient kynge of Grecia.

The propre fourme, or maner of speache, which in one countraye is oftentymes dyuer • e • • s Southerne, Northerne, Deuenysshe, Kentyshe, Frenche, Picard, Gascoyne, walon: some do set the negatife before the affirmatife, some contrary, some speache is quicke, some graue, some flouryshynge, some temperate.
The mydryfe, whyche dyuideth the vmbles of a man or beaste, frome the bowelles.
He that is vexed with a frenesy.
A countraye in Asia the lasse.
A syckenesse, in the which lyse do growe in suche multitudes, that they deuoure the body.
People dwelling nyghe to the greke see, which lyued onely by fisshe.
He that hath the consumpcion of the lunges.
A great fyshe in the Frenche Occean see, whyche ryseth lyke to a pylar aboue shippes.
A consumption of the body by a distillation frome the heed into the lunges, whereby the lunges are exulcerate.
A plante or herbe, which some call Valeriane.
A lytle swellyng or botche, harde and redde, burnynge and prickinge.
A woman, doughter of Lycurgus, kynge of Thrace, which hynge her selfe, despayriuge of the commyng of Demoophon, whome she loued, whome poetes fayne to be turned into an Almonde tree.
Warkes treatynge of the nature of thinges, or the operacion of nature.
A rule to knowe a mannes naturall affections by his vysage or fourme of his membres.
One of the names of Apollo.
He or she, whyche hath a spirite within theym, that gyueth aunswere of thinges to come.
For the whych satisfaction maye be made, and god pleased.
That whiche is gyuen or offred to god for satisfaction.
That which maye be pourged or satisfyed.
Tokēs in sacrifice of some heuy chaunce to come.
Any thinge done for satisfactiō of some greuouse synne: sometyme a greate & haynouse offence.
That which was gyuen or occupyed aboute satisfaction.
A table, pertaynynge to Iuges or bysshoppes: it is sometyme a playster for the stomake or heed.
Imbroudred apparayle, or rather of bawdekyn.
A lytle byrde, which maketh a hole in trees, wherein he breedeth: it was also the name of an olde kynge of Latines.
A mountayne in Grece, dedicate to the Musis.
More and moost mercyfull, most louynge towarde his parētes or countraye.

The reuerend loue towarde a mannes propre countraye and parentes, of dyuines it is taken for the loue and honour due vnto god. Lactantius calleth it iustice,Lact. lib. • . and deuoute worshyppynge and knowlege of god.
It greueth, it dulleth, it lyketh or contenteth not▪ Facti piget, he is sory for that, that he hath done: sometyme, I am sory.
Payntinge: also false colour in speakynge, disseytefull wordes, pleasaunt lyes.
A maker or sellar of payntynge.
That which is layde in pledge.
To laye to pledge or gage, sometyme to take pledge.
A pledge or gage, or pawne.
To holde backe, or tary one.
A mortar, wherein any thinge is beten with a pestill: also a pilar, a ball, or any thinge rounde as a ball.
A certayne stone that is whyte.
A slaue that is solde with his cap on his heed.
A cappe, sometyme lybertie, for asmoche as bondmen, whan they were infraunchysed, ware copped cappes.
To begynne to be heary, or growe in heare.
A lytell ball: also pilles made for purgations.
A barbours knyfe or rasour, also a dart of fyue foote longe and a halfe.
A man which founde the maner to dunge lande, and to grynde corne.
It is also a pestell to braye or breke any thynge withall in a mortar.
A fysshe that hath twoo grete shelles.
A case or place wherein tables are put or set.
An auncient house or famyly in Italy, of the which were the preestes that sacrifised to Hercules.
A mountayne in Thessalia: also a cytye there.
Gardens that brynge forth good herbes.
He that loueth that thinge, whiche is fatte.
Fatte, he that is fatte, corsy, vnweldy.
A quyll, or penne, the harder part of a fether.
Imbatelmentes of a walle, a muskle, which is founden in muddy waters.
The ouer part of the eare, a lytle quyll.
He that gryndeth in a qwerne: also a baker.
A rouer or robber on the se, a pyrate.
The practise of pirates or robbers on the see.
A citie in Grece betwene the two moū taynes of Olympus and Ossa: also a citie in Arcadia.
A citie in Italy, called Pise.
People of the citie of Pise.
A fysshe ponder: it is also generally euery ponde, allthoughe therin be no fish.
That may be fysshed, or is full of fysshe.
People of the citie Pisa in Gretia.

A noble man of Athenes, whiche chaunged the commune weale of that cytie from the rule of the people, to the rule of one gouernour: and therfore he was called a tyraunt, notwithstandinge that (as he wrate vnto Solon, which mayntayned the populer astate) he rulyd by their owne lawes, and was rightwyse and gentyll vnto the people.
Is proprely to braye, for in the old tyme men vsed to braye or breake corne in mortars: but after that they had quernes to grynde with the hande, they vsed Pisere to grynde, and Pisor for a gryndar.
The name of a noble famyly or house in Rome.

o: Pistoricus, ca, cum, & Pistorius, a, um,
n: pistoricus ca cum amp pistorius a um

d: A bakehouse, or grynding house: somtyme it signifieth for paynfull seruice.
A woman baker: also a monstruouse fysshe in the Indiane see.
Iles in the se agaynst Campania.
A certayne tyle, sometyme made in Spayne, which beinge cast into the water, wolde not synke.

He which first brought vppe the name of a phylosopher: who was borne in Samia, and was a beautyfull man, and of excellent wytte, and therewith of a pure and cleane lyuynge, absteyninge from the eatynge of any thinge that lyued: whose Phylosophy was mysticall and secrete, & declared by numbres and proporcions.
A Comete or impression in the firmament, which is lyke a turine, and doeth appiere as it were through a myste.
A defourmed or yll fauoured woman.
A place in Asia, where after the Idus of August, great flockes of Storkes do assemble togither.
In the olde tunge of Oskes sygnified quicquid, whatsoeuer.
One of the seuen sages of Grecia, and was of the cytie of Mytelene.
A worme which is in a pyneappull tree, whose bytinge is venymouse.
The lady and presydent of eloquence to persuade.
Flewme, or rowme, descending from the heed: alsoo the pyppe, whiche chykens haue.
An exercise, where a man goeth fast on his toes, and moueth his armes forewarde and backwarde.
Religiouse, deuoute, pitiouse, gē tyll, chaste: he that loueth his parentes or countraye.
People of the citie of Placentia.
To please, to lyke, to glory.
Studyes or exercises. Ipse placita maiorum colebat habitu seuaero: He in a sage garment, haunted the studyes of the auncient fathers.
A firme consent in an opinyon, an ordinaunce.
A disease, whereby the eye lyddes waxe feble, and wyll vneth be plucked vppe.
A wounde, also a nett to take beastis▪ sometyme the armyng cordes: also a great space in the erthe, called a Cooster alsoo a shete for a bedde: moreouer a great space on the erthe, called also Clima.
A lawe made agaynst theym, whiche were called Plagiarn, whyche for theyr offence were whypped.
He that whyppeth men. Alsoo he that byeth a man for a slaue, knowinge hym to be free. Alsoo he that intyseth a mans seruant to go from his master: also a stealer of bokes.
He that is borne to be whypped.
A schoole mayster, whyche is a greatte beater.
The offence, for the whiche oone is whypped.
Fulle of strypes, or he that beateth moche.
To wepe or wayle, to strike or hytte.
A noyse made with the mouthe, as in lawghynge, or weepynge.
He that gothe withoute showes. Also a player in an enterlude.
The foote with the toes. Sommetyme onely the soole of the foote. Alsoo a plant or tre newely sette: sometyme an herbe that groweth lowe.
Settes or plantes, or the places, where plantes be sette.

A deceyuour or mocker, Also a Iugglar, whyche makethe thynges to seeme in apparaunce, where in deede noo suche thynge is: As water to come into the howse, or trees to growe, or money of leaues or stones.
The w • rke of a potter, or of hym, whyche worketh in erthe. Also a playster.
To make pottes, or any other thynge of erthe.
A warker of ymages or other lyke thynge in erthe.
The crafte of warkynge in erthe.
A place where plane trees doo growe.
A promontory or hyll in Italy.
A high waye or strete, Also a court in great places. Moreouer a see gull.
A cytie in Boeotia, not farre from Thebes.
People of the citie of Plat • e in Greece.
The Prynce and chiefe of all philosophers, as welle in wysedome and counnynge, as in good lyuynge and eloquence.
They whyche haue great hangynge eares.
That whiche the people doeth receyue with ioye, and clapping of their handes.
A reioycynge with voyce and gesture, clapping of hādes togither for ioy
One of the comminaltie,Plautus is penulo. not beinge a gentylman.
A lawe, whiche sometyme was made by the onely consent of the common people of Rome, without the autoritie of the Senate.
An instrument, wherwith menne played on the harpe or doulcymers, for hurtynge of their fyngers. Also a spurre sette on a fyghtynge cocke, whan he lacked naturall spurres.
The seuen sterres, whyche marynours do vse in tryenge of costes.
Of old tyme was v • d for more. Plera pars, the more parte.Pom. Fe • t▪

o: Plaeri que , plerae que , plera que ,
n: plaeri que plerae que plera que

o: Plerus que , plera que , plerun que ,
n: plerus que plera que plerun que
d: The more parte of any thynge.
A fygure, wherin is superfluitie of wordes.
A measure of lande, contaynyng a hundred fete.
A sycknes in the syde, callyd the Pleurilye.
He or she, whiche hath the Pleuresy.

The name of two noble lerned men, the one wrate the moost excellent warke, callyd the hystorie of Nature, the other wrate eloquente Epistles, and an oration to Tratane in his commendation, whiche oration is called Panegyricus. There is also a warke of the practise of phisyke in the name of Plinius, but whither it were of the fyrste Plinie or no, it is not verye certayne.
To make noyse with handes or feete.
That whiche belongethe to a wayne or carte.
They whiche haue playne feete without holownes in the soles of the feete.
To be in fethers. Also to enbrowder.Vopiscus.
Of fethers, a warker with fethers.
A vayne of mettalle or oore, wherin is bothe syluer and leade, it is also an herbe, whiche hath leaues lyke sorrell, and a great rote and rough.
A plummer or worker in leade.
Balles or clubbes of leade, wherwith men faught.
Of the colour of leadde, leedye.
A lumpyshe man withoute courage or spirite.
To leadde, to sowlder or ioyn mettalle.
To be fetherid, or haue fethers.
Very moche, many, longe.Ci. in Ver.
More. Pluris uendo, I selle for more or deerer.
That whiche is sette in a table or case.
Smalle Images in tables or cases.
A space or distaunce, whereby the lower pyllers were dyuided frome the higher in the fronte or foreparte.
An engyne of warre, to conuaye men to the scalynge of walles, kepynge theym frome ordynaunce. Also hutches or greatte coffers, or other lyke places, wherin bokes, tables, or suche thynges are kepte.

n: pluuialis pluuiatilis amp pluuius a um

d: Auncient writers vsed for plurima, very many.
Wherein wynde or breathe is vsed.
They whiche be sycke of the longes.
He that bryngeth cuppes to the table, or a cuppe bearer.
The goute, peyne in the feete.
One of the sonnes of Esculapius a greatte surgeon.
