A longe gowne to the feete.
A straite garment of lynnen cloth: It maye nowe be callyd the Albe, whiche priestes doo weare whan they saye masse.
The corde, wherwith the sayle is spredde.
A place made without a walle, for men to stande and beholde thynges, Also a stage, wheron is set candelles or bokes.
To be asshamed of, to be lyttell estemed.
I am in payne, I am greued.
A man, whom Homer calleth excellently lerned in phisike.
An herbe callid Pyonie. Also a region or countrey in Macedonia.
A place, whyche for the more parte is inclosed with water.
To repent, to forthynke, to be sorie for a thynge.
A manne of the cytie of Carthage.
A blasing sterre, with a long beam afore lyke a berde.
An aduerbe of swearynge, as it were by Pollux.

Was barley ordered in this forme. They stepyd barley in water one night, and dryed it, and the next day they fried it, and than grounde it, And soo kepte it longe, whyche theyr slaues and pultrye dydde eate.
Pertaynynge to barleye grounde, as is aforesayde.
They whyche are dylygente in husbandrye.
A rangynge syue, wherewith the floure is syfted from the branne, it may be called also a boulter.
To polyshe, to garnyshe or decke.
To may, to haue power, to shine.
A thumbe of the hande, It is also an ynche, whiche is a synger bredthe and a halfe.
To minister aboute funerals, also to boulte meale.
The administratour or officer in ordaynyng of funeralles.
To mynyster sacrifyce, specially to Hercules.

The pole. There be imagyned to be twoo certayne poyntes in heuen, as hit were the endes of Extree, where aboute heuen is meuyd, the oone is in the Northe, and is callydde Polus arcticus. The other in the Southe, callydde Polus antarcticus.

Was brother to Castor, bothe being borne at one bourdeyn, whych Poetes doo fayne to come of one egge, layd or brought forthe by a woman, called Leda, with whom Iupiter companied in likenes of a swanne.

A tyraunt, whyche was soo fortunate, that he neuer suffered any aduersytie, or griefe. Wherfore he at the laste dredynge the chaunge of the fauoure of fortune, hauynge a rynge with a stone of an excellent valewe, dydde caste the same rynge into the see, to the intente that he wolde suffre somme displeasure, and soo satisfie fortune: but a fysshe deuourynge the rynge, was the same daye taken of a fyssher, and gyuen to the kynge, for the greatnesse of the fysshe, whyche beynge opened, there was the sayde ryng founde and brought to the kynge: wherat as wel he, as all other aboute hym meruayled. Sone after the same kyng was oppressed by his people, and hanged.
A Troyane, oone of theym, whyche betrayed the cytie with Eneas and Anthenor.

An herbe, whyche is also callye Sanguinaria, and hath leaues lyke to Rewe, but it runneth on the grounde as grasse, the iuyce therof put into the nose, stoppeth bledynge. It is supposed to be swynes grasse, or knotte grasse.
He that knoweth moche, or of many thynges done.
A garmēt made of twisted threde or sylke.
One of the Muses, which word sygnifieth moche memorie.
A candelstycke, whiche bereth many lyghtes.
Was a gyaunt, that had oone eye in his foreheed, whiche was put oute by Vlyxes.
An herbe lyke to ferne, growynge on trees.
He that hath a soore in the nose.
A fyshe, hauyng many feete, whiche chaungeth his coloure often: Also a piece of fleshe, growyng in the ouermost parte of the nose, whiche causeth a stynkynge ayre out of the nose.
A fygure, where manye artycles comme into a sentence, as Ille trahebat, Hic vociferabatur, He drewe, and he cried out.
The daughter of kynge Priamus whom cruell Pirrhus slewe on the tombe of Achilles.
An orcharde, sometyme a place wherin fruites be kepte.
The grounde without the walles of the citie, whiche moughte neyther be ploughed, nor inhabyted, the territory.
The name of a noble Romayne.
Of Pompeius parte, or a fauourer of Pompeius.
The generall name of all fruites. It is moste vsed for an appull.
To waye, to ponder, to consyder, to esteme.

A pounde weight, sommetyme .xii. pounde. It was amonge the Romaynes the pounde of moneye, as Mina, & mna, was in Athenes, whyche was of the value of a hundred old poyse grotes, wherof .viii. went to an ounce: so that in those grotes after our rate, it contayned a poūd and a marke of newe grotes tenne to the ounce .ii. pounde and fyue grotes.
Weight.Varro. sometyme it signifieth numbre, also auctoritie.
Putte the case that he be vanquyshed.
To putte, to set, to cesse, to buylde, to laye a parte.
A kynde of fylberdes, whiche came from the countreye called Pontus in Asia.
Is a taste, whiche hath no sente to be discerned.
The see, whyche is from the great fenne, callydde Maeotis, vnto Tenedum, It is sommetyme vsyd for all the see. It is also a prouynce in Asie the lesse.
A couern • or vyttaylynge howse, where meate is eaten out of due tyme.
Pertaynynge to ryot, or places of ryotte.
To eate oute of due tyme, to be ryottous.
The hamme of a mās legge behynde the knee.
The noyse made with the mouthe and the hande, in ryding, or wanton dalyaunce.
Wastynge the countreye, or he that gothe in forragynge or robbynge of countreyes.
Pertayning to the people, accepted or fauoured of the people. Also it sygnifyeth a familiar frende, or as we vse to call countrey man.
The coniunction or amytie of people of one countrey. also affabilitie, humanitie, towarde the people.
Of al the peple. also euerich one.
A wastynge of the countreye, a fourragynge.
A forrageour or waster of countreyes.
Was a daye in the moneth of Iune, at the whiche daye by reason of a rumour, the people fledde.
To wast or distroy a coūtrey.
A sowe, a rydge of lande, a balke.
A hogge roosted with manye other beastes and fowles within his bealye.
Vsed of the auncyent wryters for porrigam, I wyll delyuer or take to one.
Poores in the bodye, out of the whiche issueth sweate.
A byrde, whiche drinketh as yf he dyd byte the water, he hath longe red legges and bylle.
Of the colours of leeke blades.
To sprede oute, to offre, to ouerthrowe.
Skales whiche do falle from a mannes heed or berde, lyke branne.
Surely. also longe before, farre of, after, in tyme commynge, beyonde, forsoth.
In the plu • ell numbre leeke.
The name of a kynge, that besyeged Rome.
To sygnifie before a thynge happeneth.
That whiche signifieth strange or monstruous thinges comming.
Monstruouse, sygnifieng some thynge to come.
A thynge monstruous or verye seldome sene, whiche may sygnifie somme what to come.
A porcion. portiuncula, a litle porciō.
The pylate of a shyppe, whyche ruleth the maryners.
The customer of a hauen. Also a porter, that dothe beare thynges that be bought, whither as the byer wyll haue hym. Also he that beareth men fro the hauen to the shyppe.
The frayte payde for passage or caryage of merchaundyse.
An herbe callyd Purselan.Salustius in iugur.
A sawce made with vyneygre and water.
To aske, to requyre, to prouoke, to assayle.
He that hath the possession, the owner.
To leaue behynd, to cast back.
That whiche commeth after. Postera dies, the day after Posteri pedes, the hynder • ete.
To sette after or behynde, to set lesse by. Post habere, idem.
A chylde borne after that the father is deade.
All that is behynde vs, lyke as Antica is all that is before vs. It is also a line whiche diuideth the feldes from the caste to the weste.
Is whan any man happeth to go from vs to oure ennemies, and after retourneth home.
The day after to morowe, the day folowyng the day before expressed.
A braake, wherewith a horses mouthe is broken, and is made to beare his heed easyly.
To require, to demande a thing whiche is dewe to the asker. Also to accuse or sewe oone in the lawe, or to complayne on one. sometyme to desyre.
A supplication made to a prince.
To suffre men to come to hym, or to speake with hym.
To haue in possessyon, to optayne, to take pleasure of.
I maye, potis est, it is possyble.
To drynke: Also to gyue drynke to one.
That which hath drunke, and that whiche is dronken.

Before, in regarde, or in comparyson, for. Prae amore, for loue. Also of. Prae studio, of study. Praeut, sygnyfieth than. Modestior nunc quidem est de uerbis, praeut dudum fuit, He is more softe or gentyll of wordes, than he was wonte to be, or than he was late.
To passe by, or passe forthe in iorney. sometyme perire, to lese, to cast away.Plautus. Pom. Fest▪
That whiche is songen or playde at the beginning of a songe or balade.
He that first singeth. it may be taken for the chaunter in a quyre.
He that is to haslye in his busynesse, and doth thynges vnaduisedly.
A precepte, a rule gyuen, a cō maundement.
A swine, which the Paynims dydde sacrifice before they dyd cut downe their corne.
That which is fyrst kylled.Cice. in Achad. que ••
To speake or tell precisely, or certainly, to strike, to cut of, to beate, to denye styffely.Ci. ad A • . lib. 8. Plane sine ulla exceptione praecidit, Truely he styffly denied it without exception.
To synge before or fyrst, also to tell a thynge before it hapneth.
To preuēt or take first▪ to forsee: also to commaunde.
A downe right place or steppe, whiche maye not be gone on.

Harde, intractable, cutted, verye shorte,Quin •••• ▪ lib. • . Qui praecisis conclusionibus obscuri, Salustium at que Thucydidē superant. The whyche beinge harde to be vnderstand in their cutted sentences, doo excede bothe Saluste and Thucydides.
Very noble: sometyme it signifieth goode.
A cryar, a publysshar of thynges.
A solemne cry: sometyme it signifieth prayse or glory.
The skynne, whiche dyuideth the ouer part of the body from the nether: it is also taken for the place vnder the rybbes: sometyme al the numbles, as the hart, the splene, the lunges, and lyuer.

n: praecox cocis amp praecoquus a um

d: A proye, a thynge goten or taken in warres.
Goynge on foragynge in the tyme of warre.
A man of lawe expert in actions reall, or maters concerning landes.
To publysshe, to tell a thynge openly, to prayse.
Adourned: also Praeditus moe rore, replenyshed with heuynesse: Praeditus lachrymis, wasshed with teares, or full of teares.
To robbe a countraye, or to take prayes.
To be harder than it was wōt.
Not honeste to be spoken or reherced.
Was with Emperours the principall officer in his court: as nowe in Fraunce the great master.
A great bason, which was caryed before hym that dyd sacrifice.Pom. Fest.
To make to moche ha • te.
A woman, which is hyred to lamēt at the buryenge of men or women.
To put in auctoritie, or to gyue rule.
To determyne before, to assigne or appoynte.
Harde and vnflexible, whyche wyll rather breke than bowe: also that which was before broken.
The mouth of an ouen or fournayse.
To begyn, to brynge in first. Nolebam ex me morem praegigni malum, I wolde not that an yll custome shoulde be brought vp by me.
To take.Cic. in P ••• . & ad Atti. Ti. Liuius. Manum praehendere, to take by the hande.
A solicitinge or laboringe for the attayninge of some greate office.
To imbrace or set honde on one, to solicite.
To ministre or gyue an othe.

A thinge which being ones decyded and determyned, maketh a rule or example to men that do folowe, to discusse semblably in a lyke mater. As those which we do cal rulyd cases or maters in the law, which be as examples to iuges.
To iuge before: sometyme to condemne, also to let.
The othe that is taken by hym that first sweareth.
He whiche firste taketh an othe, as the fore man of a Iury, or the first witnesse, or any other, after whome other men do sweare, accordynge to the othe gyuen vnto him.
Which I suppose to be so called, eyther bycause it is fyrst runned or put into vesselles, or els bycause it is put into a sacke, which is fast knytte afore.
Batayle also the fyght in batayle: sometyme the acte of generation.
The begynninge of a communication, or thinge spoken, as that which in thetorike is named exordium.
To beare lyght before one, as a torche or candel: also to gyue more light than another.
To shyne in vertues before other.
A proheme, or that which Musicians and Mynstrelles doo playe at the begynnynge, er they come to the songe▪ which they purpose to playe.
To pourge or wasshe cleane afore.
To soone, or before the iust tyme. Praemature vita careo, I dye afore my tyme.
To aduyse before a man do a thinge.

o: Prae me sero, prae me tuli, prae me ferre,
n: prae me sero prae me tuli prae me ferre
d: To declare by deede, worde, or gesture. Prae te fers iracundiam, thou shewyste thy selfe to be angry: also to confesse: also to haue before him a thynge (as it were) in remembraunce.
A sacrifyce or offrynge to Ceres, of the cares of corne that was fyrste repyd.
Theues which steale by nyght, as we mought saye, whyche commytte burglary.
To be better than another or excel aboue another in astate or vertue.
A rewarde, gyuen to hym which hath done any notable and laudable thing.Cellius.
To playe before on an instrument.
Feare of a thinge to come.Ci. Tus. •
He that telleth or sheweth a thynge before that it happeneth.Terent. in Heau.
To dye er the tyme come.
People of the citie of Preneste in Italy.
The firste name: as Marcus. Quintus, Lucius: and as we now haue the name at baptysme.
The first messenger, he that fyrst bryngeth tydinges.
A fygure in Rhetorike, whan we will saye that we will not tell a thinge, and yet therby couertly we wil declare the matter, or make it suspected.
To take or possede a thinge by preuencion.
He that made the fyrst ordynaunce.
Were the byrdes, which shewed them selfes first to the diuinours called Augures, whereby they supposed to knowe what shulde ensue.
Hedded with yron, as a Iauelyn or dart: also sharp afore lyke the heed of a dart, thoughe it hath none yron▪ as the hornes of a lopster, wherewith he swymmeth.
To waye more, to be more worth.
Set or aduaunced aboue other, set in autoritie.
He that is in autoritie, or chief in any office.
To drynke afore, to brynge good lucke in drinkinge.
They that do that thing last, whiche they shulde haue done first.
To be done against all good ordre. As whan the seruaunt commaundeth his master, the peple their rulars, or a foole a wyse man.
The skynne which couereth the heed of a mans priuey membre.
He that laugheth a fore one.
To gnawe or eate very moche.
A prerogati • e, where one is preferred afore another.
All to broken. it is sometyme taken, where a hyll is broken by the sydes, and harde to go on.
Places broken here & there, that no man maye passe.
To perceyue or knowe a thinge before that it happen.
A pronosticatour, or perceyuer of thinges er they happe.
Amonge the auncient writars, a perceyuing of a thinge before that it happeneth, sometyme a coniecture.
An vnderstandinge and perfyte knowlege of all that shall happen.
He that knoweth perfytely thinges er they happen.
To assigne, to note or intitle, to put, to laye before, to telle before, to appoint or determyne.
A rule, a lawe, an ordre, a fourme.
A precepte, a fourme, a rule.
To cut before, sometyme to cut on sonder.
The parynges of a mannes nayles.
Present. In praesentia, & in praesentiarum, at this present tyme.
The greatest and moost feruent poyson: also stronge.
A stronge or good courage, also fauorable. Deum praesentem haber, he hath god fauorable vnto hym.
A stable, a stall, a shepehouse.
He that hath autoritie in a prouince next vnder the prince: sometyme it signifieth a defendour, alsoo sure. Locum praesidem, a sure place.
To be in more autoritye, or of a more dignitie: also to haue authoritye or rule.
Tempest, whiche commeth at the begynnynge of wynter, sooner than it is loked for, or is accustomed to happen.
Where tempest commeth very soone, and before the tyme accustomed.
That which is ordayned to be ayde to another thinge.
A garyson of men with a capytayne, set by the chief capitayne, to defend a fortresse: sometyme it is taken generally for all maner of ayde or defence: also for a fortification of a thinge.
To lepe before, to sterte oute.
To stande or be set afore.
To take the blame on hym.
A place open afore, and keuered behynde lyke a porche, where men do syt for recreacion after their busynesse.
A venymouse serpent, of whome he that is stryken, dyeth for thurst.
Of the auncient wrytars called a prelate.
A iugglynge caste, an inchauntment, a delusyon.
To prepare in byenge a thinge.
To determine before, to prescribe or appoynt before, what shal be done. Istam enim culpam, quam vereris, ego praestabo, Ci. de ora. for the blame, which thou fearest, I will take vppon me.

To be better than another thinge, wherewith it is comparyd, to excell: also to vndertake, to waraunt, sometyme to graunte, also to do, to be beneficiall, to beware, to exchue, to feare, to do or perfourme,Ci ad Q. 〈◊〉 . to gyue, to exhibite, to represent or shewe, to lende, to assigne or appoynt, to do a thinge.
An aduerbe, redy, at hande. Praestosis, helpe me. Praesto esse, to appiere, as mē do in places of iugementes.
To tary, to be at hande, or redy to do seruice.
To bynde fast, to shut, to dasell the eyen, to touche quickly, or shortly, to shaue, to greue somewhat.
To be afore or aboue an other, to be of more dignitye, to be in autorytye.
To be chief in the busynesse.

A takinge or receyuynge before: it is also that, which is called preoccupation, whan we declare first what our aduersary will saye, or what is the iuges opynyon: and against that we do argue, to dissolue it with reason.
To laye for a thing er it come: also to cary or beare afore, also to shew or pretende, to allege, to set a thinge aboute for an inclosure. Praetendere sepem, to make a hedge aboute.
To leade afore, to leade forth.
To passe by, to go beyond.
Deed, departed, decessyd: also they which in suynge for an office, dyd suffre repulse, or were put backe.
For an other cause than that which is reherced.

Except, also besyde, ouer and aboue, before. Praeter oculos, before the eyen, Against or contrary. Praeter morem, againste the custome or facion. Praeter spem, vnloked for. Praeter opinionem, otherwyse thā I thought. Praeter caetera, more than the other. Praeter aequum, against raison.
Moreouer, besyde, none els. Mihi credis praeterea nemini, Thou beleuest me, and none els. also it signifieth afterwarde.
To go ouer or passe, to leue oute a thynge, which shulde be spoken of.
To leue vntouched, to forgete, to leue oute.
Forgetynge, or leuinge out of a thynge.
To make or ordayne firste, to couer or hyde.

A longe garment myxte with purple silke, whiche was the vesture of noble mennes sonnes, vntyll they came vnto .xvii yeres of age: and therfore suche children were called Praetextati, but they had alsoo aboute their neckes, a lytell round iewell of golde, facyoned like a hart, wherin was inclosed some thinge of great vertue.
Was also the robe of astate, whiche the kynge of Romaynes, or the other chief officers dyd weare, whan they sate in their maiestie.
An enterlude, wherin are personages of highe dignitie.
Dishonest,Suetonius Gellius, Macro. or vnclene in speche or actes. Festus taketh it in the contrary sence.
Officers which went before the prelates called Flamines, proclayming openly, that all men shulde ceasse of theyr warke, bycause it was not lefull to those prelates to beholde any man warkynge.
To sheere or klyppe, or rounde before.
A chief capitayne in warres, in a citie or contraye.
Whiche hath autoritye to sit in iugemente, and to gyue sentence in causis.
He that is attendant to him that is Praetor.

The house or pauylyon of hym that is Praetor. it is alsoo a princes palayce or manoure: it is somtyme the place, where iugementes are gyuen, sometyme the coū sayle, wherevnto Praetores are assembled.
Belonginge to the office of Praetor.
The dignitie and ministration, of him that is Praetor.
To preuayle, to be better or of more value.
Very stronge or myghty, sometyme very greate.
Is a collusion: alsoo it is where one toucheth a thing lytely, which ought to be inculked with a more playn declaracyon, or els repeted, as makynge moche to the purpose.

To swarne from truthe, to go out of the right waye, to leue vnsayd that, which shulde be spoken, to touche a thinge shortely in spekynge, to warke by collusion, in suffringe his aduersary to optayne, to hurte another person.
He that leueth the ryght waye, or speketh not that whych ought to be spoken: also he that in spekinge for him selfe aydeth the cause of his aduersary, or doeth any thinge by collusion.

To set more by, or to care more for.Plautus in Amphi. Nec me vxorem praeuortisse dicant, prae repub. Nor let them not saye, that I set more by my wyfe, than by the weale publyke.Plautus in milite. Also to tourne or set a syde. Ne que praeripio pulpamentum, ne que praeuorto pocu lum, Nor I take awaye thy meate, nor set or tourne asyde thy drynke.

Also to go afore. Inde illico praeuertor domum, from thense I went home afore. also to be tourned furth. Foreis enim clausit, Plautus in Amph. ne praeuorteretur foras, he hath shyr fast the doore, leest he shulde be turned forth. Also to do any thinge firste or before any other thinge. Praeuorti hoc certum est rebus alijs omnibus, Surely this shall be done before any other thinge.
To turne it to ernest.Plautus in amph. Si quid dictum est persocum, non aequum est id te serio praeuortier. If any thinge be spoken in iape, it is not rayson to tourne it to erneste.
To be taken with slouth Caue pigritiae praeuortier, beware that thou be not taken with slouthe.
That which is done or sped first, or before any other.
Lyghtenynge whyche is not knowen, whyther it be by daye or by nyghte.
Is in latyne negociatio, an acte or busynesse: alsoo an exercise of marchaundyse.
A determination of practisians of the lawe.

n: prandeo prandi amp pransus sum prandere

d: He that is at dynar, or he that is boden to dynar.
A stone of the coloure of leekes.
That whiche is borowed, as the wyll of the lender, that which is occupyed, at another mans pleasure.
By desyre at another mans will.
To take. Et manuta prehendi, & osculum detuli tibi, I toke you by the hande, and also gaue you a kysse.
To presse: sometyme to vexe, to dygge, to prese on, to thruste, to destroye, to thrust downe, to constrayne, to restrayne.
To hyde heuynesse or sorowe. Premit alto corde dolorem, he hyd his sorowe in the secrete parte of his harte.
To shyt or close. Pressi que oculos, ac vulnera laui, Verg. I closed his eyes, and wasshed his woundes.
To cut awaye. Et ruris opaci, false premes vmbram, Ver geo. 1 and with a sythe thou shalt cut awaye the shadowe of the darke feldes.
To trede doune. Veluti qui sentibus anguem, Vergili. 2. pressit humini tens, lyke as he, which thraslyng his fote to the grounde, tredeth doune the snake, that lyeth in the brembles.
To conuicte a man by witnesse.
A swyne which was offred in sacrifice to Ceres, in satisfaction for a hole housholde, for as moche as a part of that sacrifice was made in the presence of the corps, which than was to be buryed.

He that vndertaketh, if any incommoditie do happen,C • o • Nep. A •• • ian. that he shall make sufficient recompence: it is also he that is bounden for suche money as is borowyd of a commune treasure or stocke.
An auncient, or father in yeres or dygnytye. It is vsed for a preest.
The pryce or value: alsoo the rewarde: sometyme peryll or daunger. Pretio emptas meo, Terent. in ptol. Hec. bought with my peryll or daunger.
Of olde tyme was vsed for Prae.
The noble kynge of Troye, whose history is to no man vnknowen.
A sickenesse, wherein the pryuy membre of a man allway standeth, without hauinge any appetite to lechery.
An ydolle, vnto whome the Paynymes, commytted their gardynes to kepe.
That which is done the days before.
To haue the preeminence, to be chief, to holde the bettar part.
He that assigned tribute to the first legion.
The chief prayses. Cui primae sine cō trouersia deferebantur, to whome the chief prayses were gyuen withoute any controuersye.
Sacrifice of the eares of corne▪ which were first gathered after that they were repyd.
The toppes of any thynge.Plautus. Digitulis primoribꝰ, with the fingar toppes. Labris primoribus, with the fore part of the lyppes.
To touche a thing skantely, to smater of a thinge, and not to knowe it substancially or perfitely.
That commeth naturally of it selfe, and is vnmixt.
The tytle of the eldest childe in inheritaunce.
She that hath her fyrst childe.
He that in batayle fyghteth fyrste with a sworde, and after chaungynge his fourme of fyghtynge, vseth a Iauelyne or darte.
Is he that fyghteth nexte to the standarde. It is mooste proprely the Capytayne of a companye in the fowewarde.
A capytayne of a company in the forewarde or vauntgarde, whiche hadde vnder hym fower hundred Souldiours.
That whiche hath none other begynnynge.
A stake, whereto a cabell or rope of a shyppe is tyed.
Wordes whyche be not dyed from any other.
The fyrste, the chiefe. Primores uiri au • feminae, Noble men or womenne, or gentyll men and gentyll women.
An aduerbe, whyche sygnifyethe fyrste, or euer.
Fyrste, beste, the chiefe. Primo quoque tempore, arre the fyrste tyme. Prima qua que occasione, at the fyrste occasyon that shall happen.
A prince, the fyrste or chief.
Principall, also, pertaynynge to a prynce.
An aduerbe, fyrste, or at the begynnynge.

The place in a Campe, where as are pyghte the pauilions of the heed capitaynes: but the more propre sygnification therof is, that it is the seconde warde in battayle, where in olde tyme were the princis and noble men. Also it was taken for the order of ray of noble men.
Auncient, or of the old time.
That whyche was many yeres passed. Sometyme it sygnifyeth the fyrste, auncient.
A fysh, of wonderful length, & sclender, whyche cuttethe the wawes, as he swymmeth.
He that is in none auctorytie or dygnitie.
That is proprely a mannes owne, that whyche pertayneth to oone man or fewe, also particular. Sometyme it signifieth depriued.
The chylde by an nother husbande, or other wyfe, whiche is deed, son or doughter in law to the husband or wife.
A lawe concernynge pryuate persones▪ also a priuate or speciall lawe.
Pryuate, synguler, euerye mans owne or propre.

For, before. Pro rostris, at the barre or place of pleding. Pro tribunali, in the place of iugement. also after or accordyng. Pro Platonis sententia, accordynge to the sentence of Plato. Pro opere, in the warke.
Accordynge to his deserning.Salust. in Iugurt.
Before the courte. Pro uirili, to my power.

o: Pro deum at que hominum fidem,
n: pro deum at que hominum fidem
d: O the faith of god and man.
A ponde, where sheepe are wasshed.
A vertuous man, a good man.
A sentence purposed, hauing a demaunde therto annexed.
To proue, to prayse, to approue.
A longe snowre, as an Olyphant or swyne hath.
A reprocheful act. Also a reproch or rebuke, an infamie.
Malaperte in askynge, or desyrynge, shameles, wanton in crauing, yll tounged.
Malapertnes, or wantonnesse in askynge or crauynge.
To wowe, to craue, to be ymportunate.
A progenie, whyche commeth of one heade.
To go forthe, to procede, to prosper.
A foote in meter of foure feete shorte.
To streeke, to turn vp so downe
The company or felowshyppe of yonge men in the cytie, as we beholde in London the Bachelers togyther, whan the Mayre taketh his othe.
The heed men of a towne.
An aduerbe, whyche sygnifyeth longe, or of lengthe.
Incensed or prouoked with an yll spiryte, madde or woode.
Let hym prouoke, let hym appeale.

A galerye to goo frome oone chambre to an other. Also the ouermoste parte of the walles within the imbattylmentes, where men maye go: some doo calle it a trenche before the campe, in defence therof from artyllery.
An Ile in the see, in the gulfe or rode of Puteolis, a citie in Campania.
Whan the bone of the fundement appereth oute.
To prouoke or cal from far of.
A nauy p̄parid redy to fight
The prouysyon before that any thynge is done.
To pronoūce in singing, to synge out.
Redy to falle, inclyned. Alsoo redy or easy to be done.
A noble phylosopher of the secte of Plato.
To aske malapertely. Also to dalye with wanton language, to eye or beholde a woman wantonly.
He that was sent with an extra ordinarie power of Consul into a prouynce of the Romayns.
To prolonge the tyme, to deferre.
He that kepethe watche and warde without the campe.
To stryke or beate a thynge. to make it lesse or thynner.
Old writers vsed for promittunt, they promyse.Pom. Fest.
He that is borne whan his father is farre out of the countrey.
To lye flatte or prostrate, to come narowe togyther.
To do or solicite an other mannes busynesse, to inserche dylygentely, to helpe or sustayne, or succour.
Pertaynyng to a proctour or factour.
Mynystration of thynges concernynge an other man.
A wower, to haue a womanne in mariage, but moste proprely where there be two, whyche woweth euery oone for hym selfe.
A sterre called the Doggesterre, whyche appereth in the canycular days.
To goo forthe or oute of a house, to come before one.
A thynge seldome seene, whiche sygnifyeth, that somme thynge shall happen veraye good or veraye ylle, as blasynge sterres, fyres, or fygures in the fyrmamente, thynges monstruouse or agaynste nature.
To lasshe oute moneye in vayne, or in thynges not necessary. somtyme to signifye somme straunge thynge to happen.
To forsake, to differe, or putte of, to caste forthe, to putte oute or farre of, to shewe or disclose. also to differ, to spreade, to betraye.
To leue in remembrance. Also to wryte.
To go agaynst one, or to go to mete with one, whiche is commynge.
To goo abrode, to go in the stretes.

To speke more or prate. Quamobrem excutiemus omnes istorum delitias, omnes ineptias, si prodixerint, Cicer. pro Caelio. Wherfore we wyll set forthe al these mennes pleasures and fantasyes, if they wylle prate any more.
That whyche pertayneth to the procuryng of strange tokens or sygnes.
He that by straunge tokens or sygnes, tellethe before what shall afterwarde happen.
That whyche makethe straunge signes or tokens.
Vsed of Ennius, to issue or come forthe.
To put his lyfe in daunger.

He that rounneth before, as a lackey, or he that brynge the tydynges of ones commynge. Prodromi, he also sterres in heuen, the whyche doo ryse in the Northe easte .viii. dayes afore the canicular dayes.
To prolonge, to bryng forthe, to consume or spende. Producere aliquem falsa spe, Vergilius. to holde or kepe one in a fooles paradyse, to put forewarde: also to folowe.
That whiche is made out at length with beatynge.
To sette forthe to hyre. Audientem dicto mater produxisti filiam, Thou beinge hir mother,Pl • utus in A •• nar. and she being obedient vnto the, thou haste sette hyr to hyre.
The makynge of a thynge longe.
Made longe or sette out at lengthe. also brought or put out.
That whiche being a priuate place, is made commune or publyke.
The churche suspendyd, where any horrible cryme is therin commytted.
To conuerte thynges beynge halowed to a temporall vse.
That whiche is not halowed, temporall, men vnlerned, and that do hate lerned men. Also that whiche is ioyned or annexed vnto the temple.
A passage or. settynge forthe towarde a vyage, a departynge frome the place, where a man is.
To profyte or goo forthe, proprely in study and lernynge.
The pretertence of proficiscor, I wente.
To brynge forthe, to shew forthe, to pronounce, to inlarge, or dylate,Plautus in Ca •• na. or make greatter, to prolonge.
To put a disceit in experiēce.
To profyte, to procede.Ci. de sen • ctute, & de amicitia.

To promyse openly, to tell frankly or boldly. Also to tell or declare, howe moche a man hath of money, cattal, corne,Plautus in capt. Ci. de am • . or any other thynge. Also to speake or auaunt, Also to discouer or confesse a thing. Also to rede openly a lesson.
An open confession, an open redynge or lecture.
To ouerthrowe, to dryue awaye, to brynge to distruction, to putte to flyghte.
Ouerthrowen, dryuen away, put to flyght, distroyed. somtyme it signifieth finished, brought to a poynte.
A ryuer: being a participle, is signifieth flowynge.
To runne out of a thynge, to runne from farre.
To profite. Quae nocuere sequar, Horatius. fugiam quae profore credam, That whyche hath done harme wyl I folowe: & eschew wyll I those thynges, whyche I beleue shulde profyte me.
A place, whereto a man flyethe for succour.
He that gothe farre oute of his owne countrey.
Insaciable auaryce.Salust. in Iugur • . Profunda cupido, insaciable couetyse. Profunda libido, insacyable lecherye.
To poore out largely, to spende excedyngely.
The husbande of my dowghters dowghter, or sonnes dowghter.
Prescience, or knowledge afore that a thynge happeneth.
A marchynge forthe, or passynge forthe.
An assay or profe in exercise.
To prohibite, to forbyd, to tourne awaye.
The ouer partes of a howse, which do leane outwarde from the neither part, as they be nowe in some rownes toward the stretes: some men do cal thē garrettis.
A chylde caste forthe and nouryshed of a straunger.
A penthowse to conuaye rayne from the walles.
A chylde whiche is layde abrode in the strete, no man knowyng who is the father or mother.
To throwe or cast, to set forth, to leaue, to extende or holde oute a thynge at length.
An extendynge forthe. Also pronouncyng, or pronunciation, sommetyme bringynge forthe or shewyng of a thynge.
To deferre or purre of, vntylle a longer ryme.
That which tickleth or plesantly moueth one.
A fygure in speakyng, where we doo preuente, to dissolue by reason that, whyche we thynke to be in the opinion of our aduersary, or of the iudge.
Issue or fruite of a mannes bodye. Also of a beaste.
Amonge the Romains were they whiche for pouertie were not able to goo to the warres: and therfore they were lefte at home to gette chylderne.
To tast, or to sacrifice afore.
To induce or drawe. Eius amor cupidā huc me per tenebras prolicit, Plautus in Curcul. The loue of hym hathe drawen me hyther in the darke, beynge desyrous of his company.

To make a thynge sharpe in lengthe. Quare magnopere mouendus putator est, Colum. 5. ut prolixet aciē ferramenti, & quā tum possit, nouaculae similem reddat, wherfore the cutter of the vyne oughte to be warned, that he make sharpe in lengthe the pointe of the instrument, and as moch as he may, that he make it lyke to a raser.
The fyrste speche or fyrst entree into communication.Plautus
The begynnynge of an oration or sentence.Fest •
To speake at length, to telle a longe tale. Also to speke before, to speake that whyche we thynke, to declare our opynyon.
To flourysshe, as musytians doo, before they come to the principalle mattier: and as fence men doo with the sworde or the two handstaffe.
To mourne longer than hath ben accustomed.
To wasshe moche, to drowne or surrounde.
The fylthe or ordure, whyche is washed of any thynge.
To promote or sette forth suit • in the lawe.

Thynges set forth to be solde, specially that whiche is solde by retaylle. Promercale aurum, golde solde in suche wyse, that besydes the iuste value, so moche golde remayneth to the seller, as may serue to his propre vse, as our nobles and royalles solde beyonde the see at a greatter price than they be valewed at here in this royalme.
To bie thynges good cheape, to the intent to sell them deere, to bye at the fyrst hand, to sel them at retail.
Also to bynde oone by his actes to do for hym. Also to helpe, to profytte.
To doo a man a good tourne.
He that dothe pleasure or seruyce.Plautus in As • ua • . Promerenti optime hoccine preth redditur? He that hathe done verye good seruyce, shall he haue this rewarde for his laboure?
Olde writers vsed for monet,Fest •• . he exhorteth or warneth.
He that fyrst found and taught astronomie in Assiria, and also the craft to make ymages of erthe.
To extend or set out at length.
The extendynge or settynge out at lengthe.
Olde wryters dyd vse for promiscue.
Confused, myngled one with an nother.
To promyse, to lette growe in lengthe. Also to thretten.
To speake out, to tel, to take out of a coffer or other lyke thyng.
A mountayne or high place of a lande or countrey, whyche lyeth as it were an elbowe into the see warde.
A prison from whens men be brought to be whipped or hanged.
That frome whens any thynge is brought or taken:
Prompte, redye to doo a thyng without tarseng. also redy. Promptum ingenium, A redye wytte. Res est in promptu, The thynge is redy. also manyfeste. In promptu res est, The thynge is manyfeste.
The shyppe is drawen with a bote.
He or she that dothe publyshe a thynge.
A countermure, one wall without out an nother.
He that hath the kepynge of the stoorehouse or drie larder.
My sonnes or daughters sonne or daughter.
Olde writers vsed for prona, prostrate or on the grounde.
She that attendeth on the bryde, and is housewyfe durynge the feaste.
To haue a rule in weddinges or ioynynge of couples.
He that leadeth the bryde home to her husbandes house, and hath the surueyenge of the house, durynge the tyme of the solemnisation.
He that dothe celebrate the solemnitie in mariage, it may be nowe taken for the prieste, whiche dothe mynister the solemne wordes of matrimonye.
A pronunciation or vtterance of speeche.
To pronounce, to declare openly, to gyue sentence, to saye.
The wyfe of my sonnes sonne, or daughters sonne.
Redy, inclyned, stowpinge downe, nygh hande.
A proheme or begynnynge of a marrier.
To sprede as a tree dothe on the toppe, to make to spreade, to sende farre of.
An olde vyne spred in many braunches. Sometyme it sygnifyeth kynde or generation.
Openly, clerely in the syghte of all menne.
To telle abroode, to growe in lengthe.
To dryue or putte awaye, farre of.
To hange vp. Propēndere, to examyne or consyder farre of.
To go quyckely or hastely, to say or do any thynge quyckely or hastely.Festus.
To commande that a thyng be doone.
To prophesye, to syng prayses to god: somtyme it signifieth to preache or interprete.
A prophete, he that telleth thynges, whiche shall happen.
A place by the commune baynes, where after baynynge menne toke theyr refection.
To drynke to an nother manne, to quafte, to brynge to, Sommetyme to gyue. Propino tibi salutem, I salute the.
A neyghbour. Also a kynnesman, of alyaunce.
That whiche is sone bowed or inclyned to desyres.
Sacrifyce to appease or pacyfye goddis displeasure.
Sommetyme sygnyfyeth veray deuoute or louynge.
Peasyble men, or men soone appeased or satisfied.
The crafte to make mouldes, in the whiche any thynge is caste or fourmed.
The place in a bayne or hotte house, in the whyche fyre inclosed, sendeth forth heate.
A table sette on the arke of the olde testament.
To appease, or to make mercyfull, or fauourable.
He that sellyth any thynge at retayle, specyally vyttayle, a hukster.
A subburbes of a towne. It is also that whyche bees doo make at the entrie of the hyue, wherby colde and other annoyaunce is defended.
To purpose, to be aduysed, to promyse a pryce or reward for any notable acte, to sette oute to the shewe.
A see betwene Grece and Asie.
A matter pourposed to be dysputed or reasoned. It is also that, wherby we shewe generallye, whereof we wyll speake.
He that was in the steede of Praetor, or Mayre.
Whervnto the propretie of a thynge belongeth.
For. Sommetyme nyghe. Alsoo at or in.
A dysease, where the eyen meuyd with inflammation, doo falle oute of their places.
Shame, dishonestie. Alsoo the moste abomynable vse of lecherye, in an inconuenient fourme.
To fyght farre of, to syghte valyauntly, to defende.
He that resysteth a thynge, or dryueth any thynge away.
To put of, to dryue away.
He that exercyseth the offyce of Questor in his absence.
He that hath the rule of the foreshyppe or decke.
To withdrawe or depart. ioyned with me or se, Domum se ex curia proripuit, He departed or withdrew hym homewarde from the courte.
Vtterly, alway, in any wyse, strayght towarde a place, surely.
Lymyttes in boundynge of landes directed into the easte.
To breake forthe, to sende forthe with vyolence, to leape or go out of a place with violēce, to brast out
To dryue downe, or beate downe.
A progenye, a dyscente of blode, a petygree.
The place, wherein enterludes were played by the personages.
To cutte out or vnder, to infame, to rebuke shamefullye.
To sell openly, to proclayme any thynge to be solde, to banysshe, to condemne.
A disease, which happeneth to Rammes at blysomynge tyme.

To folowe after, to pursue. Prosequor amore, I loue. Prosequor odio, I hat • . Prosequor honore, I honoure. Prosequor verbis, I • ha • e him with wordes. Prosequor officijs, I shewe to hym great kyndnesse, I do him many pleasures. Prosequi praemio, to rewarde.
To creape or slyde furth lyke a serpent.
A prayer to God: alsoo a beggynge.Iuuen. No. Mar.
That whiche is cut of frome any thinge, and cast awaye.
The father of my wyfes father.
Olde wrytars vsed for propositum purposed.
The lykenesse of one worde or name to another: as locus and lucus, orator, and arator.
Where as personages are supposed or fayned to speke, as one man to an other: a man to a beaste: one beaste to an other &c.
A syght farre of, a prospecte.
He that beholdeth a thinge farre of.
That which geueth felycitye. Felix, he that receyueth it.
To see farre, to foresee, to prouyde, to beware.
An addicion of a lettre: as gnatus, for natus.
To ouerthrowe, or to vaynquysshe in batayle.
A commune brothelhouse: also a commune harlot.
To be a commune harlot. Prostituere pudiciriam, to be commune to al men or women in the acte of lechery.
To stande ferre of, or afore: also to stande to be folde or hyred.
A place withoute the walles of Rome, where the bysshoppes of the gentyles made their diuinations, or toke their significations of thinges to come.
To excede, or haue more than ynoughe.
To differre, or tracte the tyme, to put oute, to dryue awaye, to vexe.
To set forth, or put forth, to stretche forthe.
Wantonnesse: it was also a sacrifice, wherein the maner was, that as moch as was left vneaten, shulde be consumed with fyre.
He hath consumed all that is lefte.

Proudely, immoderatly,Plautus in Ruden. shamefully. Quis est, qui tam proteruè, foribus facit iniu • iam: who is he, that so proudely rappeth at the doore? Ecce au • em tu quo que proterue iracundus es, Lo and thou also arte shamefully angry.
The sonne of Occanus, a iugglar, whyche coulde shewe hym selfe in sondry fourmes.
To declare manyfestly. what shulde be exchued and not done.
He that manifestly declareth, what is to be exchued and not done.
Wanton, malaperte, shamelesse, and (as I mought saye) knauysshe▪ or lewde.
A farre of▪ Also forthewith, without taryenge.

Promptitude: also gentyll entertaynement.Plautus in Seye. Proh Di immortales quot ego voluptates fero, quot risiones, quot iocos, quot fuauia, saltationes, blanditias, prothymias? O lorde god, howe many pleasures haue I, what lawghingis, what pastymes, what bassinges, daunsinges, daliaunces, & swete entertaynementes?
A porche at the vtter doore of a house.
An image or fourme, wherof mouldes are made, in the whiche thinges be cast of metall or erthe.
Of the first kynred or famylyrit was also the name of an excellent paynter.
That whiche is firste made or writen, which requireth correction.
The daughter of Deucalion and Pirrha.
The chief phisicion aboute a Prince.
A protonotary, or chief scribe or Secretary.
Firste made or wrought, or late made.
First fourmed so was Adam called.
A woman late bringynge forth her first childe.
The stalke which is first cut.
A boke to instructe one, a doctrinall.
A longe proued wytte: also to promote, aduaunce.
To come forth: alsoo to growe or increase,Plautus in Menech. to happen or chaunce. Nimis prouentum est nequiter, It is vngraciously chaunced.
To prouyde, to foresee, to beware.
Prouidence, foresight:Cice. & Quint. somtyme it is vsed for god.

Were countrayes, which the Romans gate farre frome Rome, where only their officers did rule. Prouincia is somtyme taken for the rule or autoritye of an officer: also an office, alsoo for a countraye or royaulme.
He that dwelleth in a prouince.
Frome countray to countray, or one countraye with another.
To see or beholde, to goo to see.
More prouident, moost prouident or circumspect.
He that prouoketh one, or he that appeleth, the appellant.
To call from a farre, to stere, to inuite, to prouoke, to exhorte, also to appele to an hygher iuge.
An appele to an hygher court.
To flye awaye, or beyonde, also to runne frome aferre.
To rolle or tumble a greate stone or other lyke thinge: sometyme to lye downe prostrate.
Of olde wrytars was taken for Proba vox, a good voyce or noyse.
A place withoute the walles, ioyninge to the cytie, where bysshoppes dyd assemble in their conuocations.
To publysshe, or declare openly to the people.
Wysedome in desiringe and exchuynge of thynges.
Olde wrytars vsed for Pronum, prone or apte.
An orcharde sette with damlyne trees, or plumme trees.
A damlyne tree or plumme tree.
A • syne, prune, plumme, slo, or bullase.
Ychinge with a delectation, as in the sterynge of lechery.
A kynge of Bythin • a, vnto whome Hanniball fledde after that he was banysshed frome Carthage.
A post or stake, where vnto the cabull of a shyp is tyed.
A nymphe or mayden of the see, one of the dawghters of Oceanus.
A counsayle assembled of great of fleers and iuges.
The president or chief of the counsayle.
A songe proprely to god, or of God.
An instrument lyke to a harp, also the Psalmes called the Psalter.
The pouldre or dust, which cometh of the fylynge of brasse.
The name of an olde writar, whiche wrote of diete.
An auditour or caster of accompte.
False or countrefait: and euery other nowne ioyned therewith, is thereby made false or countrefayt: as Pseudopropheta, a false or countrefayt Prophete.
An oynement to take awaye heares.
That which we do call Ceruse or whyte ledde.
A fysshe, whyche we call a playce.
He that delyteth to bathe in colde water.
A place where Nigromance is do call vp spirites.
People in • ibia, whose bodyes are v • enyme to se • pe • e • : and they also do cure the slyngynge and poysonynge of serpentes by soukynge the place, whyche is venymed.
A syllable ioyned oftentymes to the ablatyne case, as meapre, tuapte, suapte, myne owne, thyne owne, his owne.
Greate arches ouer the roofes made lyke wynges.
A lytle skynne, whyche groweth frome the corner of the eye, and keuereth the syght: it is alsoo a grief vnder the fore part of the nayle, whan the flesh goeth frō the nayle with payne.
The lower part of a sayle.
The water, wherin barly is soden, also barly husked, or excorticar, also frumēty made of barly.
An adder hauynge the coloure greene, drawynge towarde the colour of golde.
A rauenouse byrde, whyche taketh his praye by nyghte: and sometyme fyghteth with the Egle so valiantly, that in crab bynge togither, they fall both doune to the grounde, and are taken by Shepehardes.
Is spettyll: it is alsoo an exulceration or soore in the lunges, with a consumpcyon of all the bodye, and spettynge of bloode.
A morter, wherein barley is brayed.
An hospitall for beggars, a spyttell house.
The name of kynges of Egypte.
Ruy • e, also the case of a nowne.
He that is betwene a yonge man and a boye, of the age of .xiiii. yeres.
To growe as a childe doeth towarde mannes stare.
To begyn to haue a bearde benethe: sometyme to sprynge, as herbes done.

A yonge mosy bearde, whyche spryngeth in the nether partes of a man at .xiiii. yeres of age▪ of a woman at yonger yeres, wherfore a man or woman at those yeres is called Pubes: sometyme youth, or a multitude of yonge men: also the priuy partes of the body: also beynge an adiectif, it signifieth yonge or tender.
The yonge age of men and womē, whan they begynne to be apte vnto generacion: it is also the first commynge forthe of beares aboute the pryucy membres.
Were they whyche toke in ferme of the people of Rome the rentes and reuenues due to the cytie at a rent certayne.
A saulfe condute, a generall lycence.
Openly in the face of the worlde. Sumptus publice dati, his expenses borne of the citie or towne.
A fauorar of the people: the whiche name was gyuen to Valerius, whiche was one of the first consules of Rome.
To publysshe, to manifeste, to make openly knowen.
Commune, but more proprely, publike, that is to saye, pertaynynge to euery state of the people ioyntly and seuerally: See the true definicion therof in my booke called the Gouernour.
Wyne growynge nyghe to the gulfe of Venice.
To be violated in the acte of lechery.
Asshamed. Nonne esset puditum, si hanc causam agerent seuere? had it not bene a shame, yf that they had pursuyd that mater rigorously?
A moderacion that letteth the mynde, that it do not any thinge wantonly, or dishonestly, shamefastnesse, to saye or do any thinge dishonest.
A wenche, in Cambrige shyre they cal her a modder.
To waxe yonge agayne, to be maydenly.
A chylde, a boye: also a seruaunt.
Of a chylde, chyldysshe, or boyisshe.
A woman that lyeth in of chylde.
The tyme of a womanne to trauayle of chylde, sometyme the chylde, also the byrth.
A payre of tables to wryte in.
A ball fylled onely with wynde, which is stryken with a mans fiste, and not with the palme.
A handfull, in gatheringe of herbes or other lyke thynge.
Batayle, the acte of lechery: also an assault, a disceyte.

An aduerbe, signifyeth fayre, 〈◊〉 beautyfully, well fauoredly: somtyme valiauntly, also wysely: sometyme it is put for valde. Ac dum accubabam, quam videbar mihi esse pulchrè sobrius, Terent. 〈◊〉 Eunuch • . And whan I layde me downe, I thoughte my selfe to be very sobre.
A wesyll or Stote, whiche kylleth chyckens.
A mourner. Somtyme a manne in poore apparayle, somtyme rude, vnlernid.
A bryngynge forthe or hatchynge of chyckens. also the folynge of coltes.
Of a colte. Pullini dentes, coltes tethe, whiche be fyrste caste.
A spryngynge forthe of a thinge in growynge.
To sprynge, to come vp yonge.
Yonge, tender, in all kynde lyuinge. also a colte or fole, also a chycken.
Russette, sometyme blacke, but rather puke color, betwene russet & black.
Potage made with fleshe or fyshe, as forced gruell, or coleyse.
He that is disesid in the lūges.
Be certayne apples, whyche be called in some place a hundred shyllingis.
A lyttell synewe lyke to a vayne.
A meate made of meale, water, hony, cheese, and egges. It maye be taken for potage.
The poulses of a manne or womanne.
Striken as a harpe or other instrument is, whyche hath strynges.
To beate, to stryke, to hurte, to play on a harpe, or other lyke instrument.

The wreste of the arme, wherto the had is ioyned▪ but it is more proprely the poulse or stroke that the arteries or beatyng vaines do make, wherby the strēgth or debilitie of the syckenes is knowen in touchynge them.
To lay with doust, to be dusty.
To be tourned in to poulder or duste.
A layenge of fyne erthe aboute vynes.
A bolstar of a bedde. also a bedde whyche was wont to be made in temples, as it were for the goddis. It is taken somtyme for a temple. also a tabernacle, wherin an ymage standeth.
A pyllowe, somtyme a fetherbed, also a cusshyn, also a bedde of herbes in a gardeyne, also grauelle, also an engyne, wherewith shyppes are broughte into the docke.
A pomeyse to make parchemente smoothe, also to take cleane oute spottes or letters.
A dwarfe, or any thynge lyttell in stature.
A moment, the leest part of tyme.
A yonge wenche, a gyrle, a modder. it is also a poppette, lyke a gyrle.
The balle or apple of the eye.
The noueage of hym that is in warde.
He that is in warde, or within age not able in yeres to occupye his propre lande. Also he that hath no father alyue.
The foreparte or decke of the shyppe.
A yonge chylde, a baby. also a poppette or ymage lyke a chylde.
The pretertence of purgo, I haue pricked or pounched.
Fylthe, whyche cometh of any thyng that is clensed.
To make cleane, to purge. also to excuse.
Old wrytars vsed for purissime, most purely.
A Purple, whiche is a shell fysshe. wherof purple colour commeth. somtime it signifieth a garment of purple.
Be the noble men of a Royalme, callyd peeres.
Redde payntynge, wherewith harlottes doo paynt their vysages.
Matter, whyche commeth oute of a soore.
Blystars, which do ryse on bred whā it is baken.
Olde wrytars vsed for Pucrum & Puellam, a boye and a gyrle.
Roughe syluer whan it is newe molten.
The shale of a nutte, or parynge of an apple or peare.
The seate of a great offycer, also the couerynge of a welle.
He that diggeth a pytte or well.
Places where the commune people was buryed.
To cutte of or plucke awaye. that, which is superfluous, proprely from trees. Also to suppose, to consyder, to discusse, to gather, or conferre, to esteme, to iuge. Putare rationem, to make accompt.
To waxe leane, to be resolued into stynkynge matter.Vide cōp.
A house or place buylded, where pylars stande thicke togither.
A table, wherein the names of Iuges were wryten.
A beaste lyke to a falowe deere: it is also a byrde lyke to a hawke, hauynge a whyte tayle, I suppose hym to be that, which we call a ryngetayle.
People betweene Inde and Cathay, which are but one cubyte longe.
A bonfyre, wherin deed bodyes were burned.
A fly, which commeth of the fyre, & as longe as he is therin, he lyueth: & whā he is farre frome it, he dyeth incontinent.
One of the names of Vulcanus.
A yonge man, whyche slewe hym self for the loue of a maydē called Thisbe • it is also a ryuer in Cilicia.
A great thynge of stone or other matter, whiche he is brode beneth, and vpwarde is smalle and sharpe on the top.
A kynde of Sydar, callyd Pery.
A worme lyuynge in the fyre, It is also a kynde of spyders, whiche hurteth hony combes.
Mountaynes, whiche do dyuyde Fraunce from Spayne.
A howse buylded lyke a towar.
Was a cūnyng grauer in stones.
In latyne a towar: also a boxe, oute of the which men do cast dyse, whan they playe: it is also a certayn company of horsmen in batayle.
A boxe, oute of the whyche dyse are throwen.
A certayne playster to asswage the burnynge of a feuer.
Euery stone, out of the whych fire may be striken.
A smythes hammer, wherewith he beateth on hotte yron.
Arowes or dartes, whiche sende forthe fyre, whanne they be shotte or caste, and do burne the thynge that they doo touche.
They whyche doo shoote suche dartes.
A crowe with a redde bylle. I suppose it to be of the kynd, wherof cornyshe chowghes are.
He that fyrste strake fyre out of a flynte. also a stone of fyry colour.
A fourme of dansynge, with moche mouynge of the bodye and gesture, lyke to them whiche do syght in battayle.
They that daunce in the fourme of daunsynge, called Pyrrhica.
A foote in meter of two shorte syllables.

In latyne Flauius, siue Rufus, he that hath a ruddy or fyrye vysage, by the whyche name the sonne of Achilles was calledde, and a kynge of Epyre was soo callyd, whyche dydde make warre to the Romaynes.
An excellente Phylosopher, whose Phylosophye was in mystycalle sentences, and alsoo in the Scyence of noumbers.
He that was of the secte of Pythagoras. Pythagorista, idem.
One of the names of Apollo.
Playes made in the honor of Apollo.
A Dragon, whyche was slayne by Apollo.
A cytie in Asye, in that parte, whyche is callyd Mysia.
A spyrtynge oute of smalle spyttelle.
A lyttell boxe, proprely wherin medycines are putte.
People of Boeme, or Boemia, which dyd eate the fleshe of horses and wolfes.
A trencher, wheron meate is cut: sometyme a lofe of breadde cutte square.
A certayne coyne, whyche we may call a ferthynge: all be it proprely it is the quarterne of a pounde weight. Also it is the somme in accompte where the receyte and the expenses do accorde.
A fygure square lyke to a dyse. Also a certayn mesure, contaynyng .xlviii. measures, callyd Sextarii.
A harlotte that wyll company with a man for a ferthynge.
Certayne coyne, hauynge in them the prynte of a charyotte.
He that speaketh fowre sondrye languages.
A chyld of foure yeres old.
That whyche dothe waye foure poundes.
That whyche may be slytte in foure partes.
That is of foure dyuers fourmes or facyons.
A carte drawen with foure horses. somtyme a carte horse.
A child of four yere olde.
A shyppe with foure rewes of oores, or with foure toppes.
Where as foure wayes doo meete.
To brynge in square, to consente or agree.
To double foure tymes, or to make a thynge foure tymes as moche as it was.
A cytie, vnto the whyche doo come, or are broughte all the people, beinge lefte in foure cities, • estus by the whyche name the citie of Athenes was callyd of Actius the poete.
Were they, whiche for accusynge of other, hadde the fourth parte of the goodes of theym, that were condempned.
To appeache a man for to haue parte of his goodes.
The whyche woman or other female kynde.
Colde, with a shakynge, as in a feuer.
Stu • s or dilygente in seekynge.
To demaunde, to aske, to get, to serche, to examyne.
To seeke, serche, or inquyre dylygently.
A ius • yce or commyssyoner to inquire of crymes, defaultes,As. pedia • . or abuses agaynste the lawe.
An inquirie, an exaīation, a serch.
The treasourer of the commune Treasourye, a Treasourer of the warres, a Lyeuetenaunt to the chyef capytayne in warres. Alsoo a Iustyce by Commyssyon of Oyer and Determyner.
Iustyces to inquere, of treason, or murder. We maye calle the coroners by that name.
Were as the chaumberlaynes of London be nowe.
Offycers of the Receypte, as the Chaumberers and tellers be nowe.
Was suche a place as the eschequer is.
A generall receyuour: but it seemethe to be suche an offycer, as the eschetour is nowe in Englande.
He that hadde bene in the offyce of Questor.
That pertayneth to the offyce of Quaestor. Vir quaestorius, a man, whiche hath ben in that offyce.
Craftes, wherby men do gayne money.
Of moche gayne, studyous of greatte lucre.
Qualytyes, as fowle, fayre, wyse, foolysshe, stronge, weake, dylygente, slowe. &c.
A baskette, oute of the whyche wyne runneth, whan it is pressed: Alsoo a baskette or hamper, in the whyche womenne doo putte their spyndelles, their bottomes of threede, and suche lyke thynges.

Thanne, Sommetyme after that. Sommetyme byfore that. Pridi • quam occideretur, The day before that he was slayne. Quam bene, howe well? Quam fortiter, howe valyauntly. Also it is often ioyned with the superlatiue degree, to make it more vehemente: as, Quampaucissimi, As few as may be. Quam doctissimus, excellentely lerned. Somtyme it importeth as moche as veraye. Cum quo quam familiarissimé uixerat, With whom he lyued very familyarly. Alsoo it sygnfyeth as. Duplo accepit quam perdiderat, He receyued dowble as moche as he loste.
Wherfore? for what cause? what to doo?
Almooste, hit lackydde but a lyttelle.
Howe manye, verye manye, a greatte sorte.
Howe late sens, howe longe agoo?
For howe moche, of what pryce or valewe.
Howe moche, whyche is referred to noumbre, weight, and measure.

Howe moche, as to, as concernynge. Quantum intelligo, as farre as I vnderstande. Quantum suspicor, as farre as I suppose. Also, accordynge as. Id de imperatore Romano, quantum euentus postea praedictum patuit Iudaei ad se trahentes, rebellarunt, The Iewes gatherynge that of the Emperoure, accordynge as the thynge, whyche was afore shewed of that whyche shoulde happen, appered afterwarde, made rebellyon.
In al spede that thou mayste.
Howe moche, or howe many soo euer it be.

The fowrthe tyme. All be hit proprelye Quarto sygnifyethe the fourthe in order, as Quarto Consul, he that hadde three in the offyce afore hym. Quartum Consul, he that hath ben the fourthe tyme Consul.
He that hathe a quartayne Feeuer.
A Mulettour or keper of mules, whiche taketh but the fourthe parte of the wages or gayne.

Lyke as. Amas me quasi filium, Thou louest me, as yf I were thy sonne. Alsoo, as who saythe, as thowghe. Tu obiicis, quod uxorem repudiauerim, quasi tu idem non feceris, Thou imbraydest me, that I haue forsaken my wife, as who laythe, thou haste not doone soo to.
He that shaketh or moueth his heade.Plautus.
To shake moche or often, alsoo to breake.
To make or cause to shake or moue.
Howe moche, to the intent. also for as moche, also howe.
A quayre as in a booke, a leafe beynge folded into fowre partes.
A coniunction, whyche sygnifyeth for, for as moche.
To shaake a thynge.Vide com. also to vexe, to caste out.
Fowre dayes, the spaace of foure dayes.
For & sygnyfyeth and. Also that is to saye.
A measure of the Iewes, containyng two ounces and .ii. drammes.
Olde wryters vsyd for potentia, puissaunce, power.

o: Quercicus, ca, cum, idem quod quernus.
n: quercicus ca cum idem quod quernus

d: Quyuerynge or shakyng for colde. somtyme it was taken for great and greuous, as Festus sayth.

That which complaineth, or is full of complayntes. It is put some tyme of the Poetes for shrylle or lowde in syngynge.V • rgiliꝰ in georgie. Cicadae querulae, grassehoppers, whyche doo synge lowde, or with a shrylle voyce.
Amonge the Iewes dydde sygnifye a coyne, sometyme a lambe, somme tyme a sheepe.

The whyche. Alsoo sometyme it sygnifyeth howe. Efficite, qui detur tibi, Doo what ye canne, howe or by whatte meanes thou mayste haue hyr. Qui uocâre, Plautus in Amph. Howe arte thou callyd? Alsoo yt sygnyfyeth why. Dauo istuc dedam negoti. Te • . in An. S. Non potest. P. Qui • S. Quia habet aliud magis ex sese. I wyll commytte th • e mattier to Dauy. S. That may not be. P. Why? S. For he hath an nother greatter mattier to doo for hym selfe. Alsoo it sygnyfyeth frome whense. Qui istaec tibi incidit suspectio? Ter. in An. From whens is this suspycion happened vnto the? Also it sygnyfyeth wolde to God. Qui illum Di omnes perdiunt, Terent. in Phorm. I pray god that a vengeaunce lyghte on hym. Alsoo yt sygnyfyethe bycause.Terent▪ in prolo. An. Nam in prologis scribundis operam abutitur, non qui argumentum narret, sed qui maleuoli uaeteris Poetae maledictis • espondeat, For he spendethe his laboure in wrytynge of Prologues, not bycause he wyll telle the argumente, but for as moche as he wolde make aunswere to the yuell reportes of the olde enuyouse Poete. Alsoo it sygnyfyeth Wherefore.Cice. T •• Qui enim beatior Epicurus, quod in patria uiuebat, quam Metrodorus, quod Athenis? Wherefore was Epycure moore happye, that he dydde dye in his countreye, than Metrodorus that he dyed at Athenes.

For. Alsoo hit sygnyfyeth that.Ci. de 〈◊〉 ▪ Sed tamen recordatione nostrae amicitiae sic fruor, ut beatae uixisse uidear, quia cum Scipione uixerim, All be it I take this pleasure in remembrynge oure frendeshyp, that I maye seeme to haue lyued moste fortunatelye, that I lyued in Scypyones companye. Alsoo it sygnyfyeth for as moch.Salustias in Catil. Sed quia multis & magnis tempestatibus vos cognoui fortes, fidosque mihi, eo animus ausus est maximum atque pulcherrimum facinus incipere, But for as moch as in many great stormes or daungiers I haue proued you to be valyaunt, and faythefull vnto me, therfore my hart is bolde to begynne an excellent and commendable enterprise.

o: Quias, a, um, for cuius, a, um.
n: quias a um for cuius a um

o: Quibus in extremis, for quorum in extremo. Literae dantur mihi a te, quibus in extremis scriptum est?
n: quibus in extremis for quorum in extremo literae dantur mihi a te quibus in extremis scriptum est
d: I receyued letters frome you, in the laste ende of the whyche hit is wrytten.
All that is, what so euer it be, what so euer.

o: Qui cum, for cum quo. Qui cum loquitur filius?
n: qui cum for cum quo qui cum loquitur filius
d: With whome dothe my sonne talke?

What. Quid causae est? What is the cause? Quid aetatis? How olde? of what aege? Quid animi? What mynde?Plautus in mercarore Quid animi est? What mynde is he of? Quid captiuo • um? Howe manye prysoners? Tum Captiuorum quid ducunt secum? Plautus in Epidico. Thanne howe many prysoners doo they bryng with them? Quid id sit hominis, cui Lyco nomen sier? Plautus in praulo. Terent. in Hea •• . What man is he, whose name maye be Lyco? Quid mulleris uxorem habes, What maner of woman haste thou to thy wyfe? Quid rei est? What is the mattier. Ibo intro ut quid husus sit rei sciam: Terent. in Eunucho. I wyll goo in, that I may knowe what the mattier is▪ Quid rei est tibi cum illa, What haste thou to doo with hyr?

What is his or thyn opinyon? Quid istue uerbi est? what meanest thou therby? Also quid is taken for Aliquid, somewhat. Also ob quid for what, or wherfore. Quid? senem quoad expectas uestrum. Terent. in phormi. But nowe? how longe wyll ye tary for your maister? Note here that after the dayly forme of speakynge, quid is rehersed,Donatus. whā we passe from one matter to an other. Quid mecum est tibi? what haue I to do with the? Quid faceret aliud? what shoulde he doo els? Quid eo, what to doo? Propere curre ad Pamphilum. P. Quid eo? D. Die me orate ut ueniat. Rūne quyckely to Pamphilus. P. what to do? D. Say that I prayed hym to come. Quid uerbis opus est? Plautus. what nede manye wordes? Quid multa uerba, idem. Quid multis moror? what shall I longe tarie? Quid mea refert, Cicero de •• icitia. what care I? Also quid signifyeth wherin. Quid enim indigens Affricanus mei? wherin had Scipio any nede of me?Terent. in Iunucho. Quid istic? Si certum est facere, facias • uerum ne post conferas culpam in me, What woldeste thou I shoulde doo? If thou be determyned to doo it, goo to on goddis name: but afterward put not the fault in me.
What is hit, or wherfore is it?
What is it that he commeth soo chaufed? Also it sygnifieth what.Terent. in Eunucho. Reuiso quidnam Chaerea hic rerum gerar, I come to se what Cherea doth here.

Why not? Quo ore appellabo parrem tenes, quid dicam? S. quidni, With what countenaunce shall I speake to my father▪ Wotest thou what I wyll say? S. Wherfore shuldest thou not do so? Also it signifyeth ye. Archimedem nosti? P. quid ni? Terent. in Eunucho. Knowest thou Archimedes? P. ye mary doo I.
One, any man, in the plurell numbre it sygnifieth some.

An aduerbe, affyrmyng that, whiche ye spoken. Sommetyme yt sygnyfyeth verylye. Sommetyme it hathe no sygnyfycacyon, but ys oonely a dystinction of thynges: as, Ego quidem scribo, tu uero legis, Ille autem dormit, I doo wryte, thou reedyst, he alsoo slepethe.
What wylt thou more? What nedeth any more wordes?

o: Quid rum deni que , Quid ergo, quid •um poliea, Quid ita que , quid interea, quid demum,
n: quid rum deni que quid ergo quid um poliea quid ita que quid interea quid demum
d: All these doo sygnifye, whereto speakest thou this? What than, or what meanest thou hereby?
Holde thy peace,Plautus in milite. Leaue.
To take reste,Vide com. to ceasse.
Was a name of Pluto, callydde god of Helle.
Who thou wilt. also it sometyme signifieth vyle or base in estymacyon.
What I, thou, or he wyll.
But, why not. Quin uenis, why commest thou not?
Why goste thou not?Ter. in An.
Go to, tell me what it is.

Alsoo. Pudet me. S. Terent. in Heauton. Credo, neque id iniuria: quin mihi molestum, I am asshamed. S. I beleue, and not without a cause: And I am alsoo sorye therfore. Quin taces? Terent. in Andria. Wylte not thou holde thy peace. Also it sygnyfyethe but yet, or but for all that. C. Perij. S. Quin tu animo bono es. C.Terent. in Adelp. I am vndoone. S. But for all that be thou of good cheere. Alsoo therfore. Quin tu uno uerbo dic, quid est quod me uelis, Therefore telle me atte oone worde, whatte thou woldest haue me doo.Plautus in Aulularia. Also more ouer, or that moore is. Quin, ipsi pridem tonsor ungues dempserat, collegir, omnia abstulit praesegmina, And that more is, the other daye, the barbour paryd his nayles, he gathered the parynges togyther, and caryed them all away with hym.

Of fyue ounces. Alsoo the gayne of fyue in oone hundrede by exchaunge amongeste Marchauntes. It was alsoo an order of settynge of trees in a gardeyne or orchard veraye exactelye, that whyche waye soo euer that a manne dydde looke, the trees stoode dyrectely oone agaynste an nother.
The nombre of fiue. quinarius lapis, a stone of fyue pounde weyght.
Was amonge the olde Romains their halfe peny, whiche was fyue pounde weight of brasse, callyd As, It is two soulces of frenche money, whyche is of our money.
Of olde wryters was vsed for quingentum, fyue hundred.

Wherfore then. Quin ergo quod iuuat, quod charū aestimant, id semper faciant, Wherfore than, what so euer lyketh them, that whiche semeth pleasant vnto them, let them doo it as longe as it pleaseth them.
A feast dedicate to Pallas, whiche duryd fyue dayes.
A feast so called, bycause it was after the fyfth Idus of Marche.
An herbe callid cynkfoyle, or fyue leauyd grasse.
That whiche hapneth or is done euery fyfthe yere.
The exercyse of fyue sondrye craftes.
They whiche exercised fiue sondry craftes.
A barge with fyue oores, it may be nowe taken for a shyppe with fiue toppes, or with fyue sayles.
An office or auctorite, wherin fyue men were associate.
Oone whiche is in the sayde authoritie.
Was a gate in the Campe, where the armye was lodged, whyche was the chiefe gate next to that whiche was called Praetoria, where the market was wont to be kepte.
Was a gaate and medowes at Rome, whyche tooke their names of one Quintius, a noble cō sule of Rome.
The boye or seruaunt of Quintus.
An hylle at Rome, where the temple of Romulus was sette.
The gate next to that hyll.
Dayes, in the whyche men dydde sacryfyce to Romulus, callydde Quirinus.
Was a name, wherby the Romans were callyd of their fyrste kynge Romulus, called Quirinus, as hit were Quirinus people.
Was the name of Romulus, after that he was taken for a god.
To crye out, to styrre vp the Romayns with a crye.
Any manne. It is somtyme vsyd in the femynyne gender for any woman.
Euery manne. Doctissimus quis que , Euery welle lerned man. Decimus quis que , Euery tenthe.
Be those thynges whyche in makynge cleane of a garden or orcharde, be caryed oute, as stickes, leues, •• d At. 1 and weedes: it is vsed of Cicero for noughty men, the refuse of all other.
A lytle braunche of a kynde of holy, whyche beareth grayne, wherewith scarlet and crymsyn colours be made.
In the genitiue case cuius cuius, who so euer.
In the genitiue case cuiusuis, any mā: one of them
Is sometyme taken for some man.
Whyther. Quó abis, whyther goest thou?

o: Quo non. Perreptaui vsque omne oppidum, ad portam, ad locum, quo non?
n: quo non perreptaui vsque omne oppidum ad portam ad locum quo non
d: I went all the towne aboute, to the gate, to the lake, there is no place but that I was in it. Also it signifieth frome whense and where. Illuc quaeso redi, Terent. in •• delph. quo coepisti, I beseche the tourne backe agayne, where thou begannest:Terent. in Eunucho. also, bycause. Non pol quó quenquàm plus amem, aut plus diligā, eo feci, In good fayth I dyd it not bycause I more louyd or fauored any man:Ter. in An. also, wherfore. Forma bona memini videre, quo aequior sum Pamphilo, I remembre she is well fauored, wherfore I am the lesse displeased with Pamphilus.

Whyther: also Quo, signifyeth,Plinius. that. Neque enim id feci, quo tibi molestus essem, Nor I dyd it not, that I wolde displease you: also, to what purpose or vse. Quo mihi fortunam, si non conceditur vti, For what purpose shall fortune serue, if I may not haue commoditie by it?

o: Quoad quenque peruenit, aut peruenerit expraeda, ex manubijs, ex auro coronario?
n: quoad quenque peruenit aut peruenerit expraeda ex manubijs ex auro coronario
d: How moche of the praye or spoyle, garlandes or crownes of victours is comē, or shall come to any of your handes?
As moche as I may do.

That, wherein. Sed si quid sit, quod mea opera opus sit, Terenti. aut tu plus vides quam ego, manebo, But yf there be any thynge, wherein ye shall haue nede of my seruice, or that ye perceyue more than I do, I will tary:Plautus in A •• nar. also it is put for Quem. Allenum hominem intromittar neminem, quod illa aut amicum, aut patronum nominer: She maye let in no man, whome she will call derlyng,Plinius. or master. Nube grauida candicante, quod vocant tempestatem albam, grando imminebit: whan there doeth appiere a greate clowde, that waxeth whyte, whiche they call a whyte tempeste, ye shall haue hayle shortly after: also it sygnifyeth for as moch or bycause. Senatusconsulta duo facta sunt odiosa, quod in consulem facta putantur, Cice Atti. Catone & Domitio postulante: Two actes of counsayle were made very displeasant, for as moche as they were supposed to be made, at the desire of Domicius and Cato:Ter. in. 〈◊〉 also it signifyeth but. Quod si quiescem, nihil euenisset mali, But if I had let it alone, there hadde none yll happened, or it had bene well ynoughe: also, as moche.Cice. Te • Tu velim, quod cum commodo valetudinis tuae fiat quàm longissime poteris, obuiā nobis properes: I wolde that ye, as moche as maye be with the heithe of your persone, make speede to meete with vs, as farre frome home as ye can. Also it signifyeth why.Vergilius in • uc. Si ad vitulam spectes, nihil est quod pocula laudes: If thou consyderest the caulf wel, there is no cause why thou shuldest prayse so thy pottes.Cice. Ter. In uiam quod tedes hoc tempore, nihil est, There is no cause why thou shuldest take thy iournay at this tyme: Also it signifyeth wherfore.Hor. in ep. Quod te per genium, dextram que , Deos que penates obsecro & obtestor, vitae me redde priori: Wherfore I beseche and praye the, for thy good aungelles sake, and for the loue betwene the and me, and for the sainctes which be thyn auouryes, restore me eftsones, to my fyrst lyfe, or to the state that I was in erst.Ter. in Eu. Also it signifyeth, as to that. Sane quod tibi vir videatur esse, hic nebulo magnus est. As to that, that thou thynkest hym a man, surely he is a stourdy vagabunde.

o: Quod abs que molestia fiat, Cice. Sulp.
n: quod abs que molestia fiat cice sulp
d: So that it be no displeasure vnto you. Quare pergratum mihi feceris, si eum in amicitiam receperis, atque eum (quod absque molestia fiat) si qua in re opus ei fuerit: Wherfore ye shall do me singuler pleasure, if ye take hym into your fauour, and (so that it be no displeasure vnto you) whan neede requyrethe, be good lorde or master vnto hym.
No that. Non nouisti me? P. Plautus in Epidico. quod quidem veniat in mentem. Doeste thou not know me? P. No that I remembre me.

Somewhat.Ci. de. am •• Quamobrem vt hi, qui superiores sunt, summittere se debent in amicitia, sic quodammodo inferiores extollere, Wherfore lykewyse as they, which are superior in state or degree, shuld humble them selfes in frendshyp, so they whiche are inferior shulde aduaunce and sette them selfes forewarde.

o: Quodcun que militum contrahere poteritis, contrahatis.
n: quodcun que militum contrahere poteritis contrahatis
d: I aduyse you, that as many souldiours as ye can gete, ye gather vnto you.

o: Quominus, for Vt non. Si poterit fieri, vt ne pater per me stetisse credat, quo minus hae fierent nuptiae, volo:
n: quominus for vt non si poterit fieri vt ne pater per me stetisse credat quo minus hae fierent nuptiae volo
d: If it may be brought to passe, that my father maye beleue, that it is not in my fault, that this mariage is not concluded, I am content.

Howe, by what reason, in what maner,Plautus in Aulul. Plautus in milite. Plautus in amph. by what meane. Quomodo tibi res se haber, Howe is the matter with the? Sed quomodo dissimulabat? But in what maner dyd he dissemble? Primulo diliculo abijsti ad legiones, By tyme in the mornynge thou wentest to the armye. Amph. Quomodo? In what maner or facion? also it signifieth wherfore.Plautus in 〈◊〉 . Illa quidem nullū sacrificabit. G. Quomodo? quid igitur me volt? She will doo no sacrifyce. G. wherfore? what thynge wolde she than with me?
Howe so euer it be. Sed tamen quomodocun que , quamquàm sumus pauperculi, est domi quod edimus: Yet how so euer it be, thoughe we be poure folkes, we haue at home somewhat to eate.
Sometyme, ones: signifyenge the tyme past,Virg. or tyme to come. Quondam tua dicere facta Tempus erit: The time shal be ones, whan thyne actes shall be declared. Alsoo it is put in the tyme present.

o: Quondam etiam victis redit in precordia virtus,
n: quondam etiam victis redit in precordia virtus
d: Ye, and in them that are vaynquysshed, sometyme good courage eftsones imbracith their stomakes. Sometyme it signyfyeth allwaye. Vt quondam in stipulis magnus sine viribus ignis, Lyke as in stubbyll or holme syre is allwaye greate without any puyssaunce.
Whyther, Eamus intro, sequere. S. Quo tute agis? C. quonam, nisi domum. Let vs go in, folowe me. S. whyther wylt thou go? whyther shulde I goo but home to my house?
Any whyther. Itut • ne Thais quopiam es? Thais, wylte thou goo any whyther?

In any maner of wyse.Ter. in A • . Tum si maxime fateatur, cum amet aliam, non est vtile hanc illi dari: qua propter quoquo pacto caelato est opus, Than yf he vtterly cō fesse it, for as moch as he loueth another, it were not conuenient, that he were maryed to this woman, therfore in any maner of wyse, this thinge must be kept secrete.

Euery waye, on euerye parte. Eius imperio classem quo quouersum dimittunt, Caes. in. 〈◊〉 . By his commaundement they dyspeched the nauy in euery part. Rates duplices quoquouersum pedibus triginta é regione solis collocabat: he lette shyppes double agaynste the sonne, thirty feete euery waye.
Whyther, to what place, or thinge.
A commune beautye or facion, euery daye sene.
A thynge that is or happeneth dayly or daye by daye.
Howe moche in measure or wayght.
Of what numbre, howe many, Hora quota est, what is it a clocke?Horatius. Dic quotus es? Telle howe many be of you.

o: Quotas aedes dixerit, id ego admodum incerto scio:
n: quotas aedes dixerit id ego admodum incerto scio
d: How many houses he spake of, I am not well assertayned, or I remembre not well.
Whyther, or to what place ye wyll.
Olde wryt • rs vsed for Rabies.
Madde or woode, as a madde dogge.
Madde or very angry, woode angry.
To be madde or woode as a dogge.
One which is hasty or wilfull, in any cause, ianglynge, or full of wordes.
A twygge of a vyne, out of the which the grapes do springe.
The gatheringe of grapes after that the greate clusters be gathered to make wyne, the glenynge of grapes.
A grape or a cluster of grapes.
A reprochefull worde of Hebrewe, which signifyeth, thriftlesse, braynlesse, fynally it is a rebukefull worde sygnifyenge the extreme ire of the personne that speaketh it.
Frome the roote, or vppe by the roote, Radicitus euellere, to plucke vppe by the roote.
An herbe, the iuyce whereof is good to wasshe woulle: also a lytle roote.
To sende forth beames lyke the sunne.

A beame of the sun, or other bright sterre, sometyme of the eyes: also a rodde or yerde, that Geometricians haue to describe lynes: also a wayuers shyttell, wherwith he throweth the yern in to the webbe also the spoke of a wheele, alsoo an instrument, wherwith measures be shauen: alsoo longe olyues or oyle beryes.
To shaue, or make smoothe, to cut or pull vp, to hurte, to rent, to offende, to fatigate. Aures delicatas radere, to offende or fatigate delicate eares.
That whiche is shauen of, frome any thynge.
Cleftes or choppes in the fundament.
A see fysshe called Raye or skete.
The staffe, wherewith plowghmen in tyllynge do put the erthe frome their share.
A lytle piece of any thynge.
That whyche is of a bowgh.
A kynde of rupture, whan the bowels do fal downe into a mans coddes: also a rayle or barre, whiche goeth ouerthwart a pale or a gate.
A frogge: also a sickenesse which doth anoy cartell.
Is a prouerbe applyed to thē that canne not speake in tyme conuenient.
Rankled, mouldy, or putrifyed: also vnsauery, or vnpleasaunt.
In olde tyme was taken for aes, brasse.
In the olde tyme was a quartern • of a pounde.
A plant and roote called Rape.
A plante, and roote called Radysshe.
To arrest one, or cause him to be arrested to appere before iuges.
To take by violence, hast, or fury: also to rauysshe a woman.
Rauysshynge or deflourynge of a woman.
A lytle roote, whyche is eaten in salutes.
A byrde seldome seene▪ whereby is signifyed any thynge that seldome happeneth.
To waxe thynne, or not thicke growen, to be or happen seldome.
A sonder, here and there one or a few.
Selde or not ofte, thynne, not thicke growen or set.
That maye be shauen or made smoothe.
A barbour, or shauour, alsoo a • ydler.

Are pieces of tymber pynned togither, wheron haye or other lyke thinge beinge layde, they are drawen on ryuers, as on the great streames of Germany and France is now sene: but they be communly vsed and taken for shyppes, or the syde beames of a shyppe.
