Rayson, counsayle, purpose, care, respecte, cause, the maner, the waye, the fourme, proportion.
To rayson, to gather in argument, to accompte.
That whiche hath the vse of raison: alsoo that whiche a preest weareth at masse on his heed, & after putteth it backe lyke a hoode.

o: Ratio de integro ineunda est mihi,
n: ratio de integro ineunda est mihi

o: Rationem subducere, Nunquàm ita quisquam bene subducta ratione ad vita fuit: quin res, aetas, vsus semper aliquid apportet noui,
n: rationem subducere nunquam ita quisquam bene subducta ratione ad vita fuit quin res aetas vsus semper aliquid apportet noui
d: There was neuer man in the ordre of his lyfe so well aduysed: but that mater, age & experience bringeth to hym somwhat at that is straunge.
The matter appiereth, or is shewed.
A boke of accompt: also a boke belongynge to the counsayle of Princes. wherin actes done and to be done are writen: also an auditour.
Whan accomptes be examyned and tryed.No. M • r.
Olde wrytars vsed for Ratificare, to ratify, to confyrme.
A voyce that maye not be well harde.
Wormes, beinge in the rootes of trees, and careth them.
A thynge vnwrought, and vnpolysshed: it was also taken for aes, brasse.
Horse: also Rauus color, a dull or sadde colour, or broune.
In the selfe or very thinge.

To retourne. At vnum hoc te quaeso, si hue rebiter è Philocrare, vt eius mihi facias conueniendi copiā. But one thinge I praye the, if he retourne frome Philocrates, finde the meanes, that I may speke with him.
To stryke with the heele, to kicke.
To charme awaye or charme out a thynge, which was brought in by inchauntement, as the witches called wyse women are wont to do.
A rehercynge of thynges in chapiters.

o: Recedere a conditione, a persona, a statu,
n: recedere a conditione a persona a statu
d: Is to chaunge or alter the condicion, person, or state.Cic. de off. Quanquàm id nomen durius efficit iam vetustas, à peregrino enim iam recessit, All thoughe auncienty maketh that name diffuse, yet is it now altered from beinge a straunge worde.

To runne eftsones after that he hath rested him, to make a fresh course.Plautus in • tin. Postquàm thermopotasti gutturem, recipe te, & recurre pede recenti: After that thou haste warmed thy throte with good drynke, take thy harte to the, and make a fresshe course.
To numbre or tell, to reken.
The place, which receyueth thinges: also a place of suerty or comfort.
They whiche of straungers • e made Citizens.
That whiche is reserued from other.
To blowe the retrayte: also it is a prouerbe, which signifyeth to fynysh or ende the contention.
An aduerbe, whyche signifyeth, goynge backe.
Those rebukes shall lyght on the.
It is come to a fewe personnes.
Eftsones restored: somtyme eftsones decayed or fallen.
To fall eftsones: or to fal backwarde.
To cut agayne, to cut behynde.
A square garmente, whiche they that dyd weare them, dydde caste the one part thereof ouer their shoulders at their backe, lyke to frenche clokes.
They that dydde weare suche clokes.
To retourne or come agayne.Terent. in Phorm. Percuncta tum ibo ad portum, quoad se recipiat frater, I wyll go seeke at the hauyn, vntyll my brother come agayne.
To come to souper.Plautus in Capt. Hic homo ad coenam recipit se ad me, This man will come to me to souper.
Come hyther to me.Plautus in Per.
To heare: Nō aedepol istaec tua dicta nūc in aures recipio, Plautus in cist. In good soth I do not heare now what thou sayest.

o: Recipere se in Principem, Plinius in panegyr.
n: recipere se in principem plinius in panegyr
d: To take on hym as a Prince.
To fetche brethe or wynde. Priusquam recipias anhelitum, Plautus in mercatore vno verbo eloquere, vbi ego sum, Or euer thou fetchest breth, tell me at a worde, in what case I do stande.
Take breth.Terent. in Adelph. Cicero in Cato. Cato speketh here of Fauius the wyse Captayn •

To recouer. Cum quidem me audiente Salinatori, qui amisso oppido fugerat in arcem, glorianti atque dicenti, mea opera Quint. Fab. Yarentum recepisti: Certe, inquit ridens, nam nisi tu amisistes, nunquàm recepissem: For in my hearynge, to Salinator, which (the towne of Tarentum being lost) fledde into the castell, sayenge vnto hym, Thou hast recouered Tarentum Q. Fab. by my meanes: That is true sayde he, lawghinge: for if thou haddest not lost it: I had not recouered it. also to reserue to a mans owne vse.
A retourne backe,Plautus in Asinar. drawynge or bryngynge agayne. Quid tibi huc receptio ad te est meum virum? Why draweste thou my housbande eftsones backe vnto thy house.
A goynge backe, or retournynge to the place that he came fro.

To receyue or take, to admitte, to call agayne, to brynge in faulsgarde, to delyuer, to vndertake, to promyse: also Recipere, is to reserue to hym selfe, or to excepte a thinge in gyuynge or bargaynynge.
To turne backe, to repete, to go backe.
That whiche is repeted or eftsones reherced.
To reade that other maye here and vnderstande: to recite or telle eftsones.
To denye with a lowde voyce or crye.
Is whan the skynne of the fyngar is loose frome the nayle.
To open. Infernas reserat sedes & regna recludat pallida, Vndo he the lockes of places infernall, and let hym set wyde open the pale regions of deth. Iustinus putteth Reclusus for clausus, shut.
To recognise, to knowe perfectly, to ouerloke.

To assemble or gather togither: also to reconcile. Quod scribis, etiam si cuius animus esset in te offensior, a me recolligi oportere, quid dicas? Where thou wrytest, that moreouer yf any man be displeased with the, that he shoulde be reconcyled by my meanes, whatte sayeste thou?
To repute, to repete, to calle to remembraunce.
To remembre, or call to remembraunce.
To reconcyle, to restore vnto fauour.
To newe make, to make meete, proprely a garment.
To boyle or seeth eftsones, to amende with study.
To recreate, to refresshe, to restore.
To renewe a fault made by Princes to their familiars.
A souper, where they sate all in a rewe.
Is where lynes are soo ioyned, that no part is longar or shortar than another.
An aduerbe signifyenge strayghte.Terent. in Eunucho. Cur non recta introibas? why wentest thou not strayght, or the strayght waye in.

Well ynoughe. Quid tu igitur lachrymas? aut quid es tam tristis? Pamp. Terent. in Hecy. Recté mater. S. Quid fuit tumulti? Than wherefore doest thou mourne? or why arte thou so heuy? Pamph. It is well ynoughe mother. S. what was all this noyse?
Of good right, with good raison.
It is ynoughe, or I haue ynough. Tum quod dem ei, recté est, Terent. in Heauton. I haue alsoo ynough to gyue hym.

To do good to a man, Stultus & sine gratia es, tibi rectè facere: Plautus in Aulularia. quando quod facias perit, Thou art a foole and without thanke, to do hym any good, whan all is lost that thou doest.

To take paciently. Si sapis, ne que praeterquam quas ipse amor molestias habet, Terent. in Eunucho. addas: & illas quas habet, rectè feras, If thou be wyse, adde to no more griefe than loue bringeth with hym, and them that he bringeth, suffre paciently.

Signifyeth sometyme nothynge, as Donate sayth. Rogo, nunquid velit. rectè, inquit: abeo, I asked if he wold any thyng, Nothinge, he sayde: I went than my way. also ye, straight waye. S. Tu rus hinc abis? Ter. in Ad. D. rectè, goest thou now into the contray? D. ye strayght waye.
He or she is in good helth.
The gutte frome whense the ordure passeth.
Straight, which is not crooked, vpright, iust.
To newe hamer, or newe worke, as it were on an anduylde: also it is taken for, to make newe, or newe prynte.
Iuges assigned, or commissionars, for a pryuate mater.

To sytte at a table, or at meales: sometyme to leane on one. Recumbebat mecum vir egregius Fidius Rufinus, super eum municeps ipsius, There satte with me that worshypfull man Fidius Rufinus, and aboue hym his neyghbour.

Was of olde wryters sayde, where there was a lawe made betwene the people of Rome, and other nations & cities, wherin they accordyd, that pryuate thynges taken, shoulde be redelyuered, whyche is nowe vsyd in our leagues and entercourses with straunge countrayes and prynces.
To desyre moche. Quin ita faciam, ut récupias facere sumptum, & si ego uetem: And yet wylle I soo handle it, that thou shalte moche desyre to spende, although I wolde fordyd the.
To rounne agayne, to goo or come agayne quyckely.
To runne often back or agayn.
An aduerbe, signifieng bowid bakwarde, crokydly.
That whyche is worthye to be refusyd.
He that is circuncysed. somtyme exulcerate.
To discharge or dispeche. Sequere hac, te redabsoluam, qua aduenisti gratia, Folowe me thyther, I wylle dyspatche thy mattier, for the whyche thou camest hyther.
To retourne. Cura quam optime potes. Er. bene ambula, & redambula, Do the beste that thou canste. Er. wel get the hens, and come agayne quyckely.
To render or yelde, to delyuer, to restore, to gyue, to make.

To putte in other. Tempestas uenit, confringit tegulas imbrices que , ibi dominus indiligens reddere alias ne uult, The tempeste camme, and brake the Tyles, and the Eueyses, where as the neglygente owner wolde not putte other in theyr places.
To cause one to make haste, to haste hym forwarde.

o: Reddere dictum ac factum. Videre egisse ia nescio quid cum sene. S. De illo quod dudu? dictum ac factum reddidi,
n: reddere dictum ac factum videre egisse ia nescio quid cum sene s de illo quod dudu dictum ac factum reddidi
d: It seemeth thou haste done late, I wote not what with the olde man. S. Meanest thou that, the other daye? thou haddest not so soone spoken, but it was doone.
I brought it to passe.Plautus in Epid.
To requyre a good turne or an ylle.
To resemble or be lyke to oone.
To redeeme or bye agayne often.
To cause the seller to haue ageyne that whiche he solde.
To brynge by force or cunnynge. sometyme to restore.
To compelle menne to lyue according to their astate or professiō
Thou doest after thyne olde facion, or as thou arte wonte to do.Terent. in Hecy. Ter. in An.

o: Redire ad se. Sed paululum sine ad me ut redeam,
n: redire ad se sed paululum sine ad me ut redeam
d: But lette me take breathe a lyttelle. Tandem reprime iracundiam, arque ad reredi: Nowe leaue thy fume, and remember thy selfe.

o: Redeam ad pauca, Vt ad pauca redeam, Terent. in phorm. ac mittam illius ineptias,
n: redeam ad pauca vt ad pauca redeam terent in phorm ac mittam illius ineptias
d: To the intente that I wyll be shorte, and passe ouer his foly.
Goo to the pourpose,Terent. in Heaut. or to the mattier.

o: Redijt ad restim res. Opera tua ad restim mihi quidem res redijt, Terent. in phormi.
n: redijt ad restim res opera tua ad restim mihi quidem res redijt terent in phormi
d: By thy meanes I am brought to the poynte to hange my selfe.

o: Redijt ad rastros. Nam si illi pergam suppeditare sumptibus Menedeme, mihi illaec ueré ad rastros res redijt,
n: redijt ad rastros nam si illi pergam suppeditare sumptibus menedeme mihi illaec uere ad rastros res redijt
d: Surely if I shuld mayntayne his expenses Menedemus, it wolde brynge me to rake corne or grasse for my lyuynge.
The thynge is come so to passe. In eum iam res redijt locum, ut sit necesse, The matter is come so to passe, that there is no remedy.

o: Redit mihi animus, Terent. in Hecyra.
n: redit mihi animus terent in hecyra
d: My courage is comme vnto me.
Idem, Also to be eftesones in fauour.
The ornamentes or apparaylle of a womans heed: as a veluette bonette or frenche hode.
To adorne or apparayle, or trymme.
A temple at Rome withoute the gate callyd Capena, where Hannyball beynge aferde, retyred backe.
To redeme, to bye, to recouer, to recompence, to take in bargayne.
They that hyre lande, or taketh any thyng in great or taske.
With courage reuyued, with a freshe courage.
Whan the skynne commeth withoute the nayles of the fyngers. alsoo an adders skynne.
That whiche retourneth eftesones to lyfe. Also that whiche of an old thynge is made newe or yonge.
A worme callyd a tycke, whyche souketh bloode from a man or beaste.
A gyuynge agayne of the thing that is taken.
Of olde wryters was taken for to gyue thanke.
They do cal such whiche are brought out of exile or captiuitie.

To brynge saulfe. Méque oppido in arcem reduco, Apulcius. And I conueyed my self quyckely into the Castell. Alsoo to pacyfye or appease.Vergilius Numen que reducant, Lette theym appease the wrathe or dyspleasure of god.
To brynge backe, or plucke backe, to delyuer or set out of peryll, to reconcyle.
To ouerflowe, to reflowe or retourne backe, to redounde.
To impostume or make an impostume in some parte of the body.
To proue fals, to repreue of falsehode, to denye that whiche is obiected.
To aske one counsayle in any matter.

o: Referre de re aliqua ad Senatum,
n: referre de re aliqua ad senatum
d: Was whan the Consuls purposed a matter in the Senate, desyrynge the Senatours to reason and consulte therof.
To set forthe a foote, or goo.Plautus in mercatore Eutyche hāc uolo rem prius agi, quam meū intro refero pedem, I wyll that this thyng Eutyche be doone, or I go oone foote in.
He came toward me.Plautus in Epidico.
These thinges pertain to the matter.

o: Refero acceptum, Omnia quae uidimus, Cicero. si recte rationabimus, uni accepta referemus Antonio.
n: refero acceptum omnia quae uidimus cicero si recte rationabimus uni accepta referemus antonio
d: All that we see, yf we recken well, we may impute it onely to Antonie. Quod uiuit, mihi acceptum refert: He confesseth to be longe of me, that he nowe lyuethe.Cicer. pro C • uen. Verum omnem tranquillitatem & quietem senectutis refert acceptam clementiae tuae, But all the tranquyllytie and quyetenesse of his age, he confesseth to procede or haue receyued of your mercy and goodnesse.

To gyue thanke.Plautus in Mostell. Nunquam ego illi possum gratiam referre, ut meritus est de me, I canne neuer gyue hym thanke suffycyent for that he hathe doone for me. Spero ego mihi quoque tempus tale euenturum, Plautus in merca. ut tibi gratiam referam parem, I trust the tyme shal come, that I shall doo you as moche pleasure.Ci. in Sal. Non enim sperasti mutuam tibi gratiam relaturum, ut uicissim tuos compellarem, Thou dyddest not thynke, that I wolde in this wyse haue requyted the, in remembrynge thyne auncetours, as thou haste doone myne.

To be brought in a reckenyng. Posteaquam reus factus est, primo negabat opus in acceptum referri posse, after that he was accused, fyrste he denyed, that the warke mought be brought vnto a reckenynge.
To turne it to a better vse.
To expresse the condicyons or maners of an other.
To caste the loke vpon one.Plin. epist. 156.
To requyte. Ille quem beneficio adiungas, ex animo facit, studet par referre, Whom thou gettest with benefytte, he dothe all thynges with a good harte, and studieth to requyte the.
To shewe or tel. At illa retulit, quaesiuit que , quidnam mihi uideretur, She tolde me all, and asked what I thought therin.

o: Refert. Cuius consilii magni referebat te inter esse.
n: refert cuius consilii magni referebat te inter esse
d: Atte the whiche counsayle, it hadde bene very necessarye, that ye shulde haue bene.Terent. in phorm. Parui retulit non suscepisse, It made lyttell matter, that he tooke hir not. Mea quid refert? What care I? Mea nihil refert? I haue noughte to doo with it. Tua refert, It is for thy profyte. Quid refert me fecisse regibus, ut mihi obedirent, si me hodie hic umbraticus deriserit? What auayleth it, that I haue made kynges to obeye me, yf nowe this lewde knaue shall laughe me to scorne? Refert, It is expedient or necessarye.Ver. geor. Neque enim numero comprehendere refert: It is not necessarye, to reherce them in numbre.
To brynge agayne, to resemble, to reporte, to referre, to reuoke. Referebam me, I retourned. To adde to, or ascribe, to turne, to renew, to brynge, to declare or expresse.
I make accompt of that whiche is bestowed.
To recreate, or restore, to amende, to make agayne.
To be restored, recouered from sicknes, Also renewed or new made.
To make faste or sure, to thruste in harde. Sometyme it signifyeth the contrarye, to drawe out that whyche is fastned.

To vndoo or destroye lawes. Acta Antonij rescidistis, leges refixistis: Ye haue cancelled the actes of Antony, and vndoone or dissolued his lawes.Ver. aenei. Fixit leges, pretioque refixit, He stablyshed lawes, and for money eftesoones dissolued them.

To bowe backe, to tourne back or agayn. Qu • neque fides, ne que ius • urandū, ne que illum misericordia repressit, ne que reflexit, Whom neither promyse, nor othe, nor yet pitie, withdrewe or pulled backe.
The tyde, whanne the water floweth.
A comfortynge or refreshyng, or recreation.
To recomforte, to refresshe,Plinius in panegyr. Plin. in epistol. 156. Plinius in panegyri. to recreate, to fortifye.
To nourysshe or comforte eftesoones, to restore or set in his fyrste state.
To resyste with wordes, or clamour.
To pull backe one from a purpose.
To renewe a sore or grief, whiche was out of remembraunce.
That whiche cooleth or maketh colde.
A recreation or aduauncynge of the mynde.
To coole, or make colde, to refreshe or recomforte.
A beane, whiche the olde Romans were wont to bring home out of the felde,Festus. to doo sacrifyce for the good lucke of their corne.
An vnrulye persone, whiche wylle not be ordered.
To flee or run away or backe.Colum. 4. also to refuse.
Refuge, succour, or place where one may be succoured.
That whiche gothe away,Sidonius. or is layde aparte.

To restore that whyche lacketh. Quicquid deerit, Seneca. ex meo refundam, Whatte soo euer dothe lacke, I wylle make it vppe of myne owne. Alsoo to paye home agayne, or to yelde. Id erat non tam accipere beneficium, quam refundere, That was not soo moche,Seneca de benefic. to receyue a good tourne, as to doo a good tourne. Alsoo to caste vppe by vomyte. Quod hesterna crapula ingurgitauerat, Plinius. palam refudit, That whyche in his yesterdayes ryotte he ingourged or deuoured, he openely dydde parbrake or vomyte hit vppe.
A denyenge, a replycation, an argument to the contrary.
A byrde, betwene whome and the egle is contynual hostilitie, and is yelowe of colour.
To thawe, or resolue that, whiche is frosen.
To putte in wrytynge, to brynge backe, to vomyte vp.
Olde writers vsed, for crescere, to growe.
That whereby a kynge is made.
A lyttell kynge. Also the name of a ryuer in Italy.
Place by place, by euery region or coste.
A region or countrey, also a coste, as easte, weste, northe, and southe.
A cytie beyonde the mountaynes towarde Italye.
A returne backe, a resorte backe.
That whyche is vnder a rule.

A Prynce or lorde of a lyttelle countreye, proprely Reguli, be the chylderne of kynges. Also Regulus is a lyttell byrde, callyd a wrenne, and a serpent callyd a Cockatryce, whiche sleeth a man with his syghte. It was alsoo the name of a Consule, whiche for kepynge of his promyse, was putte to cruelle deathe by the Carthaginensis. Also a great Rhetorician in the tyme of Plynie.
Sheepe drawen out of the folde for aege or syckenesse, kebbers, crones, or cullyars.
Of phylosophers be taken for thynges to be abhorrid, as sycknesse, pouertie, and sorowe.
The yssuynge oute of bloudde atte the mouthe, the noose, or the vaynes.
Caste out, caste awaye, or put forthe.

To caste awaye, to dryue backe. Tityre pascentes a flumine reiice capellas, Tityre dryue thy gotes, that doo fede, awaye from the ryuer. Also to refuse, to put away.Apulcius. Me uero tanquam inutilem reiecerunt, As for me they refused, as a person vnprofytable.Terent. in Phorin. Si altera illa magis instabit, forsitā nos reiiciat: If the other wil be importunate, perchaunce they wyll put me away.
To parbrake or vomyte.Se • tonius in August. Senos sextantes non excessit: aut si excessisset, reiiciebantur, He exceded not twelue ounces, yf he passed that, they were caste vp agayne.

A reporte, a respecte: Amonge Logycians, it is the effecte of the Relatyue, as the father, the sonne, the mayster, the seruaunt, the husbande, the wife. For withoute the oone, the other canne not retayne his name, for a sonne may not be withoute a father: nor a wyfe withoute a husbande, nor a seruaunt withoute a mayster.
Were they, whiche for some defaute were by the maysters of maners, called Censores, put out of the numbre of Citisens, and dyd only pay tribute, or heedsyluer, as straungers.
A relatife, whiche hath relation to some thynge.
A banysshemente oute of his countreye.
To banysshe, to remoue, to seuer oone frome an nother, to sende awaye.
He that hathe a good busshe of heare, well trymmed behynde.
A fayre large and hygh forheed, without heare.
Relygion, a reuerende drede. doubte leste be shall offende.Plautus in C • rgal. Also conscience, or as a man mought say, a scruple of conscience.
To feare leeste god were displeased.
To brynge in feare of goddis displeasure.
It is not lefull. Huc introire, nisi necessario, & caste, religio est, To enter in there, but for necessitie, and chastely, it is not lefull.

To open that whiche is stopped. Releui omnia dolia, I haue broched all the vesselles. Nolo ego nos pro summo bibere: nulli relerimus postea, I wolde not that we dranke all out: for I wyll for no manne sette any a broche afterwarde.
Whiche is commonly sayde to haue conscyence in a thynge.
To leaue. Relinquere animam, to dye. Relinquit eum animus, His harte fayleth hym.
They whyche bene in arrerage on theyr accompte. Also any other, whiche haue in their handes some part of that, whiche they ought to haue payde.
To paye agayne that which is borowed, to fetch home a gage or pledge. Also to washe eftesoones.
To tourne backe to a place.
Lyttell shyppes, whiche men of Lemnos vsed.
A fysshe, whyche cleanynge to the keale of a shyppe, causeth hym to tary.
To amende or correct a faut.
To retourne or go back ageyn.
They whyche doo rowe in a galaye or boote.
The rowynge of a shyp or bote.
The remembraunce of that, whiche was ones in the mynde.
Fayntly, without courage, humbly: Sometyme meryly.
Remyssion, forgyuenesse, a recreatyng of mynde after study or labour.
Gladde, remytted or forgiuen, sente agayne.
To sende, to sende agayne, to sende backe, to release or forgyue, to graunt, to lette downe, to commytte, or remytte, to relinquishe or leaue.
To putte awaye care, to vnbende or louse.
To cesse. Remittere aliquid adolecentiae, pardon him somwhat for his youth.

o: Remittere nuntium. Gratiam habeo tibi, qum copiam istam mihi & potestatem facis, Plautus in cap. ut ego ad parentes remittam nuntiu:
n: remittere nuntium gratiam habeo tibi qum copiam istam mihi amp potestatem facis plautus in cap ut ego ad parentes remittam nuntiu
d: I thanke the, that thou gyuest me this leaue, and also authoritie, that I maye sende to thy frendes, to prouyde for the els where.
A release, a losynge, a withdrawyng. Oculorum remissio, a withdrawing of the looke.
A lyttell fyshe, whyche retayneth a great shyppe vnder sayle.Ci. de ora.
To tourment the mynde, or make one heuy.
Byrdes, whyche by their flyght or voyce sygnyfyed, that the thyng purposed was not to be folowed,
A place on the toppe of the hyl callyd Auentinus, where Remus stoode, and by the flyght of byrdes, aduysed the buyldynge of Rome.
To tary or make to abide.
To belowe or lowe agayne, to render a great sowne.
Is proprely to drawe a greatte shyp or barge with a lasse vessell, by translation it signifieth to drawe a thynge easyly.
Instrumentes, wherwith shippes be dryuen on lande.
To reward to recompense a good tourne.
The brother of Romulus, whyche buylded Rome.
To swym back, or swym agayn.
To shyne, to sauour or smell.
To vnknytte, or vndo a knot.
Garmentes made of skynnes of wol • es or other beastes, wherin the anci-Almayns were wont to lye in the warres.
A kynde of wylde roses, whyche haue neither good sauour nor facion.
To paye agayne moneye, whiche is receyued.
An Ile by Ethiope, soo ryche, that the inhabytantes doo giue for a hors by exchaunge, a talent of golde.
To report, to signify, to shew openly, to renounce, to refuse, to resigne, sometyme to restore.
A report, also a resignation of an offyce. also a summons by an offycer.
They whyche do carye tydynges from one to an other.
A refusalle or denyar with countenance.
A doore or wyndowe or other thynge that shutteth or closeth.
Bent or bowed, and brode backwarde, as ores were in the old tyme.
To repayre, to restore to the fyrste astate.
A newe dyggynge aboute vynes. Also a bryngyng of grounde to temper with moche labour and dyggynge.
Newe digged or brought in temper.
To dygge agayne about vynes, to alter lande or grounde, with ofte dyggynge or labourynge.
To be eftesones dygged, or brought into temper.
To go awaye, to go backe.
To ponder, to ouersee, to iuge.
To fynde by auenture. sometyme otherwise.Plautus.
To calle agayne. Hem repudiatus repetor, Howe nowe, beinge ones refused, I am callyd agayne. Alta repetita, Ter. in A • . rehersed from the begynning, farre sought, or farre fette.

I remembre. Me quidem adolescē tulo, repeto quendam principem nomine alternis diebus declamare, alternis disputare, I remembre me, whan I was a boye, that one, whyche was a prynce of name, dydde one daye declame, an nother daye dispute.
To aske again, to aske often, or eftesoones, to reherce agayne, or repete, to reuolue.

Is proprely where a man sometime beinge in great auctoritie and hauyng the rule of a countrey, is accused and callyd to a reckenynge, for all that he hath receyued, being in his office, aboue that whiche is his ordynarye allowaunce, also for all thynge that he tooke wrongefully from any persone or towne▪ whyche was the mooste necessarie action for a publyke weale, that mought be deuised, to be nowe put in execution.
He that redemeth or quiteth his gage or pledge.
To quite or redeme a pledge or gage. It may be taken sometyme with vs, that whyche in our lawe is callyd to repleuy: and repignoratio, a repleuy: and repignoratitia actio, for a replegiare.
To make noise with the handes beaten togither.
A replycation or vnfoldynge of a thynge.
To vnsowlder.I •• ecō, 〈◊〉 d▪ auro & argent • .
To crepe, to runne as rootes do in the grounde.
To be moche able, to be of power to doo.
To be eftesoones stronge or in force.
• s also to put in by writing. Scriptor honoratum si forte reponis Achillem, Thou that writest, if peraduenture thou puttest in Achylles.

To putte or sette agayne in his place, to laye vp, to recite agayne, to hyde, to redelyuer or restore, to reuoke, to represse, to lay to more, or exaggerate, to heape one on an other, to make to grow agayne, to brynge agayne. Et quantum longis carpent armenta diebus, Vergeo. 2. Exigua tantum gelidus ros nocte reponet: Loke howe moche the sheepe in the longe dayes shall byte. The colde dewe in oone nyghte with growynge shall requyte.
To aske agayne that whyche is myne owne, or is as it were dewe to me.

Layd vppe, to hyde. Manet alta mente repostum, Iudicium Paridis, Depe in his minde, remayned the iudgement, that Parys gaue betwene the goddesses, of the whiche sprange the occasyon of the destruction of Troye.
Whan the day after the mariage frendes do come & drinke with the bride.
To plucke backe, to reproue. Reprehensi, caught.
To represent, to render, to brynge in presence, or present a thynge, to laye before one.
To crepe moch: also to go softly lyke a snayle.
To forsake, as a man forsaketh his wife, also to refuse, to abādon, or leue.
I wyll nowe leaue the counsayle that I fyrste intended to folowe.
To declare a deuorce. Is me nunc repudium renuntiare iussit tibi, Plautus in A • i •• . He wylled me to declare to the, that he hath forsaken the.

Mariage, after the which foloweth sone after a deuorce,Plautus in Persa. Necessitate me mala ut fiam facis, uerum uideto, me vbi uoles nuptum date, ne hac fama faciat, repudosas nuptias, Thou compellest me to be nought, but take hede, that where thou wylte mary me, by that reporte he shall make suche a weddynge as shall soone after be dissolued or broken.
To repugne or say contrary, to resyste.

An aduerbe, whiche signyfyeth contrariously, displeasantly.Cicero de amicitia. Vt igitur monere & moneri, proprium est uerae amicitiae, & alterum libere facere, non asperé: alterum pacienter accipere non repugnanter, sic habendū est nullam in amicitus pestem esse maiorem, quam adulationē, blanditias, assentationem, Lyke therfore as to giue counsayle, and to be counsailed, proprely belongeth to very frendeshyp, also the tone to do euery thyng frankely, the tother to take all thynge pacientely, not displeasantly: So it is to be consydered, that in frendshyp there is no more pestilence, than flatterye, fayre wordes, and consentynge to all thynges.
Repugnācy, where one thing agreeth not with an nother.
To prycke agayne, or mutually displease or offende.
A puttynge backe of hym, whiche eyther demaundeth or looketh for authoritie or offyce.
He that putteth an nother man backe.
To thynke often, to consyder moche, to reuolue in the mynde, to compt▪ Also to cut of eftesoones.
To seke eftesones or often, to requyre.

Occasion. Ere nata melius fieri haud potuit, quam factum est, Terent. in Adelph. Of the occasion begon it coulde not better haue ben doone, than it is. Also it sygnifieth meane. I am repperi rem, quo pacto nec fur, nec sotius sies: Plautus in Ruden. I haue nowe founde the meane, howe thou shalt be neyther a thefe, nor a companion with hym.
To gayne or wynne. Nunquam rem facies: abi, nescis ine • care homines, Terent. in Adelph. Thou shalte neuer gayne penye: Gette the hense, thou cannest noo skylle to angle menne.
To haue to do with one, to meddell with one.

To haue or make warres. Scipione Aemiliano res in Affrica gerente, Polybius annalium conditor, Plinius. lib. 5. ab eo accepta classe scrutandi orbis illius gratia circunuectus est: Scipion Emilianus making warres in Affrike, Polybius the wrytar of Histories, with a certayne numbre of shyppes, was conuayed aboute that coste, to inserche that parte of the worlde.

To helpe with deedes & not with wordes onely. Is amicus, qui in re dubia re iuuat, vbi re est opus, He is a frende, which in a case that is doubteful, helpeth me with his deedes, where deedes are required. Quid isti credam? Terent. in Eunucho. res ipsa indicat: what shal I trust hym? the deede selfe declareth. Verba ad rem conferre, to doo as he sayth. Vs que adeo ego illius ferre possum ineptias, Terent. in Eunucho. & magnifica verba, verba dum sint, verū enim, si ad rem conferentur, vapulabit: Hitherto I can suffre his lewdenesse, and bragges, as longe as they are but wordes: but yf he do as he sayth, he shall smart therfore.
In deede, in very trouthe, matter in dede.
A courtayse speakynge to hym that speaketh to you, a resalutinge.
To salute hym that saluteth you.
A thinge, the thinge, the matter: sometyme astate, condicion, busynesse, contention, cause, rychesse or substance, profyte, weale, experience.
It is all come to a bagge and a staffe, or a staffe and a walet.
A mater adiourned or deferred vntyll the thirde daye.
The matter or cause finally determyned and adiuged.

To cut or breake in sunder,Vergil. • eor. • i. 1. to take awaye, to destroye, to make voyde or repell an acte or lawe, to breake vp. Coelum rescindere fratres, Ter sunt conati: Thries the brethern assayed to breke vp heuen, for to enter.
To knowe a thinge, which is hydde and kepte secrete: also to knowe a thinge after that it is done, whiche was not knowen before.
To wryte agayne, to redelyuer, to repay money.
To cut awaye that which is superfluouse.
To pare to the quicke, to touche the quicke in a mater.
To praye or desire eftsones: also to assoyle one of his auowe.
The paringe of a mans nayles.
To open a thinge that is closed.
A reseruation, a kepyng of some thynge.
To kepe a part frome other thinges, to reserue.
Ydell frome accustumed labour or occupacion.
That which is cut and springeth agayne, and beareth more fruyte than it dyd before.
To rest, to sytte, to stande fast.

To syt downe, also to abide.Plinius in Episto. Nam Viennensium vitia inter ipsos residunt, nostra late vagantur, For the faultes of men of Vienne, doo abyde with theym, oures runne abrode, and be euery where knowen.
There doeth rest or appiere in the vysage.Cic. de 〈◊〉 Quorum non in sententia solum, sed etiam in nutu residebat autoritas, In whose sentence not onely, but also countenaunce, autoritie rested.
To open that which is sealed: sometyme to seale fast, also to shyt, sometyme to restore agayne, also to resigne or surrendre.
Wages stopped for negligent seruice in warres.
To lepe backe, or steppe away quickely.
He that hath a camoysenose, that is to saye, tourned vpwarde.
All lyke gumme whyche runneth out of trees.

o: Resipio, pui, pere, idem quod Resipisco.
n: resipio pui pere idem quod resipisco

d: To retourne to perfect vnderstāding, to be eftsones wise, where before he erred.
To resolue, to destroye, to pay dettes, to remoue, to vndo or vnlowse.
To sowne agayne, to make an Eccho.
To poure out or disgorge the licour that was receyued.
To see often, to loue, to helpe.
A looke: also, respect or regarde. Ne que eo respectu commorus discesserat: Plini. Hauynge no regarde thereunto he departed.
To cast water or other licour about, to sprynkle.
A sprynklynge or castynge about of licour.
To helpe or socour. Age, me in tuis secundis rebus respice: Let se, nowe in thy prosperitie, socoure me.
God hath pytie on vs. Tacemodo, Plautus in •• cch. deꝰ respiciet nos aliquis, peace now, some god will haue pitie on vs.

To take hede or haue regarde of hym self.Plautus in •• udo • o. Non soles respicere te, cum dicas iniuste alteri? Art thou not wont to take hede of thy selfe, whan thou sayest wrong of another man?Terent. in •• caut. Non tu te cohibes? non te respicis? non tibi exempli satis sum? Wilte thou not beware? wilt thou not take hede of thy self? am not I a good example vnto the?
To loke backe, to haue regarde, to prouyde, to remedy, to kepe, to reserue, to loue.

To take brethe, also to take cō forte, to retourne to the fyrst state. Si armis aut conditione positis, aut fatigarione abiectis, aut victoria detractis, ciuitas respirauerit: & dignitate tua tibi, & fortuna vti licebit: If that harneyse, eyther by condicions of peace beinge layde away, or by werynesse of both partes beinge throwen awaye, or pulled awaye by victory, the citie shall recouer her fyrst estimation, thou than shalt enioye thy possessions and dignitie.
To aunswere, to appiere whan one is called, to agree, to consent or be lyke or equall, to be against, as one thing set or lyenge agaynste another.
To make or gyue aunswere: it pertayned proprely to lawiars: and them whyche hadde the interpretation of ceremonyes.
Where one thinge doeth agree with another, a consent, a conueniencye.
To be or remayne of that thinge, that is lefte, to stande backe, to resyste. Hoc me restat, that remayneth or abydeth for me.
That which is renewed, or sowen agayne.
A feelde which is sowen two yeres togither.
To stint or put oute, or cesse, as fyre, lyght, and thurst.
A roper: alsoo he that hangeth hym selfe.
A puttynge in of pledges,Plautus. put in gage or pledge, for to make aunswere to an action.
To make aunswere in the lawe.
To be redy to be sowen, ploughed, or dygged.
A halter or corde, a rope or bunche of of garlyke or onyons.
Whan maydens and childrē daunse togither hande in hande, or with napkens, leadynge one another. Ad reftim res redijt, the mater is in despayre, or desperate.

To remayne, to tary. Hic nunc me credit aliquam sibi fallaciam portare, Ter. in An. & ea me hic restitisse gratia: He weeneth, that I warke hym some falshede, and that I tary styll therfore.Cicero de finibus. Nullam querentes voluptatem Stoici restant. The Stoike Philosophers do resist or sticke to their opynion, sekinge for no pleasure.
It taryeth for merit shal happen vnto me.

To bynde or strayne backwarde, to bynde agayne, to restrayne: sometyme it signifyeth to lowse. Apulci. Iumentum restrinxit, abire que stabulo liberum sinit: he lowsed his horse, and let hym out of the stable at libertye.
To lepe agaynste a thinge, to rebounde, to rebelle, to leape or steppe backe.

To sowe agayne, or make a double styche: also to ryppe or vndo that whiche is sowen, to vnstytche.Suct. in an. Sumenti virilē togam, tunica laticlaui resuta ex vtra que parte, ad pedes decidit: Whan he came fyrste to mannes age, his Senatours cote beynge rypte on bothe sydes, fell downe to his feete.
To tourne vpwarde, or vpright, to reuoke or calle backe, to differ, to peruerte.
Trees growyng on the bankes of ryuers, or in the ryuers.
To retayne often, to tempte eftsones.
To vntwyste or vntwyne, or vnwynde: sometyme to twist or wynde eftsones, to dissolue.
He that casteth a nette, proprely in syghtynge to apprehende his aduersarye.
Nettes, sometyme it signifyeth one nette.
To holde ones peace, to speake no worde, to kepe secrete, to saye nothynge.
Silence, whan one holdeth his peace.
A lytle net, wherin a mans heare or womens is trussed.
A cawle or coyfe: also a bagge, wherin meate is caryed.
What so euer holdeth any other thinge, a staye.

To holde vppe, that a man fall not. Ab retine me obsecro. Terent in Heauton, B. obsecro quid tibi est • An. Disperij. B. perij misera, quid stupes Antiphila? Oh holde me vppe I praye the. B. alak what ayleth the? A. I am vndone. B. alas that euer I was borne, why doth thy hart fayle the Antiphila?
To holde agayne, to retayne, to kepe in remembraunce.

To restrayne or let one frome doinge that, that he wolde. Pudore & liberalitate liberos retinere satius esse credo, quam metu: I thinke it better to restrayne children frome their wanton willes, by shame and liberalitie, than with feare.
To cast backewarde, to throwe or shute agayne.
To be burnedde with the sunne.
To calle backe, or reuoke a thinge that is done, to drawe backe, to excuse, to laye to another man, to drawe vp.
To pull or drawe back, or to drawe to.
Old writars called the water, wherwith gardens are watered.
The dragges of a thynge: somtyme ordure or dung.
To make blunt or dull, that whyche is sharpe: also to beate often on a thynge.

Dull, blunt, contrary to sharp. Aliae agrorum partes, Cic. de D • quae acuta ingenia gignant, aliae quae retusa: Some partes of cō trayes there be, whyche do bringe forth sharpe wyttes, some bringe forth dull.
To brynge or cary backe, or agayne.
A reuelynge or a disclosynge of a thinge.
To plucke backe, to pull agayne.
Reuerence or honour doone to one.
To bynde backe or behynde, as to bynde ones handes behynde hym.
Whyche the lawyars do saye, Paratus est verificare, He is redy to auerr̄.
To calle backe, to reuoke, to brynge agayne, to drawe backe, to rayse frome deth.

To restore or renewe. Item circa omnium ordinum statum domi, foris que , aut correxit, aut exoleta reuocauit, aut etiam noua instituit: Moreouer concernynge the state of al degrees, as wel within his house as withoute, eyther he dyd amende them, or renewed those thynges that were oute of vse, or els ordayned newe.
To reherce the deposicions of witnesses, Publication.
To turne vppe and downe, to reuolue, to tourne backe, to remoue.
To be tourned backe, to be remoued.
A tournynge backe to the firste place or poynt: a reuolucion or tournynge of celestiall bodyes or spheres.
Olde wrytars vsed for Reuertor, to retourne.
He that is sued or accused, sometyme he that is gyltye.
To accuse one of gret offence
Was a chief minister of sacrifices amonge the Romayns onely.
Rubarbe, a preciouse roote, medicinable to pourge coler. also to corroborate the stomake and lyuer.
A spyder, hauynge a lytle blacke heed, and is somewhat whyte, and hath short feete, whose bytynge is as venymous as the styngynge of a Scorpion.
Was kynge of Licia, which was a strayghte executour of iustice: and therfore was supposed of the Paynyms to be afterwarde one of the iuges in hell.
Certayne kleftes or as it were Scrachis aboute the siege or fundament.
A kynde of brembles, whyche is whyte, and beareth more frute than other do, and also hath floures, & sendeth forth brāches with strayght prickes, not croked as other are, and hath brode leues.
A man of a town called Rhamnus, by Athenes.
The propre name of a kynge of Egypte.
A ryuer in the mouth of Bosphorus, a countraye in Thracia.
Was called the mother of goddes, called also Cibele.
The mother of Romulus and Rhemus.
A citie on the bordure of Italy towarde Sicile: also an other citye not ferre frome Parma.
A man of the citie of Rhegium in Calabre.
People in Fraunce, called also Rhemenses.
Cotes made of the skynnes of beastes.
A noble ryuer in Germania, called the Rheyne.
People dwellynge on the ryuer of Rheyne.
Kynge of Thracia, whiche came to the ayde of the Troianes, and was slayne of Diomedes: of whome a ryuer aboute Troye was called Rhesus.
A countraye in Germany, whyche some men doo suppose to be Bauaria, or Beuer, called in Duche, Berue.
Rhetorike, or the crafte of eloquence.
A gyaunt, whome Dionyse, beinge tourned into a lyon, slewe.
An oratour, or a man cunnyng in the craft of eloquence.
To speake in the fourme of Rhetorike.
A rewme or distillation of humours.
A best that hath an horne in his nose, whyche naturally is enemy to the Olyphant: it is also an oyle vessell, out of the which oyle is dropped.
Is sayd of them that he witty. Iuuenes que , senes que , Et pueri na sum, Rhinocerotis habent, Yong men,Horatius. olde men, And children, and all be witty.
A ryuer in Fraunce, called the Rone.
A certayne precyouse stone, of the colour of a rose.
A tree, hauynge leaues lyke to an almonde tree, but greatter and fatter sedes, open lyke a horne, which hath in them wulle lyke purple silke, a longe roote, salte in tast, it groweth in watry places.
That part of Syria, that goeth ouer the mountayne of Taurus.
Pertaynynge to the mountayne, of Rhodope.
A fygure foure square, hauynge the sydes equall, the corners crooked. it is also a fysh called a Birt: also a spynnynge wheele or tourne.
Whan the corners of the eyen are open, so that there doo still frome theym continuall dropes.
A mountayne of Troye, where • ax Thelamonius was buryed.
A water lyly, called communely Nenuphar.
People on the north part, of the ryuer of Danubius, or Danowe.
A people in Fraunce called Rhodes.
A ryuer, which runneth in to the see called Pontus.
A paynter of tryfles, a Stayner.
A vessell lyke to a moone.
Numbre or at meny in speakinge.
A garment of purple, hemmed or purfled. also a kerchief, whiche women do weare.
Euery garment that is foure square. also it is a kynde of Cucumbres. also an herbe lyke a fygge tree, but lesse, hauynge leues lyke to a plane tree.
A cloke, whereof part was cast ouer a mannes sholder.
A grynnynge or scorneful openynge of the mouthe: also the fourme of the vysage, whan a man grenneth, or a dogge brawleth.
To laughe: also to skorne or mocke.
A proppe, wherwith a vyne, or other lyke thinge is holden vp.
A man whome men doo mocke or lawghe at.

o: Ridicularius, a, um, idem quod Ridiculum.
n: ridicularius a um idem quod ridiculum

o: Ridiculosus, a, um, idem quod Ridiculus.
n: ridiculosus a um idem quod ridiculus

d: To be feruently colde, alsoo to be harde or styffe.
Colde, harde, styffe, sharpe or cruell.
To make weate, or to water a garden or felde.
That maye be easyly weate or watered.
A chynke, or kleft in woode or stone, where it is not close ioyned.
To be clouyn or chynked, as tymber or bourdes are with lyenge in the wynde.
To fynde an excuse,Plautus in Cur. & in Casina. or meane to escape.
To serche diligently, also to kleue as tymber doeth.
To grynne or shew the teeth, as a dogge doeth whan he will barke or byte. also to be angry, to brawle, to barke.
A byrde whyche breedeth in water bankes.
A cofer couered with lether: also a lytle wyndowe.
A lawghter without myrth, as of them that be madde or cruell, such as Irish men vse whan they be angry.
Dyrectely, truely, euen as it shulde be.
Bookes, wherin the fourme of ceremonyes, and old maners and customes are wryten.
They whiche equally doo loue one womanne, or be woars togither. also they, whose landes be deuyded by a ryuer or brooke: also they which dwel vpō ryuers.
Enuy or obseruaunce betwixt the louers of one woman.
Is to go to watryng, as bestis do.
The Ceremonyes pertaynynge to Robigus, the preseruatour of corne.
Was honored of the Romains for a goddesse, whom they supposed mought preserue their corne from blastinge. it is also that vice in corne called blasting.
Whome the olde Romaynes named the god, that preserued corne from blastynge.
The old wryters vsed for robore, an oke.
Hard oke. It is also strēgth and hardenes of the body. sommetyme the strength or hardnes of any thing generally

Olde wryters called redde of colour. Also al maner of matter, which had many redde vaynes, was called Robus. It is also a kynde of wheate, that yeldeth fayre meale, whiche we nowe called redde wheate.
To gnawe as a mouse or other lyke beaste dothe. sometyme to detracte or backbyte.
A thyng vnperfect or rude, vnpolyshed, vnwrought.
Notaryes, whyche requyred the partyes, that eche of theym shoulde promyse.
A begger frome doore to doore.
To intreate or demande, to inquyre often, to aske for a thynge.
To requyre, to pray, to inquyre, to aske of one, to inacte.
To sweare oone, or to gyue to hym an othe.
Was amonge the Romaynes, whanne the Tribunes, whyche were the heed officers of the people, were content that any acte shoulde passe, whyche was made by the senate, or by the same Tribunes deuysed.
A great fyre, wherein deed bodies were bourned.
He that commeth from an nother countrey, and dwelleth at Rome.
A tree, vnder the whiche Romulus and Remus were founde.

o: Romuleus, a, um, & Romulidus, da, dum,
n: romuleus a um amp romulidus da dum

d: Men in the vauntgarde, or a forwarde of a battayle.
Is a disease in vynes, by the occasyon wherof the chiefe grapes doo falle away.
To dewe, or droppe downe lyke dewe.
A gardeyn or bedde of Roses.
A lyttell beake or bylle of a byrd.

Was a place in Rome afore the court callid Hostilia, wherin was a pulpite, in which the oratours of Rome were wonte to stande, whan they preched to the people, or declared any matter, of the whiche proceded this worde Pro rostris, in the pulpit, or at the barre.
A beake of a byrde, a snowte of a beaste or fyshe, also the stemme of a ship or boote.
To turne a thynge lyke a whele.
Roundly, aptely, elegantly, handsomly, proprely in wordes.
Rounde, sommetyme well compacte or facioned. Ore rotundo loqui, to expresse moche in fewe wordes.
A ryuer in Italye, whyche dyuideth Italy from Lombardy.
A swarte redde. Alsoo rowghe or course, as bredde, hauynge moche branne.
Red chalke, or ruddell, wherwith shepe are marked.
Coloured with redde, or ruddelyd, as shepe are.
To belke or breake wynde vppe warde.
To be discharged of attendāce proprely in warres.
To laye on olde stoones and rubbell.
To daube or lay on morter.
A place, where lyeth moche rubbyshe or rubbell. Also lande, whiche hath lyen • ley, and is newly put in tylthe.

They whyche are dyscharged of fyghtynge with swordes, as they whiche were calledde Gladiatores, that openlye faught, one with an other, to animate the Romaynes, with shedyng of their blode. They be also bodgers or amēders of old garmentes, also seuiars, or makers of sieues.
A citie in the further parte of Italy, ioynynge to Apulia.
To teche one, which is vnlernid.
A rodde or yerde, whiche was gyuen to sworde players, whan they came to .lx. yeres olde, in token that they were sette at libertie. sometyme lybertie frome labour.
Shardes or pieces of stones broken and scattered, rubbell or rubbyshe of olde houses.
Rudenes, lacke of lernyng or wit.
To braye lyke an asse. It is sometyme spoken of a man. sometyme of a woman.
Certayne Captaynes made by the consul, who afterward were called Rutuli.
The staffe, wherwith the ploughman clenseth his culter.
Was of the olde writers callydde a teate, also it is the throte bolle.
The dewlappe of a beaste. alsoo a place in the bely, a panche.
A brastynge oute, an aposteme that brasteth out of the fleshe.
A goddesse, whom the paynyms did suppose to be beneficiall to womens brestes, and to suckynge chylderne.
A chewynge of the cudde, as a beaste dothe.
A figge tree, vnder the whiche it is supposed that a wolfe gaue sucke to Romulus and Remus.
To chewe the cudde. Also to calle eftesones to remembraunce.
Wylde sorell. also a weapon like to a speare.
To gyue the teate to a chylde.
To breake, to make werye, Rumpere moras, to make haste.
A busshe, whiche groweth in France, of whom Columella writeth, that no corne shulde be sowen within twentye foote therof.
The place where suche bushes doo growe.
A weapon, sommetyme vsed in Fraunce.
A sawe, wherwith tymber is sawen.
A whypsawe, wherwith tymber is sawen, it is also a bushesythe, or bylle, to cutte busshes.
Oone of the names of Pluto, callyd god of Helle.

Is also to ouerthrowe, to rūne forth heedlynge. Quo moriture ruis, maioraque uiribus audes? Whyther runnest thou hedlynge to be slayne, and attemptest thinges aboue thy puissannces Also to lyfte vp. Et ruit atram, ad coelū picea crassus caligine nubem, Ver. geor. And beinge thycke, it lyfted vp to heuen a cloude, as blacke as pytche. sometyme it sygnyfieth to make a great noyse. Ruit arduus aethey, The highe firmamente rumbled, or made a great noyse.
To falle, to poure out, to be deceyued, to subuerte, to make playne, to plucke vppe, to breake a sonder, to throwe downe.
Be hylles, bankes, or rockes: soo stepe downe, as noo manne maye clymme theym.
Thou shalte paye or yelde damages.
Broken or braste, weryed, torne or rent.
Of the countreye, not of the citie or towne.
Borne in the countrey, oute of a citie or great towne.
To do after the countrey facion.
To dwelle in the countrey, or out of the citie.
Eftesones or bakwarde, on the other parte.
The countreye, oute of the Citie, where as housbandrye is vsed and exercysed.
To serche dilygently. It is proprely to shrape, as an henne dothe, whan she seketh for meate.
A byrde lyke a partryche, but he hath a longer byll.
Rustycall, of the countrey or vyllage.
Carlysshenes, sommetyme fearefulnesse. Et si rusticitas non vetat, Ouidius. ipsa rogat, And yf that foolyshe basshefulnesse lette her nat, she makethe requeste.
To dwelle in the countrey, or exercyse husbandrye.
Is also the propre name of a man.
Rewe, callydde alsoo herbe Grace. It is amonge the lawyers all that is dygged oute of the grounde, as stone, cole, leadde, and other mettalle.

All be it Mutius doth saye, that in Rutis & caesis are those thynges, that be not faste in the grounde, nor are any parte of the buyldynge or the couerynge of a hous. Perchance we mought name theym heyre lomes.
A coole rake, to make cleane an ouen.

o: Ruto, tare, for ructo, Fla•. Cicero.
n: ruto tare for ructo fla cicero
d: To belke or breke wind vpwarde.
Trouble. Id postea uiderimus, Varro. nunc sumus in rutuba, We wyll afterwarde see, nowe be we in trouble.
A brighte redde lyke to coles that be kyndled.
A goore or elbowe of lande in Englande, lyenge into the see, whiche I suppose is in Norfolke.
He that kepeth the sabbath daye.
The day of reste from labour.
In the plurelle numbre, in the hebrewe tunge, signifyeth of hostes, or armyes, or powers.
A propre name, wherof cometh Sabatheni, the name of a people.
In the tunge of Siria, is the moneth of February.
People, whiche dwell in the mountaynes betwene the Sabines and Marsi, in Italye.
Amonge the Arrabiane doth signifye god.
A weapon lyke a bore speare.
A gate at Rome, out of the whiche men went to the Sabines.
Lastage, or balese, wherwith shippes are euen poysed, to go vpryght, whiche is commonly of grauell.
A kynde of ambre founde in Egypte.
To apparelle or amende wynes putte into sackes.
A clothe to wype a thynge with. a napkyn, also a territorie.
An hylle by Rome, an other by Galatia, wherin golde is founde.
Amonge the Indians, sygnifieth a bryght purple colour.
A precious, stoone of a bryghte purple colour.
A crafty deceyuour, whiche in sellynge of grayne out of sackes, wylle conuey away parte.
A sycknes, wherin is vehement inflamation and burnyng of the body.
Priesthode. sometime a benefyce or spirituall promotion.
A streete in Rome, where peace was made betwene Romulus and Tacius, and through the whiche the vanquyshers passed with their triūph vnto the capitol.
Is taken for men of warre.Iuuenall •
An othe amonge vs christen men, it signifyeth a sygne, wherin is contayned a diuyne mysterie, and is callyd a sacrament.
A sextrie or vestrie, wherein are kepte thynges halowed, and relykes.
Lawes, in the whiche it is enacted, that who so dothe offende agaynst theym, is accursed.
To do sacrifice, to consecrate to aske forgyuenes of god.
Theft, or taking away of thynges halowed, callyd Sacrilege.
An errant thefe in stelynge of thynges halowed.
He that violently taketh awaye or stealeth thynges halowed, or thynges vnhalowed out of a holy place.
He that keepeth the kynges letters or Recordes, concernynge the Crowne, or bokes of great affaires.
A kynde of aumbre, whiche commeth out of Scithia.
Consecrate or halowid with a solemne othe taken.
Any thynge dedicate to god. Also sacrifice. sometyme a temple or churche. Paulus Iureconsultus. Sunt aurem sacrilegi, qui publica sacra compilarint. Also sacra do signifye holy wordes. also charmes.
A great mountayne or rocke in the southwest part of Spayne, lyenge on the see, callyd nowe, Capesainct Vincent.
Men of a speciall seete among the Iewes, that beleued not of any resurrectiō, or that there be any angels or spiritis.
Is proprely the space of a hundred yeres: it is commonly taken for a space of tyme, wherin one facion of the worlde hath contynued.
To be very angrye, to do valyauntly, to be cruell, or exercyse tyranny.
Rudely▪ Magis cogito, saeuiter, blanditer ue alloquar, I thynke more, where I may speake to hym rudely, or gentylly.
Cruelle, horrible. sometyme angry, valyant, myghty.
A wyse or subtil woman, also a witch.
A gumme or rosyn, which runneth out of a kyxe or tree, callyd Ferula.
The craft to make clokes to weare on harneyse.
A grene stone, whyche the Caldees haue made fast to their handes.
That whiche is franked or made fatte.
Meate, wherwith all thynge is fatted. sometyme superfluous fatte.
A place wherein any thynge is franked or made fatte.
An arow, also the top of a twygge or rodde.
An archer. It is also one of the xii. sygnes amonge the sterres.
A packe saddell, or sumpter saddell. also an heape.
Grasse, plucked vp with the erthe, whiche in the olde time the ambassadours of the Romanes dyd, whan they denounced warres to other people.
A citie in Spayn, whiche for the constant fydelitie, kepte to the Romains, was distroyed by Hanniball.
Extreme famyne, a prouerbe made of the famyne, whyche was in the cytie of Saguntus, whan Hanniball besyeged it.
A citie of Egypte, where is one of the entries into the ryuer of Nilus, the entry or porte is callyd Saiticum.
Salt. somtime it is put for wisdom, myrth. Sales, quycke or sharpe sentences, iestynges. sometyme it sygnifieth the see.
Water that ryseth out of a quycke springe.
A beaste in fygure lyke to a lysarde, full of spottes, which beinge in the fyre, dothe extincte it, and is not burned.
A kynd of salt founde vnder sand, which is lyke to alume, & is medicynable, in dissoluynge & purgyng of fleume.
A very hygh hylle betwene great Brytayne and Irelande, nowe callid our ladyes hylle.
May be callid a mery iesting boy. It was a name giuen to Caluus an orator, which being of a childes personage, vsed moche iestynge and tauntynge meryly.
An hygh way, by the whiche salt was caried to Rome.
Vnplayne, where a manne can not goo, excepte he do leape.
Thynges condite or conserued, as peares, figges, grapes, and other lyke.
A kynde of byrdes, whiche be greatte breders: as partriches or hennes, I suppose them to be hethecockes.
A banket or supper made by the priestes of Mars.
Maydens, whyche were with the priestes of Mars, and did sacrifyce with the byshops, wearyng on them cote armures, and bysshoppes myters on theyr heedes.
Ꝑtaining to the pristis of Mars.
A kynde of wylde vyne, rounnynge vpon wyllowe trees.
The cockes or pipes of cundites, oute of the whiche water spouteth.
A place, where salte is made.
The name of a noble mā of Rome.
That whiche is salte in taste.
A plant, hauynge long leaues, somwhat yelowe, and a yelowe flowre, & groweth shorte, and hath many rootes. It is taken for the Spikenarde, that groweth in Fraunce, and is commonly vsed.
People in the mountaynes of Alpes, confynes to the Swycers, and the people called Boii.

The kynge of Elides, which takynge foolyshely vppon hym, to haue diuine honours doone vnto hym, and wolde seme to caste lyghtnynges, lyke vnto Iupiter, being ouerthrowen with lyghtning, was caste into helle.
Salte peter, whiche is putte into gunne powder.
A ryuer callyd also Bibilis, wherwith yron is tempred, and made stronger.
Is interpreted peasible, the name of a kynge of Iewes, the sonne of kynge Dauid, who exceded all men in wisedome and knowlege, and neuer the lesse was by dotage on women brought to ydolatrie.
A countrey of Bithinia, very cōmodious for the feedynge of cattell.
A cytie in Liburnia betwene Dalmatiam and Illiriam.
A fyshe whiche wylle not be sodden, excepte it be beaten, as stockefyshe is.
A kynde of emotes or pysmeres.
Pertaynyng to sauce. Vas salsamentarium, a vesselle, whereinto sawce is putte.
A tree, that bereth maste, which nothyng wyll eate, excepte onely swyne.
Pertaynyng to daunsyng. Ludus saltatorius, a scoole of daunsynge.
People ioynynge to the see callyd Pontus Euxinus.
A keper of a wod, a wodwarde.
A thycke wodde, also a leape.
A sauyour, he that kepeth or saueth a thynge from distruction or losse.
God spede you. ye be welcome, sometyme contrary, farewell, God be with you.
To be saufe, or spede well, to be well at ease.

o: Salue. S. satis est mihi tuae salutis, nihil moror non salueo,
n: salue s satis est mihi tuae salutis nihil moror non salueo
d: God spede. S.Plautus i • trucule • . It suffyseth me that thou arte in helthe: but in fewe wordes I am not well at ease.
A drench for a horse or other beest.
To make safe, or to saue.
My sonne Cicero commendeth hym vnto you.Ci. ad A •
A chamber, where men do stande and abyde to salute a prince or noble man in auctoritie, callyd nowe a chamber of presence.
In the old tyme was vsed for saltē.
To salute or to haue recommendation to any man.
He that bryngeth recommendacions from another person.
To salute, aswell at commyng as at departinge: also to honour.
Saulfe, hole, sounde, withoute damage or harme.
An hil in the east Oceā se, at the further ende of the mōtayne called Caucasus.
An instrument of musyke, now called doulcymers, an engyne of warre, wherwith fortresses were assaulted.
A woman whyche playeth on doulcymers.
Vesselles made in the Ile of Samos.
Of the Ile of Samos: the olde wrytars dyd vse it for sharpe, and Samiare, to whette or make sharpe.
People of Samnium a contraye in Italy called nowe Aprurium.
The name of an Ile in the see, called Icarium.
An Ile by Thracia in Grece.
One of the names of Hercules.
A lawe, a thynge decreed and stablysshed.
Holy, inuiolable by a lawe, pure and cleane, vncorrupted. Vir sanctus, a blessed man.
A colour founde in mynes of siluer, or golde, yelow ocker.

n: sandastros amp sandaphorion amp sandarison amp sandassites
d: A preciouse stone, hauynge in a bright colour yelowe speckes, and is called also, Garamandita.
An herbe of a delicate odour, hauynge a short stalke, in the residue lyke to fenell. it is also a colour called a bryght yelowe.
An aduerbe, whiche signifyeth, ye, or certaynely, on goddes name. Bellum sané difficile gessit, he fought a very daungerouse batayle.
Ye hardely.Ter. in An. Nempe ergo aperte uis, quae restant me loqui? D. Sanè quidem. But wilte thou than that I shall telle playnely all the rest? D. ye hardely.
A ryuer of Galatia, whyche runnynge through Phrygia, falleth into Propontis, the see.
Bloode. alsoo a tree, the barke whereof is of the coloure of bloode.
Full of bloode. also cruell. sometyme of sanguyne or bloody colour.
The bloode of a kyd or swyne, wherwith pouddynges are made.
A worme, which is in standinge waters, and doeth sowke the bloode of men or beastes that come in to it. it is alsoo called Hirudo.
A dysarde in a playe or disguysynge: also he which in countenaunce, gesture, and maners is a foole.
Muste or newe wyne sodden to the halfe deale.
The kunnynge of thynges diuine and humayne, wysedome.
To tast or sauour, to fele, to be wise, to haue a right opinion.
I knowe what I haue to doo.
Thou knowest howe to make good chere.
The lower parte of a fyrre tree, whiche is without knottes.
A drynke, made with salte and the fruite callyd Sorba, whiche helpeth men that haue the colyke.
Of olde writers was vsed for ipsa.
A maner of iestynge or scoffing bytyngely.
A trusse or packe, or fardell. sometime it is taken for an vnprofitable burden.
Is proprely of menne of warre, whanne they remoue or departe from their campe.
All stuffe that is closed or shutte vp in coffers.
To make hole agayne, to amende a thynge decayed or appaired, to make amendes.
A red stone, wherin seales ar grauē.
A kynge of Assiria, monstruouse in all kyndes of lechery, and therfore was slayne of one of his lordes as he satte spynnynge amonge harlottes.
An Ild in the see callyd Ligusticum, by Geane.
An herbe lyke to smallage,Neulu • . whiche groweth in Sardinia, wherof if a manne eate, he shall grenne and make countenance of laughynge, and so dye.
A grennynge or laughyng without cause, a longe laughter.
Hauynge apparayle garnished with the stone called Sardonix.

n: sardus amp sardinensis amp sardous a um

d: A stone of the colour of a mannes nayle.
A towne in Siria, where Hely the prophete was borne.
People in the northe parte of the worlde, ioynynge to the greatte mere of Meotis.
A fyshe beinge in the see of Egipt.
An herbe, growynge in waters, hauing an harde roote, and wounden, necessarie for smythes.
A bosome of the see agaynste Isthmus.
All that great countrey, wherein is contayned Russia, Liuonia, & Tartaria.
Twiggꝭ or shroude of trees cut of.
Made of twygges or smalle boughes.
The kyng of Lisia, whiche came to the ayde of the Troyanes agaynste the Grekes.
An Ile callyd sometyme Tyrus: also the wyfe of Abraham.
A worde of Caldey, signifienge breches.
The name of two cities, whereof the tone is in Media, the tother in Felici Arrabia, or the ryche Arrabie.
A certayne carre, wherin wodde or stones be caried.
An olde citie in Italy, where Plautus the writer of comedies was borne.
Houses letten to certayne persones to kepe them alway repaired suffyciently, for a certayne somme of money.
To sette oute houses at a price certayne to be repaired.
To charge a man with reparations.
An entrie in to the ryuer of Nilꝰ.
An harower or weder of corne.
To keepe hoole and sounde, or vncorrupted or hurte.
The bealye of a swyne stuffed with meale.
An yle fyue myles frome the citie of Brundusium in the realme of Naples.
Inough. Quantum sat • est, asmoche as is sufficient. Sat habet, it is sufficient. Sat scio, I knowe well inough.
People in the countrey nowe called Tartarie.
To be dylygent, to do with spede, to be busy about a thynge.
Is interpreted an aduersary, by the whiche name the diuel was called, bicause that he was aduersarye to Christe. Alsoo what so euer is contrary to peace, is callyd Satanas.
People in Scythia, which excluded from them the vse of golde & syluer.
One retayned to garde a mās persone. Also a catchepoll or baylyff, that dothe attache men.
A garde, the offyce of suche a person or offycer.
A beaste, whiche doth lyue some tyme in water, sometyme on lande.

Sacietie, fulnes or werynesse in moche vsynge of a thynge, sometyme it signifieth abundaunce. Hi, saltibus occupatis, externorum agros inuasêre, ••• ustius. frumenti que ex inopia graui, satias facta, After that they had gotten the woddes or forestes, they inuaded the landes of them that were borderers, and from scarsitie of corne, they happened to haue their fylle or haboundaunce.
That whiche may be easyly satisfyed.

o: Satin, for satisne, Satin sana es?
n: satin for satisne satin sana es
d: Arte thou not well at ease?
The acte of sowinge of corne.
To satiate or fylle, whyche hath relation not only to the body and sences, but also to the mynde.
Ynough, as moche as dothe nede.
A couenaunt, wherby a man is bounden, and sureties with hym.
The suertie or bonde, wherby menne are bounden for an nother, for perfourmance of couenaunte, or the couenantour and suerties with him.
He that is bounden for perfourmaunce of couenant
To put in sureties for perfourmance of couenantes. also to be bounden with suerties for the performynge of couenauntes.

o: Satis praesto, tare, idem quod satis dare,
n: satis praesto tare idem quod satis dare

d: The comparatiue degree of satis, it sygnifyeth better.
That may be sowen, or is sowen.
Amonge the Persians were as dukes and Erles be here.
Full fedde, sometyme aboundant or plentuouse.
He that hathe eaten ynoughe,Plautus in Persa. and to moche.
Fertilitie, or plentuousnes. Alsoo abundance in excesse.
Fyue dayes assigned to Saturne in December, wherin men vsed to feaste one an other, & to sende mutual presentes.
Pertayninge to the ceremonies of Saturnus.
Was the name of a towne. Alsoo high places were called Saturnia.
Were heretikes, whyche affyrmed, that onely seuen aungelles made the worlde agaynst the conscience of god the father.
A mountayne at Rome, whiche was afterwarde called Tarpeius.
One of the seuen planettes: alsoo a god of the paynyms.
To saturate or fyl with any thing superfluousely, moste commonly in eating.
A citie of Calabria, not farre from Tarentum.
A matter or poesye made in the rebuke of some astate or persone.
A syckenes, wherby the membre of a man standeth alway without appetite or dilectation.
Was a comedye, wherin Satyres were brought in.
An aduerbe, whyche sygnyfyeth sharpely and with reproche.
A beast hauyng the heed of a man, and the bodye of a gote.
An herbe, hauynge leaues lyke a lyllye, but smaller, a knappe with manye smalle purple floures, and a roote lyke the genytours of a man.
A lysarde, whiche lyeth in hedges.
A stoone, whiche is founde in the bealye of a grene lysarde.
Peple called also Sarmatae, Russes, Tartariens, Moscouites.
Stonye. Pisces saxatili, fysshes bredde amonge stones.
Full of great stones or rockes.
To tourne the stone. A prouerbe applyed to theym that be fatygate or weryed with contynuall and vnprofytable labours.
A fote stoole, or lowe settle.
A roughnesse of the skynne, as whan it dothe wrynkle.
A worme, which is ingendred of the carrayne of a deed horse.

A place, whyche seruyth onely for enterludes or comedyes to be playde in, whiche was in the fourme of halfe a cerkle. It is also where trees or busshes, are cutte and layde ouer the heed, in suche fourme, a • men may vnder them walke or sytte in the shadowe. It is alsoo where a vyce or offence is openly detected, in suche wise as mē do cry out or wonder at it.
For a player in comedies or enterludes.
People of Arabie, whiche dwelle alway in tentes, couered with the heares of gotes, amonge whome yf a swyne or hogge be brought, it dieth.
The feaste of the tabernacles, wherin the Iewes did set vp tabernacles or tētes in similitude of them, wherin they dwelled whan they came out of Egipte.
In greke, is a tent or shadowe.
The lefte hande, also he that vsethe the lefte hande for the ryghte.
Ylle,Fest •• . sometyme it sygnyfyeth good, as Scaeuū omen, good lucke or chāce.
A ladder. Alsoo a payre of stayres.
A lyttell piece of wodde, whervnto shyppemen doo bynde their oores, to rowe the more easyly.
To scratche, also to graue in mettalle.
An instrument, wherwith any thyng is scraped or rubbed, also a surgeons instrument, wherewith he taketh corrupte flesshe from the bones. It is also a grauynge yron.
Pauement made with stones, of dyuers colours, ioyned togither.
To scrape as a Cocke dothe, or other fowles.
To scrape as a henne dothe.
A ryuer, whiche dyuydeth Europa from Asia.
A towne by the hauen of Iliū, not farre from Troye.
A benche or fourme. Also a step or grise, wherby a manne gothe vp vnto a high bedde. Also a balke vntilled betwene two forowes.
An herbe, the iuyce whereof is vsed in medicine to purge coler vehemētly. All be it that it is venemous, & leaueth wars matter behynd, than it doth expell.
Occasyon to synne, gyuen by an nother to hym that synneth.
An yle in the north occean see, the quantitie wherof was neuer founde.
An herbe lyke to cheruyll, but it is sweter, and hath a whyte floure, and a lyttell roote.
An herbe, whiche runneth vppon corne, as iuye dothe on trees.
Shyngle, whiche be tyles of wod, wherwith dyuers churches be couered.
A house couered with shyngle, or wooden tyles.
That whiche maye be clymmed or gone vppon.
A bason or vesselle to receyue vryne or ordure.
A knyfe, wherwith vynes and other lyke thynges are cutte.
A place in Macedoni • , where syluer was dygged.
An olde citie in Italy, wherof came Scaptia tribus.
The hynder parte of the shulders.
A boye or wenche, whiche is oft beaten aboute the shulders.
A garment, whiche couereth onely the shoulders.
The heade of popie or other lyke herbes, wherin be the sedes, lykewise the huske of grapes, wherin the graynes be contayned.
A fly with a blacke shell or huske called a bytell: whiche breedeth in cowe shardes, and is black. Also there is a kind of thē, which hath hornes like to an hart.
A prouerbe applyed to suche as endeuour them self to do displesure to those that be more puissant thanne they are.
To launce or open a sore, that the matter corrupted may issue.
A fyshe, whiche dothe chewe lyke a beaste. some menne doo suppose it to be a Gylte heed.
The bollynge or rysynge vppe of water out of a spryng or sourges of water.
To runne or brast out, as water dothe out of a narowe or strayte place.
Brastynge oute of water or other thynge in lyke maner.
To runne out or abrode, also to springe or growe abroode, as somme herbes done.
They whiche haue their toes swollen, or their ankley croked, that they may not goo faste, it was alsoo an honourable house of the Romaynes.
He vnto whome a myscheuouse dede is done. sometyme it signifieth hym that dothe an yll dede.
A felde at Rome, where the nunnes of Vesta were buryed quicke, if they were founde to lyue incontinently.
He that hath done an vngracious or myscheuous dede.
Vngracious, ful of vnhappynesse, myscheuous, vengeable.
A myscheuous dede. also an vngracious person.
A pauyllyon or halle. Also a scaffold.
Were a secte of Phylosophers, whiche affirmed nothynge: the chiefe of that secte was Pirrhus and Herillus.
A leafe of paper, a scrowe.
A thynge lyke to a brydge with trees pynned togither, wheron thynges are caried in the water, in the steede of a barge, as it may be sene on dyuers greate ryuers in hygh Germany.
Any thynge sodaynly made, and without moche labour.
A lyttel scrowe or leafe of paper.
A figure. also an ornamēt, specially in spech. somtime a garmēt.
Where a multitude of wordes are brought in togyther vnioyned, as, Nubila, nix, grando, procellae, flumina, venti, Cloudes, snowe, hayle, showres, flouddes, wyndes.
Amonge the Iewes was a weight of foure ounces.
A diuisyon, specially in the churche.
The mylke that remayneth after that the mylke is sodden, whiche is callyd well courdes.
He that gothe on a corde.
Harlottes, whiche dresse theym selfes with stynkynge oynementes.
People, whiche do dwelle in pauyllyons.
A ryuer by Athenes, also an other in Archadia, and also a tree callid Lentiscus.
A space of grounde contaynynge thre score furlonges.

A schoole. Also a place in a bayne, where men dyd abyde, whiles other were bained, lykewise in a porche, wherin men taried for answeres. Scholae, are taken for dysputations betweene the mayster and his scholers.
That which may be easily knowē.
To be perfytte in playenge on instrumentes.
As who sayth. It is moche, surely, moreouer. Sommetyme it implyeth a negatyue.
An herbe, whiche hath a rote lyke an oynyon. some call it Squilla.
A kynde of small cockodryls in the ryuer of Nilus.
To ordeyne and inacte, as it is in our parlyament.
I knowe what I haue to do, also I can accommodate my selfe to other mens maners, & to the condycions of the tyme and place present.
A part of nygromancy wrought by shadowes.
People, whiche lyenge vpryght do shadowe them selfes with their feete: all be it euery one man hath but one legge: and yet be they wonderfull swifte.
A dyalle sette vppon a walle, to knowe by the sonne what is a clocke.
They whyche were of the progenye of Scipyons, the noble captaynes of Romaynes.
The surname of a noble howse in Rome.
Rockis in the see by Athenes.
A dunge potte or colne made with roddes.
A lyttell hooke, wherwith russhes, or any thynge is cutte of in bynding of thynges.

A rushe, or an osyar. Nodum in scirpo querere, To seke for a knotte in a rushe is a prouerbe, wherby is signified, to seke to diligently for a thyng that maye not be found, or to make doubt of a thing, whyche is playne.
A thynge growen in a man or womans bealy, specially in them, which haue the dropsy, & causeth the bely to be great.
A disease in the eyes, commynge of a longe inflammation, fleshe growyng in them somwhat blue.
Is a kynde of oynyous, growyng in wynter, callyd scalyons.

n: sciscitor taris tari amp scisco sciscere
d: To demaunde. Alsoo sciscere, is to ordeyne or inacte.
Gyue thou sentence or iudgement, gyue thy voyce or consent in election.
To knowe, Also to decerne or gyue sentence.
Wyse or wyttie, alsoo propre or feate.
People in the northe parte of Asia, whiche were cruell, and harde to be vanquyshed, they be nowe callyd Russyans, Moscouites, and Tartariens.
The name of all the countrayes togyther.
A swellynge of the eye lyddes, with payne and rednesse.
Where the eye lyddes ben harde, and waxe heuy with ache.
A sowne, which is made with puffynge of the chekes.
An instrumēt, wherwith any thing is shauen. sometyme the shauyng selfe.
That which comith of the sha • yng or boryng of wodde or mettall▪ also grit of stones, wherwith metal is scoured.
A kynde of ruste or canker.
A worme with many feete and rough, callyd a palmer.
A scoffe, or sentence spoken in myrthe, whiche sowneth otherwyse thā is ment of hym that speaketh.
A brome or besome to swepe▪ houses.
He or she that dothe swepe.
Dyssolute men without wyt or coūcil.
To say or do a thyng without any purpose or reason.
An hygh place, where men stande to beholde or espie.
A brushe, suche as payntours and pargettours doo vse.
An high rocke, also it is a marke, wherat men do shote. sometyme it sygnifieth any thynge, wherevnto that whiche is spoken, hath a principal respect.
Be grapes, after that the wyne is pressyd oute.
The refuse of metal tried out by fyre. Somtyme it signyfyeth care or grefe.
A fyshe, whyche kepeth hyr selfe to one make.
They whyche doo shoote in crossebowes.
A stone of the colour of a scorpiō.
An herbe and floure called ruddes or marygoldes. It is also a worme like to that whiche is callyd Locusta.

A venimous worm called a Scorpyon, whiche stryketh with his taylle, and neuer ceasseth to serche, where he maye haue occasyon to stryke. Also a sygne in the fyrmament. It is also a crossebowe. Som men take it to be an arkbushe. Also a whyppe, hauing plummettis of leade at the endes of the cordes. It is also an herbe, whyche hathe seedes lyke to Scorpyons.
That which is of lether: as Scortei numi, lether money.
The codde of a man or beaste.
That whyche is made of skynnes.
To haunt or company with harlottes.
An harlote or strumpette: it is also the hyde of a beaste.

Scottes, or Scottyshmen, of whom sayncte Hierom writeth in this wise. Quid loquar de caeteris nationibus, quū ipse adulesceniulus, in Gallia •• derim Scotos, gentem Britannicam, humanis uesci carnibus: & quum per syluas porcorum greges & armentorum, pecudum que reperiant, pastorum nates, & foeminarum papillas solere abscindere, & has solas ciborum delitias arbitrari? Whatte shall I speake of other Nacyons, sens that whanne I was a boye, I sawe in Fraunce, Scottes, a people of Britayn, eate mennes flesshe: and whanne they founde in the forestes herdes of swyne, beastes, and cattayle, they wolde cutte of the buttockes of the boyes, whyche kepte theym, and alsoo the womens pappeo, and toke that to be the moste deyntie and delycate meate.
In Greke, darknes: It is more aptly callyd in the northerne tunge, myrke.
A skynne, wherin arrowes are putte: it may be callyd a sheafe.
A worme, whyche is founden in leaues. Also a vyle and stynkyng harlotte, a driuelynge queane.
That whiche may be spette or retched out of the lunges or stomake.
A Secretarye, a Notarie, a Scribe, a Clerke.
The olde wryters vsed for Scribo.
A delycate meate made of paste stuffed and wounden lyke a rope. I thynk it to be suche as fartes of Portyngal are.
To write, also to make sometyme to paynte.
An vntrue fourme of speakynge or wrytyng, callyd also soloecismus.
A coffer, or other like place, wherin iewelles or secrete thinges ar kepte, as euydences and recordes of iudgementes or inrollementes.
An inscription, or any other writing
Writynge. sometyme style. Alsoo reckenynge of a baylyffe, whiche byeth and selleth cattell.Budeu • ▪
He that writeth thynges whiche be commonly done, or bokes of reckenynge for baylyffes and reues.
The codde or skynne, wherein be the stones of a man. Scrota, be also lyttel ymages made of paste, whyche are wont to be gyuen to chyldren.
A thynge wherin there seemeth to be some difficultie.
Scrupulous or doubtfull in lyghte thynges. sometyme it signifieth dyffuse or difficulte.
To bring into a mans mind, doubte, carefulnesse, or thought.
To put away dout or care.

A lyttell sharpe stoone, whiche sometyme hapneth to falle into a mannes showe, and hurte his heele. It is also taken for moche sollicitude, also for dyfficultie, or spiced conscience. Also a poise, whiche is the thyrde parte of a dramme: and than is it also writen with y, as Scrypulus.
A lyttell stone or piece of a stone.
Old garmentes, horseshoen, and such other baggage, solde for necessite. also litle ymages made in paste, sold to the people.
He that selleth olde stuffe, or maketh suche ymages.
The bely of a swine farcid or stuffid
Olde wryters vsed for sequester, an arbytrour.
To carue ymages in stoone. sometyme to graue in mettall.
He that dothe weare woullen sockes.
That whiche is carued or grauen.
A railer, a scoffer. Scurrilitas, railyng.
A buckeler maker, or a maker of tergates.
Armyd with a shielde or tergate.
A rounde fygure, such as spynners or spiders do warke. also a vessell, whyche contayneth .viii. ounces. also a staffe, wherwith flaxe is beaten.
Rounde and wroughte 〈◊〉 the fourme of a copwebbe.
A custrell▪ or page, which beareth his maisters shielde or bucklar.
A diminutiue of scutra, or scutula.
A garment of sylk, wherin be wrought fygures lyke to roūd copwebbes.
Is a colour, I suppose a wachet.
A t • rgat or shielde, a buckelar.Palladius

A daungerouse Rocke in the see by Sycile. Alsoo a ladye, daughter of Nisus, kynge of Megarensis, whyche for loue of Minois, hyr fathers ennemye, stale a pourple heare frome her fathers heed, whiche caused hym to be vanquysshed: But she being forsaken of Minois, threwe her selfe into the See, and was transfourmed into a byrde of hir name. It is also a kynde of fyshe in the ryuer of Liris in Campania.
A towne in the furthermooste parte of Italy, fyrste buylded and inhabyted by men of Athenes.
Places wherein is taken the fysshe callyd Scilla.
A promontorie or hyl in the part of Grecia, nowe callyd Morea.
The name of a Greke, whych swimmynge vnder water, dyd cutin sonder the Cables of the shyppes of the Persyans.
