The name of a manne, whyche hauynge foure score sonnes, whanne he dyed, he callydde theym afore hym, and delyueryd to eueryche of theym a sheafe of arrowes, commaundynge theym to breake the sheafes incontynente: whyche whanne they moughte not doo, he toke out of the sheafes oone arowe after an nother, and brake theym all lyghtely, declarynge therby vnto his sonnes, that yf they contynued and agreed well togither, they shoulde be puyssaunt: and yf they varyed and were dysseuered, they shulde be feble and shortly distroyed.
A blonket colour or light wachet.
An ile in the see callid Egeū, where Achilles was hid in a maidens garment.
A lytel beaste callyd a shyrewe.
People in India, whiche haue noo noses, but in the stede of a nose they haue two holes in their vysage.

Is a great countreye, whiche stretcheth into the east from the ryuer of Tanais, & hath on the south part Sacos and Sogdianos, people vnder the kynge of Persia, and on the southe parte be countreyes vnknowen and deserte, and is nowe vnder the dominion of the greatte Cane of Cataye.
A man or woman of Scithia.
A countraye nowe called Thracia in Grece.
Is a pronowne, and sygnyfyeth hym or hyr.
A fountayn at Naples, which serueth the citie, running throughout the cite.
A certayne grayne, whyche serueth onely to putte away hunger.
To goo backe, or to go out of company, to go away, to goo to play or sporte from labour.
To diuide, or laye oone frome an nother, to laye or putte by it selfe.
A cuttynge knyfe, wherewith the paynyms diuided their sacrifice.
A departyng, a vacation from busynesse, a secrete place.
A cake of breadde cut in sacrifice.
Later. Nec eo secius, neuer the later.
The space of one hundred yeres.
Ceremonies, that be secretely vsed, to be hadde in the more reuerence.
To cutte. Viam secare, to leade the waye.
Hartelesse, apte to no purpose, profytable neyther to hym selfe nor to any other.
Thynges secrete. A secretis, of the pryuie councyll.
A dyuers consent in sondrye wylfulle opinions, a secte of philosophers, a sect of heretikes.
The bell wether, that goth before the flocke.
A cuttynge, a diuision, the partynge of a praye in takynge of a towne.
All that is taken in pray at the wynnynge and sackynge of a towne.
To folowe, to rounne after one. Also to folowe in maners or fourme of speakynge, or lyuynge. Also to hunte or chase a beaste.
Byers of forfayted goodes. Also they that do take profyte by the condemnation of other.
A cuttīg, caues vnder erth, or mines
A sythe, wherwith hey is mowen.
Some do suppose it to be the space of one hundred yeres,Plini. some of one thousande yeres, other of .xxx. yere. sometyme it is taken for tyme. Seculum sterile, a barrayne tyme.
The laste course, wherein commeth fruite and conserues.
The seconde tyme or place, alsoo eftesoones.
The nexte daye. Caesaris interdicta, si re secundo lumine hic offendero, respuentur, If I find the here the next day, I wyll set litle by Cesars cōmandementis.
Browne bread. Pasti siliquis, Horatius. & pane secundo, Fed with beane huskes, and browne breadde.

An aduerbe, signifieth nye, or by. Secundum aurem, by the eare. Also nexte after. Secundum patrem, next after my father. sometyme for. Secundum te litem do, I iudge the matter for the▪ also in. Secundū quietem, in rest. also vppon. Secundum ea, thervpon. Secundum Platonem, After the saying of Plato. Secūdum Pythagorā uino, I lyue lyke to Pythagoras. Secundum flumen, Alonge by the ryuers syde.Caes. in cō.

Seconde or nexte to the fyrste. Also prosperouse. Secunda fortuna, Good or prosperous fortune. Res secund • , that whiche dothe folowe our desire or appetite, good fortune. Secundo flumine nauigat, He gothe, or sayleth, or roweth with the streme. Secundus uentus, A good wynd. Secundum praesentem, as if he were present. Et post edictum secundū praesentē iudicabitur, And after the decre, iugement shall be gyuen, as if he were present.Vlp • anus.
An axe. sommetyme it is taken for an offycer, whiche hath auctoritie to commytte men to thexecution of dethe.

Nyghe to the ryuer, wyllowes are sette. Also it sygnyfyeth otherwyse, or other, Non dixi secus ac sentiebam, I sayde none otherwyse thā I thought▪ Quid diximus tibi secus, quam uelles? What sayde we vnto the, other thanne thou woldest haue vs to say?
To sytte, to be ydelle, to content, to tarye or abide, to take council.
A seate or place to sytte on, Alsoo a mansion house. sometyme a sepulchre.
A sedition or discorde amonge the people.
To mitigate, to pacifie, to asswage, to restrayne, to extincte.
To leade asyde, or leade away sometyme to deceyue.
Dylygente, he that playnely without crafte dothe a thynge diligently.
An herbe callydde Syngreene or howseleke.
Corne, whan it standeth. some tyme the grounde falowed, and redye to receyue corne.
Was the strawe that was layde in a lyghter, wherin greate men were borne by their seruantes.
Be certayne lynes ymagyned, by the whiche Cosmographers doo deuyde the worlde into porcions, whiche be callid also Paralleli, wherby the distance of places are founden.
The cuttynges of, of any thynge, sometyme the partes of the worlde diuyded by the sonne. also gardis, or other like thynges sowed to garmentes.
He that maketh cloth of gold

A piece cutte of frome anye thinge, be it mettall or stone. It is alsoo a bee or colar, whiche is aboute womennes neckes. Some doo take it for the purfyll of a womannes gowne. It maye as welle be taken for a garde or border aboute any garmente.
May be sayde of anye thinge, whyche hathe borders or trayles synely wroughte, with small peces fastned theron, be it of mettall or tymber.
A towne in the parte of Spaine, whiche is nowe called Byskay.Plautus i • Trin. & i • Asinar. Plautus i • milite.

To speake no wordes. Si quis ibi est odiosus, abeo domum, sermonem segrego: If any man be there, whom I loue not, I gette me home, and speake neuer a worde. Segrega sermonem, taedet, Plautus i • paenulo. Holde thy peace, I am weary, or it irketh me to here the.
Is a vayne of erth in mynes,Plin. li. 33 cap. 4. whiche declareth, that therein golde maye be founde.
A cytie, whyche was preseruyd by the prayer of Loth, whan Sodoma was dystroyed by the vengeance of god.
A mountayne in the countrey of Edon, where Esau the brother of Iacob the patriarche dwellyd.
Chosen amonge other. also chiefe amonge other.
Amonge the Romans were iudges appoynted of the state of gentylmen, callyd ordo equestris.
A stone, wherin is a whyte, whiche decreaseth and increasethe, as the mone dothe.
The principall cytie of Siria, whiche is .xxx. furlonges from Babylonia.
Kyng of Siria, next after Alexā der the greatte.
To gather a part, or the chiefe thynges amonge many.
An herbe called also Apium, wherof be dyuers kyndes, as Hipposelinon, Petroselinon. Seke for them in their places.

A Chayre, whereon the chiefe officers of Rome sate in a charyotte, and were soo caried, whanne they came from their houses. some do suppose that it was callid curulis, bicause the fete were crokid the iugement therof, I remit to the reders.
Places, wherin were fourmes and stooles for men to sytte on.
Ones, also at one time, shortly, brefely, summaryly.
Sede, sommetyme settes of yonge trees, or nursgardeynes, sommetime the kynde.
The acte of sowynge, sometyme sede, sede tyme.
Holye dayes ordeyned to praye, that corne beinge sowen, moughte come forthe and increace.
Beastes ingendred betwene a wyld beast and a tame, as betwene a wolfe and a dogge, or betwene a wylde boore, and a tame swyne.
To goo to dwelle in an nother place.
A lyttell cake made with meale, chese, and water.
They whyche are not perfytte men, as those, whiche are gelded.
A place frome whense settes and plantes be translated or remoued. also a tree of the whiche settes are taken.
The .xii. part of a greke drāme.
Halfe an husbandeman, halfe a carle of the countrey.
Halfe a foote in quantitie or heyghte.
Were showes, whyche couered but halfe the fote: whiche the Romaines did weare on, whan they went in hunting.
That whyche is halfe fyue in numbre.
The wyfe of kyng Ninus, and queene of Babylon, a woman of incomparable power.
He that is halfe slepynge, halfe wakynge.
Half a cubite. It was also a certain coyne or money, that was halfe a piece of golde, as the halfe noble or halfe crowne.
The gayn of syx in a hūdred.
He that weareth a shorte gowne.
A feuer, whiche is a tercian and a halfe, and of fourty and eighte houres, and vexeth one .xxxvi. houres.
The accustomed gentyl •• sse or myldenesse.Terent. in Andria. Donatus.
A councylle howse. Also a lyttell Senate.
That whyche is of the nū ber of syxe. Senarij uersus, & senarioli, verses hauynge sixe fete.
An acte of councill, or an ordinaunce made by the senate.
An herbe, which groweth on walles, and tyles, and is hore in sommer, and hath redde stalkes, called groūdswel.
A syce, or numbre of syxe marked in the dyse.
The fielde, where the towre of Babylon was buylded.
The senses, or those thynges, whiche we do meane.
Was called Fauna, or Bona dea, the good goddesse.
Sentence, iudgement, opinion, or councill spoken or writen concernynge the lyfe of man.
The pumpe of a shyp, a place where all fylthe is receyued.
To auoyde peryl: also to pumpe vp water out of a shyppe.
To perceyue, to vnderstande, to fele, to iuge, to suppose, to know.
A parte. also namely, or specially. Omnibus gratiam habeo, & seorsum tibi praeterea Demea, Terent. in Ad • lph. I thank you al, but namely the Demea.
I am of an nother opinion than thou arte.Plautus in cap.
Separate or diuided from an other thynge.
To putte aparte, or departe one from an nother.

n: sepius piuntis amp sipus puntis amp sipontum
d: A citie in the royalme of Naples.
A shop, where swete oynementes are solde. It was a strete in the citie of Capua, wherin were dyuers delicate oynementes.
A venymous worme, of whose stroke or bytynge the fleshe rotteth.
The generalle name of all places inclosyd.
An officer, hauynge equall auctoritie with seuen other.
The seuen sterres, which are sene by Charles wayne, or Vrsa maior.
The offyce, wherin be seuen ioyntely.
By that name Rome was called, bycause of the seuen hylles, whiche were in it, Palatinum, Quirinalis, Auentinus, Coelius, Viminalis, Exquilium, & Ianiculum.
Seuen maner of facions or wais
Was a holyday kepte the daye folowynge the sixt Idus of euery month.
The mydrefe,No. Mar. whyche dyuydeth the stomacke frome the lower. bowelles.
Buried or hydde. also lyke as it were deade.
A ryuer in Fraunce called Sein.

o: Sequan que , for seorsum quan que ,
n: sequan que for seorsum quan que

d: An arbitrer. Also he, with whom money is lefte.
To lay or sette a thynge indifferently, or in the kepynge of an indifferent person.
Is a terme appropried nowe adayes to kinges onely, and is vsurped for moste famous, or moste renoumed.
A people in Asia, hauyng great plentie of sylke.
To be fayre and drie. also to be tourned into whay.
Ernest wordes, and graue or sadde.
An erthen vessell, whiche is longe.
Apparayled in sylke, or he that weareth a garment of sylke.
Botes or shyppes calked with towe.
An Ile by Grecia in the see called Aegeum.
A speche, a fourme of speakynge: sommetyme an oration, also communication.
To sowe, to plant, to ingender.
An aduerbe, signifyeth late, to late, after the tyme that it ought to be, Alsoo in the euenynge.
That whiche is in the euennynge. sometyme late or latewarde. Serotini fructus, latewarde fruites.
An herbe, whiche growethe on olde walles aboute welles or pondes, and in some places it smelleth lyke tyme, and in some places lyke to sauery.
Of olde wryters was vsed for serpens, a serpent.
Is to syght in battayle, sometyme marchynge forwarde, sometyme reculinge, as a sawe goth, whā it is drawen.
An herbe, which is callyd Germander.
Of seruyle or bonde condycion or propertie.
He that soweth seedes, or settethe herbes.
Sette with flowres, as in a garlande.
To kepe, to preserue, to possede,Vergil. or dwelle in a place.
To kepe touch, to be faithful.
To obserue tokēs or signes in the heuen or firmament.
Take good hede what thou dost.Plautus, in Amph.
He that preserueth or delyuereth one from harme.
The laste parte of the daye, the euen tyde. It is also whay of mylke.
A seruant, proprely whiche is compellyd to serue, as bondemen or apprentyses doone.
Is a prouerbe applied to him whiche in speakynge or writyng, dare not digresse from an other mannes steppes or fourme of writynge.
A whyte grayne, whyche growith in Inde, wherof oile is made whiche is called oleum Sesaminum.
The hole and the halfe parte.
As moche and half as moche. ioyned to an nother worde, sygnyfyeth halfe as moche more.
So moche and halfe so moche, a proportion in musyke.
One iourneye in tyllage and a hal • e.
Great and stoute wordes, as some noble men do speake to their inferiours, whan they are displeased.
That whiche is also callyd obolus, the syxt parte of a dramme.

Was two pounde weighte and a halfe of copper, whiche amonge the auncient Romayns was alway estemed to the value of the fourthe parte of their syluer coyn called Denarius and Dragma, of the whiche .viii. went to an ounce.
Contained .ii.li and a half weight of syluer, estemed to two hundred & fyfty grotes, wherof .viii. went to an ounce, that is to say iiii li.iii.s.iiii.d.
The fourthe parte of the syluer coyne of the auncient Romaynes, called Denarius and Dragma, amonge vs it may be named a sterlynge peny.
Wyne made aboute the cytie of Setia.
A tree, lyke to whyte thorne, whyche doth neuer rotte: wherof moch of the tymber in the temple of Salomon was.
Olde writers vsed for obscurus, darke.
Grauitie, constantnesse, proprelye in mynystrynge Iustyce.
Graue, constaunt, cruelle, sharpe, daungerous to meddle with.
To calle aparte or away, to call asyde from other.
He that receyueth a hundred strypes.
Syxe double, or syxe tymes so moche.
The syxte parte of a pounde.
A vessell amonge the olde Romanes, whiche contayned .xx. ounces of water or wyne.
Is the monthe nowe callid August.
The syxte parte of an ounce.
A kind. sexus uirilis, the male kind, sexus muliebris, the woman kynde.

If god wyl, or on goddis name: a worde spoken eyther in dysdayne, or in mockage, for any thynge not well doone. Etiam latini, si dijs placet, Ci. in ••• tore. hoc biennio, magistri dicendi extiterunt, Ye and also the latines, on goddis name, haue ben these two yeres maisters of eloquence. Quinetiam, si diis placet, nephas aiunt, Ti. Li • i •• consulem plebeiū fieri, They say also, on goddis name, that it is vnleful for a communer to be made Consul.
An Ile in the brytysshe occean see, on the northe parte.
An old towne .xii. miles from Rome. Also a citie in Calabria▪ sometyme it is taken for delycate and wanton lyuynge.
A woman prophete, of the whyche were eyght, as Varro writeth.
So, in lykewyse, accordyngly, so lightly. Mirabar hoc, si sic abiret, Terent. i • A •• ria. I wolde haue meruayled, if that it shoulde haue passed soo lyghtly.
So am I wont to do.
The people of Nasson, and Hessen in Germanye.
A countrey in the Ile of Sicile.
Of that facion, in suche facion.

o: Siccine tu illam? Plaut••. Siccine nos habes ludibrio omnes?
n: siccine tu illam plaut siccine nos habes ludibrio omnes
d: Wylte thou handelle her of that fasshyon? Wylte thou in suche fasshyon moc • e vs all.
All maner of drynke made of corne or frutes.
To cut agayne that whiche was not wel cut afore, proprely grasse in a medowe.
People dwellyng in Sicile, whiche were borne els where.
To speake the language of Sicile.
A poyse or wayght, wayinge two drammes: and is the fourth parte of an vnce.
The ounce of the iewes, which is the fourth part of our ounce.
A kynde of daunsynge, wherein they that daunsed dyd synge, as they doo in Christmasse, whan they synge Carolles: and as maydens do nowe vse to doo in the streates.
An Ile in the se of Aegeum.
A sickenesse, which in suche wyse taketh some part of a mannes body, that it sodaynly becometh drye, so that he felith it not, women do cal it takynge, or benummynge.
He that is so taken in any membre or part of his body, that he can not feele it or stere-it, the homely people calleth benummed.
An herbe, which groweth on tyles and olde walles.
To be blasted, or taken, that a man maye not stere or moue his membres.
A numbre of sterres gathered, which do make a sygne or celestiall figure: sometyme it is taken for one sterre.
A great mountaygne in the see by Troye.
Warkes wherein were set small ymages.
To seale, sometyme to close or shut.
Standardes and baners aduaunced in batayle, in marchinge againste enemyes.
The twelue signes, by the whiche the sonne and other planettes doo passe.
He that beareth standard or baner in a felde.
A warke made with shelles and mortar, or tyles and mortar.
To make a signe, to signe or seale, to signifie or shewe by a signe or token, to wryte.
A signe, token, or marke, a miracle.
Be alsoo ymages of metall, stone, or woode.
Quiete places, wherein is no noyse.
To kepe sylence, to speake nothinge.
A kynde of wythy growing in water: it is also a ryuer in the royaulme of Naples.
To be in silence, or quyete.
A certayne puddynge, eaten onely at the tyme of funeralles, some doo take it for a feaste or dyner made at the funeralles or termēt of a man or woman.
Is named of Terence for an olde Cryppel, redy to haue suche a dyner made for him.

The huske or codde of any thinge, also a certayne fruyt in Italy, which is in length of a mannes fyngar, and brode, & somewhat hooked, the wayght of sixe of them made a poyse called Scrupulus, a scruple: wherof thre do make a dramme. It is now called a Characte, and is vsed among fynars of golde and syluer, and also coyners in the fynynge and alayinge therof.
To growe in huske or codde.
A chuntraye in the more Britayne.
Is spoken in a prouerbe of hym, whiche bostith hym selfe of ryche garmentes.
A camoysed nose, or a nose whiche is tourned vpwarde.

A prouerbe applyed to theym, whiche beinge of lyke yll condicions, be matched togither, as a lewde seruaunt with an yll master, an vnruly people to a negligent gouernour, a shrewde wife to a frowarde husbonde &c. Lyke master lyke man. Lyke will to lyke.
Symony, that is to saye, ambitiō in spirituall thinges.
Symple thinges or of lytle value.
They which doo weare hostinge harneyse.
That is not double, syncere or playne, without deceipt.

A chalice or cup of erth, wherwith they sacrifyced in the olde tyme before that golde and siluer were in great estimacion It is of Varro taken for a cruet with a Pipe, out of the which wyne came droppynge by lytle and lytle.
An ymage of a manne or woman.
To indeuour, to be lyke to one, also to fayne.
Pryuy displeasure or hatered, with dissemblynge countenaunce.
To be at varyance with one, to hate one pryuyly.
Senuy sede, wherof mustarde is made.
People in Affrike, whiche do go as they crept.
A countraye beyonde the lyne equinoctiall.
To euery one, or of euery ouche, one after another.
Synguler, excellēt, one without any mo.
The lefthande, sometyme it sygnifieth, contrary to prosperouse.
A cite in the contray of Pontus.
A redde stone, communely called Sinoper.

To tourne or winde in the fourme of a serpent, makinge holowe bosomes or furrowes: it is also applyed to garmentes that are pleyghted or gathered vp: also to streames of Ryuers, which do in runnyng make dyuerse tournynges. also to bankes which haue holow creekes or bosomes.
That which hath many turnynges and wyndynges.
A bosome. also the tournynges or holownesse of water bankes: somtyme the holownesse of eyen: sometyme a sayle. also a cuppe for wyne: also nettes. sometyme a sayle, whan the wynde fylleth it.
Pittes, wherin corne was layde to be preseruyd.
A Sterre, whiche ryseth the .viii. Calendis of Iune.
Mattes, or other thinges made of russhes.
Were instrumētes made with teeth lyke to a sawe, which beinge drawen with oxen, plucked vppe by the rootes flagges and greate weedes, which grewe in medowes.
To bynde, or wynde with russhes or osyars, or other lyke thinge.
A russhe. Nodū in Sirpo quaeris, thou fyndest difficultie or doubt, where there is none. Sirpi, be also warkes or verses, which be very harde to be vnderstande.
A maner of poulce or corne.
A delicate roote to be eaten, whiche some men do suppose to be redde Carettes.
An herbe growynge in Euboea, the flower wherof is moost pleasaunt to bees. it is also called Erica.
To make to tarye or stande styll, to retayne or kepe backe, to appere, as a mā doeth beinge sued in the lawe.

o: Ore sistere. Eminor, interminor que , ne quis mihi obstiterit obuiam, nam qui-obstirerit, ore sistet.
n: ore sistere eminor interminor que ne quis mihi obstiterit obuiam nam qui obstirerit ore sistet
d: I threten, and I menace, that no man let me of my way, for whosoeuer letteth me, shall kisse the grounde.
An instrument lyke a horne, whiche was vsed in battayle, in the stede of a trumpet.

Was a great thefe, whiche was slayne by Theseus, of whom it is fayned, that in hell he tourneth a stone vppe to a great hill, but whan it is at the toppe, it falleth downe agayne, and remeueth his labour.
A bagge, or gardeuiandes, wherin meat is put.
A countraye in Macedonia vppon the se syde.
He that dyd blowe in a trumpet whā men were buryed.
To thyrst or be a thirst.
A lytle potte, wherinto lottes were putte.
He that is allwaye a thirst.
A lytle cofer, wherin lottes were put, at the chesinge of officers: also a buckat to drawe water.
Fylthynesse gathered of moysture, by lacke of klensinge. also of sluttisshnesse. also the settynge or standinge of a place, which is now called the syte or situatiō of a maner or countraye.
A preciouse stone called an Emeraude.
Sope, & all other thinge that doth put awaye spottis or vnclennesse.
A tree, whiche hath leues lyke an yuy, with beryes, and a whyte floure, and smelleth lyke a lyly.
One of the names of Apollo▪
People of Asia, dwelling about the extreme part of the mountayne, called Caucasus.
A socke, which women and players in Comedies onely ware.
That warre, whiche is made with confederates.
To haue familiar cōmunication with one.
A felowe or companyon. also Socij, be confederates, they whiche in all counsayles and actes doo participate one with another. Loke for Comites and Sodales, in their places.
He that folowethe the doctrine of Socrates.
They that kepe company togither, at meales or passetyme. they be also they, whiche be of one fraternitie or company, or gylde.
A fraternite or brotherhode. Also a company incorporate of any misterie or crafte, generally al felowshyps priuately assemblynge amonge the people.
A citie in Iudea, whiche for synne, done agaynste nature, was by almyghty god consumed by celestiall fyre.
To commytte or vse the syn of Sodoma, agaynste nature.
A countrey in Asia, extendyng to the northe parte of Scithia.
Sygnifyeth sometyme the day, sometyme the beames of the sonne.
A place where by the sunne, houres are knowen. Also a soler of a house. Also a pencion payde to the prince, to liue out of commune busynesse.
They whych be dyseased or sycke by the heate of the sonne.

A showe, callydde a galage or paten, whiche hath nothyng on the fete, but only lachettes. Also a fishe, called a sole. also a ground soyl, wheron standeth the wall of a house. It is also a shoe, wherwith horses and oxen be shodde.
Annuall or yerely, that whiche is done euery yere.

o: Soleo, solitus sum, uel solui, solére,
n: soleo solitus sum uel solui solere

d: It was wont, or the vse hath ben.

o: Solens, for ut soleo, Ego abcessi solens paulum ab illis,
n: solens for ut soleo ego abcessi solens paulum ab illis
d: I went a lyttell from them, as I was wont.
Sharpenes or quyckenes of wytte, craftynesse or subtiltie in practysynge, or wyttynesse.
To shewe both hope and feare. Also to inquiete, or make sorye, to solicite or procure by meanes: sommetyme to labour the erthe.
To close togither, as a woūd dothe, whan it healeth.
They whiche do selle in grosse.
That hath fete hole without toes.
Hole, contynuall, not holowe, not broken or cutte.
He that keepeth hym oute of the sonne, or fleeth from the heate of the son.
A flye, whiche in the heat of the sonne prycketh moste sharply.
Communication, which a man beinge alone, hathe with god in contemplation.
An offryng of thre thynges of sondrye kyndes, as a bulle, a ramme, and a boore.

A place of astate, where a kyng sytteth: it is also a great vessell, whiche serueth to dyuers vses, as to translate lycour from one to an other, to washe linnen clothes, and for men and women to be bathed in. It sygnyfyeth also a coffin, where deed bodies are put.
A vyce in speakynge, wherein the trewe congruitie and ryght speche is peruerted.
One of the seuen wyse men of Grecia, which made lawes for the Athenienses.
An herbe, whyche dothe beare floures onely at the tyme, whan the sonne is at the hyghest, or as some menne suppose but one daye.

The stay of the sonne, whan he can not be eyther hygher or lower, which is twyse in the yere, that is in wynter, the eyght calendes of Ianuarie, and is callyd Solstitium hyemale, and in sommer, the .viii. calendis of Iulye, & is callid Solstitium aestiuale.
A lyfe whyche dureth but a lyttell space.
A sycknesse whiche kylleth men shortly.
Is of somme men taken for the burnyng feuer▪ whiche happeneth aboute the canicular dayes, of excedynge heate of the ayre.
He i • not able to pay.

The soyle or grounde, generally it signifieth all thynge, whiche doth susteyne or beare any other thyngs on it. It is also the sole of the fote, also the sole of a shoe. Natale solum, a mannes naturall countrey.
To lowse, to paye, to recompense, to put a way, to delyuerꝭ, to resolue or melte. Soluere fidem, to breake promise. Soluere uenas, to open the veynes.
That whiche wyll be soone lowsed or vndone.
That whyche causeth one to sleepe.
That which induceth or bryngeth slepe.
To sounde or make a sounde.
To sounde or make a noyse.
Lowde, or makynge a great sounde.
A contynuall syckenesse▪ or wherwith all the body is greued.
The parte of logyke, whyche is capciouse and subtylle.
A craftye and deceytefull sentence, • n Oracyon or inuention, whiche seemeth to be trewe, whan 〈◊〉 false.
A dissemble • of wysedome, a deceyuer vnder an eloquente or crafty speakynge.
In Greke, is Temperance in englyshe, wherby carnall appetites and lustes be refrayned.
To sette at rest, to brynge aslepe.
Brought aslepe, or to rests, or into a sowne with a sodayne stroke.

o: Sorbeo, bus, bere, & sorbo, psi, bere,
n: sorbeo bus bere amp sorbo psi bere
d: To suppe, as one suppeth potage.
To be fowle,Plautus in Penulo. or vnkleanly.
A ratte, or a fielde mo •• .
The Iewes do calle vynes, whiche contynually do brynge forthe moste pleasant and dilectable fruyte.
A subtil & captious forme of arguing.
People whyche are diuyded frome Inde by the ryuer callyd Arabis.
Shyppes whiche are calked or stopped with hempe or flaxe.
Is proprely of may dens brestes, whan they begyn to be imbosed.
A cofer or baskette wherein are caried the instrumentes or apparayle seruynge for comedies or interludes.
Chaunce, lotte, portion in enherytaunce: the hole somme in a commune banke or stocke, wherin many haue parte. It is also destyny, iudgement.
Were also the aunsweres of Idols.
The scrowe, wherein the lotte is wrytten.
Ben they, whiche do tell mennes destenies by rakynge of lottes or verses of holy scripture.

n: sortior tiris tiri amp sortio tire
d: To make lottes, to take or haue any thynge by lotte or chaunce. Also to dispose or order.
To receyue the rule of a countray by lottes. It is vsurped to haue auctoritie by election.
An aduerbe, sygnyfyenge by lotte or chaunce.
Taken by lotte. also chaungynge to haue a thynge.
Hole or saulfe. also he that gyueth helthe.
One of the names of Iuno.
A date with the braunche plucked from the palme tree. It is also scarlette colour.
A geldyng, be it man or beest.
To make warre in sondrye partes of a countrey.
A prouerbe signifienge the astate or office, whiche thou haste, order or applye it welle.
The roote of an herbe called cynquefoyle.
The sonne of Thomiris the quene of Massagetes.
Was a famouse sworde player, whiche gathered an host of slaues, & made battayle agaynste the Romayns, and was vanquyshed by Crassus.
Be callyd caltroppes, sowen in tyme of batayl, to woūd the fete of men & horsis.
Out of the whyche any thynge is plucked.
A two handed or bastarde sworde. it is alsoo an instrumente of the kytchen, to tourne meate that is fryed.
A space as wel in tyme, as in place.
Among olde writers was taken for Inspicere, to looke in.
Speciall, peculiar, propre.Cicero de reditu su •

A fygure or image, a forme, kind, beautie, fauour. It is defyned by Logicyens, to be that, whiche is sayde of many thynges varienge in noumbre: as Homo, whiche is spoken of Plato, Socrates, Cicero, whyche doo not varye in fygure but in noumbre. Sommetyme species, doo sygnyfye spyces. Alsoo it is apparaunce. alsoo a syghte or thynge sene, spices.

o: Per speciem legationis in Asiam ablegatus est.
n: per speciem legationis in asiam ablegatus est
d: Vnder the coloure of ambassade,Plin. de 〈◊〉 ri • illustr. he was banyshed into Asia.Plautus.
A smalle Instrumente, wherewith Sourgeons doo serche the deepenesse of woundes and soores. Alsoo to annoynt sore eyes. It is also a Spectakle to loke with. also an eare pycker.
An example, a profe, also beautie.
To shew a proufe of a mannes counnynge.
A thynge to be sene or looked on. Sometyme the selfe beholdynge. alsoo the place from whens menne doo beholde thynges.

A Sygne or token.Plautus in Men • . Spectame • bono seruo, id est qui rem l • erilem procurat, uidet, collocat, It is a token of a good seruant, that is to saye, whiche attendeth aboute his maisters busynesse, and dothe suruey all thynge, and sette it in order.
To behold, to approue, to tende to some conclusion, to compare.
A tryall or proufe of money.
An ymage or fygure in a mannes ymagynation.
An hygh hylle or towre, whereon thynges be espyed far of. also lyttel hope, a diminutiue of spes.
Any thynge, wherby a manne may see the better.
To see farre, to consyder, to espye, to serche out.
Olde wryters vsed for spes, hope.
Seede, mooste commonly vsed for the naturall humoure, whereof all lyuynge thynges be ingendred and fourmed.
Looues of breadde made in haaste.
A noble phylosopher cousyne to Plato.
A fygure in al partes equally round a speere.
A rounde place in a bayne, where men are exercysed, a tenyse play.
A balle made of lether or cloth, greatter than a tenyse balle.

A monster, whiche had the heed and handes of a mayden, the bodye of a dogge, wynges lyke a byrde, nayles lyke a lyon, a tayle lyke a dragon, the voyce of a man, which purposed to men subtyl questions. It is also a beaste lyke an ape, but more rough, & with a longer tayle, I suppose it to be a munkay or babyon.
A ioynt or knotte of the backe bone .xii. of them do make the chyne, and the .v. resydue do make the loynes.
The eare of corn. also a spice called Spikenarde.
An eare of corne, hauynge no berde.
Eared, or in care, as corne is.
That whyche hathe eares lyke to corne.
The surname of Ceres callid goddesse of corne.
They whiche be called of the kynges garde. Some men do take Spiculator, to be a hangeman, or other persone, whiche putteth men to deth by execution of the lawes.
To make any thynge sharp • atte the poynte.
A pynne, also a tache, sometyme a braselette.
A byrde whyche was wonte to comme to the aulters, and carye awaye a burnynge cole, whyche was taken for an vnlucky byrde.
A plumme tree or damsyn tree.
Liuely, or that wherby we liue.
Out of whyche the ayre or brethe passeth.
A capitayne in the fore warde.

Thynges whyche doo tourne and wynde in dyuers cerkles lyke a trendell, or an adder lyeng rounde. Also spira, is an ornament of a womans heed. also the turning of cables or ropis, whā they be woūd vp. also the band or lace, wherwith a cappe or hat is made fast vnder a mans chyn. also the base of a pyllar. Also a cake made like a trendell. also a multitude of people.Ennius.

n: spirituale amp spiritale idem quod spiritus

d: To blowe as wynde dothe, to sende forthe odoure.
To go thycke, or make many feete.
An aduerbe sygnifienge clere or bryghte. also rychely.
Bryght, clere. Also he whyche vseth to haue his house rychelye decked with abundaunce of all thynges, is called Splendidus, contrarye to Sordidus & auarus.
Lyght, bryghtnesse, somtyme honour or noblenesse in lyuynge.
He that is sycke in the splene.
A plaister of cloth or lether made to lay to the body of him, whiche is sicke.
That whiche receyueth spoyle or thynges taken by robberie.
A foote in meeter of two longe syllables.
A whe • ue, whyche is a rounde thynge of stone, or wodde, or leadde, put on a spyndell to make it runne rounde. It is also a whyte harde thynge in an oyster, whyche is couered with the fyshe.
That whiche cometh of lead like to soote, whiche is about vessels of brasse, that do hange ouer the fyre.
A spounge, or that wherwith any thynge is wyped.
Lyghte, and full of holes lyke a spounge.
The spousage, or betrouthyng of a man and womanne, before that they be wedded.
He that promyseth or bargaineth. Sometyme a suretie, whiche vndertaketh an other mans acte.
Naturally, willingly, of his free wyl.
That whiche dothe, or is done willyngly, naturally, without constraynt or helpe.
Yl • s nygh to Crete or Candy.
A basket or maunde, sometyme money or meate distributed by pryncis vnto the people.
A littell gyft or almes, also lyuerey of courte, callydde bowge of courte, was callyd Sportule.
The fome or frothe of any thynge lyquyde.
To fome or gather vnto fome.
That whiche speaketh dishonestly or vnclenly.
That maketh thynges vncleane or fylthy.
Verses fayned, the authour beinge false named or vnknowen.
A bastarde. also it was the surname of dyuers Romaynes.
To be filthy, shuttishe, soiled or stainid with som vnclene thing
Sluttishe, filthy, causing one to abhorre the sight therof. Somtime it signyfieth spotted. also carrayne leane.
Grounde out of tylthe. also shynynge.
A sole fyshe with a rough skynne, wherwith fletchers doo make theyr arrowes smothe.
Rough and sharpe, lyke to a thynge whiche is skalye.
A certayne herbe, growynge in the see, also a fyshe.
People in Italy callydde Sabelli and Samnites.
A voyce of him that commandeth silence, as we say in englishe, busht, whā we wold haue one to holde his peace.
That whiche kepeth a thing stedfaste.
Women whiche keepe vyttaylynge houses, for to refresshe wayfarynge men.
An inholder. Also he that hath the charge of the howse, where cattayle is kepte.
Falowe deree or redde dere to be lodged or harborowed.
To stande as cattayle dothe in a stable.
Standynge or lyenge of cattelle, also harborowynge or lodgynge of d • re.
An inne, where men do lodge or bayte. Also it is the generalle name of the place, where cattelle doo abyde, whanne they come from their pasture. also a stable wherin horses or mules are kepte.
The floure of myrre, or fatnesse, whiche fyrste distilleth out of it.
A place, wherin runnynge is exercysed, as welle of men as of horses. It is also a furlonge or the eight part of a mile.
The place ordeined to run in.
He that rounneth in a cours of rounnynge.
Proprely of water is to stande and not to flowe.
A standynge water, a poole. alsoo a certayne mettall called tynne.
A thyng to hange at ones care, as Egyptians haue.
Clothe, whanne it is in the lome or frame. Also slaxe or woulle, whan it is on the dystaffe. also stamyne or worstede.
He that dyd fyrste myngle water with wyne.
A kynde of vynes, whiche hathe a blacke stemme and strayt, and hath a fruite more lyke to a lyttelle bladder, than to a grape, which be grene, within the which is a kernelle thre cornerde.
Sacrifyce customably doone at certayne days of an olde ordynance.
An ymage, whyche was sette vp by the people in euerye strete at Rome.
Fyrme, or stable, alsoo ordeyned or decreed.
A certayne coyne, whiche was in value foure drammes.
A beam to way without the balācis.
A certayne wanton meuynge in daunsynge. somtyme a lyttell cart.
Dayes ordynarie, dayes in banke, for apparance, or for the parties to plede.
Was callyd a priuate god, whiche men supposed to be alway with them.
Idem, or a lyttell restyng place.
A place, where eyther menne of warre or shyppes doo abyde or reste for a certayne tyme.
That whyche standeth faste or abydeth.
Souldiours, whiche are assigned to abyde stylle in one place, or to kepe a towne or fortresse, or the marches of a countrey.
A certayne place fortyfyed, where men of warre lay at the siege of a fortresse.

A sernaunt, whyche is alwayes redye attendynge aboute an offycer, to be at commandement. wherfore in that word be included pursyuantes, postes, sergeantes, baylyffes, and catchepolles. Also Iupiter, was called Iupiter stator of Romulus, bycause he supposed that he made the Romaynes to tarye whan they fledde, the Samnites pursuynge them.
An ymage of mettalle, yuorie, stone, or tymber.
The crafte of caruynge or yetting of ymages.
He that carueth or yetteth imagꝭ.
To iudge or determyne. accordynge to equitie, lasse than the rygour of the lawe wolde requyre.
To sette a price on thynges vendible.
That whiche is sette vp to sustayne or beare a thynge, a proppe.
To proppe vp, to vnderset, to make sure.

To ordayne, to determyne, to set faste, to stable a thinge, to dedicate, to beate one thynge to an nother. Sublim • illum arriperem, & caput primum in terram statuerem, ut cerebro dispergam uiam, I wolde lyfte hym on highe, and beate his heed to the grounde, that I mought scatter his brayne abrode in the hygh waye.
The particyple future of sto, stas, stare, to stande.

State, it is amonge oratours and lawyers the case, whiche rysethe in contention, wherin the matter resteth, whiche muste be replyed vnto, and eyther be denyed, confessed, or trauersed: of Tullie it is callyd Constitutio causae.
A gatherynge of greace or fatte in some place agaynste nature.
A cabyn of a shyppe. alsoo a cote or cotage.
Feuers in the whiche a man maye haue neyther syege, nor vryne, nor sweate, nor none other euacuation.
A sterre, also a sterrefysshe, also the name of a poete.
Was an extorcion of capytaynes in takynge from the souldiours the porcions of vyttayle appoynted vnto them by the Emperour.
A beaste lyke a lysarde, hauynge on his backe spottes lyke sterres.
A dysceyte in dyssemblynge a thynge, to take profyte of an other iniustely.
A kynd of byrdlyme made in Euboea.
To shyne or glysten lyke sterres, or be made lyke sterres.
A garlande of floures, alsoo the stocke or bloudde of a gentylle house. sometyme the degrees in kynrede. Alsoo an inscription grauen in a stone.
The wyfe of Pretus kynge of Ephyri, whiche loued Bellorophon, that vanquysshed the monster callyd Chimaera.
Was a man, whiche hadde a voyce as lowde as .xx. men.
Euery herbe that seruethe for garlandes.
The surname of Saturnus, bicause he fyrste founde and vsed doungynge of grounde.
Olde writers vsed for steril • s.
To be barrayne or waxe barrayne.
To throwe downe, to spreade, to couer, to lay the table, to make playne or smothe, to lye downe to reste.
They layde them downe to slepe.
A kynde of frankincense callyd cōmonly olibanū, or in latin thus masculus.
Is the numbre of eight in dise, so called of the sepulchre of Stesichorus the poete, whiche was made in figure like to eyght dyse.

A famouse poete, of whome it is writen, that whanne he was an infant in his cradelle, a Nyghtyngale satte on his mouthe, and dyd synge, sygnyfienge that he shulde be the sweetest poete, that euer was afore hym. Also he founde fyrste syngynge of songes in a daunse.
A chaire or couche made of herbes wounde togyther: somme doo calle it an herber or sommer parler.
A whyte stone founde in syluer mines, which stoppeth the runnyng of eies, and dothe make them seme very fayre.
A verse or an order in a thynge.
A marke made with fyre, or with a hotte yron. Sometyme it sygnyfieth infamy and reproche obiected openly.

A phylosopher borne in the cytie of Megara in Grece, whiche his countreye beinge burned, and his wyfe and childern loste in the fyre, escaped, and departynge alone, whan the kynge Demetrius asked of hym, yf he had loste any thynge, he answered, I haue loste nothyng: for all that is myne, I carie with me, meanynge therby, that vertue, whiche is onely the propre goodes of a wyse mā, and may not be taken from hym, he toke away with hym.
A pryckynge or feruent mouing to doo a thynge.
That whyche is done with pryckynge.
A gode, wherwith oxen ar driuen.
Pertaynynge to stoppyng or beatynge harde togyther.
They whiche do frayte the shyp, or lay in suche fardelles or burdeynes as are to be caryed. Also they whiche be of the kynges gard, alway about his person.
Enuyronned with men, to be defended, as princis are with their garde.
Whiche payeth tribute, of some callyd contributarie, to the fyndyng of an army, or defence of a contray.
He that hath bene oftentymes hyred or retayned in warres.
To be hyred or retayned in warres.
Wages proprely gyuen to souldiours, Also subsidie payde to princis.
To stop chynkes or clyftes, proprely in shyppes or botes, with towe and pytche. also to enuyronne to the intent to defende one.
To serue in warres, as a souldiour. 〈◊〉 Liuius. 〈◊〉 . 34.
Wages to men hyred: also money gyuen to beggars.
Medycines that doo bynde or restrayne.
Holme, erige, or straw, apt to thatch houses. it is of some taken for the huske that closeth in the strawe.
A bargayne or promyse, or obligation to pay money, or to perfourme a thynge, whiche is requyred.
To make a bargayn, to promyse effectually that whiche he is requyred to do. It hath both the actiue and passiue signification. Stipulor abs te, I require of the, or I am requyred of the.
An ysykle or droppe of yse.
To pull vp by the rote.
In the femynyne gender sygnyfyeth a stocke in kynrede, beinge the masculyne gender it sygnifieth the stemme of a tree or herbe.
To haue brought forth suretie or pledges.
Is that in a plough, which the plough man holdeth, whan he dothe eare.
A brode shyp or bote, callid an hulke.
Any thyng that is borne on the see.
A maker of hulkes or botes.
Old writers vsed for litem, variance.
A sowne made with the mouth, whā the chekes are blowen.

To stande, to indure or abide. Stare promisso, to abyde by his promyse. To be full. Stat ager sentibus, Caecilius. Vergil. the felde is full of brembles. Iam puluere coelum stare uident, Nowe sawe they the skye fulle of duste. To bose oute.Lucilius. Hic corpus solidum inuenies, hic stare papillas Pictor marmoreo, Here in this marble stone shalt thou fynde paynted, the body sounde, and the pappes imbosed. Also to be immouable, or alway certayne. Sic stat sententia, so the sentence abydeth immouable, or is determyned. Also Stat, my mynde is.Vergilius. Stat conferre manum Aeneae, my mynd is to fight with Aeneas Stat, is sette. Omnis in Ascanio chari stat cura parentis, Vergilius. All the care of the render louynge father was sette on Ascanius. Also stare, to coste, Neque ipse hoc periculum ignoro, expertus non leui documento, quanti steterit mihi, quod semel imperata non feci, Nor I am ignorant of that daunger, hauyng experience of no lyght warnyng, howe moch it cost me, that I dyd not those thynges, that I was commaunded.

o: Stat per me, per te, per illum,
n: stat per me per te per illum
d: Whanne I, or anye other is the cause, that a thynge is not done. Si poterit fieri, ut ne pater per me sterisse credat, quo minus hae fierent nuptiae, uolo. I wolde if it may be, that my father shulde thynke, that it was not long of me, that this mariage toke none effecte.
He is of myne opinion.Plautus in pseudo. Ter. in E • .
Thou arte of a small credence.
Foure Iles in the frenche see agaynste Languedocke.
A secte of philosophers, which affirmed, that no griefe moughte happen to a wyse man: and that felicitie was onely in vertue.
A womans gowne, It was also a long garment, whiche the prynces of Persia dyd vse, and was the only garment of honour, as we do cal suche apparell a robe.
He that weareth suche a robe. also it may be callyd honourable.
Braunches whiche do spryng out of the stemmes or rootes of trees.
He that is sick in his stomake.
To haue indignation, to be vexed in mynde.

Is the pipe, wherby meate goth downe. It is also that which is called Vē triculus, wherevnto we haue none other name but the stomacke. sometyme it sygnifyeth indignation, vehemente wrathe, hatrede, and abhorrynge of a thynge that lyketh not vs, Sommetyme facylytie or gentylnesse.Plinius.
A swete incense or gumme, whiche is also called styrax, whereof be two kyndes, the one is callyd Storax calamita, the other is callyd Storax liquida.
Any thynge that is spredde on the grounde. It is also a matte.
He that looketh a squynte, or gogle eyed.
A slaughter of mē, or a discomfiture.
Euery ouermoste garment. Also a counterpoynte or couerlyd.
That whyche is made of strawe.
A polycie or wyse councille in warres.
A generall captayne of an armye.
An herbe, whiche groweth on waters without any roote.
Idem. Also the name of one of the sonnes of Nestor.
He that helpeth his mayster to horsebacke, yeman of the styrope.
Any thinge that is strawed, Also a bedde. Strata, all that is layde on the bed.
A horse harneyse, a streate or caulsey, paued with stone.
In the olde tunge of Vmbri was a piece of the flesshe that was offered in sacrifyce.
A newe yeres gyfte, or present.
A noyse made with the handes or fete.
To make a greatte noyse, proprely in goinge or clappynge of handrs, sometyme generally.
Certayne beastes in Affryke, hauynge croked hornes.
A rabat or smal furrowe made in stone or tymber.
Be also creuyses or small lines, whiche are sene in herbes.
A viciouse fourme in speking where the wordes agree not, and the partes of speche be out of order.
Breade made lyke to ropes or cordes wounden.
Shortly touched one after an other
To reporte moche in fewe wordes.
Sparkes whiche doo issue frome mettall whan it is taken oute of the fyre, and beaten with hammers.

o: Strideo, dui, dére, & strido, dis, dere,
n: strideo dui dere amp strido dis dere
d: To crashe or make a noyse lyke to cordes, whan they be drawen.
A towne in Dalmacia, where saynct Hierome was borne.
A rewe of thynges whanne they be layde in lengthe. Alsoo a ridge of lande, wherof commeth strigatus ager.
Shrycheoules, also women whyche are supposed to come by nyghte into houses, and sucke the bloudde of chylderne, some calle them hegges.
Wyde garmentes made of lether vsed in warres.
An horsecombe, alsoo a thynge wherewith wrastelers bounde theyr bodyes, whan they had wrasteled. Alsoo a certayne vessell.

Were rubbynge combes made of swete wodde, wherwith in India the men were rubbed for an exercise. Also kerchifes, wherewith wrastelers after their labours wyped their bodyes. also certayne vessels.Budeus. also pieces of fyne golde founde in mynes, vnmyxt with any other matter. also lyttell fyshes moste commonly taken in wynter tyme.
Fylthynesse, whiche commethe from a mans bodye, whan he is wasshed. also the corruption of oyle.
A well pightman, or well compacte or stronge.
Carrayn leane, it is proprely spoken of horses or routher beastes.
To strayne or wrynge. Also to stryke, to make thynne in curtynge, to gather, to shaue, to wounde. Stringere ensem, to drawe a sworde.
To make rabattes in stoone or tymber. Alsoo to make furrowes. It is proprely whanne beastes in carynge atte the ende of a furrowe tournethe to make a newe furrowe. Somme doo calle hit, to wende.
Is also to plane or to polyshe.
To abyde or tarye with an yll wyll, or with moche payn.
Olde writers vsed for Tritauo, my grandfathers grandfather.
A sparowe, whiche hauntethe the see costes.
A shryche oule, a wytche that chaungeth the fauour of chylderne.
A pyne apple tree. sometyme the kernels, or fruite.
A tree, wherof ꝑfumes were made, myxte with the wyne of dates, whyche perfume was swete, but it made the heed heuy, all be it without any peyne.
A shelle fyshe of the see, whyche hath a kynge, whom they folowe. It was thought sommetyme that he whyche had seene that fysshe, shulde haue good lucke in his affaires.
An Ile in the see called Aegeum, nowe callyd Axos, sometyme it was callyd Dia.
Two Iles in the grekysshe see.
Garlandes whiche priestes were wonte to weare.
A maydens neckerchefe or lynnen partlette.
Made of many pieces, or of diuers thynges.
A caruer of meate at a table.
Buylding, settynge of thinges in good order.
A pyle of wodde, also a cake.
An ordynaunce of many thynges togyther.
They whyche dyd carye cakes to the temple to be offred, as they do now carie the holy lofe on the sondaye.
They which dyd sacrifyce at the trees that were burned with lyghtninge.
They whiche broughte meale to be offered.
A swellynge within the throte, whiche is gathered matter and bloode. some thynke it to be that, whyche is callyd the kynges euyll.
He that hath the kynges euylle.
A medycyne or playster for the kynges euyll.
Holydayes amonge the people callyd falisci, at the whyche daye, the people do go with garlandes on their heedis.
Is a lyke holydaye amonge the people callyd Tusculani.
Were lyttell wrethes made of leaues putte on the heedes of ymages in the temples, as nowe superstitious sooles do sette on images heedes in the churches.
The priuye membre of a man.
A rounde foote lyke a sparowe.
They whyche haue lyttelle rounde fecte.
An herbe, whiche maketh hym madde that eateth of it.
A prouerbe sygnyfyenge the man is madde.
To studye, or to applye the mynde, or care for a thynge, to endeuour.
Studious, dylygent, constant, addicte or feruently disposed.
Studye. sometyme exercyse, wylle, or appetite, desyre.

It is knowen by foure thynges, or if he hath not in remembrance that he shulde haue, or if he hath, he dothe not retayn it, or doth not folow good council, or dothe approue yll councill or affections.
He that neglecteth his owne busynesse at home, and applyeth other mens abrode, It is alsoo a prouerbe touchynge them, whiche do thynges, that cause them to be laughed to scorne.

A prouerbe applyed to fooles, whiche wyll assaye to do a thynge that is aboue their wytte or lernynge: for Choroebus, was a felowe, that assayed to number the wawes of the see, whā he him self coude not tell any number aboue fiue.
He that talketh or speakethe foolyshely.
Was a tyme in the monethe of February, that fooles kepte holy, fooles holy daye.
He that dothe a thynge vnaduisedly or without discretion.
Towe, the cours part of flaxe.
The hammer, wherewith calkers do beate towe into shyps or botes
To be astonyed or dismayde. somtyme to meruayle at.
To make astonid, or to cause to meruayle or be abashed.
The membres whiche haue loste all their sence or feling.
Dysmayed, abasshed, also he that feleth nothynge, or lacketh his sences.
Abashement, the sodayne priuation of sence or felynge.
To committe auoultrie or rape or to defloure a virgin.
Auoutrie, or defloration of a virgin
An yle agayne the mouthe of Tyber.
A senne in Egypte not farre from the citie of Memphis.

Pertaynynge to Styx, the greate fenne, whiche is fayned of poetes to be by the fielde callyd Elysius, whiche the paynyms dydde suppose to be a place of pleasure, wherein rested the soules of good men.
A trowgh of tymber, wherein water rounnethe, or is conuayed into a cesterne.
A style, whyche qualitie of wordes in speakynge, sometyme harde, sometyme easy, sometyme in a meane. also an elegant fourme or order in writynge or speakinge.
A coppe of fethers, whyche standeth on the heed of a byrde, as of a larke, an heron, a pecocke, and other.
That whiche stoppeth or bindeth, or straineth, if it be eaten or dronken. Also that whiche in tastynge seemeth to strayne the tunge, as a quynce or redde wyne.
A soote gumme callyd storax, wherof be two kyndes, the one is callyd storax calamita, the other storax liquida.
Sygnifieth sorowe or heuynesse, poetes doo fayne, that it is a fenne, whyche is in helle.
Callyd in greke Pitho, was callid the goddesse of eloquence or dylectable speche.
To speake fayre, to intreate with fayre wordes, to indeuour, to induce a man into our opinyon, or to beleue vs.
A kynde of ambre, whiche is yelowe, whereof beades be made, and is callyd Laumbre.
An aduerbe signifyenge, in maner to perswade.
An exhortation, a mocyon or persuasyon.
Euery colour that may tourne into an nother colour.
That wherwith a man is or may be perswaded.
To kysse sweetely or for ioye.
Sweete in taste, soote in odour or smelle.

Vnder, by, or aboute. Sub lucem, by daye lyght. Sub idem tempus, In the same tyme, or aboute the same tyme. Sub horam pugnae. About the time of the battayl. Sub eas autem redditae sunt, for they were deliuered after theym. Sub sarcinis, with the trussis or cariage.Cicer. pro Planco.

In the twye lyghte. Subuesperum Caesar portas claudi, milites que ex oppido exire iussit, Caes. in cō. In the twie lyghte Cesar commaunded the gates to be shutte, and the mē of warre to depart out of the citie.
Constrayned, subdewed, dryuen vnder, kneaded or wrought with handes, as dowe is, laboured, exercised.
That which is brasse with in, and other mettall without.
To solycite. Subagito blandis, & benedicis uerbis, Plautus in •• ell. I solicited with fayre and well spoken wordes. It is also to cō pany with a woman carnally.
That whyche is vnder the wynges.
People vnder the Mountaynes called Alpes, called Peemountaynes.

o: Subaquaneus, a, um, & subaqueus, a, um,
n: subaquaneus a um amp subaqueus a um
d: That whiche lyeth vnder the water.
Is spoken of women, whyche are as fylthye as swyne in the acte of lechery.
To be or waxe somewhat drye.
To here or perceyue a lyttel.
He that walkethe vnder the place, where iugementes are practysed.
A lyne bulter, wherwith the floure is seuered from the branne.
Rosted or baken vnder the ashes, or axen.
Tymes borowed or spared from seryous ••• ynesse.
Warkes cone at times stolē frō ordinarie basines or labours necessary.
To lay a thyng on ones necke
He that hath a curlyd heed.Plautus in milite.
That which is within the skynne, betwene the skinne and the fleshe.
To commytte to an nother any matter, whiche is commytted vnto vs by the kynge or prynce.
Thynges whiche doo stande or be sette abrode out of the house.
Abrode in the ayre withoute the house.
That is not in a howse, or vnder a couerynge.
Whiche is not proprelye his or hirs, whose it is fained to be. Partus subdititius, a byrthe fayned of an nother mannes chylde. Libri subdititij, bokes with fals titles or counterfaite auctours.

o: Subditus, ta, tum, idem quod subdititius.
n: subditus ta tum idem quod subdititius
d: Also put in the place of an other.
A iudge which is sette in the place of a iudge departed.Plautus in mostell. Plautus in epistol. & Plin. in epi.
To putte vnder, to adde to, to putte in the place of an nother, to putte in daunger or ieoperdie.
To deceyue. Etiam nunc me subducere istis dictis postulas? And yet nowe wylte thou goo aboute with these wordes to deceyue me?

To steale.Plautus in Curcu. Proximò magnum poculum ille bibit, caput ponit, cum dormiscit, ei sub duco anulum, At the laste he dranke a great draught, & layd downe his heed, whiles he slepte, I st • le his rynge from hym.
To take awaye, to remoue, to lyfte vp, or drawe vp.
To make accompt, to go or steale away priuily.
A house in the daunger of euery wynde.
To go vnder or in, to take.
A drawynge vp of a shyppe oute of the water.
To lie vnder, also to be subiect
To cast vppe, as corne whan it is fanned.
A forger of testamentes, or he that bryngeth forthe one testament for an nother.
To cōpany often with a womā.
To constrayne, to subdue, to dryue vnder, to whet, to beate or stāpe, sometyme to eare or tylle truely, to digge, to meddyll with a womanne,Vergil. sommetyme to lyfte vp.
To put vnder, to make subiecte. somtyme to cast vp, to reherse. Si meministi quod olim dictum est, subijce, If thou doest remembre, what was ones spoken, reherse it.
More ouer, forthwith or anon, often tymes. Subin, idem.
To delyuer a shepe to be kylled for hym that doth sacrifyce.
To be in daunger or peryll, to entre into peryll.
It cometh to my remembrance. also to succede, to resiste, to clymme.
To take charge of any thynge. Quis enim curae tuae molem sponte subeat? Who wolde wyllyngly take on hym the greate weight of thy charge.

To suffre or susteyne. Qui retinendi officij causa, cruciatus subierit vitró, He that wyll for the accomplyshement of his duetie suffre tourmentes wyllyngly. Alsoo to growe or sprynge vp.Vergil. Also to come to remembrance. Sera poenitentia subijt regem, Late repentance came to the kynges remembrance. Cogitationi nostrae nun quam subijt, It came neuer to our thought.
To put vnder. Aeneas subijt mucronem, ipsum que morando sustinuit, Eneas put vnder his sword, & tarieng, lyfted him vp.
To succede or come in place. In quarum Iocū subierunt inquilinae, impietas, perfidia impudicitia, In whose place succeded newe inhabytauntes, contempt of vertue, disloyaltie, lechery.
To aunswere or resyste. Poteris ne orationem eius subire? Moughtest not thou make answere to his oration?
To clymme or mount vp. Hemi excelcitas, sex millibus passuū subitur, the height of the mountayne of Hemus is clymmed or mounted in syxe thousande paces.
To sell any thynge in tyme of warres that was praysed. Hasta, a yerde, whiche was delyuered to hym that was appoynted to selle anye thynge taken in warres.
Was a whyte ornamente, foure square and long, which the nunnes, callid Vestales, ware on their hodes, whan they dyd sacrifyce.

o: Subitaneus, & subitarius, a, um, & subitus, ta, tum,
n: subitaneus amp subitarius a um amp subitus ta tum

o: Sublegere sermonem, Clam nostrum huc illae sublegerunt sermonem, Plautus in milite.
n: sublegere sermonem clam nostrum huc illae sublegerunt sermonem plautus in milite
d: Priuily they harkned, and bare away all that we cōmuned.
To steale. also to chese an other into the place of him that is deed.
Feble, faynt, lyght, of noo force or value.
To helpe, or ayde, to defende, to lyfte vp, to sustayne.
A proppe, a shore, a poste, or other lyke thynge, to sustayn or kepe a thing vp.
High, that which is aboue vs.
To annoynt or touche, to paynt or stayne.
The fyrste colour that is layde or dyed. also staynynge with colours.
The grounde colour, wheron the perfyte colour is layde, in cloth dyed, it is callyd grasynge.
To shyne sommewhat, or to gyue a lyttell lyght.
To vndershrede boughes, that that the lyght may come vnder the tree.
Places without the house to walk in without couerynges.
To go away by stelthe, that noo man do perceyue.

To be subdued, it was proprely whan a battayle was vanquished, the vanquishers caused thre speares to be set vp lykes galowes, and constrayned them that were vanquyshed to go vnderneth it, in token that they were subdued, whyche was the greattest reproche that moughte be deuysed.
To vnderwashe, as water, whyche runneth lowe vnder a banke or hylle,Caesar de • ell. galli. lib. 2. and washeth the foote thereof. Also to washe somewhat cleane.
A disease of cattell, whiche is betwixte the cleys of their fete.
To be at hande or redy.

Easily, handsomly. Bono animo es, Plautus in melite. negotium omne iam succedit submanus, Be of good chere, all the matter is come to passe handsomly. Lepidè hoc succedit sub manus negotium, This mattier commeth well and easily to passe.
To do seruice vnder one, to gyue or delyuer any thing that is asked for.
He that serueth vnder an other man, he that delyuereth any thynge that is callyd for.
Softely, proprely in speakynge. also humbly.
To sende priuily or by stelth.
To sende or brynge in the mean tyme. Also to put or set vnder proprely, as a calfe, a lambe, or a fole, is sette vnder the damme to sucke.
To remoue or carie a thing farre of. also to dryue out of a place. alsoo to discharge a man of his offyce.
To bynde to, or hange to, also to subscribe.
To leane agaynst a thing to be sustayned vp.
To make a knot vnder a thing.
To brymme as a bore dothe whan he getteth pygges.
To offende sommewhat,Cic. ad. Q. stratrem. or a lyttelle.
To sauour or smelle a lyttell.
To prayse or honour. also to suborne or brynge in a false. wytnesse, or messanger, or fayne one persone for an other, to deceyue with.
To begynne to sprynge or aryse, as the sonne dothe, to prayse or honour one with wordes. also to deceyue pryuylye.
To steale away or runne awaye priuyly.
To entre sodaynly or pryuyly into the mynde.
Letters stollen oute by a fals suggestion.
To steale, to take away secretely. sometyme to lyfte vp hastily.
To substitute or subrogate, to make a deputie in an office, to put in an nother mans roume.

o: Subrufus, a, um, & subrubeus, a, um,
n: subrufus a um amp subrubeus a um
d: Somwhat redde. Subrumi, lambes that do sucke.
To be souckeled, or putte to sucke as calfes, lambes, &c.
To enter with force, or priuily by litle and lytle. also to dygge the erthe.
A mocke with bendynge the browes, and snuffynge vp of the nose.
To write vnder, to subscribe, to fauour a matter,Ci. in Ver. Asco. Ped. to assynge a cause why, to affirme.
They whiche in causes iudyciall do fauour the parte of the accuser or playntyfe.
The vtter table, whervnto other tables are fastned.
To cutte vnder or cut a lyttell.
Bēches, which were vnder higher seates, they were also benches, on the whiche Iudges byd sytte.
To sowe or set vnder a thing
To serue, to accord, or agre.
Scoutwatches, wherby hostes of men are intrapped as they passe.
To sytte vnder, to saye in awayte for one.

n: subsilio liui lire amp subsulto sultare

d: He that hath a camyse nose.
That which foloweth or is next.
To resyste, to abyde, to be by hym selfe.
To sowne a lyttell, to make a lyttell noyse.
A deputation, whan one maketh an other his deputie.
Substance. also matter. somtyme goodes, whyche is also commonly callyd substaunce.
To strawe or laye vnder any thynge, as russhes, carpettes, and flowres.
A ryme or fallynge myste, or a droppynge before and after rayne. It • s also a sicknes, whā a man may not pisse wel
To substitute in the place of an nother.
Vnderpynnynge or groundyng of a house.
The holownes of the fote. also the paulme of the hande.
The threede, whyche in weauynge is callyd the woufe.
Places vnder the eueyse of howses.
To purpose or diuyse anye thynge, to deceyue an nother manne, or to laye any thynge in a mannes waye for the same purpose.
That whiche is vnder the grounde.
To runne or flowe vnder a thynge, as water vnder a brydge.
To aunswere nothynge to that which is spoken. Subtice sco, scere, idē
To take away, to steale,Pli • . Subtrahere se, to draw vnto quietnes. Subtrahere famae, to withdrawe from bruyte. Subtrahere inuidiae, to eschewe enuy.
Somewhat foule, in part foule or dishoneste, the matter or thinge dishoneste, couered with cleane wordes.
To tourne vp so downe. alsoo to distroy, to subuerte.
An aulle, that cordyners doo vse for a bodkyn.
An harte hauynge hornes without tynes, callyd as I suppose, a spyttarde.
A maner or ferme without the walles of the citie.
The suburbes of a citie or towne.
The strete in Rome where the brothell houses were.
That whiche apprehendeth men lyke as rauynes do carrayne.
To entre. Et nostris succede penatibus hospes, And enter thou my frende into my howse.
To go vnder a thyng. Succedere, to spede wel, to be at a good poynt. Hac nō successit, alia aggrediamur uia, This way it spedeth not, let vs go to an other way.
To be āgry for a good cause.
Was a certayne garmente, whiche onely hoores dyd weare.
He that made vp the number of the bende of men that lacked.
To make vp the number of a hundred souldiours, or of that company that was callyd Centuria.
To raunge meale in a syeue.
To depose a mā of his office.
That whyche prosperouslye happeneth, or spedeth well.
Successe, be it good or yll.
Beastes for sacrifice, whiche were kylled in the seconde place, or nexte to the fyrste.
A piece or flyche of bakon salted. also larde.
To felle or cutte downe. also to falle vnder.
That whiche dothe succede or folowe. also lowe, redy to falle downe.

To gyrde. Also to enuyron or compasse. Frustra se terrore succinxerit, qui septus charitate non fuerit, armis, n. arma irritantur, In vayne shall he enuyron hym selfe with terriblenesse, which is not wallyd aboute with the loue of his countreye. For with vyolence, vyolence is styred.
To make a soft noise, to singe a base or tenour.
Aumbre, whereof somme beade stones are made.
Tyme of leysure, vacant from busynesse.
To putte vnder the necke or shulders, to beare a thynge.
A small voyce and a shryll.
To growe vnder, or lowe, or a lyttell and lyttell.
Deuylles, whiche in the fourme of women, do company with men.
To be subdued, to be ioyned to, to falle downe vnder an heuy burdeyn, to fayle for feblenesse.
To help, to com to remēbrāce.
Iuyce or humour, whiche the body receyueth of meate and drynke, also generally all maner of iuyse.
To shake as a horse doth whan he trotteth. also to trotte.
The trottynge or shakynge of a horse.
A sowe pygge, also a certayn inner garment. alsó a certayne company of sterres, callyd the .vii. sterres, whiche do appiere the .xii. Calendes of Iune, and be callyd succulae & Hiades.
A certayne speare, whiche is burned at the ende.
To sweate, to laboure soore, to haue moche to do.
The clere parte of the firmamente betwene cloudes. Also the clere fyrmamēt without cloudes.
To get a shrewde turne. Metuo lenonem, ne quid suo suat capiti, I am aferde of the bawde, leste he gette a shrewde tourne.
To lade or bourdeyne, to trusse vppe.
He that carieth meale or floure to any place to selle in lyttell quantytie.
Is he, whyche an offycer beynge deed, or remoued, is sette in his place.
Was amonge the Carthaginensis, as the Consul was at Rome.

Was an attyre, whiche the nunnes of Vesta dydde weare on theyr heedes, whan they dydde sacrifice, and was lyke to the tyres, whiche wyues of London dydde weare, and becamme theym moche better than bonettes of veluette doo nowe, wherwith they mocke ladyes and gentyllwomenne, and thereby onely doo gette the name to be callydde Maskynge ladyes.
To sustayne, to put vnder, to suffre.
To suffyse, to indure, to minister, to substitute, to stayne.
The codde of a ramme, which was made for a purse, to conteyne money.
That wherwith a whiele is retained or stopped of his course.
To stop the breth, to strangle.
The voyce of people assemblyd in gyuyng their consent. also helpe or succour. also a wrecke in the see.
The iointes of the hinder legge of a beaste, callyd the how • , sometyme it doth signifie the pasternes, they be alsoo the yonge sprynges of vynes.
Horses, whyche haue the paynes or scratches.
To be proppid vp or vnderset
To caste downe or poure lycour on a thynge, to caste abrode.
To buylde or sette vppon a foundation.
To mynyster or gyue a thynge, to sende sorthe thynges, wherof are plentie.
A pulpitte or high place, oute of the whyche Oratours or Capytaynes made proposytions vnto the people.
The euyse of a house, whyche defendeth the walles from rayne.
To make a blacke spotte in the skynne with beatynge. It is alsoo to scorne, to detracte, or infame, to reproue, to condempne.
Is a a marke in the visage black or blue, made by some stroke, a mocke, a detraction, an infamation behynde one, a condemnation.

o: Suinus, a, um, & suillus, a, um,
n: suinus a um amp suillus a um

d: A furrowe. Serere tertio quarto quinto sulco, To sowe in the thyrde, the fourthe, the fyfthe falowe. Sometyme it is put of a dyche. Also any maner of cuttynge of the erthe. proprely it signifyeth any thynge that is longe and sharpe edged. Bisulcum animal, A beaste that hath the fete clouen with two talons.
Was a cruell tyrant of the Romayns callyd also Sylla.
A towne in the countraye of Peligna, where Ouidius the poete was borne.
A manne or woman of the citie of Sulmo.
A place where brymstone is boyled.
A sowdane, whiche was the name of the kynge of Egipte and Siria.
I am, es, thou arte, est, he is.

o: Sum mihi bis septem praestanti corpore nymphae,
n: sum mihi bis septem praestanti corpore nymphae
d: I haue fouretene maydens of excellent beautie.
I am put in the blame.
Olde wryters vsed for eum, hym.No. Mar. Plautus in milite.
It is seuen dayes agone. Howe this verbe Sum, shulde be sette and construed, rede Calepines vocabuler, also loke for Est, fuit, and such other partes of sum, in their letters before.
A great cake made lyke a whele, suche as is made at brydales and churche goinges.
To summe a booke of accompte.
Is made of the pappes of a sowe, cutte from hir the day after that she hath varowed, ad is powdred with salt.

To hyre. Quoad enim peruentum, quo sumpta nauis est, non domini nauis est, sed nauigantium, Vntylle they come to the place whither the shyppe was hyred, the shyppe is not the owners but theyrs, whiche are passagers.
To spende or bestowe on one. In mala vxore, at que inimico, si quid sumas, sumptus est, On a shrewd wyfe, and an ennemy, what so euer thou bestowest, is waste.
To drawe water out of the welle.
Is a collection of thinges or wordꝭ. also the principall poynte of a matter.
The chief ꝑsons of a realme or cite.
Compendiousely by euery parte of the matter, summarily. Ad summum duo, two at the moste.
Hoores kepte in the stede of wyues.
A place where bawdrye was kepte without the walles of a towne.
To conuay in priuily, also to suffre to growe.
To lette the berde growe, to let to departe.
That whyche is vnder the walles.
To take the rigour or extremitie of the lawe in suite.Cice. pro. A. Caesina.
To finishe a thyng perfitely, to brynge a mattier to a poynt.
Hyghest, extreme, greattest, or very commendable.
To take vppon one, to take generally,Varro de • e rust. to hyre, to consume.
Lawes made for restraynynge of outragious expenses.
That whyche dothe pertayne to expenses.
A promontorie or elbowe of the countrey of Attica.
To sowe, to ioyne or make fast togyther.
Household stuffe, all thynges mouable within the house.
A bondman or slaue, whyche is accompted for chatell.

o: Super Garamantas & Indos proferet imperium, Vergil.
n: super garamantas amp indos proferet imperium vergil
d: He shal aduance his empyre beyond the Garamantians and Indianes.
At supper.Plautus in Aulularia • Plinius epist. 87. Epist. 91. Vergilius.
Of Priamꝰ of Hector. Hac suꝑ re scribā ad te Rhegio, Of that mater I wil write vnto you frō Regiū.

o: Super for propter. Nec super ipse sua molitur laude laborem,
n: super for propter nec super ipse sua molitur laude laborem
d: Nor he takethe the peyne for his prayse.
His accensa suꝑ, Vergilius. with those wordes she beinge kendlyd or styred.
Pryde. Superbio, ire, to be proude.
He that speaketh proudely, or hautely.
Olde wryters vsed for mortuos,Plautus in Amphi. deed, bycause of the pompe, whiche was at their burienge. Faciam ego hodie te superbum, nisi hinc abis, I wil kyl the, if thou gette the not hens.
Proude, sometyme magnifyke or noble, also hyghe, ornate, or garnysshed, ryche, wycked.
The ouerbrowe. sommetyme it sygnifyeth pride, grauitie. It is alsoo the haunce, whiche is ouer the doore.
To laye aparte pryde or stately countenance.
Shall lyue, or be left on lyue. Superest, he lyueth, or is on lyue.

There is plentie or more thanne ynough. Aliis quia defit, quod amant, aegre est: Terent. in pho • m. tibi quia superest, dolet, Some bicause they lacke the thynge that they loue, be discontent: and thou arte sorye that thou haste more than thou nedest.

To be the reste or resydue. Porro ausculta quod superest fallatiae, But yet here what was the resydue of that craft or deceyte. To defende or pleade for one. Cū ctarise, ne si superesset, eriperet legibus reū, He wolde tary, leste yf he came and spake for hym, he shulde delyuer an offender.
Houses buylded on the lande of an nother man than buylded them.
He that hathe a house of his owne buylded on an other mans grounde, and payeth therfore a quyte rent.
The ouermost part of any thing.
Oone conception of a chylde after an other.
To caste on or lay on.
To cast vpon, to laye vppon.
To go ouer, or slyppe ouer.
They which haue the hinder part of the thighes next the buttockes cut away
The inwarde part and hindermost parte of the thyghes nexte the buttockes cutte of.
High, or ouer. Superna regio, the high countrey.
That whiche is in surplusage, aboue the true number.
To go ouer. Also to vanquishe or ouercome. also to ouerlyue. somtyme to kylle. Quod superat, whiche is more, or is lefte in a surplusage.
Ouerweight, that whiche is added to the iuste weight.
To omytte or leaue to doo a thynge.
Take not the peyne to come nowe, or forbeare the peyn takyng in this iourney.

o: Supersede istis rebus, Plautus in Epidico. Plautus in persa. Plin. epist. 102.
n: supersede istis rebus plautus in epidico plautus in persa plin epist 102

d: Let these wordis passe, holde thy runge.
I forbare to wryte, I left vnwriten.
He that ouerliueth or remaianeth alyue afterthat other be deed, also alyue. sometyme present, olde writers callyd Superstites, wytnesses.

He that is saulfe. Deos quaeso, ut sis superstes, I beseche god saue you, longe mought you lyue. also present. Superstitem utrun que monui, ne inuisi abeant, I aduysed them both, that they shoulde not departe with dyspleasure.

A superfluous or vayne religion or deuotion, an honouryng of that which ought not to be honored, a vaine reuerēce or feare towarde that thing, wherin is no efficacye or power, but by the illusyon of the dyuelle: as diuination by the cryenge or fleinge of byrdes, obseruation of times, and dreames, and other lyke vanites.

They which be tymorous without cause, fearinge that god is displeased, where there is none offence done: They were at the fyrste soo callyd, bycause they contynually prayid and offred to the goddis, to preserue theyr chyldern, that they mought ouerlyue them. Finally euery vndiscrete or vnreasonable deuocion or religion, may be callyd Superstition.
To make hoole or recouer frome deathe.
To abounde, to remain, to vanquishe, to be superfluous, to indure.
Was of the diuinours or sothsayers callyd that byrde, which cried from the toppe of any thynge.
To com vnloked for, to com vpon or after an other thynge.
To recouer from peryll of dethe, or whan a man semeth to be deade.
The see, which is callid Mare Hadtiaticum, wherin standeth the Citie of Venyce.
Vpryghte,Horation. the bealye vpvpwarde. somtyme it sygnifieth on an hyll or hygh place.
To folowe and flatter for a mans dyner.
A clothe or curtayne hanged vp where interludes were playde.
A smocke. it is also a topsayle of a shyppe.
To subdue, to minyster sufficiently, also to oppresse.

To endure. Ac stomacho nō queo labori suppeditare, My stomake wyll not lette me indure the laboure. Alsoo to furnyshe expenses, to gyue as moche as a man wolde haue.Terent. in Brautont. Nam si illi pergam, suppeditare sumptibus Menedeme, mihi illaec uero ad rastros res redit, Surely Menedemus, yf I wold gyue hym as moche as he wolde spende, that thynge wolde brynge me to the poynt to rake for my lyuynge.

To subdewe or treade vnder. Nunc, uideo, in iudicio mecum contendere non uis, ubi suppeditari turpissimum, superare pulcherrimum est, Nowe I perceyue thou wylte not contende with me before iudges, where it were a great shame to be subdued, and very moche honestie to haue the better.

o: Suppetunt dictis data, aut facta. Non suppetunt dictis data,
n: suppetunt dictis data aut facta non suppetunt dictis data
d: He perfourmeth not that, that he promysed. Vtinam quae dicis dictis facta suppetant, wold god thou woldest do as thou sayest, or wolde god thy dedes did agree with thy wordes.
There is gayne sufficiente. Res ita supperit, the matter so requireth.
Brynge to me succoures, ayde me.
To putte vnder the foote, to ouerthrowe, to supplant or deceyue, in preuentynge one to his hynderance or dammage, to vnderplante or set a tree or vyne.
That whiche supplyethe or maketh vp that whiche lacketh in quantitie or numbre.
To make vp that whiche lacketh, to make euyn.
He that desyreth any thynge knelynge or prostrate.
Payne, tourmente,Salust. in bell. ca • . Iugurt. or execution of dethe. sometyme supplicia, are prayers.
A makynge vp of a number, whiche lacketh or is minished.

o: Supplodo, plosi, ere, Cor. Tacitus lib. 13.
n: supplodo plosi ere cor tacitus lib 13
d: To stampe or make noise with the fete. also to reiecte or caste away.
A stampynge or noyse made with the feete.
To put vnder, to put into the place of an nother, to sette a false or fayned thynge in the place of that whiche is the very true thynge.
To brynge or carie priuily.Caesar de bell. Gall. lib. 7.
The puttinge or settyng of a fained or fals thyng in the place of the thing selfe, as one chylde for an nother.
Whan the chylde of one woman is layde with an nother womanne, whiche is not the very mother, as though she had borne it.
Countersureties, they whyche are bounden to the sureties, to saue them harmelesse.

Drowned, beaten vnder.Iustinus. Victi Persi in naues confugerunt, ex quibus multae suppressae, multae captae, The Persians fledde vnto their shyppes, whereof many were drowned, and many taken. Also hyd or concyled.
To kepe downe to kepe secrete, to kepe in sylence.
To stay or omitte a iourney.Caes. in cō. de bello ciuili. li. 1. Plautus in milite.
A butlar. Bono cella suppromo credita, The cellar or buttrie was cōmytted to a good butlar.
I am halfe ashamed, thou art half ashamed, or he is halfe ashamed.
That whyche pertaynethe to impostumes, or to make a soore to matter.
To matter or be an impostume.
An impostume or sore that hath matter.

o: Supra quam , for supra id quod.
n: supra quam for supra id quod

d: Hyghest of all, or aboue all.
The highest or greatest of all other.
The cause of the legge. sometyme the hole shanke or legge from the kne downe.
That which bringeth forth yonge settes or springes of trees
A yonge set or slyppe, a nursegarden, also a slyppe of a tree or yong greffe.
He that is somwhat deafe and can not here.
To waxe deafe or be deafe.
Deafe, also that which hath no sauour.
Olde writers vsed for surgit, wherof commeth surrectio, a rysynge.
That whiche is doone by stelthe that none other man knoweth it.
To ryse, also to growe or sprynge.Vergil.
To laye his eare to a thyng, to harken.

o: Surripere operam, Clanculum abij a legione, operam hanc surripui tibi,
n: surripere operam clanculum abij a legione operam hanc surripui tibi
d: I departed pryuyly from the hoste,Plautus in 〈◊〉 . this tyme haue I borowed to do you pleasure.
To steale his away. Vt surripuisti te mihi dudū de foro? O, how diddest thou steale away frō me late out of the market?
To steale or take awaye priuily. also to lyft vp on hygh, to preuent.
To substitute, or put in an nother mannes place.
To promyse. Quas partes impleturum te, secundum susceptam fidem confido, Whyche parte I truste thou wilt perfourme, according to the promyse that thou madest.
To awake one out of his slepe, to call one to his warke.
A prouerbe applyed vnto hym, whyche presumeth to teache or correcte one, of whome he rather oughte to be taught or corrected.

o: Sus que de que fero, & sus que de que habeo,
n: sus que de que fero amp sus que de que habeo
d: I force not, I recke not, I care not.
To take. Suscipere liberos, to gette chylderne.
To beholde aboue.Mart. sometyme to see benethe, or to loke downe.
To be hanged ouer or an high, also to appere a lyttell.
He that douteth to speake or do.
Timorously, doubtefully.Plin. epi •• 98. li. 6. Terent. in phor • .

o: Suspenso gradu, Haec ubi ego audiui, ad fores supenso gradu, placidé ire perrexi.
n: suspenso gradu haec ubi ego audiui ad fores supenso gradu placide ire perrexi
d: Whan I harde those wordes, I went to the doore fayre and softly.
To hange vp, to be doubteful or sorowefull. Suspensus animo, hauynge doubte, or beinge adradde.
To go softely without makynge noyse.
To loke vp, also to honour, to answere.
To haue suspicion, to suspecte. also to suppose.
Shorte wynded, or he whyche fetcheth his brethe paynfully.
To sygh. also to desyre feruētly.
That whiche sustayneth or beareth vp a thynge.
To holde vp, to suffre, to forbeare, to fede, to refrayne.
To be proude, or to haue an hygh courage.
To pay dettes.Plin. de • ris illu •• r.
