Is proprely of the father, as peperit, is of the mother.
I haue had, I haue broughte vp. I haue lyfte vp.
A whysterer. also he whyche with fals and secrete reporte maketh dissencyon betwene men.
A whystrynge, or softe murmurynge, or suche noyse as trees doo make with the wynde, or a ryuer whan it runneth, or byrdes whan they chatter.

His or hirs. But how this word shall be most aptely and conueniētly vsyd, rede Valla or Calepines vocabularie. For it is more abundantly and proprely declared of thē, than can be expressid in english.
Sterres callid also Hyades, seuen in number.
A prouerbe applied to feastes and bankettes, whyche doo excede in delycatenesse.
Playes whyche are wanton and costly.
A verse or poeme contaynynge wanton matter.
Peple in the north part of the world.

A great tree lyke a fygge tree, whiche hath abundance of mylke, whose fruite commeth not oute of the toppes of the bowghes, as fygges doo, but oute of the same boughes, and swete like to a wild fygge: the graynes therof be les than the graines of figgis, & they be neuer ripe, except they be scrapid wt an instrumēt of yrō.
He that falily accuseth an innocent. Also a bearer of tales, or a cōplayner.
A dysease in the fundement, which maketh a warte lyke to a fygge.
Where within the eie lyd groweth a lyttell wart or other lyke thynge.
A spyce of the fallynge euyll in men, but in trees it is taken for blastynge.
A citie in the confynes of Egypte and Ethiope.
A mountayne in Lucania, & a wod in it.
A great tyrant of Rome, whiche was of an vnsaciable crueltie.
A famous maker of images, whiche was neuer taught.
A fygure, where the plurell number and the synguler are ioyned togyther, as socijs & rege recepto.
A perfyte argumente, whyche hath a necessarye conclusion.
A wodde or place ouergrowen with wedes, also any matter hastily writen with oute studye.
Was callyd the god of woddes.
To waxe or growe into woddes or bushes.
Of a wodde or forest, woddy, wylde.
He that dwelleth in a foreste or wodde.
A mannes name, whiche was borne in a foreste.
A collation. also a token gyuen by one to an other vpon certayn appointmentes, generally a signe or mark to know a thynge by.
A signet or sele, or a signe manuel.
Ayde in battaile, or leage made amonge men of sondry countreys, to fight agaynst the other parte.
A concorde in measure, where sondry thynges be of equall proporcion.

A mutuall combination of thynges naturall in the operation of theyr powers and qualities, as water in coldenesse dothe participate with erthe, in moysture with the ayre, the ayre with the fyre in heate, with water in moysture.
A consent in tune, also harmony.
To agree or accord in one.
Women addicte to ceremonies or deuocion.
A cup seruīg for wyne in sacrifice.
A frende of hym that is maried, whiche accompanieth hym to feastes.
Warkes, in the which wrastlers, and they whyche contende in fyghtynge, are beholden.
Two yles in the grekyshe see.
He that makith a fest or bāket
A woman whyche kepeth company at drynkynge.
A secretary, or one of the pryuye councylle.
Funerals or playes, wherein playes were made.
A contraction of two wordes, as Bigae, for b • iugae.
A syckenesse in the throte, callyd the squynce.
Sincere, pure, vncorrupted symple without dissimulation.
The forepart of the heed Also a swynes heed soweyd.
A fygure, where a letter or syllable is taken away, as cōpostus, for cōpositus.
A fygure, where parte is vsyd •• r the hole, or the hole for part.
A stone, whyche is callyd alsoo Leucongia.
The wrytinge or dede, made or signed with the hande of hym that maketh a bargayne or couenaunte.
A stone, wherwith nygromancers do call vp dyuels.
An assēbly of mē, or general coūcil.
Whiche in dyuers wordes sygnifieth one thyng, as Eusis, Gladius, both do sygnifie a sworde. Occidit, interfecit, necanit, do signifie, he kylled.
Lacke, or weakenes, whiche hapneth by longe syckenes.
A short cote or ierkyn. also a vessell made of many vessels.
A curtayne hanged before minstrels whan they synge.
A great realme in Asia, whiche hathe on the east the ryuer of Euphrates, on the weste the myddell see, and the realme of Egipte, on the northe Cilicia and Cappadocia, on the south Arabia.
People whiche receyue their meat in oten redes.
A color mixt with sinoper & ruddel
Wyne boyled to the thyrde part.
Corne kepte in holes in the grounde, and couered with chaffe.
The traine of a womans gowne.
Quycke sandes or shelpes in the water made by the dryfte of sande or grauel.
A lyttell stoone founde in the bladder of a wolfe.
A man of Siria, also an Iland belongynge to Grece.
Feastes, and companyes assembled at feastes.

Synewes, whyche do come frome the brayne to the eyes, so that he, whiche cometh from the lefte syde, gothe to the right eye, and that whiche commeth from the right syde, goth to the left eye, so that the synewes do crosse eche other.
A flie, whiche hath foure wingis, & byteth a man or beest.
A caryer of letters, an auditour.
A scriuener that writeth commune instrumentes and dedes.
Euery vyle habytation, also a shop or tauerne, where wares be solde, and all thynge that is vendible, as wyne, oyle, or any other thynge.
A comedia or Interlude, wherein are base nor sonages, and no persones of dignitie or state.
He that sellethe any maner of wares also a tauerner.

Corruption in the body, also extreme leannesse, by a longe consumynge syckenesse. It is also matter and corrupte blode myxte togither. Also the impostume of the lunges, procedynge of humoures descendynge frome the heed into the stomake, and so woundynge and corruptyng the lounges.
To languishe or consume, to be extremely leane, to be corruptid.
That whiche may be corrupted, or falle into a consumption.
That whyche maketh one corrupted, or consumeth the body.
Was a wynter parlour, wherein were painted tables and bokes of stories.
A consumption, wastynge, or putrifaction of thinges.
A mountayne in the countrey of Galiles, where Chaiste was transfigurate.
A table. In the plurell numbre tabulae, dothe signifie a testament, or any commune instrument or writynge. Also tabula is a table to play on with dise or chesse mē.
Were whan detters were not constrayned to pay their dettes, that they dyd owe, and the olde oblygations were dissolued, and newe were to be made for that whiche shulde newely be borowed.
Ar places, where euidences and writynges be layde.
A cheste, in the whiche euidences and recordes are put.
Walles made of square stones, as if they were bourded. They be also the boughes of trees and bushes, whyche do growe streyght forth and not vpwarde.
Made of bourdes. Also tabulata, are walles sylded with bourdes. or made of stone playne lyke to bourdes. They be also the boughes of trees, whyche do leane playne outwarde, and do not growe vpwarde:
To make a thing with bourdes, or to ioyne bourdes togyther.
A ioynynge or closynge of bourdes togyther.
An hyll in Campania, wherin do growe many olyue trees.
Lette aloone, I my selfe wylle commune nowe with hym.
Those thynges whiche are not to be spoken.
To kepe sylence, to be in reste, to be quycke, to be sure.
Not a worde is spoken of it.Terent. in Adelph.
He that holdethe his peace, and is secrete.
Be styl, thou shalt here the sooner.
Somwhat burned or blasted with lyghtnynge.
It weryeth me, it yrketh me, I am werye of it.
An olde dotarde, of whom al men are wearye.
A darke place at the fote of the hil callyd Malea, by the citie of Sparta, whiche was supposed to be an entry into hell.

The edge of a fyllette. also a womās fyllette, or that whyche nowe they calle rolles: proprely it is a kerchiefe, whyche maydens do weare on their heedes. Also a whyte stoone, whyche in the water sheweth longe lyke a kerchiefe. It is alsoo a vyllage betwene Mirenas & Corinthum.
A cite in Laconia, an other ī Arcadia
A felon, whiche happeneth on a mannes fynger.
Was he, whyche taughte fyrste the Thuscanes the crafte of diuynation, callyd Aruspicium.
An hylle in Portyngale, where, as it is wryten, that mares doo conceyue of the wynde.
A ryuer in Spayne, wherin hath ben founde grauell of golde.
Is the name of oone of the seuen sterres, whiche soo appiereth, as it maye scantly be perceyued, which sterre is also called Maia, & Electra.
Were showes, whyche Mercurius dyd weare, wheron were set whynges.
That whiche commeth downe to the ancley, as Toga talaris, a longe gowne to the ancley.
Pertaynynge to dyse, as Lex talatia, a lawe agaynst dyse playenge.

Was a songe contayned in certayn verses, sungen at weddynges. It was also a certayne exclamation or crie vsed at mariages, the begynnynge whereof beganne, whan Romulus and the Romaynes reuysshed the maydens of the Sabines, amonge whom was one of excellent beautie, whom whan many of the Sabines wold haue reskued, they whyche caried her toward Romulus, to thintent that she shulde not be taken from them, cryed Talassio, whiche was the name of a noble prynce of the Sabinee, as if they wolde haue brought hyr to hym, and by that meane they escaped, & broughte hir to Romulus. And afterwarde they vsed at mariages to crie Talassio.
A stocke sette in the erthe, whereon men doo graffe. Also a truncheon, a staffe, a byllette.

Was a poyse, whyche after the countreye, wherein it was, it was dyuers. One was callyd talentum Atticum, whyche contayned .lx. poundes of Athenes, callyd Minas, or Mnas, and, lxxii. poūdes of Rome callyd libras: and this was also called talentum minus, the other was callyd Talentum maius, & Euboicum, which contayned .lxxx. poundes of Athenes, callid Minas, & .lxxxiii. poundes & foure ounces of Rome weight. Loke before in Libra, et Pondo. Talentū Atticum, uel minus, was in value after the rate of olde poyse grotes. Clxvi.li.xiii. s. iiii. d. after .lx. to the pounde, after the newe grotes, tenne to the once .CCviii.li.vi. s. viii. d.
Of olde grotes. Clxxxx.li.xiii. s. iiii. d. of newe grotes. CCxvii.li.x. s.
An Ile in the see callyd Hircanum, where groweth plentie of corne and frutes without culture.
The blade of an ony on or chyboll.
An equall peyne in recompence of a hurte, as for the cuttynge of a mans hande, to lose a hande, or for puttinge out of an eye, to lose an eye.
To be cutte: it is proprely spoken of wodde, whiche we nowe calle tallynge of wodde.
A fyllyppe gyuen with ones fynger or nayle.
Blynder than a molle, a prouerbe applyed to them, whiche lacke iugement in thinges that are playne.
To refourme that, whiche was negligently done, with more diligēce.
The ankle aboue the foote. It is also the pasterne bone of a beaste, Also a dye, or dyce.
As well, also, as, soo. Tam bonus, as good. Tā sum amicus republicae, quam qui maxi mè, I am so frendely, or as moche frende to the publyke weale, as he that is moste.
Whan with moche trauelle the blode commeth downe to the legge, and causeth it to swelle.
A fruite growynge in India,Vergil. the tree wherof is like to a palme or date tree, the fruite sower, lyke grene damsins, whiche is medicinable in asswagyng the heate of cholere.
People in Asia, not farre frome the see callyd Caspium.
An herbe, whyche bearethe floures twyse in one yere.

Not withstandyng. also yet. Tamen a malicia non discedis, Yet wylte thou not departe from thy malyce. Sommetyme it signifieth forthewith, at the laste, soo that. Quod potero, faciam, tamē ut pietatem eolam, I wyll doo that I maye: soo that not withstandynge I omytte not my duetie to my father.
A wild grape, growing in woddes.
Olde wryters vsed for eous que , vntyll that.
A riuer in Lucania, betwene Campania and Calabria.
A great ryuer in the northe parte of the worlde, whyche dyuydeth Europa from Asia.
Was wife to Tarquinius Priscus, the kynge of Romaynes.
At the laste, sometyme at the leste waye, also vneth, not withstandynge.
To touthe, to meue, to vnderstande, or perceyue, to come to.
To rubbe on the gaide place,Turp • ilius to speake to one of a thynge, whiche greueth hym to here it.
It came to myn eares.Plautus i • Ruden.
The principall citie of Egypte, where Moyses dyd shewe meruayles.
A stone of the kynde of Emeralde, grene and blacke.
A prouerbe sygnifienge good thynges to be at hande, whiche not withstandynge a man may not vse.
A kynge, whom poetes do faine to be turmented in hell with hunger & thyrste.
For so moche. This worde doth pertayne to byenge and sellynge. Tantidem, at that pryce. Tandidem idem.
I sette so moche by, or I so moche esteme i • .

o: Tantillus, la, lum, & tantulus, a, um,
n: tantillus la lum amp tantulus a um

d: A wylde vyne callyd also Labrusca.
An aduerbe, sygnyfienge so moche, as tanto magis, so moche more, tanto peior, so moche worse.
It is soo farre frome, or soo moche vnlyke.
Suche, sometyme so moche, or so greatte.
A stone of the colour of a pecoke.
Hangynges of houses, or clothes wherwith pauementes are couered.
Tapisrye, or clothes, wherin are wrought diuers pictures with thredes of sondry colours.
An Ile by Grecia, where dwelled the people called Telebois.
A citie in Egipt, the people wherof were callyd Taphnii.
In greke, is a sepulchre or tumbe.
A fygure, wherby a great thyng is basely described.
A noble Ile in the Indiane see, whiche yle is dyrectly agaynste this parte of the worlde, and there is abundance of all maner of spyces. And the people there lyueth aboue an hundred yeres.
An Ile by Sycile not farre frome Syracuse.
People in Parthia, whyche vse to gyue theyr wyues in mariage to other mē, after that they haue hadde foure or fyue chyldren by them.
A beaste in body lyke to a great oxe, hauynge a heed lyke to a harte, and hornes full of branches, the heare rough, of the colour of a beare, I suppose it to be a rayne dere.
A kynde of the beastes callydde Stelliones, lyke to a lysarde, of whose bytynge no man dieth, onely it stonieth hym that is bytten.
The sonne of Neptunus, who buylded Tarentum.
Whan the eyen do bolne out moch, and be redde.
Was a myscheuous kyng of the people callyd Albani.
A duke in Hethruria, whiche was also a greate diuinour or southsayer.
That whiche hath a slow pase, or gothe slowely.
He that draweth his speeche in lengthe.
Slowe, rude, somtyme well during▪ also thycke or grosse.
Of the citie of Tarent in Calabria.
A citie within the realm of Naples.
A wourme, whiche eareth flesshe, a magotte.
Was the laste kynge of Romaynes, whiche was expellyd oute of Rome for his pride and crueltie.
A towne in Campania callydde also Anxur.
The chiefe citie of Cilicia, where saynt Paule was borne.
A greate countray in the northeste parte of the worlde.
A place in hel. also a mā of Tartarie.
Olde writers vsed for horrible or terrible.
A people in Iberi • , amonge whom be cattes of excedynge greatnesse.
A citie in the vttermoste parte of Spayne, on the see syde by Gades, nowe callyd Cales, where Columella the moste ••• quent and perfyte husband, was borne.
One of the sonnes of duke Nestor.
Dady, which chyldrē call their father.
A wanton worde, wherwith one aunswereth to an nother.
A kynde of salt whyche cometh out of Phrigia, & is medicinable for the eies.
A mans name. Tatius, a mās name.
A scourge made of neates lether.
A contray in the north parte of Europa.
People of cruell maners that offered strangers in sacrifyce.
Were playes made in the honoure of infernall goddis.
One of the goddes of the see.
A mountayne in Sicile, soo callyd for the plentie of neate, whiche fed theron. Also ther • was by it a citie of the same name.
People of Scithia, dwellyng by the mountayne callyd Taurus.
A bulle, sometyme a stronge oxe, It is also one of the .xii. celestiall sygnes, also a great mountayne towarde India.
A fygure, where one thynge is twyse spoken.
A kynde of bayes or laurell, wherewith herbars are made.
A settynge of a taxe or subsidie.
They whiche doo rebuke oone an nother.
Olde wryters vsed for tetigeris, thou shalte touche.
A gray or brocke, or badger.
To touche often. alsoo to taxe, or cesse a thynge at a certayne value. also to reproue one an other.
A tree lyke to fyrre, whiche beareth bearyes, wherin is mortalle poyson. It is also callyd owe, wherof bowes be made.
A hylle, vnder the whiche is sette the cities of Sparta and Amycle.

A riuer of Thracia, at the heed wherof Darius kynge of Persia, whā he went into Scithia, pighte his pauyllyons, and there abode thre dayes. And delytynge at the mooste pleasaunt water of that ryuer, he sette in the same place a piller grauē with letters of greke, declaryng his being there, with cōmendatiō of the water.
A craft, also a wyle, or subtyl meane
Were they, whiche also were callyd Corybantes, and were feined to be the sonnes of Minerua and Sol.
The playstrynge or pariettynge of a house.
The roufe of a house. sommetyme all the house.
I pray & byseche the.Plaut. in milite.
A tree, out of the whiche sweateth a lycour, whan it is hette.
Of whom al men be wery. somtime it signifieth him, which is wery of som thīg.F • st. pom.
A course blanket or couerlyd,Varro. whiche lyeth on poore mens beddes. It is alsoo a matte.
To couer, to hyde, to defende or kepe.
A citie in Paphlagonia, where Anacreon the poete was borne.
The clothe, whiche is spoken as welle of sylke as of lynnen clothe or wollen.
Ymages, whiche do beare vppe pyllers or postes.
The sonne, whiche was nourished with an hynde. Telina, a certain garment.
A collectour or gatherer of tributes. Telonium, the place where taskes or tributes are payde.
In greke is an end, honour, a legion, a tribute or pēcion, it is also the name of an ile, where the ointment callid telina is made
A mās name whom the wise Solon iuged to be more fortunate thā the rich king Cresus.

Al thynge whiche maye be throwen or cast with the hand, be it stone, wod, or irō it is also the generall name of al that, wherwith a man doth fyght, callyd weapon. some tyme it is taken for a sworde.
More hardy than nede, or wysedome requyreth, folehardy. somtime dredefull, or to be dradde.
Vnaduysedly, foolyshely, aduenturously, sometyme it sygnifieth almoste. also without cause.
The beame, whiche contayneth the yoke.

A place in Thessalia wonderful plesaunt, hauynge trees and medowes meruaylous delectable, wherin byrdes of dyuers kyndes, doo synge contynually with excellent melody. Therof al plesant woddes haue the name of Tempe.
Temperance, which is a firme and moderate gouernance of reson against sensualitie and other vycyouse affections of the mynde.
A temperance or moderation, in the mynglynge of thynges togyther.
Proprely in heate or colde▪ sometyme it is vsurped for temperamentum, and for temperantia.
To temper or moderate in order or measure. Temperamus stylum, calamum, appetitum, whan we keepe in cure wrytynge a meane fourme, or do eate noo more than is nedefull.
A cytie in the countrey called now Calabria.
Sygnifyeth sometyme the same tyme, somtyme tempest, sommetyme wether, sometyme a fayre wether.
That whyche is done in conuenyent tyme.
A temple or churche. sometyme it sygnifyeth heuen. Alsoo the principall beame of a house, also a sepulchre.
That whiche duryth vntyll a certayne tyme.
That whyche is doone sodaynly, and at a tyme.
That whiche dureth or contynueth for a tyme. also that whiche pertayneth to tyme.
An aduerbe sygnifieth in tyme, or by tyme.
Tyme, also the state of tyme. sometyme the temples of the heed.
Hardenes in sparynge of expenses, nygardshyp, perseueraunce, retaynynge, or kepynge.
The comparatiue and superlatiue degree of tenax.
Of mooste sure remembraunce. Tenaciter, fastly, surely.
A desyre to go often to the stoole, and may do nothynge, with a burnynge and sometyme a bloody siege.
That whiche holdeth faste, as glue. somtime sparyng or nygarde, to moche constant, hard to be moued.
To assay, to holde vp. Paruum que patri tendebat Iulum, He helde vp lyttell Iulus vnto his father. Also to prepare, to go towarde a place.
A nette or snare to take byrdes or beastes.
To extende or stretche, to lay a snare, to dwelle, to go. Tendere infidias, to lay in wayte.
Olde writers callyd them, whych had great teethe.
Lyers and crafty knaues. Also they whiche wyll not be seene abrode by day tyme.
An Ile in the see callyd Aegeum, betwene Mitelene and Hellespontum, not farre from Troye.
A quick or sharp axe: a prouerbe applyed to iudges, which be hasty and cruell in their sentences.
To holde, to apprehende, to possede, to holde or kepe in, to couer, to vnderstande, to kepe backe, to performe.
To be bounden, to be beholden to one.
Tender, mercyful. Also a geldyd manne.
To do by councill Praecipe, Plautus in milite. ut teneat consilia nostra, Gyue hym aduyse that he may do by our counsayle.
Tary, tary. Redi, quo iugis nunc? tene, tene, Tourne agayne, whither runnnest thou nowe? tary, tary.
To agree or consent vnto other.

o: Tenère insaniam. Sed hoc primum expurgare tibi uolo, me insania ne que tenere, neque mi esse ullum morbum, nisi quod seruio,
n: tenere insaniam sed hoc primum expurgare tibi uolo me insania ne que tenere neque mi esse ullum morbum nisi quod seruio
d: But fyrste I wyll declare my self vnto the, that I am neyther out of my wyt, nor haue any sycknes, but that I am bonde.
To take hede of hym selfe.
To take oone with a lye.
To vanquyshe or recouer agaynste one in a matter.
The greate and stronge synewes, whiche do kepe the necke vpryght. Also a broode synewe, whyche gothe frome the hamme downe to the heele.
An order, a contynuaunce of a thynge.
An yle in the greke see, one of them, whyche is callyd Cyclades.
A showe with an yron soole, wheron the ouer lether is stretched.
To attempte, to assay or proue, to tempte one to do euyll.
A venymous beaste in an Ile on the ryuer of Nilus, whose voice the cokodryll doth feare.
Very symple, or lyttelle in estimation.
With a small threde, applyed to style in wrytynge, whyche is not elegant, but playne.
Lyttell or symple in estimation, smalle in quantitie, poore.
To make smalle, to make leane, or feeble.
A share. Beinge an aduerbe, hit sygnyfyeth vnto. Tenus urbem tendit, It extendeth vnto the cytie, or noo further than the cytie.
A preposition, sygnifieth nyghnesse, or vntyll a thynge.
A vesselle, wherein water is made temperate, also a chaumber, whereinto men do go out of a bayne.
Meane betweene hotte and colde, warme. Also kolyd from heate Somtyme noyfull or vnprofytable.
A stoone, whyche hathe the fygure of a newe moone, in colour blacke, 〈◊〉 asshe colour.
A contray in Lacedemonia, where the fayre Helene was borne. also an Iland nowe callyd Corsica.

A tree, the wodde wherof is blacke and harde lyke boxe, oute of this tree rounneth a gumme, callyd commonly Turpentyne. All be it the common turpentyne is not it, but an nother, whyche is as cleere as glasse, and is a soueraygne medycyne to clense the stomake of putryfyed humours.
The thyrd. Tertio, & tertium, the thyrde tyme.
An awgour, wherewith holes are boored.
To bore or make an hole.
A lytel worm that eteth wod.
The mooste eloquente wryter of comedyes. Terentianus, of Terence.
A place in the fyelde by Rome, callyd Campus Martius, wherein was an aultar of Pluto and Proserpyne.
Longe and rounde, lyke a tree or a pyller. Teretrum, an instrument, wherwith a thynge is made rounde.
To run away, proprely in barasle.
Three chylderne borne at oone bourdeyne. Tergestes, a citie in Italye.
That whiche is made of a beastes hyde.
A nonsuite in the lawe, whan the pleintife gyueth ouer his suite.
To turne back, to deny, in the lawe it sygnifieth to be nonsuite.
The backe of man or beaste, or of any other thynge. sommetyme it sygnifyeth a hyde.
The extremitie, the ende of a thinge, also the sole of the fote.
A lynnen clothe, wherewith the body is couered.
A braunche plucked of a tree with the fruite on it. also a worme, whyche eateth the fleshe.
A mountayne in Lycia, callyd also Chimaera.
A potte for wyne, whyche was alway sette on the table, that euery manne mought take as moche wine as he wolde.
Was a certayne holy day, at the latter ende of the yere.
A mere stone, laid or pight at the ende of sondry mens landes.
A sygne whiche declareth oone mans lande from an other, or one contrey or territorie from an other. also it signifyeth the buttynge.

Was an ydoll, whiche was supposed to haue preemynence ouer the boundes of lande, whose temple had euer an hole in the roufe, for as moche as they thought it to be vnlefulle that boundes of lande shulde be couered or hydde.
To rubbe, to breke or broise.
To go his way. Terere tempus, to cōsume tyme. Terere otiū, to lyue idelly.
An olde musytian, whyche added .vii. strynges to the harpe.
Erthe: sometyme all the worlde, also a prouynce, a territorie, a countrey, land.
A byrde lyke to a larke, whiche we calle a huntynge.
He that is come vp of nought, and no man knoweth his kynrede.
Of erthe, or lyuynge on erthe, erthely.
Of erthe. Vas terreum, an erthen vesselle.
Terryble, that whyche is to be feared.
He that dwelleth in the lande.
A feare, or a fearfull thyng.
Terryble, or that whiche induceth feare.
Begotten on the erthe.Varro de ling. latin.
The fyeldes or countraye lyenge within the iurisdiction and boundes of a citie, a territorie.
Of olde wryters was taken for a fayre daye.
Wordes not perfytely pronounced: as whan one is in feare or drede of hym, to whome he speaketh, he tremblynge in speche, vnethe pronounceth the thyrde worde that he wolde saye.
Is a mixt mettall, wherin are two partes of leade, and one of tynne.
To do a thynge the thyrde tyme, or to make the thyrde tylth in earynge.

Where two haue bene Consules before hym. Tertium Consul, he that hath ben thryse Consul. So that Tertio signifieth the third in order, and place, two goynge afore. Tertiū sygnifieth the tyme, where twyse gothe afore. The lyke is of Secundo, quarto, and other numbres.
At the thyrde retourne or comynge agayne. Tertius, a, ū, the third.
A famous and eloquent autor. whyche for dyspleasure and malyce felle into heresye.
A poyse or coyn of thre ounces.
A place where misticalle ceremonies were exercysed.

Places harde or difficile to come vp to, where the Romaynes dyd practise their diuinatiōs by fleing of dirdis, callid auguria Tessellatus, ta, tum, that whiche is wrought with smal pieces of stone, wodde, or bone, as in playenge tables or counterbourdes.

That whiche is in euery part square as a dye. also it is a dye. more ouer a watch worde or priuie tokē gyuen to souldiours. Also a token of warre and peace, a token gyuen to people to receyue corne of the kinges almes. Also a taile, wheron is scored or marked the numbre of thynges receyued, whiche is also called Tesserula.
To dispoyle or pulle of a garment or harncis by vyolence.
A sharde of a potte or tyle. also an erthen pot. also all maner of shellfyshe.
A prouerbe applyed to sodayn alteration of thinges, or of banishment vnlooked for.
He that is deed, and hathe made a wyll also openly knowen of all men.
To putte the male to the female. Testillor, idem.
He or she that bereth wytnesse.
Wytnesse borne of a ioynge done.
To beare wytnes, to calle to wytnes,Cōtestor. Protestor Varro. to pray god.
That whiche is boyled in an erthen potte.
A roufe, which is holowe in foure partes.

A snayle. Also an engyne of warre to beate downe walles, whiche was made of bourdes, and couerid with lether or other thinges, which wold not bourne. within it was a piece of tymber, that had a great hoke of yron at the ende, whyche piece mought be plucked backe, and putte forthe with the strength of men, and therwith plucke stoones oute of the walles of townes besyeged, It is alsoo the roufe or vaulte of a howse.
Is a panne, wherin tartes, and other lyke thynges of paste are baken.
A medycine, wherwith the face of a man or woman is made smothe without wrynkles.
Whan the synnes are slyffe, so that a man can nat bowe some part of his body
The fourth part of the zodiake cirkle, wherin are the .xii. signes. It is also that, whiche astronomers do calle the quadrate aspecte of planettes.
Moste foule or stynkyng, or cruelle.
The wife of Neptunus, callid goddesse of the see.
A coyne, whyche was in value foure dragmas, or olde poyse grootes, of viii. to an ounce.
The name of god, whych the Iewes do call Ineffabile, that is to say, vnspeakable.
In greeke, sygnifyeth of foure letters.
A kynde of metre, hauynge but foure fete.
The rule of the fourthe parte of a royalme.
Of foure syllables, as, Im pe ra tor.
To make fowle, to pollute, to make bytter.
The name of a kynge of Troianes. also of the sonne of Telamone the valyant Greke.

o: Teucer, Teucra, crum, idem quod Troianus.
n: teucer teucra crum idem quod troianus

d: A Lyon, whyche Hercules dydde slee, whan he was a chylde, and of his skynne made hym a cote.
The herbe whiche is also callydde Tripolium.
A quene of Illiria, which lyued euer chaste, and vanquyshed many noble capitaynes, and diuers hostes of the Romains
Was in olde time amc̄g the french men taken for Mercurius.
A piece of the coūtrey of Troy.
To weaue or wind threde, Also to make to builde, to write, to gather, to ornate.
An hearelace, wherwith the heare is bounden vppe.
That which is weaued or woundē
An aduerbe, sygnifieng in weauing or wyndynge vp.
He or she that weaueth or wyndeth.
The place where thinges be weaued or wounden. also the craft of weauynge.
A woman, whiche warketh in a frame or stole.
A chamber where the husbande and the wyse do lye togither.
A prouerbe applyed to them that promyse great thynges, as a mā wolde say, a worlde, a countray of welthe.
Is a lycour made of honye, salte water, and rayne water, and is put into a vessell rased with pytche.
A philosopher, whiche was one of the seuen wyse men of Grecia.

Was a quene of Amasones, whiche came to kynge Alexander with three hunderde womenne with her, to the intente to haue issue by hym and his menne: and whanne she perceyued, that she and her ladyes were spedde, they departed home agayne.
Are in lyekes, garlyke, and oynyons, whan they do growe, the myddell s • alke betwene the blade and the heed or rote.
One of the graces, whiche the auncent poetes dyd suppose to be one of the doughters of Iupiter, and gyuers of dilectable speche, and plesant pronunctatiō.
Was he, whiche fyrste playd on a harpe, without syngynge therto.
An herbe lyke to senell, and hathe a yelowe flowre, and a flatte rounde sede.
Pyckelle, wherein fysshe is salted, and kepte.
Menne of the Ile callyd Thasus in Egypte.
A certayn wine, which is in Egipt.
In greke is a meruaile or myracle.

n: theatralis le amp theatricus ca cum

d: A place made halfe round, wherin the people assembled to beholde playes and sondrye sbate mentes, sometyme it sygnifieth the multitude that beholdeth.

o: Theboe, arum, Theba, be, & Thebe, bes,
n: theboe arum theba be amp thebe bes
d: The name of cities, wherof one was in Egipte, buildid by Busirides, an other in Boeotia, buylded by Cadmus: an nother in Cilicia, where Andromaches, the wyfe of Hector was borne.
A countraye of Egipt, it is also the name of a boke made by Statius the poete.
A case, a shethe or scaberde, a boxe.
People of an yle callid Capreae, whiche lyeth agaynst Naples.
A kynge, whyche camme in the ayde of the Troyanes, and was slayne by Achylles.
An herbe, whyche hathe beries lyke to an olyue.
A cite in Boeotia, where Pyndarus praysed Bacchus,

A thynge purposed to be disputed or resoned. it is also a figure, wherin astronomers doo write the state of heuen, in placinge or settyng the planettes in suche signes and degrees, as they be in at the tyme of a mans natiuitie, or whan any thynge shall happen that they serche for.
An olde towne in the ile of Lipres where brasse was fyrste founde.

One of the systers of Iupyter, she was callid the goddesse, whiche cōmanded men to aske that whiche was leful. There was an other woman callyd Themis, whiche was called also Carmentis, it was somtyme taken for fas, lefull.
A cite in Capadocia, afterward callyd Caesaria.
A philosopher which wrate cō mentaries on Aristotels warkes.

A noble capitain of the Athemensis, whiche beinge expelled out of his countrey, and commen to Xerxes king of Persia, was sent by hym with a great armye agaynste the Athenienses, but whan he perceyued his countrey in peryll to be distroyed, he dranke poyson, and chase rather to dye, than eyther to be vnfeythfull to Xerxes, or els to distroy his countrey, although it were vnkynde towarde hym.
A poete of Grecia, which wrate Bucolica, or the contention of herd men.
A noble phylosopher, and of excellent eloquence.
The chiefe citie of Syria, callyd also Antiochia.
A place where wylde beastes are kepte, as a forest, or parke.
A soore of the priuye members, wherby all the partes therabout, are corrupted, and therof issueth blacke and stinkynge humour.
A thynne vayle, which the women of Palestina dyd weare.
To chaufe or make oone hotte with outragious eatynge and drynkynge of hote thynges.
A place where meates and drynkes were solde, wherwith men were made hote or warme in cold wether.
To drynke hotte or warm drynke.

A mountayne in Greece, hauynge a narowe entrie or passage, where two thousand Lacedemoniens, with their capytayne Leonidas, faught agaynst fyue hundred and .xxviii. thousande Persyans▪ and resysted them two dayes, vntylle the sayd Lacedemoniens were all slayne.
Was a prynce that came with the grekes to the syege of Troye, whyche in persone and condicyons was of all other moste defourmed.
A noble and valyant kyng of Athenes, companyon to Hercules.
A clause in writyng or spekyng, whiche contayneth a sentence.
The ceremonyes of Ceres, the goddesse of grayne.
A rushe growynge in Nabachis, whiche hath the taste of sharpe wyne.
One of the sonnes of Hercules by Megara.
He that is burste or broken in his stoones.
Was the name of the father of Diomedes.
The name of two kynges, oone of Taurica, the other of Lemnos.
Be wolfes in Ethiope, Arrianꝰ doth calle them tygres in India.
A scochen or small tergate. also the the syldynge of a house, or a round house.
Lyches of hempe, wherwith halters are made, they be also lyttel bolsters, whiche men do weare whanne they carye burdeynes, for frettynge of theyr neckes and shulders with cordes or ropes.
He that fyrste brought phisyke in the fourme of a scyence, amonge the Egyptians.
The daughter of Phorcꝰ, on whom Neptunus gate Polyphemus.
He that wearethe curettys or breste plates.
Is proprelye the hole boulke of a man from the necke to the myddelle, it is also curettes or breste plates. sometyme it signifieth a towre.
A region of Europa, wherin is the citie of Constantinople.
A ryuer in Italye nyghe to Perusia.
A lamentacyon, whyche was vsyd a • buryenge.
Be one of the .ix. orders of angels.
The seate or chayre of an Emperour or kynge.
A trewell, whyche masons, tylers, and pargettours doo vse for layenge of morter.
An herbe callyd in Italye Strella & Bipinella.
To make a perfume, or to sence.
A diminutiue of thus. Also a cite in Latium.
Whome his owne brother Atreus causyd to eate his propre chylderne.
A woman, whyche fyrst taught daunsynge in open places.
Maye be callydde daunsers of Morysdaunces.
A wart, which is as great as a bean.

The stalke of letyse and of other herbes, whiche may be eaten. somme doo take it for a speare with a sharpe heade, whiche hadde boughes and leaues of yuy wrapped aboute them: suche speares dyd Bacchus and his flocke of drunken harlottes, beare in theyr handes. Lucretius the poete taketh thyrsum, for furye or an ardent mocyon.
The stalke of euery herbe, specially of letyse▪ It is also a staffe wounde about with yuy, whiche was borne of them that dyd sacrifyce to Bacchus.
An ornament, which the women of Persia dyd weare on their heedes, whiche was rounde, and couered onely the hynder parte of theyr heedes. Princis & pristis vsed also to weare it.
A cytie in the countray of Mis • a.
People in Scithia, being in Asia.
The leg, proprely the shanke or shinne bone, it is also an instrumēt callid a shalme.
He or she that blowethe a trumpette or shalme.
Is alsoo any thynge, whereby any thynge in buyldynge is susteyned, as a shore or proppe.
A baskette or coffyn made of wickers or bulle rushes, or barke of a tree:Origenes super Ex. suche one was Moyses put into by the daughter of Pharao.
Were dayes whan menne wente with trumpettes, as it were in processyon aboute their lambes.
People in Italy nigh to Rome.
A citye in Lumbardye nowe callyd Pauia.
A Carpentar that maketh a house of tymber.
A rafter of a house, whiche beareth the roufe. It is also generally all the tymber, which serueth to a hous.
A riuer in the countray of Media.
The propre name of a kynge of Media, of the greatter Armeny.
A beaste of a wonderfull swyftenes, it is also one of the foure ryuers, whiche commeth out of Paradyse.
People of Germanye, whiche do inhabyte the fourthe parte of Heluetia, or Swyzerlande.
An Ile beyonde Scotlande, callydde also Thule.
A tree, whyche some do thinke is callyd quyckebeame.
A citie in the weste parte of Sardinia, on the see syde.

An yle in the Indian see, wherein is plentie of perle, and trees of dyuers fruites, and the leaues of trees there growynge do neuer falle. also wolle groweth on trees there, whiche do beare goardes of the greatnes of quynces, and beynge type do open, in the whyche doo appiere the wolle, wherof are made fyne and precious clothes. About that place dothe begynne the mountain of Caucasus, whiche dothe passe through a greate parte of the worlde.
An herbe and flower growyng in waters, callyd commonly of potycaries Nenufer.
A noble phylosopher of Pythagoras secte.
A ryuer in Italy besides Aquileia.
He that feareth for a tyme.
He that alway feareth, callyd tymorouse.
I feare the as myn ennemy, leste thou shallt do me harme.
I am af • rd of the as my frende, leste thou shuldest haue any harme.
I am afrayde that thou wylte do me harme.
I am afrayde that one wyll seale myn appulles.
I am aferd that he wyl die
Ingi ossers or regraters of markettes, whiche doo bye moch corne or vitayle togyther, to make it scarse and dere.

Was the name of a noble capytayn of the Athemēfes, who for the good fortune that he had in battayle, was paynted lyenge aslepe, and hauynge by hym a nette pytched, wherin fortune was taken. Also a cunnynge musitian, whiche vsyd to take of his scholers, which had lerned before▪ double salarie, that he toke of other, whiche neuer lerned, sayeng, that he toke with them double labours, that is to saye, to make them to forgette that which they hadde lernyd afore, and thanne to teache them perfytely.
Olde wryters vs • d for Eum.
A greatte bolle, whiche being ful of wine, euery man mought drynke therof as moche as he lysted.
A mothe, they be also wormes in the bealye, also wormes breding in bee stalles.
A promontorie or elbowe of Affrica.
A parte of Mauritania or Barbaria agaynste Spayne.
To deepe a thynge into lycour, to dye colours.
To rynge or make a sounde as mettall dothe, sometyme as in a mās eare.
A ryngyng in the eare of a mā.Plaut. in ruden.

A byrd, which maketh a sharp ryngynge noyse, and is of the kynde of haukes, and in some place dothe brede in houses, whiche with his voyce dryueth away other hawkes, and therfore the byrdes of hym are kepte in erthen pottes couered with claye, and hanged vp in doue-houses, whyche causeth culuers meruaylousely to loue their house.
Sharpe in sounde, as that which is made by beatinge on metall.
He that beateth with roddes, a transgressour of a lawe.
An excellent carpentar, the whiche founde first the meane to gouerne a shyp, a rother.
A wurme, whyche runneth on the water as other wurmes doo on the lande, and hath sixe fete.
Was kynge of Thebes, who had the knowlege of thinges whyche shoulde happen, and was blynde.
A ryuer in Grecia: also the contray where Hercules was borne in Peloponesso, now called Morea.
A famouse olde citie in Grecia.
One of the furies of helle, which was supposed to tourment homycydes, or s • eers of men.
Was the brother of Saturne, and is taken for the sonne, and Titanis, for the moone.
An herbe callyd werte worte, wherof the mylke woll take away wartes.
An herbe whyche is commonly callyd Spurge.
To tyckle, to prouoke or meeue pleasantly.
A fyrebrande or wodde, whiche hath ben in the fyre.
To stacker in speking or going, as a man beinge drunke or sycke.
The title or inscription of a warke or acte. sometyme dignitie, also a monumēt or other remembrance.
The moste excellent hystorien or writer of stories, in whom was the foū tayne of the mylke of pure eloquence.
Was the kyng of the Rhodes, whiche camme to the battayle of Troye, with nyne shyppes.

The sonne of Iupiter, whom poetes fayned to be slayne by Apollo, bycause he wolde haue rauysshed Latona his syster. And therfore lyeth in helle, hauyng an egle alwaye eatynge his lyuer. And it is alsoo sayde, that his bodye was in lengthe nyne furlonge. wytnesse Tibulle, whiche was a poete, and also a greate louer, and therfore coulde not lye.
A mountayne in Lidia, wheron dyd growe great plentie of saffron and vynes. It is also a lyttell busshe, whiche beareth floures of saffron coloure.
Lytell byrdes, I suppose it be the byrde, whyche is callyd a tytmous.
The common garmente of men and women, callyd a gowne. And bycause the Romaynes specially dydde weare that garment in the tyme of peace, toga was taken for peace, as arma was for warre.
A garment whiche the Romains dyd weare afore that they were of the age of .xvi. yeres. Afterwarde it was worne of them, whiche were in auctoritie.
A garment made with thredes of sondrye coloures, as motleye or bauldekyn.
A comedye or enterlude, wherein the maners of the Romaynes, were expressed.
Was a garment, whiche they dyd weare, that sued for any great office in the citie of Rome.
That wherein any thynge is put or layde to be drawen vp.Vegetius. Budeus. sometyme a buckette wherwith water is drawen vp.
An engyne to drawe vppe water, whiche hath a great poise at the one ende
To suffre, to endure, to beare, to lyue poorely, or nyghly.
To lyue, or to maynteyne his lyfe.
That whiche maye suffre or beare.
To lyfte vppe, or sette vppe.
To sette vp the crest, applyed to them that be proude or arrogante, & do stretche vp their browes with a dysdaynfull countenaunce.
Hold vp thy fynger, confesse thy selfe vanquyshed.
To sette forthe, or to marche forthe.
To take away. Tolle hanc patinam, Plautus in milite. take away this dyshe.
To haue a chylde by a woman.
To nouryshe. Verum quod erit natū, Plautus in Amphit. • ollito, What soo euer is borne, putte it to nouryshynge.
To deferre or prolonge,Plautus. Omnes tollo ex hoc die in alium diem, I put them all of from one day to an other.
To speake faste oone worde after an nother.
A certayn sorte of pouddynges, proprelye swynes pouddynges.
Floxe, which is shorne of wollen cloth. also lockes clypped of white wolle.
Hempen cordes, also colers, whiche are put on carthorses, for hurtynge of their neckes.
A pece of a boke, or a warke vnperperfyte. Alsoo a citie in the countraye of Ponthus.

Was a noble queene of Massagetis in Scithia, agaynste whom whan Cirus the great kynge of Persia came, and hadde slayne her sonne, she pytchynge a fylde agaynste hym, and of purpose hauing great plentie of vytayles in her pauyllyone, after a lyttell skyrmyshe she and her host fled. And whan Cirus had a whyle folowed the chace, and blowen to the retraicte, he came to her campe, and fyndynge greate plentie of vytayle, he and his people dyd so moche fyll theym selfee therwith, that fallynge aslepe, they were all taken by the quene, and slayne, and she causynge a great vessell to be fylled with the bloudde of Cirus, and the Persyans, dyd caste his heed therinto, sayinge, Bloode thou haste thyrsted, and nowe drynke therof thy fylle.

A certayne shaulme with a softe sounde, on the whiche in the old time some oratours vsed to haue, to playe by theym, whan they pleaded, that by the tunes of the shalme, the oratour mought moderate and order his pronunciation.
To thunder, to make a greatte sounde or noyse, to speake loude.
Shepe, which be shorne or clypped. also ores of botes or shyppes.
That which is shorne or clipped.
A poste, hauynge the one ende armed with yron, whiche is pitched into the erth, to thende that shippes or botes may be tyed therat.
A dysese within the chekes and mouthe lyke to great kernels.
He or she whyche clyppeth or sheareth.
A place where they do vse to clip or a barbers shoppe.
A tune or accent. alsoo the space or distance, whiche is betwene the erthe and the moone.
He that hathe the gouernaunce and charge of one onely countrey.
A preciouse stone of the colour of golde.
A kynde of stone, whiche is soone resolued into sande.

A warke made of trees, bushes, bryers, or herbes, for pleasure, and contayned places to sytte or walke in, as it is vsed nowe with boxe, eglantine, iacymine, and other lyke trees or thornes, that be flexible, or wyll be wounden.
Warkes in that part of logike, whiche declareth the places, out of the whiche argumentes maye be inuented, that moste proprely pertayneth to oratours.
The description of a place, as of a countrey or citie.
The olde wryters vsed for soone,Festus. shortly, or quyckely.

In plurali numero, toralia, euery thynge that lyeth on a bed, as shatis blankettes and couerlyds. In the old time it were certaine floures and swete herbes wounden togyther in ropes, and hanged before the place, where men dyd lye. Like as nowe they vse in London at Mydsommer to hange afore their doores.

Frettynge or tourmente in the bealy and guttes.

He that hathe tourmentes or frettynge in his guttes.
That whiche is tourned with a whele.
May be nowe taken for a tournayment or iustes.
To torne or warke with a whele, as tourners done.
Slouthefulnes. also a fysshe, whiche in the takynge maketh the handes of theym that doo drawe, to be stonyed or deed for the tyme.

To wynde in,Vide ••• to whirle aboute lyke a whiele, to sustayne or beare vp, to tourment.
To throwe a darte or iauelyn, that he runne rounde.Vergilius
A colar, chayne, or bye of gold or syluer, suche as is worne by knyghtes or esquiers about their neckes.
To broyle or rost at the fire, or by the heate of the sonne.
A streame, that cometh downe of hylles, whiche is caused by moche rayne or snowe. Torrens, a particyple, sygnifieth flowynge with a great swepe. Torrentior, more flowing, with a greatter violence.

That whiche is bent or bowed.
A tourmentour, or he that casteth a stone with a slynge.
Ꝓprely in beholdyng sowerly or grymly.
An apparell of a womans heed.
A bedde, it was somtyme made with herbes wounden togyther.
The brawnes of the armes and leggis, or the fleshe myxte with synewes.
Myghty or stronge in brawnes of the legges and armes.
Theodorus, Gaza, & Longolius supposed to be a sturgion. Paulus Iouius is of a contrary opinion.
Verily so many, euen as many.
As many. Toties, so many tymes.
A yron pin or gret nail wherwith bemis ar made fast to the rafters
A cerklet or kyrtell worn by kynges vnder theyr mantell.

The ouer part of a fishe callid Mutex, of whom purple colour is made.
The weson or pype of the lunges.

The chine of a mā or beast, from the heed to the haunche.
A kynde of roses, not perfytelyted, lyke to them, that we call french roses.

On length, a longe tyme or space.
To intreate. Haec arte tractabat uirum, She handlid the man craftely, or of that sorte. alsoo to vse or exercise, to order or gouerne.
A windlas to draw vp heuy thīgis Tractus, us, a space, a countrey.
To delyuer, also to teache, to commytte in trust to an other man.
To brynge from oone place to an other, to brynge ouer, to translate oute of one language into an nother.
To passe the tyme, to brynge vp or nouryshe.
Vynes or trees translated frome place to place.
A beaste in parte lyke a harte, in parte lyke a gote.
That whyche are commonlye callyd bankettynge dyshes.
Cruelly, in the maner of a tragedy.
A tragedye, whiche is an enterlude, wherin the personages do represent somme hystorie or fable lamentable, for the crueltie and myserye therin expressed.
He that exercyseth some part in a tragedye.
A tree growynge in Candy, lyke to Iunyper, the iuyce wherof is lyke to mylke, and waxethe thycke lyke gumme.
Is lyke a tyzan made of wheate, it is also a fyshers nette callyd a dragge.
An herbe nowe callid Taragon, late sene in this realme, whiche hath a tast lyke gynger: whiche herbe layde to the lefte syde, consumeth the splene.
A byrde in Ethiopia, greatter thā an egle, & hath on his hed horne like a gote.
An herbe whiche I suppose, is callyd Peny royalle, growyng wylde.
A iauelyn with a barbyd heed.
An ile in the see callyd Hadriaticū ▪
Is a fyshe callyd a thornebacke.
A dray or slyd drawen wtout wheles.
A couetous persone, the whiche draweth all thynge vnto hym.
To passe the day, the nyghte, or the tyme.

To tary. At que egomet me adeo cumillis una ibidem traho, And I my selfe taryed as longe with them. Trahere, to liue. Et uosut turā tranquillā que fortunā traheretis, mea perfeci uigilantiā. And by my vygilancy I brought to passe, that ye shulde lyue in a sure and quiete prosperitie.
To draw, to leade, to deferre, or delay, to extend, to remoue, to prolong.

n: traiicto reci ijcete to leade ouer
d: To carye ouer, to brynge ouer, to stryke through.
A citie in Lidis, an other in Phrigia.
That a man maye loke through.
A good place to reste in, a place of quietenes.
Ouer, from one place to an other.
Fraunce on this syde the mountaynes.

Is to giue or deliuer. Turne tot incassum fusos patiere labores, Et tua Dardaneis trāscribi sceptra colonis? Wilt thou Turnus suffre thy labours to be lost, & thy realm to be giuen to the inhabytantes of Troy?
The transposition of a possession from one to an other.
To write out of a copie, sometyme to translate.
A course. In transcursu, In passynge forthe.
A loupe to loke out at. also a windowe, or casement. alsoo a rope stretched out, a snare or trappe.
To go forthe, to passe euer, to passe. Transire domum, to go home.
To cary or bryng from one place to an other, to translate from one langage to an other, or from ones possessiō to an others. Translatus, a, ū, the participle.
He that departeth from his own people or capytayne vnto the parte of the ennemies, or of theym that are suspected in tyme of truce.
To transfourme, to turne into an nother fygure.
Is to goo and yelde hym to the contrary parte.

To translate frome one to an other. Libentius omnes meas laudes (si modo sint aliquae meae laudes) ad te transfuderim, Ci. Dol • . I haue more wyllyngly tourned my prayse, (yf I haue any prayse) vnto you.
To fle from place to place.
To poure oute of one vessell into an nother.
To passe or go ouer or beyonde, to excede, to transgresse a law or commaundemente.
Is a figure of retorike, where a mā leaueth the principal matter, & entreth into an other thing, & after returneth to his matter. We cōmonly call it, a digression.
To passe his or their lyfe.Salust. Plaut. in Amphit Terent. in Andria.
To dryue furth, to treate a mater, to agree or condescende, or come to a point: as hapneth betwene men, which do contend for somwhat.
A passing ouer, a going forth.
A trāslation, or brynging frō one place to another. Trāsle go, ere, to rede ouer
That whiche cōmeth from beyonde the se.
A departinge or goynge frō one place to dwell in another.
To go further, to dwell further of, to transpose my dwellynge.
A going or sēding further or ouer
To passe ouer the see.Plin. ep •• 173. Epist. 183. Epist. 16
To sende from one place to an other, to go or runne quickly, to send shortly or quickly to passe ouer a water
To remoue frō one place to an other. Transnato, are, to swym ouer.
To be sene thrugh a thinge.
In quiet or rest frō hēsforth
Transoms which do go ouerwhart a house▪ also the seates, wheron they do syt, whiche do rowe in a shyppe or bote.
That whiche is or dwelleth beyonde the ryuer of Tyber.
To waade ouer a shalowe place of a ryuer.
To tourne hastily away from the purpose which a man went about.
Not to go a nayle bredth from it. A prouerbe signifieng a litle distance. Trāsuersū digitū, idē.
Ouerthwart, not straight or direct. Transuerto, tere, to turne away, or out of the right facion or way.
To se through a clere thīg.
That which is writē out of a record, and approued vnder the kinges seale, or the sygnynge of the iudge. In the common lawe they calle it an exemplifycation. Some do also call it a Transumpte.
A figure callid also Metalepsis, wherby one signification is gathered of an other: as of Nox atra, a blacke nyghte, is gathered Nox tenebricosa, a darke nyght.
To flye ouer, or leape ouer. or to go or runne beyonde a place.
To take of or from an nother, to remeue from one to an other
A myl wherin oyle is made
A table, wheron an exchāger doth tel money. Trapezita, an exchāger or bāker
A citie in the countrey of Pontus, Trapezuntius, a man of that citie.
A certain rosine or gumme, the best of that which is callyd gummihamoniacum.
He that spekith with gret difficulti
Wine growing about the riuer of Trebia, in Lū bardye, the Italions do call it Trebiana.
An olde towne nygh to Rome.
To make to tremble or quake. Tremisco, scere, to tremble.
To quake as one doth in a feuer. also to feare. Tremulus, he that quaketh for feare. Tremor, oris, quakyng, also feare.
Fearful, also he that doth a thing hastily. Trepōdo, thre poūd weight.
A citie in Germany callid Tryre.
Were thre which spake togither in a tragedy. Triangularis, re, hauīg .iii. corners
A master of a shyp with .iii. tops.
Soudiors that be set alway in the rere warde, which were the strongest men, they faught stāding, bowing their knies, as they wold rather dy thā remeue frō their places
A festiuall day kept after the third Idus of euery moneth.
They which be worne with stripes
A fote in meter of .iii. short sillables. Tribula, & tribulum, a flayle or other lyke thing, wherwith corne is threshed.
A kynnesman that commeth of the same stocke that I do.
To be troubled with heuynes of mynde. Tribulus, a bremble.
The place where a Iudge sytteth in iudgement.
The office or dignite of a tribune

Was an offycer amonge the Romains, hauinge chiefe iurisdiction amonge the communes, also a capytaine in warres, hauynge auctoritie ouer soudiours, to view and see that they were welle armed and exercysed. Tribunitius, a, um, pertaynynge to the Tribunes.
To gyue, sommetyme to sette moche by. Also to fauour.

A part of the people, somtime diuided into thre partis. It semeth that it was somtime taken for a family or particular iurisdiction among the people, and therof cometh tribulis. And therfore the partition of the people of Israel were into .xii. Tribus. hereof be sondry opinions. rede Calepine.
By sondrye families or partes of the people. Tributum, tribute.
Fethers in the fete of chykens & pygeons, whiche do let them to go, and therfore all thinges which do let a man ar callid Tricae. Vide extrico, & intrico.
A garment, whiche was so fyne, that it semed to be made of smalle heares.
Cometh of triginta, thirtie. it is sometyme taken for tricentenum.
A vessell hauynge thre lauers, oute of the whiche water is poured.
A parlor to sup in, wherin were thre tables and thre beddes. For in the old tyme they vsed to lye, whan the • dyd eate.
The seruaunt, which doth serue in the parlour.
Pertaynynge to the parlour or dynynge chaumber.
Men hauynge soure couuntenances, and that be neuer or seldome sene to laugh. Also pykers of quarels.

Was oone whiche dranke or he rested, thre mesures of wine, callid congii, whiche as I suppose, was thre galons and a pynt of our wyne mesure. wherfore Tiberius the Emperoure promoted hym to honour, and at the last made hym Consul of Rome.
A stone, which although it be black yet sheweth he at the roote blacke, in the myddell sanguyne, at the toppe whyte.
An oyster so greate, that a manne must make of hym thre morsels.
Euery instrument, toole, or wepon, hauynge thre tethe.
A coyne whiche is the third part of a pounde, it is also a cuppe cuntaynyng that poyse.
An herbe, whiche hath leaues as great as the coyne callyd triens.
A vessel containing the thirde part of that mesure, which was named Sextariū.
The capytain of a shyppe, whiche is callyd trieris.
A greate shyppe, whiche hathe in it thre orders of seates for the rowers.
That whiche hapneth to be done euery thirde yere
In .iii. partes, or thre maner of wais.
A weapon of thre cubytes longe.
That which bryngeth frute thryse. Triferus, a, um, idem.
Is a medycyne and other delycate spyces, to expulse easily corrupt humours
The buttyng of thre feldes, whiche ioyne togyther.
Maye be taken for the generalle name of all herbes hauynge thre leues. Al be it there is one herbe callid so proprely.
More than a thefe, three tymes wars than a thefe. Semblably tri, ioyned with any thyng, signifieth more.
A carte drawen with thre horses.
A certain course with such cartis
He whiche hathe or hath hadde three wyues.
A place by campū Martiū, at Rome

To bynde or to drawe a thynge clo • e togyther.
That whiche is thre cornerde, hauyng thre lynes.

Is named of .iii. signes in heuen, whiche contayne .lxxxx. degrees or porcions. wherfore Timorion, is in calculation of natiuities from the time of the birth or cōception, the .lxxx. & tenth part or degree.
A lampe or candellstycke, bearynge thre lyghtes.
He which is thre discentes lyneall from my chyldes chylde.
A woman in lyke degree of blode as trinepos is.
The thirde faire or markette, whiche was wont to be proclaimed, to the intent that it shuld be the better remēbrid.
A man worthe thre halfe pens, of lyttell value.
Thre halfe pens, or worthe three halfe pens.
Plough oxen. Alsoo they be seuen sterres beinge in the northe.
A lyttell stone, hauynge in hym the fygure of thre eyen.
A kynde of hawkes, hauynge three stoones.
An Aduerbe, sygnyfyenge in three partis.
Three folde, treble, a table with thre leaues.
To do or fold a thing .iii. times.
A countray in Affrica, an other in Syria, the thyrde in Phenicia.
A towne in Vmbria in Italy, so callyd bycause it hath thre brydges.
A man whiche founde the vse of grayne in the countray of Athenes.
Euery thynge that hath three feete. Tripodes, were alsoo tables in the temple of Apollo, of golde.
A fygure three cornerde. It was also a name of the Ile of Sicile.
The name of Mercurius, in latyn Ter maximus.
A chamber in the third storye or floore of a house.
Is also taken for doctus, Iudex tristis & integer, A iudge welle lerned and of a good conscience.
Agaynste his wyll, not well content.Terent. in Eunucho.
Sorowfull, heuy, also cruelle, of moche grauitie, bytter, more difficile or hard▪ sometyme angry.
An herbe whiche hathe thryse in the yere flowres.
One callyd god of the see.
Commune or of smalle estimation vsed or taught in hyghe wayes, alsoo rude, not elegant.
Where ways do mete, also a place where commune recourse of people is.
Communely, in the vulgare or homely facyon.

Was spoken in scorn of hym, that wolde seeme to be a gentylle man, where he was none, whyche worde was made by this occasyon, that amonge the olde Romaynes gentylle men vsyd to wryte theyr names with three letters, as Q, F, M, for Quintus Fabius Maximus. Also this prouerbe was spoken of them, whiche were theues, bycause that Fur, contayned but thre letters.
He that tryumpheth or hathe triumphed for vaynquishyng his enmyes.
Of the whiche oone hath tryumphed.

A triumph, whiche is a solemne pompe or ceremonie, where a prince, a cō sul or principal capitayn of an armye, hath had vyctorie of the ennemies of his countray, & therfore is brought home & receyued with al reioycing & honor that may be deuised of the people. The order & forme therof ye may se in Titus Liuius, Apianus, and Iulius Capitolinus.
One of theym whyche is in anye office, wherof be thre in like auctorite.
Pertaynynge to an office or auctoritie, wherin be thre persones.
Is an offyce in the publyque weale, wherin thre men haue equall iurisdiction togyther. Triumuiratus, the office or auctoritie of triumuit.
A worme lyke to that which is callyd Locusta, but he hath no wynges.
The citie of Troy, and the coū trey aboute it callyd the lasse Phrigia.
A foote in meter, whiche is of two longe syllables, and one shorte.
A lyttell byrde, whiche is callyd kynge of byrdes.
A lyttell whele. Alsoo trochisci, be of phisitians callyd, lyttell balles flatte at bothe endes, whiche be made of sondry poulders.
A certayne stoole or chaire, whiche wyll be tourned aboute.
A top, wherwith childern do play.
A poley wherin ye cord rūneth, wherby any thynge is drawen vp. it is also the gyn, whiche is callid a crane.
A citie in the parte of Grece, callyd Peloponesus. It is also a countraye in the lasse Asia.
The citie of Troy. also the countrey wherin Troye stode.
Was a playe of chylderne on horsebacke.
He that dothe a shrewde tourne, and runneth away whan he hath done.
Was a marke or token of tymber or stone, sette in the place where enemyes were vanquyshed or put to flyghte, sometyme it is taken for vyctorie.
A kynde of bulle russhes, the sede wherof wyll make one to slepe.
Wyndes, whyche doo comme from the see.
A fygure, a maner or facion, an alteracion of a worde or sentence from his propre signification.
A Troyane. alsoo the name of a kynge of Troianes.
In the olde tyme was taken for a horsman or man of armes. It is also a person delycate, well fedde or fleshy.
A vessel wherwith water is throwē into the synke.
Wherin meate is put whan it is roste or sodden. It is alsoo a pyssepotte, of somme it is taken for a great cuppe, brode and deepe, suche as greatte masers were wonte to be.
A trewell, wherwith masons, tylers, and pariettours do lay morter.
He or she that cutteth in pieces.

That whiche maye be tourned and dryuen about with a mans hande.

A wayenge balance. sometyme it is taken for iudgement.
A puffe growyng on the groūd lyke a musheron or spunge. It is alsoo generally euery swellynge in a mans bodye or vysage. It is alsoo in a tree lyke to a greatte knotte.
A lyttell pype, wherin water runneth from a sprynge. it is also a riede.
A pype, wherin water is conuayed to a cundyte.
The pype of a cundyte. it was also a thynge, wherewith they made walles hote, before there were chymneis.
A meate made with choppid fleshe lyke to a gigot or alowe.
A ladell, a pryntynge yron, wherwith vessell is marked.
To steere, to prynte a marke.
The name of a man, so callyd bycause he had a heed as bygge as a betyll.
To defende. alsoo Tueor, túeris, to see.
Some suppose them to be ryuers, som flowinges of bloudde out of sondry membres or ioyntes.
A dungeon within the common pryson of Rome.
Than, whan he gothe before cum, it sygnifieth as welle.
A holowe place in the grounde, a sepulchre.
To make the grounde holowe, to burye.
That whyche is doone without aduysement, or in haste.
A lyttell hylle or barowe, sommetyme a tombe.
To smyte, to braye or beate as in a mortar.
A citie in Affrica callid now Tunise.
Olde writers vsed for Nosco, nosce, to knowe.
My iackette is nerer than my gown. a prouerbe applyed where we wyll signifie that all frendes are not to be lyke estemed or made of.
To beholde, all be hit that worde is not in vse.

A multitude or assemblye of people. Quid illec turba est? nūnam ego perij? Terent. in Eunucho. Terent. in Heautont, What a multitude is yonder? am not I vndoone for euer? Also it signifieth trouble. Propter eam haec turba at que abitio euenit, For hyr sake is all this trouble or dissension.
Rounde and sharpe, lyke a toppe.
To make sharpe at the ende.
Is a thynge myxte with the lycour, wherwith woulle is dyed, which maketh the dye to synke into the woull, wherby the colour is made perfyte.
A boystouse wynde, whyche dothe blowe downe trees and houses, also a toppe, wherwith chyldern do play. It is generally all thynge, whiche is round and brode aboue, and sharpe benethe.
A byrde, whiche is delycate in eatynge, a thrustell or blacke byrde, alsoo a fyshe callyd an hadocke.
A companye of souldiours, contaynynge .xxxii. horsemen.
To defyle, dyshonest, or brynge out of good facyon.
A toure or any thing made like to it.
A lyttell towne. also a boxe, oute of the whiche dyse are throwen.
That whiche beareth a towre, as an Elyphaunt.
High, also towred, or fulle of towres. also the name of the ydol, whiche was callyd mother of goddes.
A byrde callyd a turtelle. It is also a fyshe.
Pellettes of bread or past, wherwith capons or other foules ar crammed. Also a tente whiche surgeons doo put into a wounde.
Frankyncense, it is alsoo wrytten whi • h 〈◊〉 , as thus.
A countrey in Italye, wherin be the cities of Florence, Sene, Luca, and Pise.
A lyttelle piece of frankincense. also a citie by Rome.
An herbe, whiche puttethe away the cough. some men suppose it to be coltes foote.
Was supposed to be a god, whiche had the custody of men.
The wardshyp or custody of infātes.
The saint whom we do take for our speciall aduocate to god.
Was callydde a Goddesse, vnder whose custodye was corne, whyche was in barnes or rykes.
To defend. Tutor, taris, tari, idem.
A garden, he that hath the warde of an infante.
A top of the heare wounden with a purple lace on the crowne of a womans heed, whiche was only worne of her that was wife to the great priest at Rome, callyd Flamen Dialis.
Sure, defended from peryll, out of daunger.
A gret riuer, which is by Rome
The name of an emperoure of Rome.

d: The father of Diomedes the noble capytayne, whome Venus dyd wounde at the battayle of Troy.
Callyd also Thule, an ile within one dayes iourney of the frosen see.

A worme, whyche lyeth vnder stones and tyles, whiche haue lyen longe on the grounde, and is somewhat blacke and scalyd, and hath many legges, whych beinge touched, closeth hym selfe rounde as a pease, and is moste commonlye callyd a cheselyppe.
A great felde in the countreye of Troy, through which the ryuer of Tymber runneth into the riuer of Scamander.
One of the sons of king Prtamꝰ.
He that playeth on a drumslade or tymbrell.
A woman that playeth on a tymbrell.
A kynde of dropsy, wherin the bealy swelleth great, a tympany, whereof wynde is the chiefe occasyon.
To play on a tymbrell, tabour, or drumslade.

A tymbrel, a tabour, or drumslade. Seruius calleth it a couered charyotte or carte, other doo suppose it to be the strake of a carte whele. I suppose that it may be taken for that, whyche is callyd the corse of a charyotte or horselytter, made with bayles or bourdes ioyned, whiche is not moche from the opynyon of Seruius.
Is also a great whele, wherein men do goo and drawe vp water. It is also a platter, whiche serueth for meate.
People in Etholia, whyche is in Grecia.
The father of the fayre Helene, for whom Troy was destroyed, and alsoo of Castor and Pollux.
Was a great gyant, the sonne of Tytan. It is also a greate puyssaunt wynde.
Be certayne impressyons in the ayre lyke globes of fyre or dartes.
Was a carpenter, whiche fyrst dyd fynde the way to gouerne a shyppe.
A fygure, an example, or a fourme, a lykenes or shadowe of a thyng.
A cruelle or violente rule or gouernance for a priuate commoditie, and not for a publyke weale.
Of the yle callyd Tyrus, Also vyolette or purple colour.
A yonge souldiour or manne of armes. Also he that fyrst entreth into the experience of any science, art, or exercise.
Of a younge souldiour or lerner.
The fyrst exercise in any thing.
A cite in Phenicia. also an yle, where the colour of purple was fyrste founden.
A veraye younge sowldiour or yonge lerner.
The circuite without the walles of a town, wherin mē may walk for their solace.
A cowe. Also a citie in Numidia.Salust • in •• gurt.
Madde, without wytte, percloses or railes, made of tymber, within the whych some thynge is inclosyd.
To moue inconstantly, to wagge or waue, to be vnstable, or vnsure.

The flowre, whiche is also callyd Hyacinthus, and hath longe leaues, a roūd roote, a stalke of a spanne longe and more, hauynge on it many purple floures, wherwith in some places they do dye pourple. I doubte whither it be the flowre whiche is callyd Hartis ease, or Swete wyllyam.
A waggynge or wauerynge and inconstant meuynge.
Letters wrytten crokedly or out of order.
A wytnesse, whiche inconstantly dothe varye in report or deposition.

It serueth to no purpose, it is superfluous. Also it sygnyfyeth, I am at good leysure, or withoute busynes. sometyme it sygnifyeth to care or force. Et cui esse deserto vacat, And who careth to be wel spoken or eloquent.
Vacation, or tyme whan a man is out of his common busynes.

To applye wytte or studye. Vaco sapientiae, I applye my study to wisedome. Vaco rei diuinae, I apply my wytte to goddes seruyce. Also to be emptye or voyde. Fac uacent aedes, cause the house to be voided. Vacat occupatione, He is without occupation or ydell. Somtime it signifieth to be superfluous, or vnprofitable.

Voyde, emptye, or withoute a thynge.
A mynde withoute care or solycitude.
Was callyd a goddesse, vnto whom husbandmen after that haruest was cleane done, dyd sacrifyce, as to the goddesse of quyetenes after labour.
Suretie to appiere at a day • assygned.
He that vndertaketh for an nother.

To be able, to be hoole. Male ua • eo, I fare yll, I am yll at ease.
To be stronge or puyssant, to may do, or be of force or power. Neque tam imperita, ut quid amor ualeat, ne sciam, I am not suche a foole, but I knowe what loue may do, or of what power loue is.

Farewel he, I care not for hym. Imo habeat, ualeat, uiuat cum illa, well lette him wedde her, I care not for him, moch good do it hym with her: or let hym haue her, god be with hym, lette hym make merye with her.Cicero. Si deus talis est, ut nulla gratia, nulla hominum charitate teneatur ualeat, If god be suche oone, that he hathe neyther fauour nor loue to mankynde, I care not for hym.Terent. in Andria. Valeant, qui inter nos dissidium uolunt, They that wyl haue vs at variance let them get them hense.
The sister of Messala, wyfe to a noble man callyd Seruius, who beinge deed, whan she was asked, why she dyd not marye agayne, she answered, that she alwaye lyued by Seruius her husbande.
A place where men do lye, whan they be sycke, as the fermerye in a monasterye.
An instrument to make flores smoth.Plinius.
A question in rebuke of one.
He that hathe his legges or feete bowed inwarde.
Nowe and than sycke, oftentymes sycke.
Pertaining to a trench in a feld.
A garlande gyuen to hym▪ whyche fyrste entred into the trenche of the enemyes campe.
Olde writers vsed for perierit, he is loste or peryshed.

Dorc • whiche be shut on two partis.

Olde wryters vsed for fallens,No. Mar. deceyuynge.
A countray in the northe parte of the worlde.
To vanysshe, to be broughte vnto noughte.
A lyer or teller of folyshe tales.
Voyde or empty. Also folisshe or enuyous, a maker of lyes.
A vapour, or hot breth issuynge out of a thynge.
A place made hotte to sytte in in the wynter tyme.
To hete or make warm a place
Wyne, whyche hathe loste his verdure. It is sometyme taken for a manne, in whome is no wytte or perfyte reason.
Ar vaynes whiche do swelle excedyngly.
He that hath such vaynes swollē.
To transgresse, to passe ouer a thynge neglygently.
Painted or garnished with sondrye colours.
Was a noble Romayne, of all other moste excellently lerned.
A ryuer, whiche dyuydeth that part of Fraunce, that is callydde Narbonensis, frō Italy. Also it was the name of a poete
A suretie, he that vndertakethe for an other man. also a pledge.
A goldsmythe, the whiche maketh plaate.
To crye to trusse vp caryage and baggage, as whanne an armye dothe remoue.
A horselytter, or any thynge borne by two horses.
To be distroyed, to be dryed vppe, to be forsaken.

That whiche is spoken in a prophecye.
He that hath croked legges outwarde.

Where▪ in what place, somtyme whan, after. Vbiloci, idem.
In all places, euery where, in all.
Alsoo it is putte for uel, or que .
To haue moche to day, and nothynge to morowe, sodaynly ryche, and as sodaynely poore.
A tribute, a pencion, a rent, a yerely reuenewe.
He that payeth trybute, pencyon, or rente.
A barre. also a leauer, wherwith thinges be lyfte, or borne by men.
He that is caryed, sometyme he that caryeth.
Caryage, also the hyre or moneye gyuen for caryage.
A noble man that wrate of marciall doctryne.
To recreate, to quycken, to conserue.
Was callid a god which had no power to do good, but onely harme.
In the old Tuscane tonge was a cart.
A generall name to all thynges, whyche serueth for caryage.
People, with whom the Romayns had longe tyme warres.
Or, sommetyme also, chiefely, namely, at the leste.
A place in Rome. It may be also callyd a tent, whiche craftes men do sette vp, where they haue noo howses, to be in stede of their shoppes.
Clothes, wherwith tentis ar made. also the same tentes.
A souldiour that weareth light harneyse.
A f • nne in Italy, in the countreye of Calabria.
A strete in Rome, by the hyll callyd Mons Palatinus.
Battayle done by them that are lyght harneysed.
