To plucke vp, or pull a thynge.
To couer or hyde, to bynde, to apparayle.
That whiche is sette to sale.
A place where any thing is sold.
An Ile, wherein be many vaynes of mettalle.
Easy or redy to be solde.
The act and craft of poysoning.
A maker of poyson, a vser of sorcerie.
Poyson, it is the general name of all that dothe alter the nature or colour of that thinge, wherwith it is myxte.
He that dothe wourshyppe any thynge. Venerandus, idem.
Values in Brytayne. Also the people of Venyce.
Of Venyce. Alsoo the colour of lyght blewe or blunkat.
Pardon, forgyuenesse. Tua venia, by your lycence.
To hunte, to gette a thynge craftylye.
Thynges that seme to be dangerous, and yet therin is no daunger.
The bealy or panche. sometyme it is taken for the stomake.
A fanne or f • abelle, wherewith wynde is made.
A vanner or wynnower of corne.
To gather wynde, to vanne or wynowe corne, to tourne out of one hande into an nother.
To lyue by the wynde. A prouerbe applyed to theym, whiche haue noo substance to lyue on.
The wynde blowethe a good coole.
Callyd goddesse of loue, somtyme lechery, also carnall appetite, alsoo beautie, by whiche a man is styred to loue.
Beautie, proprely of women. somtime a dilectable pronūciatiō or speche
He or she that sayth truthe.
To speake to a deed mā, a prouerbe whan a man loseth his labour.

An herbe wherof be .ii. kindes: of which one is supposed to be Molin or long wort, the other is supposed to be that whiche is callyd primerose, not withstandynge other menne redynge the description, lette theym iudge at theyr lybertie.
An herbe callyd veruyn. sometyme Verbenae, are all leaues sodeinly plucked vp, to garnyshe howses or churches, or to make garlandes.
A small longe stycke or yarde.
A persone worthy punyshement, the reproche of all seruantes.
Was one of the ambassadors sēt fro the Romans vnto their enmies, whiche ware on his heed a garland of veruyn.
An aduerbe, signifienge with many wordꝭ. Verbositas, moch talking or speking.
As by example. Verbi gratia, idē.
A worde, also a sentence comprised in one worde, a prouerbe.
Was a citie in Liguria, nigh to the mountayns called Alpes. Veré, truely.
A messanger that rideth by post.
A lyght horse, a huntynge nagge, or swyfte geldynge.
Places in a man and woman, which without shame may not be named.
To feare as the child doth the father. Timêre, to feare, as the slaue or boye dothe his mayster.
I am aferde of the, leste thou wylt doo me dyspleasure.
Truthe in speakinge a true tale.
He or she that telleth truthe.
To verifie as lawyers do say, to auerre
A felde diuided amonge the people, so that euery mā may haue a porciō.
An aduerbe, sygnyfyenge in smalle pieces.
To be fulle of vermyne or wourmes.
Warkes whyche are of small pieces of dyuers colours, wherin ar sette out sondrye pyctures, lyke as we see in spruse tables or counters.
Pryckinges in the body, that it semeth wormes were cutte asonder.
The dysease of the wourmes, proprely in cattell.
Full of wormes, or that wherin wormes are.

A worme. Also it is a fishe in the riuer of Ganges, whiche is in length .lx. cubytes, and is blue in coloure, whiche hath suche strength, that whan oliphantes com to the water and do drynke, he wylle take one of them by the nose, and plucke hym into hym.
A bondeman or bondewoman, borne in the house of the lorde, or in his owne countreye.

Al that taketh beginning in our owne contrey, as Vernacula lingua, the countrey language, the cōmon speche, peculyar or propre to countrey or howse. Vernaculi, be also men of ylle maners and language, whych vse to flatter or to speake in rebuke.
Cuttynge of vynee in the sprynge of the yere.
Pertaynynge to the sprynge of the yere. also seruyle.
The olde skynne of an adder. It is sometyme taken for age.
Olde wryters vsed for a flatterer.
To sprynge, as herbes done, also to synge as byrdes done.
Lusty, freshe, as the spring time.
Truely, verily. somtime it doth affirme that which foloweth. also but yet.
Is also a ryuer in Byskay.
People dwellynge nyghe to the ryuer of Vero.
That whiche hath no skyn. It is also the myddell fynger.
An altar at Rome, wherat they prayid that children shulde not be wronge borne.
A hogge vngelded, a tame bore. as aper may be called a wylde bore.
To tourne or chaunge a thing vnto better.
An hyllocke or knappe on a hylle. also a warte.
Old writers toke for a hye place.
Thingis that ar tourned or wounden one about the other, as two cordes or two styckes woūden togyther. also pillers made of the same facion.
That whiche tourneth or maye be tourned.
Chaungeable, or that which changeth colour. also of sondry colours.
Any thyng tourned out of his naturall colour. also that whiche is of dyuers colours mixt togither.
A crafty person that wyll tourne often as he lysteth.
The needell in a shyppe, to knowe the costes. Versor, aris, ari, to be occupied in a thynge or matter.
A tournynge. it is also whan a man boroweth of oone to pay his dettes to an other. and to borow in suche wyse is Versuram face • e.
Is to chaunge creditours, as to borowe of one man to pay an other.
A verse. sometyme an order. also a songe. Versus, towarde.
A hounde whyche wylle hunte by hym selfe.
God gyue the therof good lucke. Di bene uertant, I pray god tourne it to good.
Places in the bodye, where the boones doo not meete: but are knytte togyther in suche wyse with synewes, that they may tourne the more lyghtly.
To rounne awaye, or flye in battayle.
To goo and dwelle oute of a mans propre countrey.
To repute foly in a thyng.
To put the blame in one. Quis erit, uitio qui id non uerta • tibis? Who is it, that wyll not put the blame in the?
To translate▪ or interprete oute of one tunge into an nother.
A whyrlewynde. also a whyrlepoole in a water. also the crowne or toppe of the heed. also the toppe of euery thynge.
A wherue, whyche is a rounde thyng set on a spyndel, to cause it to turne.
A sicknes of the heed, wherin it semeth to a man, that he seeth thynges tournynge.
To tourne, to drawe, to translate, to consyder.
The solemnitie of Vertunus, whiche was kept in Octobre.
Was callyd the god of bieng and selling it is somtime taken for the yere.
A castynge darte with a strynge.
An instrument of goldesmithes lyke a lyttell broche.
True, substanciall, vncorrupted, good, iuste, profytable.
An aduerbe, signifieth truly. also but.
To eate, to vse. Actius vsed it to see.
Euery thynge that may be eaten, also lyttell or leane.
Browse, leaues, wheron beastes doo feeds in wynter.
An herbe, whiche potycaries do calle Alkakengi.
A mountayn by Naples which sendeth out continually smoke & fire.
They whiche do burye deed cors • s.
The euenynge, or euentyde, also the euenynge sterre.
An aduerbe, signifienge late, at the ende of the daye.
Old wryters vsed for coena, supp.
That whyche is doone in the euenynge.
He that burieth menne in the nyghte tyme.
The doughter of Saturnus, whiche for her chastitie was honoured for a goddesse. sometyme it is taken for pure fyre.
Were virg • ns, whyche mynistred to Vesta.
A warderobe, wherein garmentes are layde.
The yomā of the robes, or he that hepeth the warderobe.
A voide place without the dore, where men do tary whyles they do knock and vntyll the doore be opened.
A yonge man, which beginneth to haue a berde.
He that seketh for a thinge.
The prynt of a mans foote in the ground. It is taken also for a sygne or token of any thynge that is doone.
To apparel, to adorne, to ke • er
A mayden whiche layeth vp her maystresse garmentes.
A vesture, a garment, sometyme it is put for a bearde.
He or she which kepeth their maister or maistres apparayle.
A mountayne in Liguria by Alpes, at the rote wherof the riuer callyd Padus or Po, spryngeth out.
Sometyme signifyeth olde. Also he that had serued a hol • yere in the citie. sometyme he that hath longe continued in warres, an olde soudiour.
Beastes whiche do serue for burdeyne, as horses, mulettes, and asses.

To shake a thynge, or to make a thynge to shake or quauer.
The sprynge whyche commethe out of the roote of a tree.
That whiche is in the steede or place of an other. Also the seruaunte of hym, whiche is a seruant.

Etenim vt circumspiciamus omnia, quae populo grata, ar que iucunda sunt: nihil tam populare quàm pacem, quàm concordiam, quàm otium reperiemus, for put the case that we mought se perfitely all thinges that were plesaunte and delectable vnto the people, we shoulde nothinge fynde, that they so moche desyre, as peace, as concorde, as vacacion from laboure.

A people in Asia whose citie beinge besieged of the captayne of Cirus, they brought into the castelles theyr wyues, seruantes, and goodes, and puttynge thervnto fyre, bourned all togyther, and afterwarde issuinge out of the citie, faught vntyll that they were all slayne.

A fygure, wherby many sences • r ioyned togyther with one verbe, as, Ne que is es Catilina, ut te, aut pudor a turpitudine, aut metus a periculo, aut ratio a furore reuocarit, Ne thou arte suche a man Catilyne, as eyther shamefastnesse canne withdrawe from dishonestie, or feare from daunger, or reason from vengeable angre.

An excellent paynter, which so painted a boy caryeng grapes, that byrdes cam to the table and pecked on the grapes, wenynge that they had ben very grapes, whiche Zeusis, beholdynge, was with hym self angrye, and sayd, If I had made the boye, aswel as I haue done the grapis, the birdis durst not haue come so nygh to the grapes.
A fysshe taken about Calys in Spain, whiche is blacke, but he is very delicate.
People, whyche we doo calle Egyptians, that wander about in euery royalme and be horrible theues.

Was a poete, whyche enuyed Homerus, and therfore the enuiers of welle lerned men are callyd Zoili.
Certayne flaxe, that commeth out of Spayne, whereof threde is made for nettes to take byrdes.

An herbe, which some do suppose to be Puly ol mountayne.

Was a man, whiche by phisnomye knew euery mās cōdicions. And whā in beholding Socrates he iudged him to be vnthrifty, & therfore was scorned of many mē ▪ Socrates answered, Zopyrus is not deceiued, for in dede I had ben suche one as he saith, if I had not by philosophy subduid nature. Also Zopirus was a noble Persian, seruant to Darius, which whan the citie of Babylon rebellid ageinst king Dariꝰ, & that he had madelong warre, & coulde not subdue thē, vnwares to any mā, did cut of his owne nose, & woūded him self, & fled to Babylon, sayinge, the kynge had so disfygured hym, bycause that he perswaded hym to haue peace with the Babylonians, whiche they heryng, made him their chiefe capitayne. Than by lytell and lytle declaryng to them the strength of the kynge, and howe they mought not indure longe agaynste hym, at the laste he caused them to submit them selues to the kynge, & to receyue hym into the citie. Wherfore Darius was wonte to saye, that he had leauer haue one Zopyrus, than twenty Babylons.
A ryuer, whiche the great water of Tigris maketh on the one syde of the mountayne Taurus.

A lawe made for the cēmon disposition of landes, as be oure statutes of inclosures and decayenge of husbandry. but amonge the Romaynes they were suche lawes as dyd appoynte, howe moche lande a Senatour shuld haue, and not excede, and howe moche shulde be dyuided amonge the people.

The ancient name of England: 〈…〉 sonnes of Neptianꝰ.

The whyte of an egge. albugo, is alsoo a whyte spotte in a mannes eye.
The olde name of the ryuer of Tiber. also a water in the felde callyd Tiburtinus, which was medicinable for fore eien.
A wodde and fountayne by the riuer callyd Aniene, in Italy.

A wylde beast in the woddes of Germany, in facion and skyn lyke to a gote, but greter, which haue no iointes in theyr legges, & therfore they do neuer ly, but only do leane to trees, whan they do rest thē, which the hunters knowyng, doo sawe the trees that they leane to, halfe a sonder, whereby they falle downe, and be taken.

A beast in France lyke a mule, but he hath his ouer lyppe so longe, that whā he sedeth, he goth backewarde, or els he can not bi • e of the grasse and herbes, whiche he shulde eate. The horsekynde of them haue hornes on their ouer browes.

The wyfe of Admetus the kinge of the people callid Pherei, who being sicke, and hauing answere of the goddis, that he shuld escape dethe, if any of his kynne or frondes wold die for him willingly, whan all men and women refused it, only Alceste his wife consented therto, and willyngly dyed.
In the Araby tongue, is the beast, whiche is callid Linx, whiche is begotten betwene a lyon and a lybarde.
A noble capitayne of the Athenienses, whiche in nobilitie, beautie, prowesse, 〈◊〉 , & eloquēce, passed al other in his tyme, nat withstandynge his yyçes were accompted equall vnto his vertues.

The name of a kyng of a peple callid Phaeaces, excellēt in Iustice, which had a fayre and 〈…〉 palyce, with or charde a which • are most plentuousely fruites • wyse in the 〈◊〉 . A • cman, a famous poete.

A good archer of Creta, which beholdynge a dragon redy 〈…〉 are his sonne of dyd 〈…〉 so craftily, 〈◊〉 as the dragon 〈…〉 of the chylde, the arowe passed vnto his harte, and hurte not his son, so that the dragon immediatly died.

The name of .ii. ladies, wherof the one was wife to Ceisis, who seing the deed body of her husband cast on land, threw her self into the see, whom the poetes fained to be turnid into a bird of that name: the other was doughter of Euene, callid also Marpesia
A dice playing, or a dycyng hous. Suetonuis calleth it aleatorium forum.
Is a sauce made of the liuers of fishes, also a fyshe, callyd a hearyng.
One of the furies of Hell.
A stone founde in a cockes gysar or mawe, of the greatenes of a beane, of the colour of christall.

The name of a man, specially of a king of Macedony, which conquered al the cast part of the world, and was in prowesse and wysedom incōparable: but being drowned in ouermoche felicitie, he felle into excedinge pride and crueltie, and was at the laste poysoned, and died in Babylon, excedynge lyttell the age of thirty yeres.
The name of a great citie in Egypt▪ also of dyuere other cities.
A kynde of radysshe, longe and clere through.
A wod at the fote of that moū tayne. Algo, idem quod algeo.
An herbe like to a lyly.
Thou thinkest on other matters. Vnde anulū istū nactus? di • mihi, ille alias res agere se simulare, Tel me where gattest thou this ryng? he made semblance as yf he thought on an other matter.
Of nōage, not of cōpetēs age.

Is vsed cōmonly for a iuyce of an herbe congeled lyke a gūme, wherof be two sortes, one is named Succotrina, which is like a lyuer, redde, bright, & bronkle: the other is callyd Caballina, and is sandy and grosse▪ The fyrste clenseth and confirmeth the stomake of a man, and therfore is mixt with purgatiue medicines, bicause they shal not anoy or hurt the stomake, the last is occupied about horse and other beastis.
Is a swete & precious wod, which beinge receiued in medicine, comforteth the stomake, and all the inferior partis of a mā, & maketh swete breth.
Vnreasonable or beastly feding, and ingurgitation of meate and drinke.
He that hath a pylde heed, that is to say, the heares fallynge with scurse.
A fyshe callyd also Laccia, and Clupea, is that, whiche by the description of Paulus Iouius semeth to be a cheuyn.
They whiche do lerne first the order of letters.
The order of letters, as a. b. c.
A riuer in Archadia, also the name of a manne.
A morphy or staining of the shinne •
An herbe callyd the seconde mouse eare.
Colde of nature▪ also whiche are soone hurt or anoyed with colde.

A woman, whiche with her syster callyd Meissa, nouryshed Iupiter with the milke of a gore. Also the name of a prophetesse.
People in Affrike, whiche haue suche plentie of precious stones, that they buylde therwith houses.

An herbe, which groweth a fote in height, & hath leues like basile, and hath a floure facionid like an ere of wheat, • f crimson colour, which neuer dieth: in frenche it is callid Pass • uelute ▪ some there be, whiche do suppose it to be callid in englysh Baldar.
To make bitter, to make angry
An herbe callyd de Mathis, or Dogge senell.
The name of a shepeherde in the bucolic is of Vergile.
A kyng of Iewes: whiche signyfieth as moche as populum tollens.

Was a noble kynge of Egypt, whiche made a lawe, that euery yere, ech • mā shulde make a rekeninge to the heed offycer of his realme, of his life, & shew wherby he liued, or by what occupation he was susteined, and he that dyd not make suche accompt, shulde be put to deathe.
A cite in Ciprꝰ, dedicate to Venus. Amathuntius, a, um, of the sayd citie.

Womē of Scithia, which wāne a great part of Asia: who slewe all the men chyldren, and kept the women chyldren, of whom they burned the right pappe, bicause it shulde not lette them to throwe their Iauelyns, or to shote.
Pertayning to the Amazones. Amazonius, a, ū, idē qd Amazonicus.
Was a sacrifice made for the fieldes, with a sowe great with farowe.

Were an oxe and a ramme, where on euery side of them lambis were brought to be sacrificed. Ambesus, a, ū, eaten rounde.

Tyles, which be layd ouerthwart betwene other tyles.

To bynde a thonge aboute any thynge.
A countrey late founde in the east by Amercum Vesputium.
A precious stone of vyolet colour, an ametyst.
A fyshe lyke to a Tuny, but he hathe no scales, but a playne skynne, which shyneth lyke to syluer mixte with blue, and his tayle is in facyon lyke a newe moone.

He that weareth a short cloke.

To breake an othe, to lose credence. Quod si non dederit, atque hic dies praeterierit, ego argentum, ille iusiurandum amiserit, If he doo not paye it, and this day do passe, I shall lose my money, but he shall lose his credence.

A man, whiche with naturall eloquence, brought rude and wilde people to a c • uile forme of lyuynge: and as some do suppose, sounde first harmony.
A nimph or maidē of the ryuers.

Playce exercysed in those places. Amphitrite, the wyfe of Reptunus. it is also taken for the see.
The husband of Alcmena, mother of Hercules.

Is proprely where in daūcing like mening or coūtenāce that one maketh, he vnto whom it is made, shal do the semblable, it was first vsid of the pristꝭ callid Saly.

They foughte mightily more than foure houres. Coeperunt amplius tria millia hominum, Liuius. They toke prisoners thre thousande men and aboue.
To deferre or delaye a thynge in iugement, to reprie.
A corde or chayne fastened to the yokes, wherby beastes do drawe a wayne.
The gret vncle of Romulꝰ & Remꝰ
A citie in Lacedemonia, where Castor & Pollux were borne. also an other citie in Italy. Amyclaeus, a, um, of that citie.

Is wheate laide in water .iii. days, and euery day the water chaunged fyue times, and being soft, to poure out the water softly, that none other thing do passe, than to poure in a litle & rubbe the corne, and to skymme away the huskes and the branne, & strayn the residue, and being somwhat dried in a clothe, than to lay it on newe tyles, and set it in the sonne, and drye it.

An herbe, whiche hath a square stalk, & leues like to peritory of the wal, but moche lesse, the male hath red floures, the female blewe. some do suppose it to be our pympernell, some take it to be chykweede.
He that rideth by post horsis. Hieronymus contra Rufinum.
A pulpyt or other lyke place, whiche standeth on hygh, whervnto a man must go vp by a ladder or grie • es.
A beaste in Aethiope,Plinius. hauynge a heed like a camell, a necke like a hors, legges lyke an oxe, and is of colour a bryght redde, full of white spottes.
A shorte recapytulation or repetition of thynges before rehersed.

A philosopher of a meruaylous wysedom, all be it that he was borne in the barbarous coūtrey of Scithia, whom Pliny supposeth to haue fyrst foūden the potters whele: And beinge in the tyme that Solon made lawes to the Athenienses, He sayde, that lawes were lyke to copwebbes, which tyed fast lyttell flyes, & the great flyes brake them, and went clene through them. In like wyse the poore & meane men are fast woū den in the penalties and dangers of lawes, but lordes and men in great auctoritie daily breake lawes, and are not corrected.
An hermite: the interpretation therof is, he that lyueth a parte, and oute of companye.

Is a doublynge of a worde,Spartianꝰ in Ceiouio. as the last worde of the fyrst verse, is the fyrst word of the second verse: as, Certent & signis ululae, sit Tytirus Orpheus, Orpheus in syluis inter delphinas Arion.
Vessell or plate of golde or siluer chaced, as cuppis or bolles beaten with the hammer, & not ingraued.
Ye craft to chace or īboce plate.
He that redeth to other men, as bible clerkes, or any other clerke, whiche redeth whyle an other writeth.
The high and subtylle vnderstandynge of scripture.
Fragmētis of meat, which fal vnder the table, & be afterward swept awaye.

Is a sicknes of the heed, which taketh away sensiblenes from the hole partis of the heed, & cometh of the weakenes of the stomak, or of to moch meat, or of to moche lechery, or drinking moche cold water, or to moche study, drinke, or of indigestion.
Conueniēcy or proporcion, whose propretie is to cōferre that which is doutfull, with that whiche is like to it, whiche is more certayne, to make it more playne.
A fote in meter of .iii. sillables, hauing .ii. the fyrst fete short, the laste longe.
A ryuer in Sicyle, tenne furlonge from the citie of Syracusis.
Without a prynce, or withoute a begynnynge.
A tournynge out of a commune order, as, Italiā contra, for contra Italiam.

A famous philosopher, noble of bloode, but more noble in vertue & wisedome, whiche abandonynge all his possessyon, gaue hym all holly to the study of naturall philosophie: and whan one said vnto him, Haste thou no care for thy countreye, he aunswered, Yes verily. I haue exceding care for my countrey, poyntynge vp to heuen with his fynger. Also whan he hadde ben longe out of his countray, and was eftsones returned, and behelde his possessions distroyed and wasted, he sayd, I had nat bē safe, except these thinges had be loste.

A philosopher, whiche fallyng in the indignation of a tyrant, callyd Nicoc • e • n, kyng of Cipres, was by hym apprehēded, and put into a great morter of stone, where he was beaten or pounde with yron pestyls: whiche tourment he toke so paciently, that he doubled these wordes, worthy of remembraunce, Beate on, beate on Anaxarchus wynd bagge, for Anaxarchus thou bearest not. By the which wordes he accoūted his body but a bagge ful of wind.
A philosopher, which fyrste sounde the description of the compasse of the see and land, and made first the sphere.
Doutfull. sometyme it signifieth double. also cuttyng on bothe sydes.
A lytle or poore wenche seruant.
A Cytie in Italye, vppon the see of Venyce.
Goddis and goddessis of seruynge womenne.
He that hath a croked elbow. it was also the name of a kynge of Romaynes.
An herbe, of whose rote commeth a redde iuyse, wherwith sanguyne colour is dyed.
The name of two cities, the one in Phrigia, the other in Galatia.
Certayne men that faughte with swordes wynkynge.
A countray in Fraunce, callyd Angiewe.
A woman hauyng a mans harte.

The sonne of Minoos, kyng of Crete, whiche by enuye was slayne of the Atheniensis. For the whyche many yeres after the sonnes of Athenienses were sent to Crete, to be delyuered to the monster callyd Minotaurus, whiche was afterward distroyd by Thefeus. It was also the name of a noble Briton, whan Iulius Cesar came hither into this realme of Britayne.
People in Asia, beinge of both kyndes in one person, man and woman.
A man hauyng both membres of a man, and also of a woman.
The wife of the valiāt Hector.
The wyfe of Perses, whom he saued from a monster of the see.
A chaumber, whereinto men onely do come, and not women. Also a space betwene two houses, wherinto the rayn falleth. Andronitis, idem.
An ile betwene Grece and Asia, directly agaynst the citie of Ephesum.
Olde writers vsed for Recurre, to runne ageyne.
A certaine serpent, after whose stingynge hapneth intollerable peynes.
Was callid the goddesse of pleasure, callyd also Volupia.
People in Affrike, of whom the women, the fyrst nyght that they be wedded, do accompany with al men, which come to the wedding, but euer after they be chast.
Some doo expounde it for a poste or a currour.
Of a serpent, or winding and crepynge lyke a serpent.
He that fetcheth his wynde often, or bloweth moche, poursike.

A Romayne woman, whyche beynge fayre & yonge, after that her husband was deed, was counsailed to take an other, but she wold nat consent therto, For if said she, I shall hap to haue as good as I haue had, I wyll not be in feare to lose him: If I shall haue an yll husbande, what shall I nede, after a good man, to suffre a shrewe?
He oweth more than he is worthe, he oweth soo moche, that he hath not his lyfe but in lone.
Somtime signifieth brethe. Dic amabo, an foetet anima uxori tue? Telle me of good feloship, doth thy wiues dreth stink?

Sometyme signifieth wynde, somme time water. Si situlam lamiam caepero, •• m quam aedepol tu mihi diuino quid credas post hunc diem, ni ego illi puteo, si occepso, animam omnem intertraxero, If I take the buckerte, neuer beleue me for a prophete after this day, if I drawe not cleane out, if I ones begynne, all the water of the welle.
From the very soule or lyfe.

For pleasure. Cur eam emit? T. Animi causa, Wherfore dydde he bye hir? T. For his pleasure.

Hauynge a fantasye or fauour to a thynge, or to be disposed. Ita animatus fui, Plautus. ita que nunc sum, ut ea te patera donem, I had suche a fantasy, and yet haue, that I wold gyue the cuppe to you. Amabo s • quid animatus est facere, fac iam vt sciam, If he be disposed to do any thyng, let me knowe it.

To take hede, to perceyue. Experrecta nutrix animaduertit dormientem, Plautus. circumplicatum serpentis amplexu, The nouryce awaked, and perceyued the childe beinge on slepe, wrapped all about in the wyndynge of the serpent.Terent. Da • e operam & cū silentio animaduertite, Take you hede, and with sylence perceyue what I wylle saye to you. It is also to punysshe or correcte,Cicero. Ea sunt animaduertēda peccata maxime, quae difficillimé praecauentur, Those offences ought to be moste sharpely corrected, whiche mooste hardlye are eschewed.Caesar▪ Hac re animaduersa, Caesar iubet signa conuerti, After that that matter was punyshed, Cesar commaunded to aduance the standerdes.
They whyche are punysshed or corrected.
A ryuer in Italye in the felde callyd Tibu • tinum.
An herbe callyd Anyse, wherof cometh anyse seede.

The moste valyant captayne of the Carthaginēsis, a mā most expert in marcial prowesse, who at .xxv. yeres of age subdued Spayne, percyd the mountaynes, callyd Alpes, where afore neuer was passage, dystroyed all Italy, and slewe the more parte of the nobylitie of Rome, and kept warres with the Romaynes .xxx. yeres.
That euery yere returneth at one tyme.

Before his eyes: but it signifieth further of than Coram oculis.
