Come before that he was loked for.
A kynde of medlars, which hath leues lyke an almonde tree, the fruite lasse then the common medlar, but moche plesaunter, and wyll be lengar kepte.
A stone called a carbuncle, whiche shyneth in the nighte: it is also an aposleme or swelling callid a carbūcle or botch.
A stone, in the which there semeth to be sparkes as it were of fyre.
People in Asia, which eate men.
Were heretikes, which of a folyshe symplicitie affirmed, that god had membres lyke a man.
A foote in metre, hauynge the firste syllable and the laste shorte, and the myddell syllable longe.
People dwellyng in the vttermost part of the world, directly against vs.

An Ile in Asia, where the herbe called Elleborus groweth, which purgeth melancoly, and there it may be taken with out any daunger: wherof grewe this prouerbe spoken to men in theyr melancholy, Nauiga ad anticyras: Go sayle to Anticyra.
Gifte for gift, one for a nother.
Olde writars vsed for very shortly, forthwith, or the thynge were done.
A fygure in speache, where wordes are repeted to a contrary sentēce: as, Non vt edam uiuo, sed vt viuam edo. I lyue not to eate, but I eate to lyue.
A great citie in Siria, another at the riuage of Persia.
The name of dyuers kynges of Siria.

Is that thinge, wherby where heate commeth colde is expelled, where colde is, heate is expelled: by this, well water in the wynter time is warme, for as moche as the hygh partes of the ayre beinge colde, the heate withdraweth him to the lowest partes. like wise in the body of man the spirite is kepte in more feruente by the outwarde colde, by the ioynt conscent & tolleratiō of al partes of the body.
Was a philosopher, borne in the citie of Tirus, of the sect of Stoici, whiche from the tyme of his byrthe, vntyl his deathe, had alway a feuer, and not withstandyng he lyued vntil he was olde.
A naturall dyfference or repugnancy of thynges.
A worde or sentence hauynge a contrary meanynge: as, Parcae, the mynisters of deathe be so called, bycause they spare no man.
People whiche doo inhabite the part of the world, in respect of the roundnes therof, vnderneth vs, that it seemeth that theyr feete be agaynst our feete.
A noble countray. Terra antiqua, potens armis, et vberae glebae, A noble countray puissaunt in warres, and of a fertile soyle.
He that stādeth before them that do worke and controlleth them.
A fygure, where one letter is set for a nother: as olli, for illi.
A fygure, wherby one contrary is ioyned with a nother.

o: Frigida pugnabant calidis, humentia siccis. Quidius i• Metamor.
n: frigida pugnabant calidis humentia siccis quidius i metamor
d: Mollia cū duris, sine pōdere habentia pōdus. Colde thynges contended with them that were hote, moyst thynges with dry, Hard thynges with softe, lyghte thynges with heuy kept not one note.
A citie in the parte of Italy called Latium.
A pumpe or lyke thynge to drawe vp water.
People whiche dwel in the contrary Zone or gyrdell, to Anticthones.
Was a god of the Egiptians, which they honoured for Mercurius.
A citie, called also Tarr • sins.
A place, whervnto no birde maye come.

o: APage, fy, fy. Apage, haud nos deceat fugitiuos imitari:
n: apage fy fy apage haud nos deceat fugitiuos imitari
d: Fy, fy, it wyll not beseme vs to play the michers.
He that can neither wrastell nor do any other maistrie.
The name of oone citie in the lasse Asia, an nother in Parthia.

An herbe that growethe in corne feldes, whiche is rough. and cleaneth to the garmentes of them, which passe by it, and hath a white floure, the stede lyke to a nauyll: I suppose that it be goose grasse or clyuers.
Were phylosophers, whiche of a frowarde and stubborne nature, held opinion that a wyse man had none affections or passions.
A by • de, whose fete be so lytle, that they seeme to haue none. I suppose they be martlettes.
The moste excellen • e paynter that euer was.
To amoue or putte of from • thynge.
The part of the mountaynes of Alpes, whiche begynne at Grane.
Openly, playnly, euidently, without dissimulation or colour.
Open, playne, euident, discouered, without colour or cloke.
A figure, wherby a letter or syllable is taken from a worde: as Pone met • , for depone metum, mi, for mihi, tun, for tu ne.
Days dedicate to Venus, or veneriall pastymes.
The some of saltepeter, callid of the Arabiens, Maurach.
Callyd also Serapis, 〈…〉 , whome the Egypri • s honored Sspan • chief god.
The parte of heuen, whiche neuer moueth.
A fygure, by the whiche a letter or fillable i • takē away, is peculi, for peculij.
•• on that be harde and myserable in lyuynge.
Bokes, the authors wherof be ••• nowen.
A lyttell bone in the left syde of a frogge, wherwith it is supposed, thinges may be done, whiche were not expedient to be openly knowen.
The place by a bayne, where 〈◊〉 whyche wyll be bayned, do putte of t •• yr clothes.
Wyndes that doo aryse out of the grounde.
To strike with the heles also to despise or set at nought.
Playes made in the honor of Apollo.
Whom the gentyles honored for god, referrynge to hym the inuencion of musyke, of poetrie, and of phisike: It is sometyme taken for the sonne.
The name of a cite in Epiro, now callid Malonis, an other in Creta, an other in •• ri • , also an ile by Thracia.
A broke of hotte water by Padus.
He that is takē with the palsy.
Where s ••• what is lefte our, specially in speakyng, and left to the conie •• u •• of them that be herers.
Rebellyon or forsakyng of a mans profyssion or allegiance.
A conuertion in speakyng from one to an nother.
A prouos ••• tion▪ or declaratiō of the signyfications of sterres at a mans natiuitie, or the beginnyng of any thynge, what therof shall happen.
A dedycation or consecration, proprely of men into goddes.
A decoction of dyuers herbes and spyces.
To serue processe as sergeantes and baylyffes done.
To apparayle or trymme, to be redy to do a thinge, to prepare or ordeine.
The name of a high way at Rome
A kynde of appulles as gret as quinces, and hauyng as great a sauour as they.

o: Applicat primum ad Chrisidis patrem se:
n: applicat primum ad chrisidis patrem se
d: He fyrste made repayre to Christs father.

An herbe called also Vitis nigra, a blacke vine, whiche runneth vp, and wyndeth about trees and stalkes of herbes, & hath a leafe lyke an yuy, but greatter, and beareth beryes in clusters, whiche at the begynnynge are greene, and blacke whan they be rype, also the rote is blacke without, and within is yelowe lyke boxe.
To approche, to drawe nyghe to.
An approchynge or drawinge nyghe to.
The fely of a carte wheele.
An Ile in the Venecian See.
A citie in the countray of Licia, and a towne in Crete.

He maye doo moste with me.Terentius Facio te apud illum deum, I wyll make hym to take the for a god. Per eam te obsecramus ambae, si ius, si fas est, uti aduersa eius per te tecta, Terentius tacitaque apud omnes sint, we bothe desyre you on her be halfe, if it may be by any meanes possible, that by your polycy her mysfortune maye be keuered, and from al men kept secrete.
To make a lye to one.
In the market, apud aedes, In the house. apud horcum, in hell.
In the tyme of our forefathers.

He is out of his wytte, or he is not in his ryght mynde. Vix sum apud me, ita animus cōmotus est metu, spe, gaudio. mirando hoc tanto, tam repentino bono: I am well nyghe out of my wytte, my mynde is so vexed with feare, hope and ioye, with this good chaunce, whiche is so wonderfull, so great, and so sodaynely hapned.
Thynke what thou haste to doo, remembre thy selfe.
By the fyre. apud aquam, Salust. apud quem, by whome, apud eum, by hym.

o: Apud te exemplum experiendi •abes, Plautus. noneges foria:
n: apud te exemplum experiendi abes plautus noneges foria
d: Ye haue the experience at home, ye neede not to seeke for it abrode.
A countraye in Italy, marchynge on the see called Hadriaticum.
A byrde lyke a swallowe, but he hath larger winges, and is most commonly about the see coste a where alway he eyther flyeth or houereth in the ayre, & bredeth in a rocke.
A stone that no fyre may damage, or deface.
Water which runneth betwene the skynne and the flesshe, the dropesy.
Boyes whiche do attende vppon common harlottes.
Partaynynge to water, as aquarius sulcus, a forow, by the which water is drayned.
A wylde medlar,Vide The • ophrastū. or a tree lyke a wylde medlar.
A gourde of water, which cometh of rayne.
A citie in Italye, in the countreye wherof the people are called Carni.
A great countrey ioynyng to Iudea and Siria, Araby.
A man or woman of Araby.
The name of a woman, whiche first inuented spynnyng of lynnen, and making of nettes. it is also taken for lynnen yarne, or the woufe.
A lyttell beaste, whiche gothe a softe pace.
Fygges brode and whyte, whiche do growe on a lyttell stalke.
A mountayne in Grece, in the countray callyd Aetolia.
A ryuer in Fraunce, whiche runneth out of the countray of Languedocke by Barbone and Burgoyn, into the ryuer of Rone.
A ryuer of Scithis, whie he r •••• oth throughe the realms of Armeny.
A countraye in A •• eny wonderfull fertyle.
To ploughe eftsones lande that is sowen, to make the grounde fatte.
A ryuer in Armeny, where it is supposed, that the arch of Noyabode, wh • n the stodde ceased.
A citie in Iudea, where Adam and other thre patriarches were buryed.
A countray in Greece, in the parte called Peloponesus, nowe Morea.
One of the sonnes of Iupiter. it is also a man or woman of Arcadia.
A philosopher, which affirmid by Sophemes, that he nor none other knewe any thynge.
To purchace or gette a thynge.
A noble man of Sparta, who being demanded howe moch money wold serue to the warre of Peloponesus, aunswered, sayinge, that warre sought for no certaynty.
The name of a famous phisition. it is also he that wold be taken for the wisest of his kynne.

Was a geometricion of Siracasts, in S • eile, whiche inuented a sphere of glasse, in the whiche all the mo • sons of heuen were playnely perceyued. he made also a doone of woode, whiche conteyned suche an equall poyse, that it wolde hange in the ayre.
A noble philosopher of the citie of Tarentum in Italy, whiche was of the sect of Pythagoras, and was a great frend vnto 〈◊〉 .
Was the chief dignitie in Athenes.
The mayster or chyefe of the players.
Certayn hare •• kes, whiche affirmed that the vniuersal state of thinges was not made by god, that by princi • , and they al • o denied the resurrection of the body.
A certayne figure of sterres, folowynge Charles wayne.
A fygure of sterres callyd Charles wayne. also Vrsa maior.
A sterre whiche is at the tayle of that, whiche is callyd arctos, or vrsa maior.
To be made bent like a bowe,Liuius. Plinius. Ouidius in Metamor. 12. or to be vaulted. Arcatus, ta, tum, idem.
People of the citie of Ardea.
To haue done, or to be in •• med of a myscheuous dede.Plautus.
To shine. Tyrio que ardebat murice laena, His mantell dydde shyne of fyne purple of Tyre.
A citie in France, callid Orleance.
Were Iudges, whiche sate in a place by Athenes, and iudged causes of murder, and weighty thynges concerning the cōmune weale.
Marces towne, where the said iudges dyd sytte in iudgement.
A cite in Araby, callid also Moab
In latine virtus, in englishe vertue. It was also the name of the wife of Alcinous kyng of Phoeacis, of whom Homere writeth in Odyssea.
A ryuer in the greate Armenye.
The companion of Diana. it is also the name of a fountayne in Sicile, and of dyuers other.
Wyne or water offred to the infernall goddes, or rather deuyls.
The sepulchre of Argus. it is also a place to here posters clay is dygged. it was also a strete in Rome, where the boke sellers •••• lled.
Boke sellers dwelling in the said strete callyd argilerum.
Thre lytle iles in Asia,S. ra. li. 13. by the iles of Mitelenae, and Lesbus.
The shyppe wherin Iason and his cō panye sayled in to Colchos, to wynne the f • y • e of golde.
Were the noble men, which accompanyed Iason vnto Colchos.
A citie not far from Athenes, a nother in Achara. it is also a countray, part of Greece.
To accuse one for stealynge of money.
A sharpe or pikyd hedde lyke a sugar lofe.
The spume or fome of syluer.
A lady, the wife of Theseus, whom he forsoke, notwithstandyng that she hadde sauyd his life.
A woode by the sayd citye where Numa kynge of Romaynes fayned to speke with Aegeria the fayry.
A dry felowe, of whom no thynge maye be goten: some do call hym, a pelt,Plautus. or a pynchebeke.
Peple in the north part of Europa whiche haue but one eye, & that is in theyr sorched, which do fyght contynually with ••• phons.

People in the north part of Asia, whiche all though that they haue onely woodes for theyr dwellynge, and onely beryes for theyr sustynance, yet kepe they iustice and peace amonge them selues, and be temperate of maners.

A famouse harper, whom the maryners wolde haue throwen into the see, for to haue his money: but he desyryng them to let hym play a songe on his harpe or he dyed, afterwarde lepte into the water, but a dolphyn receyuyng hym on his backe, & brought hym to lande a lyue.

A famouse grāmarien, whiche corrected the bookes of Homere, tryeng out what verses were his, and what verses were counterfayt. Therfore they vse to call hym Aristarchus, that is a sharpe co • rectour of other mennes workes.

A noble man of Athenes, who for his playne and iust. dealing, as well in deedes as in wordes, hadde the surname gyuen hym, Ryghtuous, or Iuste: He that readeth this mannes lyfe, in the lyues of Plutarche, shall thinke hym before all other to be folowed by a coūsaylour or gouernour vnder a prynce.
A philosopher, whiche fyrst dyd put the principall good thynge in the pleasaunt mocions of the mynde: the pryncipall yll thinge, in gryefe.
The fourme of gouernaunce of a weale publike, where they do rule, which are of moste vertue.

An herbe, wherof be two kyndestone is called longe, the other round. The rounde hath leues in facion like yuy, but somwhat rounder, wherin is a sharpe and soft odoure, the floure white lyke a lytle bonet vpon a redde knoppe, the rootes are rounde and many. The longe Aristolochia, hath lenger leues, small braunches, and a purple floure, which stynketh: and whan it spryngeth, it is of the facyon of a peare, the rote therof is long, and of the greatnesse of a mannes fyngar: bothe of them do beare beryes lyke to capers, within of box coloure, whiche are bytter and stynkynge.
A man of Messene, whiche was called Iustissimus, moste iuste. This man, whan he was dead, was founden to haue his hart all heary.
A famous poete, which wrate Comedies, wherin he taūted them, whom he dyd not fauoure: all be it he was very eloquent, and moch myrth is in his workes
A disshe, wherin meate is borne to dyner.

A philosopher, of whom Quintylyane writeth in this wyse: whatte saye you by Aristotle, whome I wote not, whither I maye iudge more excellent in knowlege of thinges, or in abundaunce of wrytynge, or in swetnesse of eloquence, or in sharpnesse of witte, or els in diuersyte of workes. Notwithstandynge he was lytle of personage, crooke backed, yll shapen, and stuttynge.
A royalme in Asia, lyeng betwene the two great mountaynes, Taurus and Caucasus, and stretcheth from Cappadocia to the see called Caspium.
A pome citron, or a Eitton, whiche is lyke an orenge, but that he is somwhat in length.
The keper of an a ••• ry: somtyme Esqui •• de Esquyry.
An instrument of falshode or craft.
Was a festiual day, in the whiche the Romaynes dyd sacr •• es armed, and trompettes dyd blowe bluddy soundes. also the place wherin suche sacrifyce was made.
The tendrels or yonge stalkes of wylde radyshe.
A ryuer that cometh from the hilles of Arabye, and dyuydeth Moabiride from Amoni • ide.
An herbe callid brode Plantain or waybred.
A precious stone, whiche hathe the sauour of Mirre.
He that selleth thynges hauynge swete sauour.
An herbe, callyd wake Robyn. It is callyd of some Serpentaria minor, bycause it hath leaue • lyke to Dragons, but broder, and hauynge blacke spottes, it groweth moche about hedges.
An auncient towne in Italye, famous and noble by the byrthe of Plautus, Tulli, and Marius.
A man or woman of Arpinum.
Olde wryters vsed for an arche • .
To smyle on one. also to lyke or seme pleasant.Plaut Aedes mihi arridebant, The house lyked me well.
Lay to thyn eares, or gyue an care to that whiche is spoken.
Walles made with tymber and parget, to diuide chambers.
To gette hym oute of the •• otes.Plautus.
To take hym at his word.

To take hede of an yll reporte.Cicero. Quare cum ista sis auth • ri •••• non debes Marce arripere male dictum 〈…〉 , aut ex scurrarum aliquo, conuitio, Wherfore in as moche as ye are in this auctoritie, or of this estimation, ye ought not Maro, to take hede of an yll worde spoken a ••• de, or of the rebuke of a raylynge 〈◊〉 ▪
Was the seueral name of the kynges of Parthia.
Beaste, whiche is both male and female as some do saye that a 〈◊〉 is one yere male, 〈◊〉 other yere female.
A measure of the Egyptian • contaynynge 〈…〉 and .xii. Romayn mesures, called Sextarii.
The name of dyuers kynges of Persia, of the whiche one of theym callyd Artaxerxes with the longe hande, vse • to say, that it was moche more kingly to giue, than to take.

Was the name of a noble princesse whiche was the wyfe to Mans • lus, kynge of Caria, who was of a notable chastitie, & in loue towarde her husband so excelled, that whan he was deade, she caused his harte to be dried in a vesselle of golde into pou • er, and by lyttell and lyttell dranke it vppe sayenge, That theyr two hartes shulde neuer departe a sonder, and that she thought, that there mought be made noo worthye sepulchre for it, but her owne body. Natwithstā dynge she made for his body suche a sepulchre, that for the excellents wark • manshyp that was in it, also the beautie, and costlynesse, it was taken for one of the meruayles of the worlde, and for the notable saame therof, all sumptuous and great sepulchres were afterwarde callydde Mausole • . She found also an herbe called Artemisia, M • gwort, or Motherwort in englyshe, of great vertue in womens diseases.
The moneth of Maye amonge the Macedonians. also a hyll in Arcadia.
A trouble, wherby ropes do runne. It may also be taken for any instrument, which hath troukles.

Callyd also Morbus articularis, the ioynt syckenesse, is thus diuided into Coxendix, callyd Sciatich, whyche is in the • uckle bone, Podagra, the goute of the legges & fete, and Chiragra, Galenus. Plautus. the goute of the fyngers.
Articulately, as whan one dothe expresse euery syllable.
• am do suppose it to be that herb and floure, whyche is callyd Prym •• ose.
Maye be callyd a pastye or pye, with fleshe or fyshe bakes.
A bakynge panne, wherein they brake tarte •• or other, thinges, made of fyne paste. Some take 〈◊〉 vesselle to 〈…〉 .
Tartes or cake shaken in a panne
People, whiche did •• offer vnto god 〈◊〉 and these.
Were supposed to be the foster brethrē of Romulus, to whom he gaue the dignitie of priesthode, to make sacrifice for growynge and increace of corne, and preseruation of the corne feldes.
An hyll on the see coste of the ile callyd Chium, where groweth the wynes callyd Aruisia vina.

An herbe, whose leaues are lyke vnto yuie, but they be lesse and roūder, and hath a good sauour, the floure is purple, lyke to the floure of henbane, but it sauoreth swetely, and groweth betwene the leaues by the roote, the stalke is edged, and somwhat roughe, the rootes ar smal, croked, & like to grasse, full of knottes: it is commonly callid Asarabaccha, som calle it wylde Spikenarde.
Pauynge tile with pictures enelyd, which may nat be swept with a besom, but the dust and other thing must be swept with a wynge and gathered vp.
A kind of onyons called scalions.

The name of a famous phisitian. Alsoo of a philosopher, whiche beinge blynde, was demaunded in skorne, what his blyndnes dyd profit him, and he answered, that he had the more company by one boye that dyd leade hym.
A citie in Boeotia, where Hesiodus the poete was borne.
Sowldiours, whose names are regystred or entred with other.
He that is regystred with other.
A lyttell or yong asse. also the name of a see fyshe, callyd an haddocke.
A surname gyuen to oone of the Scipyons, bycause that he subdewed the lasse Asia.
A great flye, whiche byteth beastes, and is callyd a horse flye.
An owle, whiche hath fethers on euery syde of her heed lyke vnto eares.
A kynde of spyders, with whyte strakes, of whom if that one be stunge, his knees shall bowe and waxe faynt.
Vnpalpable, or that cā not be felt
A thorne growynge in the easte partes of the worlde, the rynde wherof is somwhat redde, and within, the wodde is of a sadde purple, and smellith very swete, and therfore is vsed in parfumes.
An herbe callyd of cōmon apotycaries Sparagus, in englyshe Sperage.
To myxt famyliaritie and grauitie togyther.

A water in Syria, wherein nothynge that hath lyfe may be drowned. It is callyd Mare mortuū, the deed see. It is supposed, that in that place stoode the cyties of Sodoma. It is also a certayn lyme myxte with brymstone, whiche being ones hette, may neuer be extinete.
To perceyue.Plaut. Sed assentio aperiti fores, quae absorbent quicquid uenit infra pessulos, But I perceyue the doores are opened, whiche deuouren all that commethe within the boltes.

To render as moch to one as he hath deserued.Cicero Nullam partem uidear tuorum meritorum assecutus, It may not be founde in me, that I haue rendred to you any thynge after youre merytes, or haue doone soo moche for you, as ye haue deserued.
To set one at libertie or to manumyse a bondman.
To brynge in bondage or seruytude.
To defende from wronge or daunger.
To leaue al other besynes, to applye study.
He that setteth one at libertie, or defendeth hym from bondage.
A byshops seate or chaire, wherin he sytteth whan he ministreth.
To be alwaye in studye of letters.
An author apꝓued, whose sentence▪ is holden for certayne and true.
To applye hym selfe to get renoume.
To do a thynge lyke to an nother man, to 〈…〉 or folowe one.
To fayne to do a thynge, and not to doo it.
One of ye names of Pallas or Minerua
To sowne or make a sowne.
A bryngyng of one in custome.
A cytie in Iudea, buylded by kynge Salomon.
A region in Asia, callyd now Syria, in englyshe Surrye, hauynge on the easte Indie, on the west the ryuer of Tigris, on the south Medi or Mede, on the northe the mounte of Caucasus.
A kynde of crabbes of the see.
To stande by, or to be present.
To assyst or speake for one.

An olde citie sometyme belonging to Og, kyng of Basan, in the which dwellyd gyantes, and afterwarde it came to the lotte of the tribe of Manasses, and is in the countray of Bethania. There be two castelles of that name nyne myles a sonder, betwene the citie of Adara and Abella.
A goddesse of the Sirians, to whom Salomon to please his concubyne, raysed an Aultar.
A kynde of herons, I suppose that it is an Egrette.

A sycknesse, where one maye not fetche his wynde but with moche difficultie, with weasynge of the breast: whiche hapneth by straytenesse of the pypes stopped with toughe fleume, or of somme impostume growen in the pypes.
People of Indie, hauynge no mo • thes, whiche lyuen by ayre and smelle of swete thynges.
To yelde or make him self gyltie of felonie.
A stone lyke to a •• shes eie.
An astrologie • , he that studieth the speculation of astronomie.
To augment an other mans dignitie or honour.
Is putte for more ouer,Plinius in Epistolis. or furthermore.
Any thyng of Asturia, a cite in Spain.
A spanysshe horse, callyd a genette. Astur co • es, idem.
A towne and ryuer in Italy.
Lynnen threede, whiche maye nat be burned.
He that commeth to a bankette, without appoyntement, an vnboden geste.

▪ yet, or at the least way▪ Cicero ꝓ Flacco. Si non propiquitatis, at aetatis suae, si nō hominis, at humanitatis rationem haberet, All though he had not consideration of kinred, yet shulde he haue had regarde to his age, and though he caryd not for the person, yet shulde he haue hadde respecte vnto good humanitie.
A feruent wynde, whyche whan it bloweth in the realme of Naples, pestylence immediately insueth.

A mayden, whiche was doughter to the kynge of Argiues, whiche kepynge perpetuall virginitie, haunted forestes and woodes, and dyd slee wylde beastes, & was the fyrste that wounded the greatte bore of Calidonia.
A kynge in the lasse Asia, of meruailous rychesse, of whome all magnifyke and stately thynges, are callyd Attalica.
A bouthe, or place made vppe with trees and boughes.
A byrde with foure legges, hauing the longest behynde.
A place at Rome, where all scyences were radde.

A phylosopher, whiche lefte with Octauian the Emperoure this lesson, whā he toke his leue of him: Roble prince, whā thou art attached with wrath, neither say nor do any thing, vntyl thou hast by thy selfe pervsed the .xxiiii. greke letters, and remembred the order of places where they stand, to thi •• ent that the passion of yre, by withdrawyng the mind to an nother thing, mought languishe and vanishe away.
Lyttell pousshes in the necke, and vnder the armes.
He that doth not beleue that god is.
A ryuer in Italy that passeth by the cyties of Verona and Tridentum callyd Trente.
A hylle in Macedonia, of a wonderfulle heyght.
The yles callyd nowe fortunatae, where fruite and herbes doo growe without labour.
The doughters of Atlas, alsoo certayne sterres.

The name of a kynge, whiche fyrste taughte the course of sterres, and therfore it was fayned of hym, that he susteyned heuen on his sholders. It is also the name of a hylle in Barbaria, highe and small, that it perceth the cloudes.
A medicyne, which maketh a woman to be barrayne.
A certayne spyder which is heary.
Than. Illi sunt alio ingenio at que tu, They be of an nother maner of wytte than thou art. Non Appollinis magis verum, at que hoc responsum est, Appolloes aunswere was neuer truer than this is.
And that more is. Esurio hercle, at que adeo nunc haud parum sirio, I am hungrye, and that more is, I am a thyrste not a lyttelle.

An herbe, hauing a longe stemme and rough, with long leaues growyng by the toppe, the residue without leaues, the toppe full of prickes, and a yelowe floure, women were wonte to make spyndelles of the stalkes therof.
A byrde, with blacke fethers on the crowne of his heed.
A rushe that beareth a blacke sede.
An herbe callyd orache or arage.
An affecte or discra • ye, wherin the body can nat be nouryshed with any thing but consumeth with leannesse.
One of the fatall ladies, whyche is fayned to breake the threde of lyfe: it is somtyme put for necessitte of dethe.
Is he that gothe so on the soles of his fete, that he swepeth the grounde, rather than walketh.

A byrd, whiche is foūd in Ionia, and is very delycate, and hathe fethers of sondry colours, and beynge at large, is alwaye syngynge o • chatteringe, whan he is taken, he maketh no noyse, nor semeth to haue any voic • . They ar deceiued that take hym for a woodcocke.
Were comedies or enterludes, whiche onely were • iestes and mery scoffes, or bourdynges.

o: Atterere famam, Salust. Post ubi •orum famam at que pudorem attriuerat, maiora alia imperabat,
n: atterere famam salust post ubi orum famam at que pudorem attriuerat maiora alia imperabat
d: After that he hadde made theym consume their good name and honestie, he set them in hande with other greatter attemptatis.
A countray in Grece, wherin stoode the famous citie of Athenes, the nourice of all scyences.
An aduerbe, sygnifyenge in the eloquence of speche of Athenes.

A fysshe, whyche is in the ryuer of Po, very gret, and with longe rest waxeth meruaylous fatte, which Franciscus Philelphus supposed to be a sturion, but that is denied by Iouius, which affirmeth that he is greatter than a sturion, and vnlyke to hym in fourme, taste, and price.
He is nigh of my blod.Plinius.

o: Attingere partes naturae, Vergili. in Geor.
n: attingere partes naturae vergili in geor
d: To com to the knowlege of naturall causes.
To clyppe or sheare a thynge nygh.
To rydde one of his money, to take all away from hym.
Moneye delyuered to be gyuen to an nother manne.
To harken or take hede what one sayth.
Redy to doo that he is commaunded, at commaundement, obedyent▪
To commaunde or make sylence, as they doo wihche are cryers in places of iustyce.
To withdrawe hym, or go away by force from an harlotts.
A kynde of grassehoppes, which appers nat vntyll the corne be rype.
A loke in Campani • , whyche was dedicate vnto Pluto kyng of Hell, where •• on supposed, that there was an entrie or passage to helle.
To lette or prohybyte one to enter.
God whiche putteth awaye all euylle.
To gette by action or processe of the lawe. Maiore mulcta mulcta • , quam li • em auferunt, Plautus in Ruden. He maketh them to spende more than they may wynne by their suite.
Leaue these trifelynges, leaue your mockes.
To haue the thynge that he asketh.Plautus in Cur. Tuo arbitratu, dum auferam abs te id quod peto, Euen as ye wyll, soo that I maye haue the thynge that I aske or demaunde.
To take a dystresse or gage.
To make oone to confesse a thynge secrete. Suspendas potius me, quam tacita haec auferas, Thou mayst rather hange me, thanne make me confesse that secrete.
To goo quyte without punyshement. Ergo pretium ob stultitiam fero, sed inultū nun quam auferet, I am well rewarded for my folyshenes, but yet he shall not go quyte away without punyshement.
To be vexed in mynde, or frome hym selfe.
To make a newe hoste, after a discomfyte.
The dygnitie of theym, whiche were Augures, of whome was a colledge in Rome: as there be nowe of priestes in Cathedrall churches.
Dyuination or tellynge before of thinges, whiche shall happen, specially by the flyght, or voyces of byrdes.
A cytie in Spayne, vppon the ryuer of Iberus.
A goodly and beautyfulle citie in Germanye, nowe callydde Awsbourghe.
A place consecrate, full of maiestie and honour, it is also a name of addicion gyuen to emperours.
He and she that hath the charge of the kepynge of pultrie or wildfoule. It may also be vsed for a pultar, whiche selleth pultrie.
The place where pultrie is kept. also busshes sette for byrdes to haunte and sytte in.
Affectuously, couetously, ardantly. with great desyre.
Desyre of a thynge, couetyse, ardant affection.

o: Auius, uia, uium, Plaut. Vergil. Salust.
n: auius uia uium plaut vergil salust
d: Wherby there is no passage or waye.
He that gothe out of the way.
Of old writers was vsid for olla, a pot.

A lyttell potte, wherof cometh Aulularia, a comedye of Plautus, wherein is declared the couetous mynd of one, whiche hydde his money in a potte, thynkyng that noo man knewe hit but hym selfe, and yet was he deceyued of it.
Of the court,Sueton, in Nerone. as aulicus apparatus, courtely apparayle, but most proprely the apparayle of pryncis.
A lyttelle countraye or shyre in Boeotia in Grece. It was also a great cytie and hauen, where the princis of Grece assemblyd, and conspired togyther the distruction of Troy.
The name of a Mountayne and citie in Calabria, where growethe excellente good wynes. Alsoo of two other cyties, the oone in Macedonia, the other in Cilicia.
He that playeth best on a sha • me or wayte.
To withdrawe the mynde from a thynge.
Passetyme, recreation, that withdraweth the mynde from heuynesse or melancholy.

A fyshe of the see, which I suppose to be a gylte heed, for he hath in his foreheed a thinge congelate, which in the water shyneth lyke golde, and also hath a set of t • the lyke checke t • the, wherwith he hathe ben harde of fyshers in the night to crushe cockyls, and suche other lytell shell fyshes, wheron he fedeth.
To lyfte vppe the eares, to here attentyuely.
Myne cares glowe or burne to here of his mischeuous actes. Aures hebetes haber, he is dulle in berynge, or he lysteth nat to here.
To harken & beare away our sacrefies, or secrete counsayle.
To flatter, to speake that whiche shall content a mans eare.
To be fauorably harde of one.

To be caried by the eares, it is proprely vsed, where we wyl declare, that beinge in iourney with one, we delyte so moch in his cōmunication, that we fele no labour or payne by going or riding. So may we say, auribus prouehimur, in hering of hym our paynes are relieued, or in heryng him talke, our iorney semeth shorte, or is abbreuiate.
Cōfession made secretly, as priestis do here it.
A sicknes callid the yelow iaundise.
Was golde gathered of the people, to make crownes, to sende to Emperours, after their vyctories.
He wyll do as ye byd hym.
To obeye one, or be at his commaundement.
To whyster oone in an nothers • are.
Is put for audeam, as, at.
The contray callid also Hus, where Iob dwellyd.
Italy. Ausones, were the anciēt kynges of Italy.
With ylle lucke, or in an ylle tyme. Nae ego edepol ueni huc auspicio malo: I camme hither in an ylle time, or, An vnhappy or vnlucky fortune broughte me byther.
To seke for a thing by diuinatiō.

Or at the least. Quo enim vno uincebamur a victa Graetia, id aut illi ereptum est, Ci. in Bru. aut certe nobis communicatum, That oone thyng, wherin we gaue place to Grece, whiche is vanquyshed by vs, eyther it is taken cleane away from them, or at the lest we be therin equall vnto them.
People which beganne in the countray that they doo inhabyte, whyche name was gyuen to them of Athenes.
He that lernith without a master by his owne study.
Thynges without lyfe, whyche seme to moue by them selfes: as it may appere in olde horologes, and ymages, whiche by vices do moue.
Breade of cleane wheate without other mixture, sauing a lyttell leuen.

o: Author, T•. Liuius, Paulus inrecosultꝰ. Ci. in Ver. Plautus in Cur. Terentius in Prolog. Andri. Plautus in poenu.
n: author t liuius paulus inrecosult ci in ver plautus in cur terentius in prolog andri plautus in poenu
d: The fyrste Inuenter or maker of a thyng also a reporter of newes. also he that hath the custody of one within age. also he that doth sell or delyuer a thing on warrantise. also he whom a man foloweth in doing any thynge.
Authoritie, credence, puissance, opinion, iugement, the inioying of possessiō.
To deny to haue done any thynge, or to haue bene the cause that it was doone.
To refuse to do that whiche he is commanded.
To commaunde a thynge to be done.
To bynde one by couenant to doo seruyce.
An extree of a cart, somtyme the hole carte, Sometyme it is shyngle,Iuuenal •• . wherewith howses are couered in the stede of tyle.
Verses made by the priestes of Mars, called Salii, in quycke tauntynge of all men.
Olde writers vsed for nominare, to name or aske.

A sentence spoken and proued: as If Plato walketh, Plato moueth, if it be day, the son is aboue the erth. It is put by Tulli for that, which sophisters do call a proposition, whiche is a sentence trewe or fals.
Was a welle, the water wherof beinge dronke, caused menne to hate the sauour and taste of wyne.
In the tongue of Siria, signifieth lorde, & is attrybute to Iupiter.

A great citie in Caldey, and signyfyeth confusion or trāslation. where was a towre edyfied by Hembroth, whiche was in height fiue myles, and a hū dred thre score and tenne paces, afterward being enlarged by Semiramis, the wyfe of Ninus kyng of Assiria, it was so great, that it conteyned in compasse thre score myles, and the walles were in the height thre hundred fete, and in thyckenes or bredthe thre score and fyftene fete, and hadde a hūdred gates of brasse, and there ranne through the middell therof the noble and moste famous riuer Euphrates, whyche is oone of the ryuers, whereof the hedde or sprynge is in Paradyse.
The countray where the citye of Babylon stode.

o: Babylonicus, ca, cum, and Babylonius, a, um,
n: babylonicus ca cum and babylonius a um

d: Are clothes wouen with sondry colours.
A kynde of bay trees or laurell, but it hath larger leues, and great plentye of beryes. It is also called Augusta.

Is an herbe hauynge a lefe in facyon and greatnesse betwene violet leues and the herbe, whiche is called Moleyn or longwort, the stalke square, and somwhat rough, whiche is in hayght a foote and a half, hauyng a floure lyke purple, myxte with whyte, the roote blacke, but that sauouryth lyke vnto Cinamome, some do call it Asdrabacca, some our ladies gloues.
To do a thynge lyke a madde man or vexed with spirites.
A swete oyntment, made of the roote of Asdrabaccha.
A contray in Scithis, beyōd Assiria, it is also the name of a citie in that countraye.
A coūtray wherin were a thousands cities.
In the Persian tounge signyfieth a geldyng, or a man gelded.
A ryuer in Affrike by the citie callyd Vtica, where Att • hus Regulus, and the hoste of the Romans, slewe a serpent, whiche was in length one hundred & .xx. fete.
A stone, whiche is a lyght grene, and hath a vayn in the myddell lyke a flame of fyre.
A kynde of rounde Chestens or cheste nuttes.
The floures of wylde pome granades.
Two Iles by Spayne, wherof the one is now called Maiorca, the other Minorca.
The place where a great brake • or slynge is layde.
An artificer that worketh at ye fyre.
Men whiche hadde theyr visages paynted.
A stoone greene, of the colour of a frogge.

n: baptismus amp baptismum amp baptisma matis

d: An herbe called Sing • eene, and groweth on tyles.
Is an herbe, which groweth amonge stones, the leaues wherof be lyke to long heares. It is also callyd Barba petrae, it hathe a yelowe floure, and the roote therof is bytter.
He that hath a yonge berde.
A citye in Libia, also an other citye called Ptolomais.
A bote in Egypt, wherin they caried ded bodies to burieng.
The Culuers sonne. It was the surname of saynte Peter the apostell.
A garmēt that childern did wear.
A toothe. Quid tibi vis mulier, nigris dignissima barris? What woldest thou haue woman, that arte worthy blacke tethe?
A countray beyond the ryuer of Iordane in Iudea, which was diuyded to two of the Trybes: whyche may be interpreted moste fertile and fatte.
A certayn vessel, whiche came out of Englande, whan it was callyd Britayn.
An Ile in the northe occean see.
A certayne heretike, whiche affirmed to be .CCClxv. heuens.
Is a worde that is spoken to one, whan we wyl haue hym speke no more, as peace or huysht.
A countraye in Germanye, callyd Hollande.
An Hollander, or man of Hollande.
A lyttell potte, out of the whiche wyne is poured at the tablel

An herbe, whiche I do suppose is that whiche is cōmonly called goldknap, or crowefoote. It is also callyd of Democritus Chrisanthemon, for it hathe a flowre as yelowe as golde, and the leafe is somewhat lyke vnto parcily, but that it is moche greatter.

Is a measure for lycour amonge the Hebrues, whiche conteyned .lxii. measures of Athenes, callyd Sextarios, euery Sextarius contaynynge .xviii. ounces, which amounteth to foure score and .xiii.li. of englyshe galons.

Is a tree growyng in Arabia & Scithia. also a gumme commynge of the same tree, lyke to waxe, but clere as gumme, within vnctuous or fatte, verye swete of sauour, whan it is rubbed or burned, and bytter in taste.
A coūtray callid the gret Phrigia.

n: bebrytius a um amp bebrix bebricis
d: Of the countray of great Phrigia.
A towne in Italye betwene Cremona and Verona.
Lorde of the northe, an ydol set vp in the places of espiall.
An ydoll callyd god of flyes.
The deuyll, and signifieth a beast.

People of Gallia, betwene the riuers of Ryne, Marne, and Seyn, and stretchith to the northwest see, in the whiche are now conteyned the countrays of Brabant, Flā ders, Holland, Ghelder, part of Friseland, Gulyke, Hennow, Pycardy, part of Champayne, the great forest of •• dan, the cities of Acon, Colayn, Triere, Rhein • s.
The deuyll, whiche is interpreted Apostata, without yoke.
Lyttell swete harte.Plautus. Plautus in Ruden.

o: Bellerophontes, seu Bellerophon, Note here the malyce of hariots.
n: bellerophontes seu bellerophon note here the malyce of hariots
d: Was the sonne of Glaucus kynge of Ephyra, who beinge a man of moche beautie and prowes was ardātly beloued of Stenobea, the wife of Pretus king of Ephyra, next after Glaucus, and whan she desyred him to committe adulterie with her, he fearynge the vengeance of Iupiter god of hospitalitie, and remembrynge the frendshyp shewed to hym by her husbande, refused her, and dyd put hyr away from him, whiche she disdayning, and beinge in a woode rage, accused hym to her husbande, that he had rauyshed her, but he like a sober man wolde nat than slee hym in his owne house, but delyueringe to him letters to his wyues father, sent hym in to Licia, where he than reigned, who perceyuynge therby the mynde of Pretus, encouraged Bellerophon, to distroy the two mōsters callid Solymos and Chymera, and sent him therto that he mought be s • ayn vnder the colour of a valiaunt enterprise, but he acheuyng it nobly, returned with honor.
Was a pyllour in the temple of Bellona, callyd goddesse of battayle, where they vsed, whanne warres were proclaymed, to cast a Iauelyn.
A certayne fourme of daunsynge in harneyse.
The white daysye, callyd of some the Margarite, in the northe it is callyd a Banwort. It is also a fyshe with a longe beake lyke a crane, whiche is callyd of some a kekehorne.
The name of a citie & riuer in Spaine.
Full of monsters of the see.
Paynted or • erued with great beastes.
Tap • strye wroughte with great beastes.

The fyrste kynge of Assiria, father of Ninus, and is signifieth the sonne, it is also a ryuer in Syria, which hath sande of the nature of glasse, whiche it casteth vppe, also it torneth all other mettall that commeth into it, into glasse.
A towne by the forest called Nemaeus. Bembinatus, of that towne or woode.
To entreate one well, or entertayne hym.
To haue a good opinion of one.
An aduerbe, signifieng in praysing or saying wel. Cum illiciebas me ad te blande et benedice: whan thou dyddiste trayne me vnto the with plesant wordes and praisynge of me.
A benefite, a plesure, or good torne
Is not onelye lyberalitie in gyuing of money, or possessions, or other like thynges, but also in helpynge a man with counsayle, solicitation, or other labour.
To behaue me or hym well.
This matter commeth well to passe.
A purse wel stored with money.
God turne it to good: I pray god brynge it well to passe.
He that loueth well an nother.
An aduerbe, whiche signifieth curteysly, graciously, bounteously.
A mountayne and citie in Phrigia, where Cybele, callid the mother of the goddis was chiefely honoured.
A citie in Iudea, callyd also Puteus iuramenti, the pytte of the othe, where Abraham dwellid, whiche is the consynes of the lande of behest.

A stone whiche is verye clere, and somewhat inclynynge to a grene colour. it is not that, whiche we commonly do calle Berall, in drynkynge cuppes, but it is rather that, whiche we do call christall, whiche beinge wrought into squares, hathe in them a glymse of a lyght grene.
A towne two myles from Hierusalem, on the side of the mounte Oliuete.
A citie in Samaria, where the people dwelled whiche were callyd Iebus • i.

The citie of Dauyd the prophet, where he was borne and dyed, where alsoo our sauiour Christe Iesu was borne: there also dyed Rachel the wyfe of Iacob the patriarche. it was assigned to the tribe of Iuda, and was distant from Hierusalem .vi. miles, and was firste called Euphrata, and signifyeth in the hebrewe tongue, the howse of breadde.

Was a great ponde in Hierusalem, wherin the pristis washed the shepe, whiche shuld be sacrifised, and may be interpreted the house of cattell. It was also the name of a towne, where Peter & Phylyp the apostels were borne.
A citie in Galilee, where Christe dyd many myracles.
A stronge fortresse of the Iewes.
He that weareth a black or broune garment.
A prouynce or countray in Spayne, callyd nowe Granado,
A ryuer in Spayne by Granado.
I suppose hit to be Gyllofers.
A towne in Iudea, and may be interpreted the house of a mouth, or a iawe.
Wheate whiche is hard to be beaten out of the huskes.

Was one of the .vii. wise men of Grece, and was gouernour of the citie called Priene, and was very rigorouse in iutice agaynst ill men, and defended his contray longe agaynste outwarde hostilitie: at the last the towne being taken, and the people fleinge awaye, and carienge with them suche treasure as they had, he went quietly out of the towne, leuyng all his substance behynde hym: and whan he was demaunded, why that he onelye caryed nothynge with hym, he aunswered: I cary al with me that is myne owne, meanynge therby, that his wysedome and vertue were his propre goodes, al other thynges were the goodes of fortune, & by her appoynted to them that mought catche them, but wysedome & vertue were constante, and mought by no man be taken from hym.
To make a sowne as a pot doth, whan drynke is drawen into it.

o: Bibitur. Mature ueniunt, discumbitur, fit sermo inter eos, et inuitatio vt graeco more biberotur,
n: bibitur mature ueniunt discumbitur fit sermo inter eos et inuitatio vt graeco more biberotur
d: They come at the tyme appoynted, & there was among them talkynge and quaftynge, that euery man mought drynke after the Greekes facion.
Flatery, pleasaunt motion, intysement by wordes.
Losse of generation, proprelye in bees.
To speke or talke lyke a fole, or without any purpose or reson, to bable.
A babbler, he that talketh to noo pourpose.
Is also a sicknes, wherin the body is full of redde blysters.
Playes made for the helthe of oxen and kyne.
An herbe callyd a clote or burre.

A fyshe, whiche hathe his backe as it were paynted with sondrye colours, Iouius saythe and affirmeth, that he is taken in all costes in greate sculles, nat withstandynge I do nat yet fynde his name in englyshe.
A towne in Affrike, alsoo the name of a kynge.
A throw or cast at dyse. also a braught with a net in waters. it is also a morsell.
An aduerbe spokē of him,Plautus in pseudolo. that setteth nought by that whiche is spoken, as one wolde say, whanne he is rebuked of a faute, And what than? or tushe, I care not for that.
A common scoffar, or he that susteyneth all vyllanie for to gette money. It was also taken for a boye, that stode at the aulters end, to stele away the candels.
The goodes of theym that be damned, goodes escheted.
Was she that some callyd fatuá, or fauna, of whom Varro writeth, that in her lyfe neuer man did see her but her husbād, nor herde hir named.
Say well I pray you.Terentius in Andria.
A kynde of olyue, hauynge many boughes, white & spotted with sāguine.
Where oone syllable lacketh at the ende of a verse.
A verse lackynge one syllable or mo.
Or Marinum, a thinge growynge on the rockes, wheron the salte water beateth, somewhat lyke to mosse, and is called of the northern men flanke.
A •• lde vine, hauynge redde bearies, & the leaues more rough thā of a vine.
An herbe lyke greatte sorelle, but blacker, thycker, and therwith mosye, the roote blacke and litell, and in tasting straineth the tounge.
One of the names of Bacchus.
Old writers vsed for stupeo, stupere, to be abashed.
The word of yonge children whan they aske for drynke, with vs they vse to saye Bumme.
Where the bowell is braste by the share of a man toward his priuy mēbres.
A thynne huske in a beane within the hulle.
A lyttell water bell or bobill.
An herbe, wherof if catell eate, they do dye of a griefe in theyr throte.
An herbe, called also Cotula fetida, and is lyke to camomyll, but it growith more vpright, maywede.
A fly lyke to a blacke bytel, but he hath lenger legges, whiche if a beast doth eate, he swelleth, and therwith dyeth.
A fyshe, whiche by the descriptiō of Paulus Iouius, semeth to be a Carp.
Sworde players, whiche went before the ded corpsts whan they were borne to be burned.
Sygnyfyeth Caius, the propre name of a man, and therfore is ioyned with an other name, as C. lul. Caesar, Caius Iulius Caesar. Ci. signifieth Claudius.

A tradicion of the Iewes, lefte amonge them by Moyses without writyng, but from the father to his sonne, and so cō tinually in their generation, wherein is included the vnderstandynge as welle of the secretes of nature, as the mysticalle sence, included in the wordes of holy scripture.
A ••• dre of the hebrues, containing two sextatios and a half .vi. ounces, and .iii. drammes of Athenes measure, whyche amounteth to foure pounde, thre ounces, & thre drammes.
To desyre to go to the stole.
A spyce of a consumption, which procedeth of an yll disposition of the body, and the body and vysage is therwith verye leane, and yll coloured.
Viciositie, or that whiche we cōmonly do calle, a faute in a thynge.
A lyttell beaste in Egypte in the bankes of the ryuer of Nilus, whiche hath suche venenosytie in his eien, that who that beholdeth them, dieth incontinent.
A vyce or sore ingendred in oone frome his infancie, harde to be recouered or caryd.
Is an yll fourme of speakyng, or where the wordes do not sowne wel and conueniently.
A gyaunte, whome Hercules slewe in Italye.
A vesselle, wherinto are gathered scedules, billes, or lottes, where thynges at done by a consent of many counsaylours, or of the people.
A stone, whiche hath lyttell blue sparkes aboute it.
The name of a kyng of Phenicia, whiche buylded Thebes: by whome some men do suppose, that dyuers of the Greke letters were founde.
The courage faylethe, or is ••• ted.
The rodde,Plautus in Amphit. whiche Mercurius dyd alway beare in token of peace.
Ambassadour or heraulte at armes, sent to demaunde peace.
Thynges that wyll shortly peryshe or decaye, olde wryters vsed them for significations of that which shulde happen.Ci. in phil.
An inheritaunce whiche is fallen in excheate, for 〈◊〉 of heyres.
Letters whiche wyl be shortly put out.
Honours and dignities,Pli. in pan. which endure but a lyttell while.
A vessell con •• ynge the same measure that Amphora dothe.
An Ile in the see called Aegeum. It is also called Co • , where fyshe wormes were fyrst founde. the countrey of Hippocrates, the prynce of Phisitione.
Of that Ile called Caea or Coa.

o: Caeca die, Eme die caeca hercle oliuum, id uendito oculata die:
n: caeca die eme die caeca hercle oliuum id uendito oculata die
d: Bye oyle oliue good chepe and sell it agayne dere. orels, bye oyle for dayes, and sell it againe for redy money.
A siknesse that is hid, or may not be discerned.
Emoraudes or piles, whiche are within the foundement, and do not appere.
Where one may not se his way that he rydeth or goeth.
A trenche, which in tyme of warre is pyght priuily with sharpe stakes, which are hydde with brakes or bushes.
Is a bowel, which cometh from the ryghte syde, at the poynt of the houkle bone, and goeth to the left syde in length, and is also called Monoculus.
Blyndnesse, not onely of the bodyly eyes, but also of the mynde.
To sacrifice. Caedunt binas de more bidientes: Accordyng to the custome they sacrificed two hoggrelles.

Was the staffe of a Iauelyn, which had ben in the body of one of them, whiche were called gladiatores, and was slayn: with the which staffe the heade of a mayden newe maried was hempe and striken, sygnifiyng, that lykewyse as the staffe was stycked faste in the body of hym that was slayne, so shulde she stycke fast, and be ioyned with hym that maried her.
A vyce in speache, where one speketh inwardely, and maketh rather a sounde than a pronunciatiō of his wordes
The palate, or roufe of the mouth.
A sore lyke a • hony combe.
They whiche do beare candels in the churche before the crosse in procession, or do any lyke seruice in the churche
A candell stycke, whervppon tapers are sette.
An ointment, wherwith wrastelers were annoynted, to make them the more delyuer and stronge.
A cutte, a garse, an incisyon, also intaylyng or caruynge in stone or tymber.
Lerned in other thynges.Cice. de natura deo ••
Boyes whyche doo synge with a shyll voyce.
Seruauntes whyche are always callyd for.
To show an horse or mule.
The .xxxvi.Sueton. in Resp. parte of a Dramme.
To approue or allowe a thynge.
A cauldron wherin water is her.
The fyrst day of euery moneth.
Olde writers vsed for Clam, priuily.
A cole whitynge, meane betwene a haddocke and a whytinge.
To perceyue, to knowe by longe experience.
Medicines to make heres to growe in the chekes or browes.
A medicine for the eies, specially whan the eie lyddes doo cleaue togyther.
To waxe harde, proprelye in the skynne and fleshe.
To harden, to make to indure labours or peynes.
Shoes of wodde. Also scullyons and boyes, whiche do folowe an hooste to cary baggage, wodde, coled, or other like thynges.
That whiche heateth or maketh a thinge hotte.
An h • r • callid marigold •• or tuddis
A garment of the colour of M • rygoldes.
The hole heed of a 〈◊〉 or beaste. It was also a comon place of 〈◊〉 some men do suppose, that it was the place where Adam the fyrste man was buried.
The feminyne gender, lyme made of stones burned. it is taken somtyme for the ende of a thynge.
A stynking herbe, the ayre wherof prouoketh one to vomyte.
A fishe callid a creuyse, specially of the freshe water, a creuyse deaudoulx.

Is a prouerbe spoken to one, signifieng that he hurteth hym self, which proceded of a fenne so callid which being dried vp, there hapned a great pestilēce, wherfore the peple adioyning, asked of Apollo, if they shuld make it drye for euer, who answered, Ne moueas camerinā, as he shoulde saye, styrre no myschyefe to thy selfe.
Oxen or kyne, with crooked hornes.
The sonne of Cam, the son of Noe, of whome commeth Cananeus.
A part of Siria, now callid Iudea.
An yle in the see callyd Atlanticū, nygh to the fortunate yles.
An Aduerbe, sygnyfyenge lyke a dogge.
In the old tyme was taken for a scrybe or notarye, nowe it is callydde a chauncellour.
To speake for his owne profite.
To synge or wryte for his owne pleasure, and for theym that doo fauour hym, nothing caring for any other.
To monysshe or exhorte. Haec dies noctes que tibi canto ut caueas, This I exhort the daye & nyght, that thou mayste beware.

To fynde the meane. Rationem coepi ut & amanti obsequerer, & patrem non offenderem, I founde the mean to please my louer, and not withstandyng I dyspleased not my father. also to knowe the cause why.Terent. in Heautont. Scio tibi esse hoc grauius multo, ac durius cui fit: uerum ego haud minus aegré patior id qui nescio, nec rationem capio, nisi quod tibi bene ex animo uolo, I knowe wel that to you, whom the thynge toucheth, hit is moche more displeasant and greuous: but yet it greuith me no lesse, I can not tel why, but onely bycause I loue you.

To iudge by syghte. Hi loci sunt at que • ae regiones, Plautus in Pseud. quae mihi ab hero sunt meo demonstratae, ut ego oculis rationem capio, These are the places & stretes, that my mayster shewed me, as farre as myn eyes can iudge, or as farre as I canne perceyue.
To chaunge a pourpose, to tourne saylle, to doo contrarye to that he intended.

o: Capere usuram corporis vxoris alterius, Plautus in Amphitri.
n: capere usuram corporis vxoris alterius plautus in amphitri
d: To commytte aduoultrie with an nother mannes wyfe.
A see fyshe, greatter cōmonly than a Myllet is, whiche as I suppose, we do call a base
An herbe callyd Fumitorie.Plinius li. 26. it is also callyd Capnos.
To lye in awayt to take one in the acte of lecherie.
To get a supper of fre cost.Martialis.
To harken priuyly what menne talke.
A wynde that blowethe frome the Southe.
Is a faut in vynes, whan the clusters of grapes are nat sufficiently couered with leaues, by the whyche occasyon, they be wythered and dried.
Is also a kynde of erthe, the whiche with the heare of the sonne, waxeth soo hotte, that it burneth the rotes of herbes and trees.
A kynde of Carbuncle stones, whiche in the house seme of purple colour, abrode in the aire they ar fyrie, against the sonne they sende oute sparkles, and yf waxe be touched with them, it melteth.
A fysshe callyd a lopster, lyke to a Creuyse, but that he is greater, and is red whan he is alyue.
A fysshe of the see, of the kynde of Turbutte.
A Fysshe, callydde alsoo Dentix, with teethe standinge out of his lippes, & is a brode fyshe, and somewhat redde, with a chaungeable colour.
An huche or coffar, wherin bread is layde, In the Northe countraye hit is callyd an arke.
A fysshe callydde Pranes, lyke to shrympes.
To waxe rotten, or to be putrified or vinnewed.
Excesse of meate or drynke. also an herbe and sede callyd carways.
An heretyke, whiche denyed that god made the worlde.
A tree, which hath leues like to laurell.
Of a nutte: as oleum carynum, the oyle of nuttes.
An Ile in the see called Euboicum, wherin is plentie of marbyll of dyuers colours.
In the Oske tunge is an olde man.
Certayne yles, wherein tynne is dygged.
A wede that windeth about hempe or lynne, callyd Doddar.
A fygure, wherby the propretie of a worde is abused: as, Facies simillima lauro, where facies oonely belongeth to a man, and not to a tree, although it doth signifye there a similitude or fygure.
Ymages lokyng diuers ways, and in dyuers fourmes.
To sette one vp with a paper on his heed to be mocked or rebuked for some offence, as they vse to doo with men periured, or with forgers of euidences.
A fygure, where one thynge is described by an nother.
Wyse. Also the name of a noble Senatour of Rome.
A beaste full of poyson, callyd a Basylyske.
Lytell coffers of wyckers, or a iū ket, wherin eles are taken in ryuers.Plautus in Rude.
Of the stemme of a tree.
Is a dulle brayned felowe, a dulle hedde.
Pertaynynge to the stemme of a tree.
To gyue counsaylle to oone in mattiers of lawe, or concernynge contractes.
With accusatiue case, sygnifyeth to byd to beware.

To take a quytaunce or other discharge for the payment of money or delyueraunce of any thynge. At uero, Ci. in Bru. inquam, tibi ego Brute non soluā, nisi prius a te cauero, amplius eo nomine neminem, cuius petitio sit, petiturum, Truely (sayde I) Brutus I wyll not pay the, excepte I haue fyrst a quyttance of the, that thou shalte nat eftesones demaunde it of hym, of whome thou moughtest aske it.
To be bounde body for body.Plinius li. 34. plautus in Bacch.
To prouyde. Quid isti caueam? B. Vt reuehat domum, Whatte shall I prouyde for hym? B. one to brynge hym home.
Were partes of the beastes nexte to the tayle, to be sacryfysed for the byshoppes.
A cauillation, a subtyl forged tale
The iuyce of colewortes myxt with bran, and being tossed togider, was brought into the fourme of a paste.
To take the matter in hād. also to take an excuse.
To aunswere vnto that, whiche is layde to his charge.

To saye contrarye, to deny.Plautus in capt. Hoc si secus reperies, nullam causam dico, quin mihi & parentum, et libertatis apud te deliquio siet, If thou doest fynde hit other wyse, I wylle not saye contrarye, but that it is at thy pleasure, that I shall lose both my parentes and lybertie.
To aunswere in warde, or beinge a prisoner.
For my sake. Syro Ignoscas uolo, quae mea causa fecit, I wyll that ye forgyue Syrus all that he hath done, for my sake.
Is proprely where one not being able to pay his dettes, leaueth all his goodes or landes to his credytours.
To go sydelynge lyke a Crabbe.
To be in the stede: of an nother thynge. Nam pro pulmentario cedit sicuti ficus, For it is in steede of the meate, lyke as fygges be.
Certayne kynde of pytche founde in Siris.
A place moche haunted and knowen.
Olde wryters vsed for Equites, horsemenne.

o: Celeris copia. Date di quaeso coueniundi mihi eius celerem copiam,
n: celeris copia date di quaeso coueniundi mihi eius celerem copiam
d: God graunt that I may very shortly mete with hym.
To be angrye. Ne uobis censeam, si ad me referretis, Lest I wolde be angrye, if ye tolde me.
To speake or tell. G. Quid grauare? censeas. Telle me, what is that, that greuethe the?
To be had in estymation, or to be set by, also to be meruayled at.
The rebuke or checke of the maister of maners,
Was a punyshement of them, whiche were of yll maners.
Pertaynyng to them, whiche had ouersyghte of the maners of the people, whyche were callyd Censores.
An herbe, wherof there be two kyndes: The great, whyche apotycaries doo call Reuponticum: And the lasse, whiche is callyd Centorye. Alsoo fel terrae, & Febrifugia.
Were suppers on the whiche by a lawe callid Licinia, was bestowid but one hundred of the brasyn coyne callyd Asses.
Were gaines of the hundred peny value of euery thynge, for euery moneth lone.
The hundred, as Centesima pars, the hundred parte.
That which is sette in the very myddes of a thynge.
A feld in Sicile, wherof is Centurupinum crocum.
A worme, whyche is in the leaues of a peache tree.
To eate onions, was a prouerbe spoken of them, whiche do seme to wepe, or doo wepe often.
Vnprofytable bees, which make no honye, but onely with the multitude of them, do kepe warme the yonge bees.
The same mesure that amphora is
A garment of the colour of wax.
A soore lyke an hony combe.
An herbe hauing the taste of waxe and hony togither.
The meate of bees, whyche is founde in hony combes, seperate from the honye, whiche is in taste bytter and is also moyste.

To deuyse togyther,Plautus in Trinūmo. or talke oone with an nother. Verecundari neminem apud mensam decet, nam ibi de diuinis atque humanis cernitur, Noo manne oughte to be abasshed at the table, for there men doo deuise or talke of matters concernyng as well god as manne.
To syfte or range floure of corne.Pliniꝰ. 1 • .
I doo foresee or consyder before.
He that is busye to fynde faute in an nother man.Hier. con. Ruffinum.
Oyle myxt with wex.Cic. in ca. also the place where wrastlers were annoynted.
A lyttelle cowe that gyuethe moche Mylke.Ci. ad Art.
A cabyn in the hygheste parte of a shyppe.
A gyrdell, wherwith the housbande dydde gyrde his wyfe, whiche was sette with lyttell studdes.
The knotte wherwith womens garmentes were knytte about they neckes.
Saltepeter, whiche is very pure, and lyke to salte.
A kynde of ynke lyke to brasse.
An herbe growynge by riuers, hauynge leaues lyke a poplar, but moche greatter.
Is a busshe or tree, whiche hath sharpe pryckes in the leaues, & redde bearies cloustred, I suppose it to be that, whiche is callyd holy or holme.
Lyttell ymages, made folowynge a greatter ymage.
The hyndermost part of a shyp, by the whiche the anker hangeth.
A tarte or marchepayne, or other lyke delycate thynge.
A cuppe longe and smalle in the myddell, and full of handels.
A kynde of sylke, which deliteth the beholders. I thinke it be crimsin.
Amyable, pleasant, or hauynge a good grace.
I suppose to be the byrdes whiche we do call Barnakles.
A house or place where waterfoule are kepte.

A kynge of Egypt, whyche made the great steple at Memphis, wheron were so many men workynge, that the same king spent only in parcely, oynyons, and garlike, a thousande and thre score talentes, whych if it were the greate talent, it amounted of oure moneye, to CCl. thousande fyue hundred and fyfty poundes.
A certayn measure. also vessel, wherin was put lycour, whiche was offred to idols Choenix, a mesure conteining .xxvii. ounces, which is one Sextarius of Athenes, & a half
He that leadethe a daunce, and playeth hym selfe on an instrument.
A place inclosed, wherin cattelle is kepte, a barton callyd in some place.
Pultrie fedynge abrode in a barton or court of husbandry.

A measure of the Hebrues, whiche contayneth tenne tymes as moch as Batus, or Ephi, and amounteth to as moche as one and fourtye measures of Athenes, callyd Medimni, whiche in all maketh two thousand, nyne hundred .xii. pounde of measure, euery pounde being xii. ounces.

A measure of grayn, salt, and other lyke thynges, whiche conteyneth as moch as tenne of the measures callyd Medimni Attici, where in euerye Medimnus be .lxxii. Sextarii Attici, Rede in Sextarius. so that hit contayneth of our galons
A chrystal stone, wherin the colour of golde shyneth.
A stone grene as a leke, hauynge speckes of golde.
A measure contaynyng nine poundes of measure, whiche is
A tryuet or cradel, wheron pottes are sette to boyle meate.
To take meate away frome one.
To make redye meate.plautus in Truculen. Mane aliquid fiet cibi, There shall be some meate made redy betyme.
Meate set vp to be kept.Quintilla. Ci. tus. q. 1 Varro.
To strike one so that a marke alway remayneth.
Idem, also to heale a wounde, soo that onely a seame or scarre may appere.
He that coueyteth to folowe Cicero in eloquence.
A thynne skynne, whyche is within a Pomegranate.
Euery beaste or byrde, whyche ones beynge wylde, is made tame.
To trouble or make hym angry.Plautus. Quid negotii est, Pistoclerum Lydus quod herum tam ciet? What is the mattier that Lydus thus troubleth or angreth his maister?
An herbe, whiche some men do suppose to be an artochoke.
Brought into ashes, as thynges whiche are bourned.
A byrde, whiche in his flyght fetcheth a compasse.
An herbe, which we do cal buglosse.
To compasse aboute, or to make a cerkle or compasse aboute a thyng.
Wine, which after that the grapes are pressed, is taken out of the same grapes, being cut and newe pressed.
To make an oration by pecis, without comming to the purpose.

To lead one about. it is also to abolysshe or put asyde an acte. Quod si is qui edictum peremptorium impetrauit, absit die cognitionis, tunc circūducendum erit edictum peremptorium, And yf that he that hath optayned the paremptorie decree, be absent the daye whan the matter shuld be determined, than the peremptorie decree is to be dyssolued or abolyshed.
Is sommetyme to deceyue by cautelles.
To get ones money by falsehode.
To go braggynge about the streetes.
To caste water or other lycour aboute.
Gathered about, as people whan they desyre to se a thyng. somtime wrapped about lyke an adder or serpent.
To enuyron strongely, to fortifie with walles or men.
Lackayes awaytynge at their maisters styrop. also fote men of princis.
A woman that beholdeth aboute, or watcheth.
Be thinges lyke heares about oysters.
He that hath his heares brayded.

o: Cispello, puli, pellere, Plautus in Amphit.
n: cispello puli pellere plautus in amphit
d: To kepe out oone that he come nat into the house.
Lyke a citesyn. Also courteysly, or with good maner.
A bough or stocke,Varro. wherinto a graffe is sette.
The oone knowyth not of the other.
No man knowynge or witting.Plautus in Pseud.
They which in a towne were moste ryche and substanciall.
A man of warre on the see.
To turne about. Claudite nymphae Dicteae, nymphae nemorum, iam. claudite saltus, Tourne aboute ye goddesses of Dictea, ladyes of the forestes tourne youre daunse aboute.
The tēperatnes of somer.Plautus in Stich.
Olde writers vsed for cingere to gyrde.
Al thīgis hard to be brought to passe.Festus
To be added to the principall somme.
He that wereth a scarlet gowne.
Shyppes or barges made of thycke plankes.
Epistels,Suetonius sometyme it is taken for letter patentes of a prince.
The part of Siria, that ioineth to Arabie.
To sup at an other mās cost.Plautus in persa.
Thou shalte haue thy supper soone in shrewde rest.
To stynte the fyre, whyche burneth a house or other lyke thynge.
To putte vp the shepe into a stable or folde.
To be ioyned, or to cleaue to a thynge, also to come to passe. Nuptiae non cohaerent, The mariage come nat to passe. also to agree togyther.
He that is ioyntelye heyre with an nother.
To retayne or kepe to hym selfe.
Is also a company of seruantes aboute a noble man.
To be banyshed out of the citie by lottes of shelles, as it was vsid in Athenes. Se after Ostracismus.
He that sucketh of the same brest and at the same tyme.
That whyche is gathered and brought to gyther.
A company of them, which haue equall authoritie. also a companye of men whiche be of one mysterie or crafte.

o: Collibet, & collubet, collibuit, collibitum est, collibére, Plautus in Amph.
n: collibet amp collubet collibuit collibitum est collibere plautus in amph
d: To lyke, to please. Vtcun que animo collibitum est meo, Euen as it pleaseth me, or lyketh me.
To klim vp on a tree
To stryke one in suche wyse that he is amased, and lieth as he were on slepe, or to speake hit more shortly, to laye one aslepe with a stroke.
Put or set in some place.
To deuyse or talke with one.
To talke with one, or to talke togyther.
An Hogge that walloweth in the myre, and there hath meate giuen hym.
To play with one, or togither.
Money receyued by exchaunge, or in banke, as menne do whiche goo into straunge countrays, delyuering money of this realme, to receyue as moche of an other coyne, where he commeth.
He that deliuereth money by exchaunge, a banker.
A lofe of breadde, or a bunne.
To do his duetie or indeuor.Plautus.
To haue his parentes in reuerence.
Are two mountaynes in the see, where menne do entre out of the myddell see into the occean, the one is in Europa by Spayne, the other in Affrica.
The tree callyd Sene, wherof the leaues and coddes are ministred in medicines, to pourge melancoly.
To do an offence.Pla. in aul.
To go frome one place to dwelle in an nother.
A conferrynge togyther by exercise, as two lerned mens wyttes togyther, or other lyke thynge.
Commytted to the keping of oone.
To speake.Ti. Liuius. Plautus in Ruden. Plautus in Mostel.
To kembe his heed, or decke his busshe.
He that hathe borowed any thynge.
To speake thynges to the purpose.
To happē or succede well or to the purpose.
The facilitie or curteysie of one, the whiche agreeth to any requeste.
It maye not be easily done.
A man of good stature, nor to great nor to lyttell.
A bushe well decked or kempte.

o: Commodum discesseras heri, cum Trebatius uenit:
n: commodum discesseras heri cum trebatius uenit
d: Ye were scantely departed from me yesterday, whan Trebatius came to me.
To aduertise one what he ought to do.
To remembre one of a thynge.
To shewe a thyng that is hyd.

To abyde with one: also to dwell in a place for a tyme: also to tary one that is goinge. Male facis, properantem qui me cōmorate, sol abit: Thou doest naught to tary me, sens I go in hast, and the sonne is nowe sette.

To cause one to tary. Ante auspitium commoratum est? an tempestas continet, qui non abisti ad legiones ita vt dudum dixeras? Did the token shewed by the birdes, cause the to tary? or elles the wether kepe the backe, that thou wentest not vnto the army as thou saydest a whyle a go that thou woldeste?
Were vnlucky dayes to go about any thynge, suche as we do call dysmoll dayes or crosse dayes.
That whiche may be changed easyly.
An exchaunge, one thynge for a nother.
You shall see all thynges done, that ye do commaunde.
It doth appere how the money is spent.
